The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelans from going into effect. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

text:

BALTIMORE (OSV News) — A year after the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops approved a special pastoral message on immigration, “much of what we addressed at that time continues to be relevant today,” Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Migration, said Nov. 18 at their fall plenary assembly in Baltimore.

The November 2025 statement expressed the bishops’ opposition to the “indiscriminate mass deportation of people.”

While it did not name President Donald Trump, it objected to some of the policies implemented by his administration, which also included a reduction in protection from immigration enforcement actions at houses of worship and other sensitive locations, and expressed concern about access to sacraments for those detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Migration Committee Chair Highlights Impact on Children and Families

In remarks at the assembly, Bishop Cahill expressed particular concern about the impact on children and family separation.

“The reduced protections and support for noncitizen children, especially the decreased availability of legal services within this population, is a scandal,” he said.

Bishop Cahill also stressed the conference’s position that clergy should be able to provide pastoral care to those in detention centers. The Archdiocese of St. Louis recently filed a lawsuit against the federal government over a policy it said prohibits priests from distributing Communion to and hearing confessions of ICE detainees.

“Please note that our staff at the conference are eager to assist with addressing any issues that arise for dioceses attempting to provide pastoral care to those in immigrant detention,” he said.

Election Results Reshape Political Landscape for Immigration Debate

The assembly came just weeks after midterm elections in which Democrats won a landslide victory, projected to win a more than 80-seat majority in the U.S. House. In the U.S. Senate, Democrats will hold 56 seats, after Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska.

After the election and subsequent mixed signals from Trump on his willingness to work with the new Congress on the issue, debate emerged over the viability of immigration reform after the new Congress begins in January. Leaders of the USCCB indicated they would continue to advocate for what they called humane and just immigration reform.

In Vice President JD Vance’s book “Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith,” released in June, he acknowledged the USCCB’s November 2025 statement was “widely viewed as a critique of our administration’s immigration policies,” but argued that the bishops’ message was “admirably measured. Or almost too measured,” casting it as vague.

USCCB Points to Limited Progress on Religious Worker Visas

In response to a question at a Nov. 17 press conference about whether the message was effectively ignored by the Trump administration, Archbishop Paul S. Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the USCCB, said, “We did have one bit of success working with the Trump administration, subsequent to my visit with him at the end of January regarding R1 visas. So that was something that we counted as a partial win.”

“There’s a lot more work to be done,” he added.

Many immigrant religious workers — such as Catholic priests and nuns — legally enter the country on R-1 non-immigrant religious worker visas. During his address to the assembly, Bishop Cahill also pointed to a policy slightly reducing wait times for religious worker visas.

Asked about the new political landscape during an interview with OSV News, Bishop Cahill said, “I do think there is a sense that the people of America would want better treatment of human beings,” adding that it is a good “starting point.”

text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday the United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties, over 10 months after U.S. forces seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from his home and flew him to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges in New York. Hegseth offered few specifics on the military agreement, but it is expected to range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing. The deal comes as the U.S. military has been expanding focus on Latin America during President Donald Trump’s second term, while uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future.

Also Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullintestified before Congress, defending his flight to an LSU-Texas football game when travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide ground stop. Canceling his trip could’ve caused confusion, Mullin told the House Homeland Security Committee. Mullin, who oversees the agency tasked with protecting the country’s cyber infrastructure, faced lawmakers as a string of cyber and technology issues in public and private sectors have rattled Americans.

Elsewhere in Congress, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, putting him on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker in the role. Jeffries, who ran unopposed, secured the nod during closed-door voting ahead of a full vote in January by the new House — where he faces a restive party eager for a change.

Trump, meanwhile, landed in China, where he hopes to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technological power. That posture is complicated by the recent outages, putting Trump on the defensive ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Here's the latest:

Democratic lawmakers urge Trump not to sacrifice US interests in talks with Xi, Putin

Ahead of Trump’s meetings with leaders of China and Russia planned for Thursday, a group of Democratic lawmakers urged him to stand up for U.S. interests and democratic values.

“President Trump must make clear that American workers, manufacturers, and security will not be sacrificed to advance the interests of Beijing or Moscow,” said the lawmakers on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

They urged Trump to use this opportunity to directly address China’s “enabling of Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine” and to demand both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin cease their “military, economic and gray-zone coercion” of U.S. allies and partners in the region.

“The security of Taiwan’s people must under no circumstance be a bargaining chip. Similarly, the future of Ukraine must not be discussed without Ukrainians at the table,” the lawmakers said.

Hegseth uses Venezuela speech to boast about operation that captured former leader

Hegseth called the operation that seized Maduro “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America” that “lasted just 48 minutes.”

“America’s best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours,” he added.

But Venezuela’s ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.

Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader “predicted,” the operation ended with “no war, yes, peace.”

Uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future

Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela’s head of state.

Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for “working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela.”

Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by the U.S., which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.

The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.

A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers.

The fishermen allege American drones struck their boat in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador in March, according to a federal lawsuit filed Monday.

The vessel was engulfed in flames, with two of the men suffering serious burns, the lawsuit says. The men allege they were held against their will by the U.S. for around 24 hours and treated in cruel and inhumane ways.

The lawsuit is the second against the Trump administration over U.S. military attacks on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. It was filed under a U.S. admiralty law that allows for claims for severe injuries inflicted on the high seas as well as unlawful attacks, kidnapping and torture.

Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court over legal protections for Venezuelan migrants

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.

The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.

It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”

Acting International Criminal Court prosecutor tells UN the tribunal is achieving results despite US sanctions

Mame Mandiaye Niang said those trying to undermine the ICC should know they are trying to undermine justice for victims of the world’s worst atrocities — war, crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

He told a U.N. Security Council meeting Wednesday that “despite the coercive measures and despite the attacks, the ICC and its partners continue obtaining concrete results for the victims in Libya” — and for victims elsewhere.

The Senegalese prosecutor addressed the council by video because of Trump administration sanctions against the court itself and 13 current and former staff members — including himself. The U.S. opposes any investigation into American citizens or allies such as Israel.

Last week, ICC judges ended part of its investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel.

The U.S. military is down to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East with the departure of the USS George Washington from the region.

The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

Rodríguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership.

“I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level, so that … we may address common threats,” she said.

Black lawmakers reflect on Jeffries vote

The vote to nominate Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker of the House was a particularly emotional moment for longtime Black members of Congress.

Rep. Maxine Waters of California called it perhaps the most significant vote she has ever cast and a day that she never thought she would see.

“It was very emotional. You could feel a sense of presence of so many people who have worked and toiled to try and find a way to create a Congress and create a government that reflects the best of America,” Mfume said.

House hearing on worldwide threats ends

The hearing included testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

text:
Immigration policy expert highlights impact in drop in refugee admissions for Christians persecuted for their faith abroad

Contact: Lauren Rasmussen, media@wr.org, 802.310.4255

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, co-chairmen Representative Christopher H. Smith and Representative James P. McGovern of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission held a hearing entitled “Worldwide Persecution of Christians: Responding to New Challenges,” drawing attention to the plight facing many believers around the world on account of their faith.

Matthew Soerens, vice president of advocacy and policy at World Relief, presented the findings of a recent report co-authored by World Relief and Open Doors US. The report found that, despite higher levels of global persecution than ever, Fiscal Year 2026 was the first on record in which zero Christian refugees from the top countries of concern for persecution of Christians on Open Doors’ World Watch List were resettled to the U.S. He also pointed to the sharp drop in asylum approvals for individuals from those same countries.

He commented: “Religious persecution is on the rise globally. That affects individuals of many different faiths, and at World Relief – as Christians who believe that God has made every human being in his image with inherent dignity – we are deeply committed to advocating for religious liberty for all people, not just fellow Christians, consistent with Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. But the number of Christians alone who face religious persecution is staggering. According to Open Doors US, 388 million Christians face high levels of persecution and discrimination on account of their faith, accounting for roughly one out of every seven Christians globally.

“When persecution becomes sufficiently acute, some are forced to flee. In their most recent report, Open Doors reported that 224,129 Christians had to leave their homes to escape persecution just in the prior year. […] In Fiscal Year 2026, […] for the first time on record, zero Christian refugees were resettled to the United States from any of these countries. Not just a few, zero. That’s down from 29,478 Christian refugees resettled from the top fifty countries in fiscal year 2024.”

In response, Rep. Christopher H. Smith, co-chair, Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission, affirmed that, in addition to filtering out those who seek to exploit the asylum process: “This is the place of refuge, not the place where people can exploit it, […but] for those with a well-founded fear of persecution, we need to be the most welcoming in the world.”

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The Trump administration may not enforce two recent policy memos that put new limits on international students’ ability to participate in internships and other training opportunities, per a federal court order Tuesday.

For decades, the Curricular Practical Training program has allowed international students to participate in off-campus training opportunities that result in academic credit. But in August, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued two memos barring international students from participating in such training programs unless they were mandatory to complete their degrees.

U.S. District Judge Julia Kobick temporarily blocked DHS from enforcing the two memos, ruling that the higher education associations who are suing to strike down the policy were likely to succeed.

Dive Insight:

The lawsuit was brought by prominent higher education groups, including the Association of American Universities. They argued that DHS unlawfully changed decades of “settled agency interpretation” when it issued its new two memos.

DHS pushed back in court documents, arguing that the two memos didn’t alter “the legal regime” because they were simply reminders about the CPT program’s regulatory requirements. However, Kobick wrote that they “represent a marked departure” from the agency’s prior interpretation.

Since 1991, the federal government has allowed international students to qualify for training opportunities — even if they weren’t mandated by their degree program — so long as they resulted in academic credit, Kobick wrote.

Yet in the August memos, DHS put new restrictions on the CPT program without acknowledging that it was shifting long-standing federal policy. Under its interpretation, an international student could only participate in a training opportunity like an internship if it was required of all students in their degree program.

“In practice, for example, this meant that a law school could not authorize CPT for a law student on an F-1 visa to extern for a federal judge for academic credit unless such an externship was required of all students seeking to earn a juris doctor degree,” Kobick wrote.

DHS also threatened college officials with civil and criminal liability if they didn’t comply with the memos.

Many colleges responded to the two memos by rejecting or revoking CPT authorization for some of their international students or by adjusting their program requirements.

At Columbia University, in New York, officials denied CPT authorization to over 120 international students this fall, according to court documents. Similarly, over a dozen international students at Grinnell College, in Iowa, lost out on internships due to the change.

Some colleges — including Cornell and Michigan State universities — reported that they’ve lost international students due to the two directives. And college officials have reported reluctance to sign documents related to the program over fear of being prosecuted.

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which operates under DHS, said in an email Wednesday that it does not comment on pending litigation.

title: 'Gagged' immigration judges return to Supreme Court, asserting 'First Amendment black hole'
description:

text:
Another chapter in the long-running legal battle over a policy barring the nation’s corps of immigration judges from speaking publicly about their work or immigration more broadly may yet be written, as an employee association and free-speech organization have requested the Supreme Court’s assistance for the second time in the case.

The National Association of Immigration Judges, a non-recognized union representing the around 700 judges at the Justice Department’s Executive Office of Immigration Review, has said the so-called “gag rule” violates its members’ First Amendment rights. The policy, first issued in 2017, made more restrictive in 2020 and revised again in 2021, categorically bars employees’ speech on all matters concerning “agency policies, programs or a subject matter that directly relates to [their] official duties.”

With the help of Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute, NAIJ first sued to end the policy in 2020, but a district court judge dismissed the case in 2023, finding that the group must first pursue its claims administratively, via the Merit Systems Protection Board.

But last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit revived the complaint, sending the lower court on a fact-finding inquiry as to whether the Trump administration’s effort to take greater control over previously independent agencies like the MSPB had rendered the 1978 Civil Service Reform Act’s intended administrative review scheme meaningless.

The Trump administration appealed that ruling to the Supreme Court, which in turn overturned it on the grounds that the parties in the case had not yet raised such an argument, sending the case back to the Fourth Circuit. In response, the appeals court quietly affirmed the original district court ruling.

But NAIJ wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court that by doing so, the appellate court had created what is known as a circuit split: when legal precedent is in conflict, depending upon where a case is filed. In this instance, the union said the Fourth Circuit’s decision conflicts with a 1996 decision out of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, Weaver v. U.S. Information Agency, a case in which a Voice of America employee challenged a policy requiring agency employees to receive preclearance ahead of any speaking, writing or teaching engagement.

“After being admonished for violating this requirement, [Weaver] filed an amended complaint challenging that sanction in addition to the policy,” NAIJ wrote. “The court dismissed Weaver’s challenge to the admonishment, reasoning that it was remediable under the CSRA as a ‘prohibited personnel practice.’ But the court treated her challenge to the policy differently, holding that the district court had jurisdiction over ‘a simple pre-enforcement attack on a regulation restricting employee speech.’”

The union argued that its case is similar, and that because EOIR’s gag order chills constitutionally protected activity, it creates the type of “here-and-now” injury that cannot be remediated after months or years of exhausting plaintiffs’ administrative avenues for redress.

“Review of the Fourth Circuit’s decision is warranted now because it threatens to create a First Amendment black hole,” NAIJ wrote. “Under the Fourth Circuit’s application of Thunder Basin, administrations of both political parties could enact sweeping prior restraints on the speech of federal employees without any guarantee of judicial review.”

In a statement Tuesday, NAIJ President Holly D’Andrea said the gag rule not only hurts her organization’s members, but also impedes the American public’s broader understanding of immigration issues.

“Judges do not turn in their right to free speech when they put on the robe,” she said. “Our country was designed to be governed by public reason, not private silence. Silencing judges deprives the public of a key perspective on the rule of law.”

text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday the United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties, over 10 months after U.S. forces seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from his home and flew him to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges in New York. Hegseth offered few specifics on the military agreement, but it is expected to range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing. The deal comes as the U.S. military has been expanding focus on Latin America during President Donald Trump’s second term, while uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future.

Also Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullintestified before Congress, defending his flight to an LSU-Texas football game when travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide ground stop. Canceling his trip could’ve caused confusion, Mullin told the House Homeland Security Committee. Mullin, who oversees the agency tasked with protecting the country’s cyber infrastructure, faced lawmakers as a string of cyber and technology issues in public and private sectors have rattled Americans.

Elsewhere in Congress, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, putting him on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker in the role. Jeffries, who ran unopposed, secured the nod during closed-door voting ahead of a full vote in January by the new House — where he faces a restive party eager for a change.

Trump, meanwhile, landed in China, where he hopes to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technological power. That posture is complicated by the recent outages, putting Trump on the defensive ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Here’s the latest:

Democratic lawmakers urge Trump not to sacrifice US interests in talks with Xi, Putin

Ahead of Trump’s meetings with leaders of China and Russia planned for Thursday, a group of Democratic lawmakers urged him to stand up for U.S. interests and democratic values.

“President Trump must make clear that American workers, manufacturers, and security will not be sacrificed to advance the interests of Beijing or Moscow,” said the lawmakers on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

They urged Trump to use this opportunity to directly address China’s “enabling of Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine” and to demand both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin cease their “military, economic and gray-zone coercion” of U.S. allies and partners in the region.

“The security of Taiwan’s people must under no circumstance be a bargaining chip. Similarly, the future of Ukraine must not be discussed without Ukrainians at the table,” the lawmakers said.

Hegseth uses Venezuela speech to boast about operation that captured former leader

Hegseth called the operation that seized Maduro “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America” that “lasted just 48 minutes.”

“America’s best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours,” he added.

But Venezuela’s ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.

Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader “predicted,” the operation ended with “no war, yes, peace.”

Uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future

Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela’s head of state.

Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for “working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela.”

Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by the U.S., which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.

The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.

▶ Read more

Fishermen from Ecuador sue Trump administration over boat strike

A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers.

The fishermen allege American drones struck their boat in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador in March, according to a federal lawsuit filed Monday.

The vessel was engulfed in flames, with two of the men suffering serious burns, the lawsuit says. The men allege they were held against their will by the U.S. for around 24 hours and treated in cruel and inhumane ways.

The lawsuit is the second against the Trump administration over U.S. military attacks on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. It was filed under a U.S. admiralty law that allows for claims for severe injuries inflicted on the high seas as well as unlawful attacks, kidnapping and torture.

Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court over legal protections for Venezuelan migrants

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.

The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.

It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”

▶ Read more

Acting International Criminal Court prosecutor tells UN the tribunal is achieving results despite US sanctions

Mame Mandiaye Niang said those trying to undermine the ICC should know they are trying to undermine justice for victims of the world’s worst atrocities — war, crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

He told a U.N. Security Council meeting Wednesday that “despite the coercive measures and despite the attacks, the ICC and its partners continue obtaining concrete results for the victims in Libya” — and for victims elsewhere.

The Senegalese prosecutor addressed the council by video because of Trump administration sanctions against the court itself and 13 current and former staff members — including himself. The U.S. opposes any investigation into American citizens or allies such as Israel.

Last week, ICC judges ended part of its investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel.

U.S. deputy ambassador Jeff Bartos stressed to the council “our ongoing, unequivocal opposition” to the ICC.

Misinformation about a FEMA test leveraged distrust in Spanish-speaking communities

Ahead of a simulated emergency alert from the Federal Emergency Management Agency was a spate of outages that disabled Outlook and other Microsoft programs, grounded thousands of flights, blocked access to JPMorgan Chase, and halted internal communications at the National Security Agency.

The test, scheduled every three years to identify issues in the system, has previously become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories and misinformation.

Online, false and misleading claims questioned the cause of the outages. The worries especially hit Latino or Spanish-language communities.

Experts warned that these online conversations show how growing distrust in elites and institutions uniquely influences Latino media consumption.

“This sense of general distrust within many communities, but especially including the Latino community in the United States, will then feed into and be amplified by the online discourse around it,” said Dr. Arthur Soto-Vásquez, who teaches ethnic and equity studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

▶ Read more

Incoming class of House Democrats meets with Obama

Former President Barack Obama is meeting with the incoming class of House Democrats in Washington on Wednesday, according to two people familiar with the private gathering who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The meeting, convened by House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, comes just hours after House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Jeffries to become speaker, putting him on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker to hold the gavel.

Obama, the nation’s first Black president, remains one of the Democratic Party’s most prominent figures nearly a decade after leaving office, though those close to him have emphasized that he now plays a more advisory role.

US military down to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East

The U.S. military is down to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East with the departure of the USS George Washington from the region.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Pacific Fleet confirmed that the Japan-based USS George Washington was now under their control and “conducting routine operations” in the area.

The development comes just two days after the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Middle East, briefly bringing the number of carriers in the waters off Iran to three. The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in April, remains in the area.

US and Venezuela sign military agreement, Hegseth says

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking in Venezuela, said the two countries have signed an agreement to reestablish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing.

Hegseth also said that following the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by the U.S. military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”

Hegseth also praised the “close cooperation” with interim President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all.”

The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

Rodríguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership.

“I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level, so that … we may address common threats,” she said.

▶ Read more

Black lawmakers reflect on Jeffries vote

The vote to nominate Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker of the House was a particularly emotional moment for longtime Black members of Congress.

Rep. Maxine Waters of California called it perhaps the most significant vote she has ever cast and a day that she never thought she would see.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he thought back to the 13 original members of the Congressional Black Caucus. “Could they have even dreamt of this day?”

Rep. Kweisi Mfume of Maryland said he flashed back to being sworn in with the late John Lewis back in 1987.

“It was very emotional. You could feel a sense of presence of so many people who have worked and toiled to try and find a way to create a Congress and create a government that reflects the best of America,” Mfume said.

House hearing on worldwide threats ends

The hearing included testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee was aimed at assessing threats 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.

‘We are not killing people,’ Mullin says under immigration crackdown scrutiny

House members scrutinized DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin during Wednesday’s hearing on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters, shortened training, and incomplete background checks for officers in the field. U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had an unprecedented hiring spree — 12,000 new officers and special agents to double its force. In one prominent case, an ICE agent with a troubled mental health history shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine. Mullin said some agents who haven’t completed training or background checks are placed on administrative leave until they are completed. Tense exchanges centered on the deaths caused by ICE agents including those of Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Araujo Salgado. “We are not killing people,” Mullin responded to Rep. LaMonica McIver. “You are killing people,” McIver replied. “No m’am. That’s your opinion,” he said, ending the exchange.

Nike to give valedictorians custom sneakers after Mississippi’s Colom asked

The sneaker giant announced Tuesday it would be gifting custom Air Force 1s to every high school valedictorian in the country.

Democrat Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, had called on Nike to honor his historic election by gifting every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of his favorite sneakers.

Nike responded and said it would expand the giveaway to top students across the country.

Colom suggested the sneaker design give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippi senator who was the first African American to serve in Congress.

Mullin, Puerto Rico representative Hernandez spar over killings by immigration officers

A testy exchange between Mullin and Pablo Jose Hernandez, Puerto Rico’s representative in Congress, erupted over investigations into the deaths caused by Homeland Security Department law enforcement agents.

Hernandez asked Mullin for an update on the status of investigations into the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol officers in January amid the administration’s immigration crackdown. He also inquired about Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was killed in July in Maine as well as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, fatally shot by an immigration officer shortly after Guerrero in Texas.

“I cannot talk about ongoing investigations, but I can talk about the angel families,” Mullin said.

Does that justify the killings? Hernandez asked.

Mullin began responding, saying that it never justifies it, when Hernandez asked: “Why do you have to bring up that comparison? That is very disrespectful to those people.”

Mullin went on, referring to angel families — a term frequently used by the Trump administration to refer those whose family members were killed by someone in the country illegally — saying Hernandez should talk about them.

Newsom unveils proposals to crack down on AI

California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned the influence of artificial intelligence is spurring a “national crisis of confidence.”

The potential 2028 presidential candidate, who is leaving the governor’s office in January, issued a proposal on Wednesday calling on California to expand AI oversight. It calls on the industry to submit to mandatory independent testing, stronger requirements for reporting safety incidents and limits on systems improving themselves.

He proposes giving the state power to order an AI company to immediately shut down a model if officials determine it poses a potential catastrophic threat. He vetoed a so-called kill switch bill in 2024.

Newsom said he plans to speak to his successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, about his proposal later Wednesday.

Newsom said there’s an urgency for governments to address threats posed by AI. He blasted the Trump administration’s response to a series of tech outages that have surfaced over the past week.

“I don’t think there’s much trust in this administration on these issues,” Newsom said. “Too many times, we’ve been lied to by this administration.”

In Senate farewell address, Ohio’s Jon Husted says ’selfishness must be forsaken for selflessness’

The Republican, who lost his retention bid Nov. 3 to Democrat Sherrod Brown, suggested “the algorithm that we might be trapped in” has caused Washington’s elected representatives to lose perspective on “what this place is supposed to be about.”

Reflecting on his 25 years in public service, Husted observed that the national debt has exploded in his 59 years of life, as “the collective ‘we’ stopped sacrificing for the future and started taking from it.”

“From this Capitol, the harvest that was supposed to be planted for the future has been devoured,” he said.

Husted was tapped last year to fill the seat vacated by JD Vance as the latter ascended to the vice presidency.

His appointment expires Dec. 15, when Brown — a former three-term senator who lost his seat to Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024 — will finish out Vance’s final two years.

Sen. Sanders welcomes working with MAHA on issues such as food labeling, junk food ads

Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he can find common ground with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement, even though he has “profound disagreements” with Kennedy on vaccines.

The Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats said in a call with reporters that he “can work with the MAHA people” on areas of shared interest such as improving food labeling and getting junk food advertisements off the airwaves.

Sanders, who is likely to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year, also said he thinks his newly announced plan to use the role for a “ Medicare for All push ” is aligned with the MAHA mission.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is visiting Venezuela to meet with interim authorities Wednesday, underscoring efforts by the Trump administration to deepen its influence in the Latin American country since U.S. forces ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Hegseth is the latest member of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap the South American nation’s oil reserves and critical minerals. Venezuelan state television broadcast footage of Hegseth at the presidential palace in Caracas, alongside acting President Delcy Rodríguez. text:
A Colorado federal judge held an immigration official and the government in contempt Wednesday for instantly re-arresting a man she had ordered released. However, the judge declined to take further action because an official swore in court the agency had ended the practice in Colorado.

In two hearings, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials tried to justify the re-arrest to U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney. Acting Denver Field Office Director Nathan Rasper said he had ordered instant re-arrests of some immigrants released by judges after hearing from “colleagues” in Minnesota that courts had allowed it.

In Wednesday’s order, Sweeney held Nichole Black, ICE’s assistant field office director in Denver, and the government in contempt for the re-arrest.

“This should — and, in the Court’s opinion, must — shock any reader. There is not a single word in this Nation’s Constitution that sustains or could plausibly give rise to Ms. Black’s ‘belief’ that ICE and ICE agents can walk out to the sidewalk and re-shackle a habeas petitioner within a minute of that petitioner’s court-ordered release,” Sweeney wrote.

Sweeney added that “the single thing” that saves Black and the government from further action by the court in this case is Rasper’s testimony that ICE had “ceased” these re-arrests as a result of the first evidentiary hearing Nov. 4. Sweeney wrote that “cured” the contempt, but reminded the government she considers Rasper’s pledge legally binding.

In a statement to MPR News last week, an unnamed ICE spokesperson wrote: “When appropriate, ICE will address the issues identified by the court and take further action consistent with applicable law and court orders, which can include rearresting an offender.”

At least one other federal judge in Colorado has ruled against an instant ICE re-arrest. In a Nov. 3 order, U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews said ICE never really released a man it instantly re-arrested and wrote: "Once again, the cruelty appears to be the point."

Crews cited decisions from two Minnesota judges who ruled similar re-arrests violated their release orders.

Minnesota’s district court is split on the issue: while two judges have strongly condemned the re-arrests, two others have ruled the re-arrests did not violate their release orders.

MPR News has confirmed at least eight men have been instantly re-arrested at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building after they were ordered released by a judge. One man was re-arrested twice.

Elizabeth Jordan, a law professor at the University of Denver, teamed up with the ACLU of Colorado on an amicus brief asking Sweeney to take ‘necessary steps’ to stop the re-arrests.

The brief called the re-arrests “part of a pattern in this District and nationally of ICE’s circumvention and violation of federal court orders.”

For now, it appears the re-arrests have stopped in Colorado.

Court records show ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people between Oct. 27 and Nov. 4, sometimes in batches. Those people have since been re-released.

But Jordan said damage has been done to the immigrants, their families and the rule of law.

“All of these people who thought they were going to be released and put their confidence in the word of a federal judge probably felt betrayed,” she said.

“U.S. citizen children were taught the lesson by ICE that a court order doesn’t mean something,” Jordan added.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

A look at some of the highlights:

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.

Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.

Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.

Mullin defends ground stop response

Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.

Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.

The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda.

Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.

“You are killing people,” McIver replied.

“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.

Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.

Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.

___

Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

text:
Several Los Angeles County community groups and public housing residents are suing to block a new rule from the Trump administration's Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that would require all public housing residents to verify that they are either citizens or immigrants who are eligible for federal housing assistance.

The plaintiffs, which include three pseudonymous individuals, as well as the People Organized for Westside Renewal (POWER) and Union de Vecinos, argue that the new HUD rule will result in thousands of "mixed-status" families, whose households might include an illegal immigrant, losing benefits to which they were otherwise entitled.

"No family should have to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads. Yet HUD's rule would force precisely that choice on families across the country," said Amanda Mangaser Savage, strategic litigation counsel at Public Counsel, a public interest law firm representing the plaintiffs.

Since 1980, federal law has generally prohibited anyone who wasn't a citizen or qualifying legal immigrant from receiving federal housing assistance.

Congress over the years added several "family preservation" provisions into the law to allow "mixed-status" families to stay in subsidized units while also receiving smaller overall subsidies.

One such provision allowed mixed-status households to live in federally subsidized housing provided that the ineligibility of any household member had not been affirmatively established.

Benefits to these households would be prorated so that only eligible citizens or legal immigrants would receive financial assistance.

This led the federal government to create an effective "don't ask, don't tell" rule for families applying for federal housing benefits. When asked about their immigration status, individual family members could opt to "not contend" they had an immigration status that would allow them to receive benefits.

The financial aid provided to the family was reduced for every member who took this "do not contend" option. But because no member's ineligibility for benefits had been affirmatively established, the whole family could still receive a voucher or live in a subsidized unit.

The Trump administration's new rule ends this de facto "don't ask, don't tell" system. Instead, it will require every member of a household receiving federal assistance to verify that they're a citizen or an eligible legal immigrant.

Since the confirmation of one non-eligible family member is enough to deprive a whole family of federal housing benefits, this new rule will effectively require mixed-status families to forfeit their benefits or expel the ineligible member from the household.

Since many mixed-status households are composed of citizen children and illegal immigrant parents, the family as a whole will have to forfeit their benefits and move.

There are an estimated 80,000 people in mixed-status families currently who would lose their assistance under the rule, according to the Center for Budget and Priorities.

The administration argues the new rule preserves scarce housing benefits for the American citizens they were intended for.

"It's unacceptable that America's homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system," said HUD Secretary Scott Turner last week, when the new final rule was published.

Critics of the Trump administration rule make two primary cases against requiring all housing benefit recipients to verify their citizenship or immigration status.

The first is that it will cause mixed-status families to either break up or forfeit their benefits. That will be disruptive to the families themselves and runs contrary to Congress' intent when it added various "family preservation" amendments to the general ban on illegal immigrants receiving housing aid.

The second is that the Trump administration's change will mean fewer families overall will receive assistance under current funding levels. Since mixed-status families receive prorated benefits, they are cheaper to subsidize. Replacing them with families that qualify for full benefits will result in larger subsidies going to fewer people.

The Los Angeles plaintiffs' lawsuit primarily argues that the Trump administration's rule is illegal because it fully excludes mixed-status families from benefits Congress clearly intended them to have.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.

The court determined that the broadcasts constituted final agency action subject to judicial review under the APA.
For approximately 35 years, the government recognized that elective training students received academic credit for qualified for CPT.
The court concluded that the balance of equities and public interest favored relief, explaining that there is, generally, no public interest in perpetuating unlawful agency action.

text:
On November 17, the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted a nationwide stay and a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and its agencies from enforcing two August 2026 broadcast messages issued by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) that restricted Curricular Practical Training (CPT) for F-1 student visa holders. The broadcasts effectively prohibited CPT authorization for elective, for-credit internships and practicums unless the training was required of all students pursuing the degree.

The court found that SEVP had departed from its longstanding interpretation of the CPT regulation without acknowledging the change, explaining its rationale, or considering the significant reliance interests of institutions and students. For now, institutions may rely on the prior interpretation to qualify elective training for academic credit for CPT, provided the other regulatory requirements are satisfied.

The ruling is significant, but it is not a final resolution of the underlying dispute. Importantly, the court did not confirm how institutions should interpret the regulatory requirement that CPT be an “integral part of an established curriculum.”

Litigation and the court’s ruling

On October 5, the Association of American Universities (AAU), the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), and NAFSA: Association of International Educators filed suit against DHS, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Department of Justice. Association of American Universities v. US Department of Homeland Security, No. 1:26-cv-14520-JEK (D. Mass. Nov. 17, 2026).

The plaintiffs challenged the broadcast messages issued by SEVP under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), alleging that they were arbitrary and capricious, impermissibly retroactive, contrary to law, and procedurally invalid. They sought a stay of the broadcasts and a preliminary injunction preventing their enforcement while the litigation proceeded.

Judge Julia E. Kobick granted the motion, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the broadcasts were arbitrary and capricious. The court’s principal findings were:

Standing. The associations had standing to sue on behalf of their members, including SEVP-certified institutions and designated school officials (DSOs). The court rejected the government’s argument that the plaintiffs had not suffered an injury because no enforcement action had yet been taken. The broadcasts directly addressed regulated institutions and DSOs and threatened legal consequences for noncompliance. Institutions were not required to wait for an enforcement action before challenging the guidance.

Final agency action. The court determined that the broadcasts constituted final agency action subject to judicial review under the APA. Although SEVP characterized them as informational guidance rather than rules or final agency actions, the broadcasts used mandatory language, established a concrete interpretation of the CPT regulation, and threatened specific consequences for noncompliance. Their disclaimers did not insulate them from judicial review.

Arbitrary and capricious agency action. The court found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that SEVP violated the APA by changing its longstanding interpretation of the CPT regulation, without acknowledging or explaining the change. For approximately 35 years, the government recognized that elective training students received academic credit for qualified for CPT. The August broadcasts adopted a contrary interpretation without addressing the prior rulemaking or agency guidance, explaining the departure, or considering the substantial reliance interests of institutions and students that had structured academic programs and educational opportunities around the longstanding interpretation.

Importantly, the court did not reach the plaintiffs’ other APA arguments, including their claims that the broadcasts were impermissibly retroactive, contrary to law, or procedurally invalid.

Irreparable harm and public interest. The court found that institutions had already incurred substantial, unrecoverable costs responding to the broadcasts, including revising curricula, modifying student guidance, and addressing increased student inquiries. The threatened loss of SEVP certification and potential liability for DSOs further supported a finding of irreparable harm. The court concluded that the balance of equities and public interest favored relief, explaining that there is, generally, no public interest in perpetuating unlawful agency action.

Scope of the court’s relief

The court granted two forms of interim relief under separate legal authorities. The distinction is important for institutions assessing the extent of the decision’s protections.

Under 5 US Code §705, the court stayed enforcement and application of the two broadcasts nationwide to preserve the status quo and avoid the confusion that could result from institution-specific relief. Accordingly, institutions do not need to establish membership in one of the plaintiff associations to benefit from the stay.

The preliminary injunction provides additional protection to the plaintiff associations and their members, expressly extending to members’ employees and students and covering both future conduct and CPT approvals predating the August broadcasts. Institutions should confirm their membership status to understand the full scope of the relief available to them.

Continuing risk: The meaning of “integral” remains unresolved

Although the ruling allows institutions to return to the longstanding CPT framework, it does not resolve the underlying regulatory question. The court’s decision rests on SEVP’s failure to acknowledge and adequately explain its departure from its prior interpretation, rather than an independent determination of what constitutes an “integral part of an established curriculum.”

The government continues to maintain that its narrower interpretation is the correct reading of the regulation. The court did not decide on that issue, and the government may continue to pursue its interpretation in further proceedings or through new agency action that addresses the deficiencies identified by the court. The preliminary relief also remains subject to further judicial review and potential appeal.

There is also separate concern for current and former F-1 students. Their CPT history may be relevant to future immigration applications and adjudications, including applications for optional practical training (OPT), STEM OPT extensions, H-1B status, changes or adjustments of status, and new visa applications. Questions about whether prior CPT was properly authorized could arise in connection with an assessment of whether a student properly maintained F-1 status.

For students whose CPT involved elective, for-credit training, the unresolved regulatory interpretation creates some uncertainty. If SEVP’s narrower interpretation is ultimately reinstated or adopted through new agency action, questions could arise later about the treatment of prior CPT authorizations. The court’s preliminary injunction expressly protects pre-broadcast conduct and approvals for the plaintiffs and their members, but it does not finally adjudicate the validity of all historical CPT authorizations or resolve how future immigration adjudicators will approach those records.

Institutions should not assume that the November 17 ruling eliminates all potential questions about prior CPT participation. Maintaining a clear record of the academic basis for each authorization will remain important.

text:
Jorge Linares, a Venezuelan professional boxer and former world champion in three divisions of the sport, was detained over the weekend by U.S. immigration agents in southern Texas near the Mexican border, according to federal officials and his attorneys.

Linares, 41, was arrested at the El Paso International Airport, a spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement to CBS News on Wednesday. Linares is based in Miami, CBS News' partner network BBC News reported.

"ICE has me at the Texas border crossing," Linares wrote in a post on social media early Sunday. "This is crazy."

The ICE spokesperson confirmed Linares was detained and would remain in custody pending deportation proceedings. The agency said he had permission to enter the U.S. temporarily in October 2023 but stayed longer than the term permitted, which the spokesperson didn't specify. Their statement didn't provide information about why Linares had sought or received the immigration authorization, or which type of authorization he was granted.

"To be clear, a pending application or work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States," the ICE statement said, claiming Linares acted "in defiance of our nation's laws" and "overstayed his welcome."

The agency spokesperson said "being in detention is a choice" and that undocumented immigrants could choose to "self-deport" in order to avoid the ordeal.

Attorneys for Linares, from the U.S. immigration law firm Wilner & O'Reilly, said in a news release Tuesday that Linares is authorized to be in the U.S., adding that they're confident in their client's position in this case. They also said Linares "has cooperated fully with immigration authorities."

"We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time," the attorneys said. "Mr. Linares and his family are deeply grateful for the outpouring of support from Venezuela and from fans around the world. Out of respect for his privacy and the legal process, we are unable to comment further on his case at this time."

text:
United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, announced today that HENRY YAU, a former supervisory deportation officer in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”), was sentenced today to 37 months in prison for conspiring to solicit and accept bribes and gratuities. In exchange for bribes and gratuities, YAU abused his influence and status as a supervisory deportation officer to disclose confidential law enforcement and immigration information to unauthorized recipients, provide expedited processing of foreign nationals entering the United States, tip off an individual about an ongoing investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”), and arrest a particular individual (“Victim-1”) that members of a bank fraud conspiracy were seeking to silence and intimidate. YAU previously pled guilty on March 26, 2026, before U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon, who imposed today’s sentence.

"For years, Henry Yau repeatedly abused his position of public trust as a Supervisory ICE Deportation Officer in New York City by soliciting and accepting bribes and gratuities,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. ​“Today’s sentence exemplifies the consequence awaiting law enforcement officers who sell public authority and influence for private gain.”

According to the Information, court records, and statements made in Court:

YAU was a Supervisory Deportation Officer with ICE, which is a law enforcement agency within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”). ICE’s stated mission includes protecting the U.S. through criminal investigations and enforcing immigration laws to preserve national security and public safety. Between in or about 2016 and in or about November 2024, YAU was employed as a Deportation Officer with ICE. In or around September 2021, YAU was promoted to Supervisory Deportation Officer. YAU was assigned to the ICE New York Field Office, located in Manhattan. As an ICE Deportation Officer, YAU was given access to several password-protected law enforcement databases operated by DHS and other law enforcement agencies, including U.S. Customs and Immigration Service (“USCIS”) databases containing the status of immigration-related applications filed by aliens, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) databases containing information about border crossings, criminal history databases containing people’s arrest and conviction records, and ICE databases containing records relating to arrests and removals of aliens from the U.S.

From at least in or about 2016 through at least in or about 2024, YAU participated with others in a scheme to obtain bribes and gratuities in exchange for disseminating confidential law enforcement and immigration information, processing the entry of foreign nationals and other individuals into the United States, and arresting Victim-1 at the request of members of a bank fraud conspiracy. The confidential information that YAU disclosed to others included confidential law information regarding the status of a pending federal investigation into a particular individual by the FBI, as well as information about the immigration status of foreign nationals and border crossing histories. In total, YAU improperly disclosed confidential law enforcement and immigration information regarding at least 28 individuals to approximately 12 co-conspirators, and he accepted over $12,000 in cash, dinners at expensive restaurants, top-shelf bottles of alcohol, and other things of value in exchange for these official acts and violations of duty.

Additionally, YAU conspired to assist various foreign nationals and other bribe-payors by expediting their entry into the United States. YAU did so by circumventing the policies and procedures at JFK Airport and arranging for these foreign nationals to get expedited entry into the United States without secondary inspections, thereby allowing these foreign nationals to be subjected to less scrutiny at the border.

YAU also defrauded the Small Business Administration (“SBA”), the New York State Emergency Rental Assistance Program, and the Federal Employee Education and Assistance Fund, falsely claiming business and rental income losses relating to the COVID-19 pandemic or other natural disasters. YAU and others also participated in a fraud on New York State Medicaid by submitting fraudulent timesheets dramatically exaggerating the number of hours spent providing home care to YAU’s elderly parents between at least in or around 2018 and in or around 2024.

* * *

In addition to the prison term, YAU, 43 of New York, New York, was sentenced to three years of supervised release and ordered to pay forfeiture of $12,600, restitution of $177,000, and a fine of $25,000.

Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding work of the FBI. Mr. McDonald also thanked CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility, the DHS Office of Inspector General, and the New York City Department of Investigation for their assistance with the investigation

This case is being handled by the Office’s Public Corruption Unit and Violent Organizations & Crime Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew K. Chan, James Ligtenberg, and Ni Qian are in charge of the prosecution.
