text:
WASHINGTON | Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

A look at some of the highlights:

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.

Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the Louisiana State University-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and that there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.

Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.

Mullin defends ground stop response

Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.

Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.

The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda.

Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.

“You are killing people,” McIver replied.

“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.

Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.

Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.

Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

BOSTON — A federal jury convicted Eric Tabaro Nshimiye, also known as Eric Tabaro Nshimiyimana, 54, Oct. 27 on charges related to concealing his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

Nshimiyeof Uniontown, Ohio, was convicted of four counts of perjury and one count of obstruction of justice. Homeland Security Investigations special agents arrested Nshimiye in March 2024 after an extensive international investigation found Nshimiye lied to a federal jury during the 2019 trial of the subject of another HSI investigation, convicted Rwandan genocide perpetrator Jean Leonard Teganya.

“Eric Nshimiye is a wolf in sheep’s clothing, masquerading here in the United States in an affront to the thousands of Rwandans terrorized and displaced by the genocide he violently participated in. For decades, he lived the American dream by building a life based on the continuation of lies. Today, a federal jury has brought his deceptions to an end,” said HSI New England acting Special Agent in Charge Jeffrey Grimming. “This verdict belongs to the dozens of victims who bravely shared their stories, traveling across the world to relive the most horrifying moments of their lives and bring Nshimiye to justice. We are deeply grateful for their contribution and their sacrifice.”

According to the evidence presented at trial, while he was a medical student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, Rwanda, in the early 1990s, Nshimiye participated in killing Tutsi men, women, and children by hacking them to death with a machete.

Nshimiye fled Rwanda in the summer of 1994 and made his way to Kenya. In 1995, he gained admission to the United States by failing to disclose his violent participation in the Rwandan genocide to immigration authorities. Nshimiye continued to provide false information about his involvement in the Rwandan genocide to obtain lawful permanent residency and ultimately U.S. citizenship. Nshimiye has lived and worked in Ohio since 1995.

HSI New England investigated this matter with the assistance of HSI’s Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. Established in 2009, the HRVWCC furthers the government’s efforts to identify, locate, and prosecute human rights abusers in the United States, including those who are known or suspected to have participated in persecution, war crimes, genocide, torture, extrajudicial killings, female genital mutilation, and the use or recruitment of child soldiers.

Currently, HSI has more than 227 active investigations into suspected human rights violators and is pursuing more than 1,773 leads and removals cases involving suspected human rights violators from 95 different countries. Since 2003, the HRVWCC has issued more than 80,500 individual lookouts and stopped over 423 human rights violators and war crimes suspects from entering the U.S.

Members of the public who have information about former human rights violators in the United States are urged to contact U.S. law enforcement through the HSI tip line at 1-866-DHS-2-ICE (1-866-347-2423) or internationally at 001-1802-872-6199. authors: Greg Sargent, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling, Sophie Jager, The New Republic Staff, BAD COMPROMISE Timothy Noah, Michael Tomasky, Job Reference Michael Hardaway
description:

text:
By all indications, Stephen Miller is set to respond to the biggest electoral wipeout in a half-century by doubling down on unchecked anti-immigrant thuggery. Miller is privately vowing to expand his mass deportations, and Donald Trump has elevated him to White House chief of staff, where he hopes to execute his scheme from commanding new heights.

Unfortunately, Miller will have far more resources than you might expect to carry out his predations. That puts new pressure squarely on the incoming Democratic congressional majority to take those resources away from him.

As of right now, Immigration and Customs Enforcement still has an eye-popping $91 billion in funds on hand to spend on deportations between now and the end of Trump’s second term, a striking new report from the American Immigration Council finds. Importantly, the report—which The New Republic obtained before its release—shows that this is all no-strings-attached funding, which means ICE can spend it without any serious guardrails or constraints.

Where did this money come from? The report details that in 2025 and 2026, the GOP Congress passed two major chunks of funding for ICE, $75 billion in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and $38 billion in the Secure America Act. The report looks at recent government spending data and concludes that of this money, only $17 billion has been “obligated” (spent or committed) from the 2025 bill and only $5 billion has been obligated from the 2026 measure.

That leaves a total of $91 billion left for spending on mass deportations and other ICE activity between now and 2029, the report concludes. The office of Senator Jeff Merkley, the ranking Democrat on the Budget Committee, believes this calculation is accurate.* As Merkley told me in a statement, the GOP Congress basically handed ICE “an enormous slush fund to wreak havoc in our communities.”

That’s right. Because all that funding originally passed without serious constraints, the huge amount that remains is now functionally a slush fund for ICE recruitment, deportations, long-term detention, and the stockpiling of paramilitary equipment.

“ICE still has essentially a blank check of tens of billions of dollars to use with no conditions attached,” Nayna Gupta, policy director of the American Immigration Council, told me. “Unless Congress acts, ICE will continue to expand its agenda, which has been lawless, violent, and undermined public safety.”

Democrats are already discussing how to claw this money back next year, and the report details many paths toward that end.

The first is for the Democratic House to simply pass a measure canceling the unobligated appropriations. That’s the cleanest option, but as the report notes, it would have to pass the Senate (it’s not certain 51 Democratic senators would support this, though they might), and if it did, Trump would veto it, leaving the fund in place.

That’s why the second path—attach a clawback of the money to a different appropriations bill that Trump and Republicans want—should also be considered. A third approach involves attaching riders to Department of Homeland Security funding that impose tough restrictions on various types of ICE enforcement. These could bar racial profiling, indiscriminate and warrantless ICE arrests, and enforcement in sensitive places, among many other things.

“Congress can make a meaningful difference right away in how ICE is behaving just with the appropriations process,” Gupta says. All these paths could end in government shutdown fights, something Democrats should prepare for right now.

There is a strong case for the Democratic House to pass a complete clawback of the ICE slush fund and then see how far it gets. True, some Democratic members in districts carried by Trump might balk, fearing Republicans will accuse them of “defunding ICE.” But they shouldn’t.

ICE is hideously unpopular. And those Democrats can say they want to channel the money to, say, health care spending; Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries hinted at this Tuesday, suggesting such funding should be “redirected.” Taking taxpayer funds away from the widely hated ICE raids and using them to provide material benefits for voters would be a popular stance.

What’s more, Democrats worried about the politics of “defunding ICE” can say they oppose funding immigration enforcement with no strings attached, as opposed to an end to all immigration enforcement. Being for accountability, especially after this election, will resonate with the very voters who powered the blue wave. Skittish Democrats can also call for clawing back the slush fund and then support passage of baseline Department of Homeland Security funding with many serious restrictions built in.

All these positions should be pretty easy sells. Stephen Miller wants you to believe otherwise: Someone close to him has been furiously leaking to reporters that there will be no moderating ICE operations in the slightest. This is supposed to make Miller look as if he’s operating from a position of strength. But it’s actually one of weakness.

Indeed, Miller’s reading of the postelection landscape borders on delusional. Axios reports that Miller now wants to rebuild the shattered Trump coalition by winning back young and nonwhite men, including Latinos. Miller apparently believes they were driven away primarily by the Iran war and by costs and won’t care if ICE brutality rages on.

Naturally, war and prices were major factors. But as I’ve argued, MAGA figures are heavily invested in blaming only the war and costs for their electoral debacle because it insulates mass deportations and MAGA ethno-nationalism from blame. In a new analysis, G. Elliott Morris shows that ICE activity may have helped drive key constituencies to Democrats, including the young and nonwhite voters Miller wants to win back.

Adding to Morris’s analysis, it’s plausible that revulsion at the underlying ideological vision of a purified nation achieved via mass ethnic purges—that is, disgust with the white nationalist project, not just the ICE operations—also helped move many voters. Tellingly, podcast bros like Joe Rogan who have turned on Trump aren’t just pillorying ICE’s tactics. In his widely discussed response to the election, Rogan—who reaches a huge audience of young men who deserted MAGA—said the only crime many undocumented immigrants have committed is “they don’t have the right paperwork.”

In other words, most Americans grasp that these immigrants are only guilty of trying to better their prospects and have a reasonable claim to a place in American life. The exit polls show that huge majorities say that immigrants are good for our country. Miller, a bone-deep ideologue and unrepentant ethno-nationalist, cannot fathom that anyone, let alone most Americans, could possibly believe such heresies.

The consensus position for Democrats should be a simple one: ICE cannot continue in anything remotely like its current form. In fact, not doing everything possible to zero out ICE’s massive slush fund might be politically worse for Democrats. It could allow ICE to continue its operations with quasi-impunity and make Democrats look weak and feckless.

Democrats were elected, at least in part, to put a check on an authoritarian president. text:
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.

The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.

It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”

President Donald Trump has moved to withdraw protections that have allowed immigrants from multiple countries to remain in the United States and work legally, some for decades.

The Supreme Court also allowed the Trump administration to end temporary legal protections for people from Haiti and Syria in June. An appeals court subsequently paused the judge's decision that kept the program in place for Venezuelans, but that pause is set to expire Friday.

The program known as TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It is granted in increments of up to 18 months.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9 and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan, in October.

About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections. After the administration ended TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also ceased to be valid. Thousands of people were subjected to removal proceedings, detained and deported. Many Venezuelans chose to leave the country voluntarily. It is not clear how many Venezuelans who had the protections are still living in the U.S.

——

Salomon reported from Miami.

text:
The GEO Group has sold the Northwest Processing Center in Tacoma to the federal government's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for $453 million, while retaining a contract to provide support services at the facility through 2036, the company announced Wednesday.

The sale of the 1,635-bed facility was made to the United States and its assigns through the Department of Homeland Security. The GEO Group previously owned the NWPC while contracting services with ICE.

SEE ALSO | Lawsuit targets Tacoma ICE facility amid reports of neglect, squalor from detainees

The facility is used to hold noncitizens while their immigration cases or deportation proceedings are processed and hosts the Tacoma Immigration Court on-site.

GEO said it expects to receive about $340 million after taxes, transaction fees and expenses. The company plans to use the proceeds, along with operating cash, toward a $500 million accelerated share repurchase agreement.

GEO said its new 10-year contract to provide support services at the center is expected to run through Oct. 27, 2036. The company also said it is negotiating sales of several other facilities to ICE, but has no final agreements or firm timelines for those potential deals.

The sale comes amid ongoing controversy and legal disputes over state oversight of the Tacoma detention center.

In July, a federal judge issued preliminary injunctions requiring GEO to allow Washington health inspectors into the center, except in administrative and medical areas controlled by ICE. The judge found the company was likely to lose its challenge to the inspections.

Washington also sought inspections to investigate more than 3,500 complaints from detainees about conditions at the facility. The complaints included allegations of spoiled or contaminated food, unsafe drinking water, unsanitary bedding, mold, and limited access to functioning bathrooms.

The state’s 2023 law set health and safety standards for private detention facilities and authorized unannounced inspections. GEO had challenged the law, while the company has argued that state regulation of a federally contracted facility is unlawful.

The center, while under GEO ownership, also drew protests from immigrant rights advocates, who had urged Tacoma leaders to revoke its business license and seek to shut it down.

In light of the sale, U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, released the following statement:

“I am deeply concerned by what appears to be a gross misuse of taxpayer dollars to pad the pockets of the GEO Group, a private, for-profit company that has overseen real mistreatment and abuses of detained people across the company. In the height of this Administration’s complete disregard for the real pain that families are suffering with higher gas and grocery prices and skyrocketing healthcare costs, it is unfathomable that GEO has announced it intends to use the net proceeds from this sale for stock buybacks, in yet another move to put profits over the safety and health of the people it detains.

“Let me also be very clear: if this is a thinly-veiled attempt by GEO Group to shield themselves from answering for any of the mistreatment of detained people at the Northwest ICE Processing Center, it simply will not work. In Congress, we intend to investigate every one of these sales and to demand accountability from these private, for-profit detention centers that have engaged in pay-to-play schemes with this Administration and completely ignored basic human dignity and safety.

“Since Trump returned to office, for-profit prison corporations, including GEO Group and CoreCivic, have raked in federal funding and taxpayer money, while avoiding oversight every step of the way. Under their watch, 62 immigrants have died in detention. I have visited facilities that were completely unlivable, and have heard reports of moldy food, disgusting water, and a lack of medical care from multiple other detention centers around the country.

“Now GEO and ICE are teaming up in Washington State to avoid having to answer for any of their abuses, while also taking home more of Americans’ hard-earned money. I will be investigating this corruption, and we will hold them accountable.”

Jayapal claimed that under the Trump administration, GEO and CoreCivic have reaped "enormous financial gains." In 2025, both companies reportedly received an additional $2 billion in profit each, and a 13% increase in revenue. Jayapal said there has been a "revolving door between the Trump administration and these companies," including border czar Tom Homan and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, who were previously employed by GEO.

KOMO News has reached out to the GEO Group for comment.

title: 5 EU nations push ahead with plan to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
description:
London — Five European Union countries have announced a plan to establish a deportation center in Rwanda next year to which they hope to send migrants whose asylum requests they have rejected.
According to a statement from the Netherlands government, migrants deported to Rwanda under the proposed program would initially be accommodated in an "open, temporary facility."
If they choose to remain in Rwanda, they will "have access to education, the labor market, healthcare and the legal system."
The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal based on concerns that asylum seekers transferred to Rwanda could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution or other serious harm.
"Instead of fixing existing EU asylum and return systems, Member States are creating a costly new mechanism and calling it innovative."
text:
London — Five European Union countries have announced a plan to establish a deportation center in Rwanda next year to which they hope to send migrants whose asylum requests they have rejected.

The plan has echoes of President Trump's controversial initiative to deport migrants to third countries to which they have no links, and an effort by a previous British government that failed to clear legal hurdles. It is an attempt by the five European nations to address widespread concerns about mass-migration that have fueled political change across the continent, but it is far from guaranteed to succeed, or even to get off the ground.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have reached an agreement in principle with Rwanda to open a so-called "return hub" in the landlocked African nation in 2027. Unlike the U.S. program, the plan would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in Europe and subsequently been placed under a deportation order.

Rather than being returned to their countries of origin, some migrants would instead be transferred to Rwanda, where they would have the option of staying or returning to their home countries. The plan is intended to provide the European nations an alternative for cases in which deportation to a migrant's country of origin is not possible, either because those countries will not accept them, or due to circumstances that could endanger the migrant if they return.

Many European governments have sought to reduce the number of migrants entering their countries, or already present without permission, in the face of mounting political pressure from voters.

As an example of the kind of statistics fueling that public concern, there were some 230,000 foreign nationals in Germany at the end of 2025 who were legally required to leave the country, according to the Die Welt newspaper, yet government figures show fewer than 23,000 deportations were carried out during the year.

"If people without the right to remain in the EU cannot be removed from the country, our entire asylum system becomes absurd," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said this week. "If the state sets limits, then these must be respected."

According to a statement from the Netherlands government, migrants deported to Rwanda under the proposed program would initially be accommodated in an "open, temporary facility." If they choose to remain in Rwanda, they will "have access to education, the labor market, healthcare and the legal system."

"For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system, a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said during a news conference on Monday.

"Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries," Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said.

Legal and logistical hurdles

But some big questions remain unanswered about how the proposed deportation program might work in practice.

"The countries will need to negotiate the detailed arrangements with Rwanda, including who would be eligible for transfer, what legal status and rights they would have in Rwanda, how the facilities would operate, who would pay for them, and how the authorities would monitor people's treatment after transfer," Dr. Peter W. Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, told CBS News.

"A big open question is what Rwanda will receive as part of the deal, such as financial payments, as was the case with the U.K.-Rwanda agreement," he said, referring to a similar plan the former Conservative U.K. government embraced, but failed to get past a challenge in Britain's Supreme Court.

The new Labour Party government scrapped the policy completely in July 2024.

There are important differences between the British and European proposals, however.

"The U.K.'s Rwanda scheme was designed to transfer asylum seekers to Rwanda for their asylum claims to be decided there," Walsh said, whereas the European proposal "is intended for people who have already been determined to have no right to remain in the participating countries, rather than people awaiting an initial asylum decision."

"This distinction may avoid some of the specific legal problems that affected the U.K. scheme, particularly concerns about whether Rwanda's asylum system could reliably assess claims for international protection," he said.

Another significant difference, Walsh said, is the EU has adopted legislation explicitly allowing member states to establish migrant return hubs outside the bloc, providing a clearer legal framework for the European proposal.

"However, this does not mean that transfers to Rwanda would automatically be lawful," he cautioned.

The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal based on concerns that asylum seekers transferred to Rwanda could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution or other serious harm.

"The European countries would also need to address concerns about safety, individual rights, and the treatment of people transferred to Rwanda — especially to ensure that people were not sent on to countries where they could be at risk of serious harm," Walsh said. "The existence of an agreement with Rwanda would not, by itself, settle these questions."

Would the program deter illegal migration?

Even as a proposal, the plan has drawn criticism from humanitarian organizations questioning not only its potential legality, but its likely effectiveness as a deterrent to unauthorized migration.

The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) told CBS News it was "deeply concerned and disappointed" by the announcement.

"While European states have the right to return individuals who do not have a legal right to stay, sending people to a third country with which they have no connection is not the answer," said Céline Mias, the organization's EU director. "Instead of fixing existing EU asylum and return systems, Member States are creating a costly new mechanism and calling it innovative."

The organization said its research also showed "that restrictive migration policies fail to deter people from migrating, while carrying severe consequences for human lives."

Rwanda has long been criticized for its human rights record. In a statement this week, the rights group Amnesty International said "sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights."

The participating governments have said the return hub will be developed in accordance with EU and international law, including human rights obligations, and that relevant national agencies were already working with the European Commission and international migration organizations to ensure compliance.

Whether the countries will be able to begin deportations under the program next year, or ever, however, remains uncertain.

"The proposed timetable is ambitious," Walsh told CBS News. "It is possible that a small pilot could begin in 2027, particularly if the participating countries initially limit transfers to a relatively small group."

"Even if the first transfers take place next year, that would not necessarily demonstrate that return hubs could make a substantial difference to the overall number of people leaving Europe," he added. "And the question of scale will be key to the plan's hoped-for deterrent effect."

title: Landlord seeks dismissal of Glenwood Springs lawsuit over ICE facility | AspenTimes.com
description:
Florida-based JG Housing Solutions filed a motion to dismiss Friday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
“JG Housing Solutions has filed a motion to ask the federal district court to dismiss the City of Glenwood Springs’ lawsuit against it.
According to JG Housing Solutions’ motion, the city’s lawsuit alleges that ICE detained 27 people at the facility between May 22 and Aug. 4, 2026, after the special use permit had been revoked.
“JG Housing Solutions has no control over the federal government or any of its actions at any of its leased facilities.
“JG Housing Solutions should not be caught in the middle of this controversy – it has done nothing wrong,” Bryan said.
text:
The owner of a Glenwood Springs property leased to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is asking a federal judge to dismiss the city’s lawsuit over detention operations at the facility, arguing the city is attempting to hold a private landlord responsible for the actions of the federal government.

Florida-based JG Housing Solutions filed a motion to dismiss Friday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. The company argues that the city cannot use its zoning regulations to interfere with federal immigration enforcement at its property at 100 Midland Ave.

Christopher Bryan, an attorney with Garfield and Hecht representing JG Housing Solutions, said the city’s legal dispute should be directed at the federal government rather than his client.

“JG Housing Solutions has filed a motion to ask the federal district court to dismiss the City of Glenwood Springs’ lawsuit against it. The reason is simple: JG Housing Solutions is a private landlord, and the dispute the City is raising is with the federal government,” Bryan said in an email to the Post Independent Tuesday.

The city, however, maintains that its lawsuit is a matter of enforcing local land use regulations against a private property owner.

“The city has followed fair, impartial, and standard practices to resolve issues and have taken the same steps toward resolving issues in this process as it would have with any other entity. This lawsuit is just about enforcing violation of the city’s Land Use Code with a private property owner, regardless of the building’s tenant,” the city said in an emailed statement to the Post Independent.

The dispute dates back to April, when the Glenwood Springs Planning and Zoning Commission revoked a special use permit that had allowed ICE to detain people at the property for up to 12 hours.

The permit was issued to the federal government in 2004, before the city’s zoning regulations changed in 2018 to prohibit detention facilities.

According to Law360, a legal news publication covering litigation and court proceedings , the city revoked the permit after obtaining records showing ICE had met or exceeded the detention limit 10 times in May and August 2025.

According to JG Housing Solutions’ motion, the city’s lawsuit alleges that ICE detained 27 people at the facility between May 22 and Aug. 4, 2026, after the special use permit had been revoked.

The Glenwood Springs City Council voted in August to pursue legal action over the continued detention operations.

Glenwood Springs filed its lawsuit Sept. 25 in Garfield County District Court, alleging that ICE continued using the property as a detention facility after the special use permit was revoked. According to the city’s complaint, as summarized in JG Housing Solutions’ motion to dismiss, the city’s Land Use Code has prohibited detention facilities since 2018.

JG Housing Solutions moved the case to federal court Oct. 26 before filing its motion to dismiss Nov. 13. The company argues that the city cannot use its zoning authority to indirectly regulate federal immigration enforcement by pursuing legal action against the landlord.

In its motion, JG Housing Solutions argues that the city cannot use its zoning authority to indirectly regulate federal immigration enforcement by pursuing legal action against the landlord. The company cites the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause and the doctrine of intergovernmental immunity, which generally protects federal operations from state and local interference.

The motion also argues that federal law gives the federal government authority to determine where immigration detainees are held, overriding conflicting local restrictions. JG Housing further contends that the federal government is a necessary party to the lawsuit but cannot be joined because of sovereign immunity, which generally prevents lawsuits against the federal government without its consent.

Bryan said JG Housing Solutions purchased the property with a preexisting federal lease allowing the government to use the space for its agencies and lawful federal operations. The federal government has leased space at the property since 2003.

He also said the company had no ability to challenge the city’s decision to revoke the special use permit because the federal government, not JG Housing Solutions, held the permit.

“JG Housing Solutions has no control over the federal government or any of its actions at any of its leased facilities. The federal government has not addressed the City of Glenwood Springs’ complaints, and the City has not sued the federal government. Instead, the City sued JG Housing Solutions, the property owner,” Bryan said.

The motion argues that an order preventing JG Housing Solutions from leasing the property for detention operations would conflict with its existing federal lease. The company maintains that it cannot direct ICE’s operations or remove the agency from the property.

Rather than pursuing the landlord, Bryan said the city could seek assistance from Colorado’s congressional delegation, offer to purchase the property or pursue legal action against the federal government.

“Suing a small, family-owned business that simply owns the commercial property will not give the City the relief it seeks, because JG Housing Solutions has no authority over how the federal government uses the space,” Bryan said.

The city’s lawsuit seeks a court declaration that leasing the property for detention operations violates its Land Use Code, an order prohibiting JG Housing Solutions from continuing that use and penalties of $1,000 per day until the alleged violations stop, according to the motion.

JG Housing Solutions is asking the judge to dismiss the lawsuit with prejudice for failure to state a legally sufficient claim or, alternatively, without prejudice because the federal government is a required party that cannot be joined.

Bryan maintained that his client has complied with the terms of its lease and should not be held responsible for the federal government’s activities.

“JG Housing Solutions should not be caught in the middle of this controversy – it has done nothing wrong,” Bryan said.

The city declined to comment further on the pending litigation.

“A ruling has not yet been rendered. No additional comments from city officials will be shared at this time,” the city said in its emailed statement.

The motion remains pending in federal court.

text:
On November 9, 10 and 12, the Federal Court in Toronto heard arguments challenging the legal validity of the Safe Third Country Agreement. Hearings are scheduled to resume on December 16.

The agreement has been in force for two decades. It is based on the premise that both countries reliably uphold the right to seek asylum. It requires asylum seekers to make their claims in the first safe country they reach. TBR

Under the agreement, asylum seekers who arrive at Canada's land or sea border after passing through the United States are generally denied entry and returned to the U.S.

Haiti, Venezuela and Colombia are currently the main countries of origin of asylum seekers returned by Canada to the United States.

Amnesty International, the Canadian Council for Refugees, the Canadian Council of Churches, and asylum seekers argue that the agreement violates the right to equality, protected by section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Julia Sande is a lawyer and strategic litigation campaigner specializing in refugee and migrant rights at Amnesty International Canada. She is not involved in litigating this case. In her view, the agreement causes harm by returning people to the United States despite knowing that they face detention and removal.

They are at risk of deportation to a country where they could face torture, persecution or other serious human rights violations.

A quote from Julia Sande, lawyer at Amnesty International Canada

Between January 1, 2025, and March 30, 2026, Canada returned at least 4,000 people to the United States. This figure comes from the plaintiffs' written submissions, based on data from Canada Border Services Agency.

According to Julia Sande, Canadian officers only assess whether asylum seekers qualify for exceptions, such as having a close relative in Canada. They do not consider what might happen to them in the United States, she says.

Twenty minutes to decide at the border

Having family in Canada is not always enough.

Carlos and Antonia fled Honduras in 2021 with their son, Alejandro, after suffering attacks and threats from gang members. In March 2025, in the United States, they were informed their asylum case had been closed and that they would be deported, according to the Canadian Council for Refugees.

In April 2025, they arrived at the Canadian border. Carlos has siblings in Canada, so officers told him he and Alejandro could enter. Antonia, however, had to go back to the United States.

I said to them: 'What am I supposed to tell my son to explain why they won't let his mother in with us?' And the border officer answered: 'That's your problem, you have 20 minutes to make a decision.'

A quote from Carlos, Honduran asylum seeker

The family refused to be separated, and Canada returned all three to the United States. After five days in detention, they were transferred to the detention centre in Dilley, Texas. There, Antonia and Alejandro were separated from Carlos.

A child shouldn't learn what a lock is before learning what freedom is.

A quote from Antonia, Honduran asylum seeker

Ottawa and the organizations defend their positions

In 2023, the Supreme Court of Canada unanimously ruled that the agreement does not violate asylum seekers' rights to liberty and security under section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

According to the University of Toronto's Investigative Journalism Bureau, the Canadian government argues that the plaintiffs’ case relies on press reports, hearsay and speculation.

Ottawa also argues that the equality rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not apply, because the challenge is about U.S. asylum law. It further asserts that, even if those rights do apply, any infringement is demonstrably justified.

Julia Sande says the court record runs to tens of thousands of pages, including expert reports and sworn statements from people detained in the United States.

The United States isn't hiding what it's doing. It is quite open and, in fact, proud of its campaign of mass detention and deportation. We have statements from the United States, executive orders, its own laws.

A quote from Julia Sande, lawyer at Amnesty International Canada

According to the Amnesty International lawyer, the Canadian government considers that the situation in the United States has not changed.

She points instead to overcrowding and to the detention of families and of pregnant and breastfeeding women. She adds that LGBTQI+ people are 97 times more likely to be sexually assaulted while in U.S. immigration detention.

Remote crossings, child detention and the Refugee Convention

Since 2023, the agreement has applied along the entire land border between Canada and the United States. To avoid it, Julia Sande explains, people must cross the border somewhere other than an official port of entry. They must then remain 14 days in Canada without being detected.

According to the lawyer, Canadians express differing views on the appropriate level of immigration, but she is confident that there are certain values on which no one in the country would disagree.

Do you think that Canada should be handing over children to ICE to throw them into detention where they will not have clean drinking water, where they'll lose weight […]? I would like to hope that answer of Canadians would be no.

A quote from Julia Sande, lawyer at Amnesty International Canada

The lawyer also recalls the collective horror after the Second World War over turning away people fleeing Nazi Germany. That horror led to the Refugee Convention.

We created this system to say: if someone isn't safe, if someone needs protection, what do they have to do? They just have to knock on your door, she said. Canada, she argues, has a duty to hear their claim.

Once the hearings have concluded, the Federal Court will decide whether returning to the United States people who come to Canada's door seeking safety violates the right to equality guaranteed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

text:
Officials in Charlotte, North Carolina, have petitioned a judge to dismiss the wrongful death lawsuit over the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee who was killed by a man on a light rail train in the city in August 2025.

Zarutska’s uncle, Frank Scott Haskell, who was hosting Zarutska and her family in Charlotte, filed the lawsuit against the city and its transit security company, Professional Security Services, claiming that Charlotte failed to take reasonable and available safety measures to prevent her murder.

Haskell alleged in the lawsuit that the city and its security knew there were safety and crime issues related to its public transit, and they “were responsible for protecting lawful passengers from known and foreseeable dangers. Their failures caused the fatal stabbing.”

Zarutska was fatally stabbed from behind while aboard a Charlotte blue line train as she was traveling home from her shift at pizzeria. The attack, which was caught on surveillance cameras, gained international attention. Zarutska’s killing became a flashpoint in a broader public debate over violent crime, mental illness and public transit safety.

She had lived in a bomb shelter in Ukraine and had hopes of finding safety in the US. Family members described her as determined to build a safer life.

She was allegedly stabbed by Decarlos Brown Jr, who was charged with first-degree murder and later deemed incompetent to stand trial. He is now in a federal medical facility to restore his competency.

Charlotte’s motion to dismiss the civil lawsuit “with prejudice” comes after mediation talks failed earlier this month.

“The City recognizes the tragic and devastating death of Iryna Zarutska as the result of an intentional criminal attack by Decarlos Brown Jr,” Charlotte’s lawyers wrote. “The City denies that it ignored passenger safety or that its conduct legally caused that attack.”

Charlotte says it “maintained an extensive security program, contracted for armed and unarmed security and company-police services, and undertook initiatives concerning public safety, security planning, training, and transit operations”.

authors: Thomas Robertson, Shannon Heckt, Virginia Mercury

text:
A lawsuit filed in Virginia accuses Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents of arresting people without warrants or sufficient probable cause, citing cases where officers arrested residents without identifying themselves, stating a reason for detaining them or even having any knowledge about whether they were immigrants or natural-born citizens.

The Centreville Immigration Forum and six Virginia residents detained by ICE are listed as plaintiffs in the lawsuit. Three of the residents live in Northern Virginia, two in the Hampton Roads area and one in Greene County.

The 84-page lawsuit alleges several other examples of troubling conduct by ICE officers, including leaving a young child to wander in traffic while detaining her adult sister, initiating an arrest by ramming into a van and pepper spraying its occupants, and deciding who to target on the basis of how their names sounded.

WTOP has reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security for comment on the lawsuit but did not hear back in time for publication.

One of the plaintiffs, Alvaro Alvarez Flores, has lived in Newport News, Virginia, for 14 years and, after providing a valid Virginia driver’s license when stopped by ICE in July, was ordered out of his vehicle and placed in handcuffs, according to the lawsuit. The officers, the complaint states, did not present a warrant or ask about his immigration status.

While he was detained in an agent’s vehicle, Alvarez Flores watched as officers relayed license plate numbers over a handheld radio approximately six times, receiving names in response each time. When a non-Hispanic-sounding name was returned, the lawsuit states, the officers took no further action and said things such as, “No, not that one.”

After receiving what sounded like a Latino surname in response to a plate number, an officer directed other agents by radio to stop the identified vehicle, according to the lawsuit.

The officer transporting Alvarez Flores then sped up to catch the vehicle, teamed up with other officers to surround the vehicle, break its windows and remove two women and two men from the vehicle and place them all in handcuffs, according to Alvarez Flores’s observations detailed in the lawsuit.

“Alvarez Flores did not observe officers using a computer or other records system during this process; instead, the officers appeared to rely on information received through the radio when deciding which vehicles to target,” the complaint states.

‘They often don’t know who the person is’

Rebecca Guterman is a lawyer with the Washington Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, which helped the group bring the lawsuit. She explained the legal threshold ICE officers must meet during their enforcement operations.

“For decades, federal law has required that ICE can make an arrest if they have a warrant or if they have an individualized determination that the person is in the country unlawfully and that they are likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained,” Guterman said.

It’s the “individualized determination” that Guterman said ICE is often lacking when making warrantless arrests. In Virginia, she said the lawsuit demonstrates that officers “often don’t know who the person is or very much about them at all.”

The lawsuit is seeking an immediate end to ICE arrests without a warrant or probable cause, as was allegedly the case during the arrest of another plaintiff, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona.

Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and lifelong resident of Norfolk, Virginia, showed up at the scene where her fiancé had been arrested by immigration agents in August and was approached by an ICE agent who demanded her name and identification.

According to the lawsuit, officers blocked access to her vehicle when she tried to go back to it, accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle and placed her in handcuffs. While she was detained, the lawsuit states, her 4-year-old sister exited the car and was left to wander around in a busy street, despite Ramirez Corona’s pleas to make sure the child was safe.

Ramirez Corona also repeatedly told officers she was a U.S. citizen, but, according to the lawsuit, they informed her she would be taken to a federal building to verify her identity because “her name was not coming up in their system.”

“Ramirez Corona’s name would not appear in immigration databases because she is a natural-born U.S. citizen,” the lawsuit states.

Plaintiffs in Northern Virginia live in fear of ICE

Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez is a 24-year-old from Guatemala who has lived in Virginia for seven years and now resides in Manassas. She was detained in April while riding in a vehicle driven by her partner in Centreville.

During the stop, the lawsuit says one of the officers falsely stated that Us Lopez’s partner was subject to a deportation order. After her partner asked about what was going on, the lawsuit states, agents pepper sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their guns.

Before arresting Us Lopez, officers did not identify themselves, ask about her immigration status “or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained,” the lawsuit states.

While detained, Us Lopez told officers she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order. She was eventually released with an ankle monitor and ordered to report back to ICE the following day, according to the lawsuit.

“Since her arrest, Ms. Us Lopez has continued to travel to work, has learned of ICE activity near her home from community members, and fears being rearrested and separated from her child whenever she must leave her home,” the complaint states.

Jose Rosito Roca Estrada’s experience with ICE has left him not only in fear but also with debilitating pain from a broken clavicle and lung injury, according to the lawsuit.

Roca Estrada, 24, lives in Woodbridge and was traveling in a work van to a job site in June when, the lawsuit states, a driver in front of him slammed the brakes, came to a stop and rammed his van in reverse while other vehicles boxed the van in.

Then, 10 to 12 officers smashed the van’s back windows, according to the lawsuit, screamed at those inside to leave the van and pepper-sprayed the occupants through the lowered side windows.

Roca Estrada thought he was being kidnapped, as the agents did not identify themselves, according to the complaint.

As with the other cases included in the lawsuit, the complaint alleges that, before arresting Roca Estrada, officers did not ask about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status or any other questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.

While he was detained, officers threw him to the ground, pinned him and punched him, causing injuries that were later neglected by ICE, the lawsuit states. For weeks, according to the complaint, the defendants failed to provide promised follow-up care.

“The physical injuries and trauma resulting from Defendants’ actions left him unable to work or drive for over a month, impacted his ability to attend church in person, made him afraid to go grocery shopping or otherwise leave home, and left him with a persistent fear that he will be detained again,” the lawsuit states.

Prior to his arrest in June, the lawsuit states, Roca Estrada had never been arrested, charged with a crime or interacted with immigration authorities, as was the case for several of the other plaintiffs.

WTOP’s Steve Karesh contributed to this report.

title: Chicago man cleared in Gregory Bovino murder plot fights deportation to stay with family
description:
Ten months have passed since Juan Espinoza Martinez heard the words “not guilty” — but he’s still not a free man.
Gregory Bovino, the controversial face of the Trump administration’s audacious Midway Blitz deportation campaign in the Chicago area.
“I’m not abandoning my family,” Espinoza Martinez told the Chicago Sun-Times.
Espinoza Martinez put his fate in the hands of a jury, in the only trial to result from Operation Midway Blitz.
I just went blank in there.” When the verdict was read two days later, Espinoza Martinez sat stoically in his chair.
text:
Ten months have passed since Juan Espinoza Martinez heard the words “not guilty” — but he’s still not a free man.

Immigration authorities have held the Little Village resident in custody since he was acquitted of plotting the murder of then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, the controversial face of the Trump administration’s audacious Midway Blitz deportation campaign in the Chicago area.

In a call arranged by his legal team this week, Espinoza Martinez said he’d rather sit behind bars than be deported — without his loved ones — to a country he doesn’t remember.

“I’m not abandoning my family,” Espinoza Martinez told the Chicago Sun-Times. “I’m going to try as hard as I can. I’m going to hold on, incarcerated, because I’m not giving up.”

His fight for freedom has now stretched more than a year, starting when federal authorities accused him of soliciting Bovino’s murder.

Espinoza Martinez put his fate in the hands of a jury, in the only trial to result from Operation Midway Blitz. The panel swiftly acquitted him in January, deliberating only about three hours.

But Espinoza Martinez knew that wouldn’t be the end of the story.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcementtook him into custody the next day. And he’s now being held in the Greene County Jail in Missouri, ICE records show.

ICE wouldn’t comment when contacted Tuesday. Homeland Security didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Espinoza Martinez, 38, said he was brought to the United States as a small child. A judge described him as a Mexican citizen who entered the United States as a minor, over 30 years ago, “without inspection or lawful admission.”

His case is another striking example of the damage done when prosecutors level high-profile charges that don’t hold up in court.

Not only did the feds accuse Espinoza Martinez of the murder plot, court records identified him as a “ranking member of the Latin Kings.” Espinoza Martinez’s criminal defense attorneys, Jonathan Bedi and Dena Singer, denied he had any gang affiliation or criminal history.

Bedi said their client “consistently worked to provide for his family while contributing positively to the community” — and even coached his kids’ sports teams.

Prosecutors eventually backed down from their claim about the Latin Kings. That prompted a judge tobar gang-related testimony from the trial. And a week later, the jury found Espinoza Martinez not guilty in one of several Midway Blitz prosecutions that collapsed at Chicago’s Dirksen Federal Courthouse.

The feds there accused 33 known defendants of crimes tied to the blitz. But charges against 28 of them have been dropped. And prosecutors are now under fire for alleged misconduct in a failed case brought against a group of ICE protesters known as the “Broadview Six.”

Espinoza Martinez says he’s “holding on” in Missouri. But the ordeal has been a struggle for him and his family.

His younger brother, Oscar Martinez, made note of the birthdays and holidays that have passed without him. “We’re a family that was always together,” Oscar Martinez said in an interview.

Espinoza Martinez is the father of three children and said he has regular opportunities to speak with his family. But he said his youngest child, just 4 years old, doesn’t fully understand why his father isn’t home.

“I lie to him a little bit,” Espinoza Martinez acknowledged, noting he tells the boy he’s “working far away from home.”

But his son still complains: “You’re taking too long.”

Deep ties to Chicago

Espinoza Martinez is 38. And he spent three decades in the United States, supporters point out.

“His entire life, his family, his children, his siblings, and his mother all live in Chicago,” a lawyer told a judge in February.

He’s been described as a union carpenter. He said he even worked on the newly opened Obama Presidential Center on Chicago’s South Side.

“For the past decade, he has worked at his brother’s construction company, showing up every day to earn an honest living,” attorney Michael Adler wrote in a court filing last winter, seeking Espinoza Martinez’s release. “He has never been convicted of a crime. He has never given anyone reason to doubt his character.

“Before this, Mr. Espinoza Martinez was simply a working man with deep roots in his community going to work and taking his children to their soccer games.”

Espinoza Martinez said he didn’t even realize he was in the United States illegally until he was in high school. He said his parents were always working and paid their taxes, so no one expected trouble.

Espinoza Martinez even participated in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, court records show. Oscar Martinez said he once tried to help his brother gain legal status but was told the process could take 25 years.

Espinoza Martinez said there’s little waiting for him in Mexico. They have no family there, his brother said.

“I’ve been here since I was 3 years old,” Espinoza Martinez said. “I don’t have memory of over there, at all.”

The trial

The feds leveled criminal charges against Espinoza Martinez one month after the start of Midway Blitz. The news came as President Donald Trumptried to deploy National Guard troops into Chicago, with members of his administration complaining about threats to federal agents.

Federal prosecutors accused Espinoza Martinez of offering $10,000 for the murder of then-Border Patrol boss Bovino. They pointed to a Snapchat message, which Espinoza Martinez sent someone in early October.

The message followed a picture of Bovino and read “10k if u take him down.”

Espinoza Martinez wouldn’t go into the facts of his criminal case during his conversation with the Sun-Times. But at trial, defense attorneys argued he’d simply been sharing “neighborhood gossip” during the fast-moving Midway Blitz campaign that hit Little Village especially hard.

Jurors also viewed a recorded interview in which Espinoza Martinez told federal agents, “I didn’t threaten anybody.”

But top federal officials called Espinoza Martinez “ruthless” and accused him of an “attack on the rule of law” in a press release.

Espinoza Martinez told the Sun-Times that, when he was arrested, “my heart just went down to my feet.”

He said he thought he’d spend a week or so in custody. But attorneys pressed for a speedy trial, instead. A judge began picking jurors Jan. 20, less than four months after the charges were filed.

Espinoza Martinez said he was “really scared.”

“I didn’t know what to think,” he said. “I was shaking. I just went blank in there.”

When the verdict was read two days later, Espinoza Martinez sat stoically in his chair. He seemed to hold back emotion for a moment, though, as he briefly lifted his eyes to the ceiling.

“I felt great,” Espinoza Martinez said. “And at the same time, it’s like, I felt really sad. Because I knew that right after that, I had to come here.”

U.S. District Judge Joan Lefkow soon entered an order that said Espinoza Martinez “shall be released as soon as practical after processing.”

But when it came time for him to leave the Metropolitan Correctional Center around 6 a.m. the next day, he said, “ICE was already waiting for me.”

Waiting for a reprieve

The feds initially took Espinoza Martinez to Clay County, Indiana. Later, they moved him to Missouri. An immigration judge denied bail to Espinoza Martinez in February, calling him a “potential” danger to the community.

The ruling came less than a month after the jury’s verdict.

Now, Espinoza Martinez’s case is before the Board of Immigration Appeals, where it could still take months to be resolved. That’s according to a spokesperson for the National Immigrant Justice Center, which is helping him with the case.

Espinoza Martinez told the Sun-Times he’s had a “tough life being an immigrant.” But, he said, his incarceration has been “the worst.”

The headlines that hit the news about him last year “really affected me a lot,” he said. People have asked him about it in jail. And, he said, “my daughter started seeing all that stuff, as well.”

Still, he shared his gratitude for the way his community stepped up and helped look out for his children. He said he’s ready to “leave whatever happened in the news in the past.”

He said he’s taking things “day by day,” waiting for news from the immigration court.

And hoping to hear six words over the intercom: “Juan Espinoza Martinez, you’re going home.”

BALTIMORE (OSV News) — Priests in the Archdiocese of St. Louis attempted to seek accommodations to ensure their ability to distribute Communion to and hear confessions for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees before it filed a federal lawsuit in October, Archbishop Mitchell T. Rozanski said Nov. 17.

The archbishop made the comments in an interview with OSV News during the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ fall plenary assembly in Baltimore.

The issue originated, Archbishop Rozanski said, when about a dozen priests seeking to minister to those in detention went to the prison and they “were only allowed to speak to the detainees on the telephone through the glass.”

“They were not able to hear confessions,” he said. “They were not able to give them Communion. Not able to celebrate Mass. Nothing of the sacraments.”

Lawsuit challenges restrictions at Missouri ICE detention center

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, said the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center — which ICE uses for migrants awaiting deportation proceedings — has refused to accommodate clergy seeking to provide sacraments to migrants held there, due to their no-contact policy that prevents priests from meeting detainees face to face. The policy has left clergy unable to provide sacraments to detainees.

“We’re just asking for a space, as we are given in other incarceration institutions in Missouri prisons,” Archbishop Rozanski said. “We’re given a space to have Mass. We’re given a space to meet for reconciliation. I myself have been in other prisons where I have been able to hear the sacrament of reconciliation to celebrate Mass, and we’ve had no problems. But it’s just in this facility.”

Archbishop says requests for accommodation were rejected

But efforts to gain the necessary accommodations to provide the sacraments to those in ICE detention were disregarded by the prison, he said.

“There was a suggestion made to the priest that they could pass holy Communion in an envelope, and somebody would give it to them on the other side,” Archbishop Rozanski said. “That’s not the way we receive Communion.”

St. Louis Magazine recently reported that the facility made some modifications, notably a window in a steel door, to allow for the distribution of Communion while conducting Mass via video.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately return a request for comment from OSV News about whether they planned to make accommodations for reconciliation.

Archbishop Rozanski said that a key accommodation they are seeking is that “there would be no electronic communication involved if the detainees are going to the sacrament of reconciliation.”

Archdiocese warns case could have national implications

The issue, he said, could have “national repercussions.”

Earlier the same day in remarks to reporters at a press conference, Archbishop Paul S. Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the USCCB, identified “providing adequate pastoral and spiritual care” to those in detention centers as being among the U.S. bishops’ key concerns about migration policy.

Archbishop Rozanski added, “The Catholic Church reaches out to everyone, and especially those who are most vulnerable and most in need. And I can’t think of anyone in a situation like that, who is a detainee who’s separated from family, who’s facing an uncertain future, who would be as vulnerable as that?”

text:
The Florida company that owns an immigration detention center in Tacoma announced Wednesday that it has sold the facility to the federal government, bringing an end to months of rumors.

The Northwest ICE Processing Center, built in 2004 and acquired by the GEO Group in 2005, sold for $453 million, just weeks after GEO entered into a 10-year, $1.5 billion contract to continue running the facility, which holds roughly 1,600 beds. GEO will continue to provide services there.

“We look forward to continuing to provide high-quality secure support services at the Northwest ICE Processing Center under our new 10-year contract with ICE,” company CEO George Zoley said in a statement. “We are proud of our 40-year public-private partnership with ICE, and we stand ready to continue to assist the federal government in meeting its immigration enforcement priorities.”

GEO Group has faced numerous allegations of mistreating immigrants detained in Tacoma, who await either release back into the United States or deportation.

The sale could allow the detention center to avoid state oversight, including a law passed in Washington in 2023.

State officials have tried for years to inspect conditions at the Tacoma facility under that law, but the company has repeatedly refused, leading to lengthy litigation. A judge ruled in the state’s favor over the summer, but the company has continued to fight.

Federal ownership adds a legal obstacle to access for inspections, since state laws can’t unduly regulate federal activities.

The state Department of Health has received thousands of complaints about the detention center, but can’t investigate them.

Many deal with air, water and food quality. For example, detainees have complained about finding burned plastic, metal string, hair, worms and rope in food served by GEO, according to the state. Other concerns include assault, medical safety, sanitation and denying access to religious services.

GEO and the other major operator of federal detention centers, CoreCivic, have been in talks to sell their for-profit facilities to the Trump administration. GEO said Wednesday it’s in active negotiations that could result in the sale of three more of its facilities by the end of the year.

CoreCivic has been urging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to quickly buy up its facilities before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

President Donald Trump has sought to rapidly expand detention infrastructure nationwide as part of his surge in immigration enforcement since taking office last year.

State and federal officials didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the sale.

text:
On November 16, 2026, five European countries announced plans to send people who sought asylum in Europe and cannot be returned to their home country to Rwanda. The “Group of Five”—which includes Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece, and Denmark—states that it will send people whose asylum claims have been adjudicated and denied to a return hub overseas because they have no right to stay in Europe. The enforcement of returns should not come at the cost of eroding human rights for migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers. USCRI strongly urges the “Group of Five” to retract their deal with Rwanda and stop pursuing return hubs.

Return hubs expose vulnerable groups to the danger of refoulement, or the forcible return of a person to a country where they face a risk of persecution, torture, or serious harm. The principle of non-refoulement is a core human rights guarantee that is enshrined in several key international treaties, including the 1951 Refugee Convention.

“The Group of Five is attempting to skirt this international legal and moral obligation by sending people to a country where they have no ties and will feel pressured to either face the danger of an unfamiliar legal process in Rwanda or face the danger of returning to the place where they fled,” said Eskinder Negash, President and CEO of the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI).

This announcement follows a meeting in September between the Group of Five, where they announced intentions to pursue a deal with a non-European country to host migrant return hubs. Despite legal controversy surrounding return hubs, the European Parliament adopted regulation in June 2026 allowing countries to pursue deals to establish them.

“The idea of sending anyone who fled their country to seek safety to an offshore site should be against our moral principles as an international community,” Negash continued. “Global coordination should be in pursuit of protecting people who face danger, rather than exposing them to more risks.”

Deals with Rwanda on migration have been widely criticized. In July 2024, a deal between the United Kingdom and Rwanda to send asylum seekers for processing was scrapped after heavy scrutiny from human rights advocates and international human rights organizations. Rwanda has reportedly received $7.5 million from the United States to accept third country removals, a practice that is currently subject to legal challenge.

The Group of Five stated that it is working with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Organization for Migration. Both organizations have stated that human rights must be guaranteed and that they will engage with the countries as they move forward.

text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta, as part of a multistate coalition, today announced the filing of an amicus brief in United States v. Colorado in defense of Colorado laws restricting state and local law enforcement from sharing noncitizens’ personal information with immigration agents and from expending state resources to enforce civil immigration laws. The Trump Administration has challenged four Colorado laws and two Denver policies limiting the use of state and local resources to aid in immigration enforcement. In the amicus brief filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that Colorado’s policies and laws are lawful exercises of states’ police powers and are not preempted by federal immigration laws.

“The Trump Administration has perpetuated an aggressive and inhumane mass deportation agenda that threatens the security of all who reside in our country, not just undocumented immigrants,” said Attorney General Bonta. “The best way for states to ensure public safety is upheld in our communities is to build trust between state, local law enforcement, immigrants, and citizens alike. Courts have repeatedly upheld states’ abilities to not use their limited resources to aid federal immigration authorities, and we urge the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals to affirm this standard.”

United States v. Colorado is one of a number of cases that the Trump Administration has filed throughout the country challenging the legality of policies that limit state or local assistance with federal immigration enforcement. During President Trump’s first term, the Trump Administration unsuccessfully challenged the legality of one of California’s immigrant trust laws, the Values Act (SB 54). On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed that SB 54 is constitutional and consistent with federal law. When the Trump Administration subsequently asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review that decision, the Court denied the request, leaving the Ninth Circuit’s decision and SB 54 in place.

Like California, Colorado and Denver limit state and local governments from complying with demands to detain people who should be released, responding to requests to notify immigration authorities of release dates for non-citizens in custody, and advising noncitizens of their rights before facilitating interviews with immigration agents. Last year, the Trump Administration filed a lawsuit, challenging Colorado’s and Denver’s laws on preemption and intergovernmental immunity grounds. In March 2026, a district court ruled in favor of Colorado and Denver, determining that the federal government cannot force the state or the city to use their own resources to carry out federal immigration enforcement. The federal government subsequently filed a notice of appeal.

In the amicus brief Attorney General Bonta and the coalition assert that:

Amici States have reasonably concluded that disentangling their state from civil immigration enforcement promotes public safety.

Federal immigration law does not preempt the challenged policies.

State laws that limit assistance with immigration enforcement are constitutional and do not serve as obstacles to the implementation of federal law, and the federal government’s contrary argument raises serious Tenth Amendment concerns.

The challenged policies do not impermissibly discriminate against the federal government. Although the policies limit state and local government involvement with immigration enforcement, they do not treat the federal government unfavorably compared to non-federal actors.
