text:
Ifirst heard​ about what was being done to migrants and refugees in Libya in the autumn of 2015. I was reporting from the port of Augusta in eastern Sicily, where ships – European navy vessels, commercial tankers, fishing boats – would dock to discharge people rescued from the Mediterranean. I had been there several times before, but this year, a doctor treating refugees told me, the injuries were far more severe. Some were caused by the boats or by the crossing itself: dehydration and sunburn from days at sea, chemical burns from leaking engine oil. Others came from mistreatment in Libya: scabies and stomach problems; injuries consistent with beatings, torture and rape. Some people, the doctor told me, arrived with broken legs and feet – injuries consistent with high-impact landings. These patients had been thrown from buildings by their jailers to speed up ransom payments.

Later, I met people who could confirm these accounts themselves. But I remember that conversation on the quayside and the powerful urge I felt to write it down, to let people know what was happening. I wasn’t alone in doing so. That year was the peak of Europe’s so-called refugee crisis, and hundreds of journalists were reporting from Sicily, the Aegean, the Balkans. A few had malicious intent: I remember seeing a reporter from Russian state television wearing a medical mask as he did a piece to camera from Augusta, as if reporting on a plague. But many, I imagine, were feeling some version of what I felt. People were suffering, and by letting others know about it we were contributing somehow to alleviating that suffering.

What changed? A recent investigation by Forensis, a Berlin-based research group, provides fresh evidence that the suffering continues, only now with a patina of official legitimacy. A short film, Escaping Libya’s Detention Industry, charts a transition from smugglers’ compounds, through which migrants were trafficked by organised criminal networks for profit, to state-run detention centres that, in theory, form part of a humane system of immigration control. In practice, the new centres are much like the old ones – and in some cases, operated by the same people.

Forensis makes its case by comparing examples of the two types of prison, reconstructed via satellite imagery, architectural models, eyewitness accounts and video footage. The first example, a huge smugglers’ compound at Bani Walid, to the south-east of Tripoli, was established after Gaddafi’s overthrow in 2011. Smuggling – of people, weapons, fuel oil – increased as the Libyan state fell apart, to be replaced by a patchwork of local militias, many of which had links to gangsters. The compound in Bani Walid was built by the Diab crime family. Its most profitable activity involved detaining people who had crossed the Sahara, extorting money from them, pimping out their labour and passing them on to other smugglers, who would charge them yet more money for a boat journey towards Europe. Moussa Diab, the head of the family, allegedly spent his profits on lavish parties in Dubai.

The more recent examples – at Ain Zara and Al Mayah, on the outskirts of Tripoli – are run by Libya’s Government of National Unity. (The GNU has been at war with a rival government, led by the military commander Khalifa Haftar.) In areas the GNU controls, which include Tripoli and its hinterland, the old smugglers’ compounds have been shut down. (Bani Walid ceased operating in the late 2010s.) Instead, undocumented migrants are detained indefinitely in centres run by the Department for Combating Illegal Migration. These facilities have received enthusiastic support from European governments: before 2011, Gaddafi positioned the country as Europe’s border cop by restricting Mediterranean crossings, and European leaders have been keen to see Libya resume this role. The EU and Britain have provided funding for DCIM centres, while the EU collaborates with the GNU’s security forces to intercept boats at sea and return them to Libya. Yet as the Forensis film shows, the centres at both Ain Zara and Al Mayah were established by militias involved in trafficking. And just like Bani Walid, both continue to be sites of abuse. Survivors of each of the three centres describe dire living conditions, violence and extortion.

I still struggle to accept that exposing the abuse didn’t end it, even though I know that simply drawing attention to a problem is rarely enough. But as the world gets more violent, the gap between knowledge and action seems larger than ever. Forensis, which was founded in 2021 as an independent spin-off from the research organisation Forensic Architecture, is part of a constellation of groups looking for ways both to expose injustice and ensure that accountability follows. In part, they take their cue from the technology we now have at our fingertips. Everyday devices – not least smartphones – have drastically expanded our ability to record and monitor the world around us, while a range of specialist techniques exist to analyse information at scale or piece it together from fragments. Almost no event, whether fast-moving and chaotic or deliberately obscured, goes unrecorded – so long as you know where to look.

Getting access to Libya has long been extremely difficult for international journalists, human rights investigators and other information-gatherers, just as it has been potentially deadly for their Libyan colleagues to carry out this kind of work. Nevertheless, the ongoing abuse in smugglers’ compounds and ‘official’ detention centres alike has been repeatedly documented, often with a mix of traditional and innovative methods. In My Fourth Time, We Drowned, for instance, the journalist Sally Hayden managed to contact people being shunted around Libya’s migrant prisons and then collate their experiences via messages sent surreptitiously from phones that had been smuggled into the detention centres.

The difficulty is that the most powerful tools for sensing – and for sense-making – are not evenly distributed. State authorities, for instance, have far greater resources than either journalists or detainees. The EU’s border agency, Frontex, uses its billion-euro annual budget to run aerial surveillance operations in the Mediterranean that help the Libyan coastguard to intercept migrant boats. An investigation by Human Rights Watch in 2022 found that the agency conceals the extent of its activities, redacting documents released through freedom of information requests and denying investigators permission to visit its surveillance base in Warsaw. Frontex’s main activity – forcing migrants back to Libya in the full knowledge of what awaits them – is further concealed by the euphemisms and distortions of the politicians who built the system. In this world, the only villains are the traffickers. Many voters in Europe accept this mutual delusion, despite what evidence they might see to the contrary.

Forensis pursues what it hopes is a more effective challenge to this status quo than the traditional approaches. Building on the work of its parent organisation, which began as a research project at Goldsmiths, University of London in 2010, Forensis carries out what it calls ‘counter-investigations’. These bring together a wide range of documentary and imaging techniques to amass evidence in a way that not only builds a case, but asks the reader or viewer to question the way the tools work and in what ways they can be manipulated.

Forensic Architecture, which continues operating separately from Forensis (much of the former’s work now focuses on Gaza, as well as theoretical research), has won plaudits for this approach to human rights investigations. Some projects, such as the digital mapping of CIA drone strikes against the Taliban, or the use of machine-learning tools to trace police violence during the Hong Kong protests in 2019, apply innovative technology to a traditional form of human rights advocacy, focused on unpicking discrete events and identifying the likely perpetrators. Others take aim at historical or structural injustice: an ongoing project examines sites in Namibia related to the genocide of Ovaherero and Nama peoples by German troops in the 1900s, while investigations into police shootings in the US, UK, Greece, Palestine and Turkey have exposed cultural and ethnic bias in the actions of officers. In 2019, Forensic Architecture was invited to produce a film for the Whitney Biennial; its response was a film investigating the use of tear gas made by a company belonging to a member of the museum’s board.

As the name suggests, Forensic Architecture has its roots in a specific discipline: its founder, Eyal Weizman, is an architect who began his career working with human rights groups monitoring Israel’s construction of the West Bank separation wall. Advanced spatial imaging techniques are central to its work: in 2016, for instance, it used a 3D model to reconstruct the layout and cells of Saydnaya prison in Syria – at the time, the heart of the Assad regime’s machine for torturing and executing its opponents. The reconstruction was made using survivors’ recollections, but since prisoners were kept in the dark, participants drew on their memories of changes in temperature, moisture, light, vibrations and sound to create the model. Like many of Forensic Architecture’s projects, the investigation was carried out in collaboration with a more traditional human rights organisation – in this case, Amnesty International. But FA brought conceptual innovation as well as art-world glitz. I first came across the Saydnaya investigation at a Forensic Architecture exhibition at the ICA in 2018, the same year the organisation was nominated for the Turner Prize. I had mixed feelings about the exhibition: the subject matter was certainly important, but it sat awkwardly in the gallery setting. What wins out in such a context: the evidence or the aesthetics?

At their most successful, such interventions have played on their surroundings. At the opening of documenta 2017, which was attended by leading German politicians, Forensic Architecture re-enacted a notorious racist murder in Kassel. (The culprits belonged to a neo-Nazi group that had been allowed to carry out a string of murders under German state surveillance; FA’s research was later used in an official inquiry into the killings.) When that doesn’t happen, though, the risk is that such work stays stuck in the worlds of art and academia – and that discussion focuses on its creators.

To what other uses could these techniques be put? Open-source intelligence – the practice of analysing publicly available information about an event – is now done by most traditional media organisations, while many NGOs have established their own high-tech investigative units. These techniques aren’t inherently subversive: in October 2023, for instance, the Centre for Information Resilience – an investigative agency founded by two Foreign Office veterans – was contracted to provide regular updates to the British government on the situation in Gaza. Its information hasn’t stopped the government from repeatedly trying to wriggle out of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and other international human rights treaties, for instance by continuing to supply parts for lethal F-35 jets to Israel. (In April the Foreign Office withdrew funding for the specialist internal human rights unit that monitored Gaza, ending the CIR’s contract altogether.)

Forensis is an attempt to make a virtue of these shifts, by focusing on practical human rights investigations and building a network of collaborators who can extend their reach. Since Forensis’s own researchers couldn’t visit Libya themselves, they established relationships with two groups. The first comprised Libyans, identified via the legal network Lawyers for Justice in Libya, who helped Forensis to collect on-the-ground footage, supplemented by testimony from locals who could describe the way the detention centres had developed over time. A striking sequence in Escaping Libya’s Detention Industry features the Diab compound at Bani Walid, visible only in footage snatched by a phone camera placed on the dashboard of a passing car. More obvious filming is impossible. Using the information compiled from the Libyan sources, the researchers at Forensis traced the development of the trafficking industry through changes in Bani Walid’s built environment. At first the traffickers held people in abandoned industrial buildings. Later, as profits grew, they constructed purpose-built sites whose layout and function closely resemble today’s government-run detention centres.

The second group comprised survivors of the prisons. Computer models of the compounds at Bani Walid, Ain Zara and Al Mayah were created with the help of former inmates now living in Europe. The tools for creating these models include QGIS, a mapping program that allows buildings to be given precise geographical locations; Blender, modelling software used to design interiors; and Unreal, a video game engine that allows the user to move through a 3D environment.

Unreal is often used for first-person shooters – the militaristic adventures that generate billions for the gaming industry each year. Here, however, it’s harnessed for what Forensis calls ‘situated testimony’: an interviewing technique developed in collaboration with psychiatrists to help survivors recover and situate traumatic memories. This serves several purposes. It helps to break down the traditional hierarchy between researcher and subject. Survivors lead the sessions, with the researchers on hand mainly to provide guidance on how to use the technology. But it’s also a way of questioning the standards by which evidence is judged. The many forms of ‘hard’ evidence – of data, documents, images – now available to us have diminished the value of individual testimony. An investigation like Escaping Libya’s Detention Industry attempts to restore its prominence by marrying it with technological innovation.

Towards the end of the film we are shown a map of the Mediterranean, on which are plotted the many sea journeys taken by two survivors of the government-run detention centres. The map, a computer-generated image that resembles the kind of material handed out at a government press briefing, is a mess of zigzags showing how each attempt to reach Europe was foiled by EU surveillance and the Libyan coastguard, returning the passengers to prison in Libya. (Martin, one of the two survivors, only succeeded on his ninth attempt.) This functions as a kind of commentary on the slick effusions of data and graphics pumped out by an organisation like Frontex and the lies they conceal. The journeys on this map have been plotted by Forensis researchers and the survivors working together, trying to visualise the latter’s necessarily partial memories. We believe them because of the film’s patient accumulation of detail.

This painstaking, collaborative approach also feeds into a wider campaign for legal accountability. Lawyers for Justice in Libya, which helped to gather information for the Forensis investigation, has submitted a criminal complaint about mistreatment in Bani Walid and elsewhere to Dutch prosecutors, who are investigating crimes committed in Libya. In January 2026, an Eritrean national known as ‘Walid’ was sentenced to twenty years in prison in the Netherlands for the torture of migrants in Libya, while the trial of another alleged trafficker is ongoing. LFJL is trying to encourage prosecutors to treat such crimes as systemic, rather than focus on isolated cases.

One of the persistent problems in discussing the situation for refugees in Libya is that attention is too easily focused on the immediate perpetrators of violence: traffickers such as the Diab family and the militias who now sport DCIM uniforms. In May, the former Libyan militia leader Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri will face trial at the International Criminal Court on seventeen counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes for the alleged torture, rape and other severe mistreatment of detainees in a militia-run prison outside Tripoli. ‘This case should mark only the beginning,’ according to a recent communiqué from LFJL and other organisations that urges the ICC ‘to pursue those most responsible – whether Libyan or European actors – who perpetrate and enable these systematic crimes’. But it’s harder to capture the way a decision taken thousands of miles away contributes to the problem; for that, it’s necessary to draw attention to larger patterns and processes. One benefit of the work of Forensis and like-minded researchers is that they provide the rest of us with a template to copy.

title: Democrats eye a reckoning on ICE tactics and mass deportation - MS NOW
authors: Joe Danborn, David Noriega, Steve Benen, David J. Bier, Irina D. Manta
description:
Will the Trump administration comply?
Boasberg started examining whether to hold administration officials in contempt for ignoring his order, but his effort was halted by a Trump-appointed majority on an appeals court.
(The Trump administration has consistently maintained, in spite of the evidence, that the men sent to CECOT were dangerous gang members.)
Nevertheless, Moriarty and others cautioned against expecting anything other than resistance and obstruction from the Trump administration.
Miller and other officials could claim executive immunity from congressional investigations, and they could bog down the process in appeals.
text:
A volley of letters fired off Wednesday by Rep. Robert Garcia to several current and former high-level Trump administration officials marks an early step in what congressional Democrats hope to make a sweeping investigation of the president’s policies — particularly his mass deportation campaign.

Democrats will enter the new Congress claiming a mandate from voters after an election shaped in no small part by Americans’ reaction to episodes of violence involving federal immigration officers.

Those affected and their advocates have high expectations for the investigations led by Garcia, D-Ca., the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, whose letter to newly named White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — the architect of President Donald Trump’s immigration policy — asserts the committee’s intentions to probe “violence, abuse, and corruption carried out by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) at your direction.”

But the prospect of congressional scrutiny also raises questions about what these investigations can realistically accomplish, and on what timeline. While Democrats will have broad powers to demand documents, compel testimony and expose wrongdoing, Congress cannot itself bring criminal charges or force the executive branch to prosecute its own officials. And an administration that has repeatedly resisted judicial and congressional oversight is unlikely to cooperate willingly.

“We’re certainly in a better position than we were before the election,” said outgoing Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, the chief prosecutor in Minneapolis, whose investigations of the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti by immigration officers have been stymied by lack of cooperation from the federal government.

“But a lot depends on the details. Will the Trump administration comply? And will the Democrats treat this as a mandate and really push for what people voted for?” she said.

An infamous prison

On the list of actions that advocates are hoping Congress will scrutinize are the March 2025 deportations of hundreds of Venezuelan migrants to an infamous prison in El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act, an obscure law from the early years of the American republic. The deportations (which are at the center of my forthcoming book, “Trial Run: How Trump’s War on Immigrants Threatens Us All”) were one of the first indications of how far the Trump administration was prepared to go in pursuit of mass deportations.

As planes carrying the deportees were in the air, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg ordered the administration to turn them around. But the planes continued to El Salvador, where the men were incarcerated at the Center for the Confinement of Terrorism, or CECOT, a prison built for hardened gang members.

Boasberg started examining whether to hold administration officials in contempt for ignoring his order, but his effort was halted by a Trump-appointed majority on an appeals court. A similar scenario could play out in a Democrat-controlled Congress, with hard questions asked but consequences comparatively few.

In the immediate aftermath of the flights, Miller described the men sent to El Salvador as “terrorists” who “relish in torture and murder,” alleging they belonged to the Venezuelan street gang Tren de Aragua. Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who was sent one of Garcia’s letters Wednesday, flew down for a photo op with shirtless, tattooed men — not the Venezuelans, but rather convicted Salvadorans — crowded into a cell behind her.

Under the Alien Enemies Act, the Venezuelans were deported without court hearings of any kind. In the weeks that followed, it became clear that most had no criminal record, and the government’s claims of gang membership fell apart under scrutiny.

In “Trial Run,” I suggest that the Alien Enemies Act deportations were an early test of the Trump administration’s ability to strip a marginalized group of fundamental legal protections and exercise unchecked executive power.

“We need to have public hearings on the record in which Trump administration officials are held accountable, and in which it’s clear as day what happened when they chose to break the law and send people to be tortured in El Salvador,” said Lindsay Toczylowski, the co-founder and CEO of Immigrant Defenders Law Center, or ImmDef, a nonprofit law firm that represents several of the Venezuelans.

The deportees spent four months at CECOT, during which they said they underwent near-constant beatings and torture. (The Trump administration has consistently maintained, in spite of the evidence, that the men sent to CECOT were dangerous gang members.) The possibility of a Democratic congressional majority investigating that is “a step forward,” said Andry Hernández Romero, a makeup artist and hairdresser who was among the CECOT deportees and whose case became emblematic for many Americans of the extraordinary injustice of the operation. “It opens up the possibility, at least, that there might be justice.”

Good and Pretti

In Minneapolis, where federal immigration agents shot Good and Pretti during a series of sweeps called “Operation Metro Surge,” the prospect of congressional investigations has taken on particular urgency: Congress might be able to obtain evidence that has so far been withheld from state and local officials.

“What I hope for is that somehow, as a result of a congressional hearing, the evidence that we don’t have would be given to us,” said Moriarty, the prosecutor.

Similarly, attorneys representing Good’s family said they hope congressional investigations can further their own lawsuits against the federal government, particularly when it comes to establishing high-level responsibility for what happened.

“One of the things that has to come out of oversight, without question, is supervisory accountability,” said Antonio Romanucci, a lawyer for the Good family. “It must start from the top, and someone has to take responsibility.”

More articles

Romanucci said his firm has had a hard time serving Miller — who reportedly lives on a military base outside Washington — with a subpoena in the family’s lawsuit. A subpoena from the House Oversight Committee would not be so easy to avoid.

Nevertheless, Moriarty and others cautioned against expecting anything other than resistance and obstruction from the Trump administration. Miller and other officials could claim executive immunity from congressional investigations, and they could bog down the process in appeals. This would be of a piece, Moriarty said, with the administration’s approach to the law.

“They’re willing to do things that are against the law and just challenge a court to decide differently,” she said.

Accountability, if not change

With Trump still in the White House, and with the ascension of Miller to chief of staff, advocates and attorneys have been careful to warn their clients and others in immigrant communities that there are limits to what Congress can accomplish.

“Accountability is different than ending mass deportations,” said Toczylowski of ImmDef, whose firm represents thousands of immigrants caught up in the crackdown.

The Trump administration turbocharged immigration enforcement with hundreds of billions of dollars in new funding. The agents, detention space and other initiatives the money is used to fund will not stop because Democrats have a majority in Congress.

Moreover, the Trump administration has made significant structural changes to much of the immigration enforcement system, including purging immigration courts of judges seen as sympathetic to immigrants and replacing them with hard-liners.

“We still have all of that machine that they built to move people quickly towards deportation,” Toczylowski said. “Those are the things that are harder for me to see changing in the short term, particularly with Stephen Miller now fully in charge.”

For Hernández, the Venezuelan man deported to CECOT, justice will not truly be done unless he is allowed to continue the asylum proceedings that were interrupted when Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act to deport him, an action that federal courts have ruled constituted a violation of due process. Whether Hernández and the others are allowed to return to the U.S. is a question currently being decided in the courts — not a question that can be resolved by Congress.

“My goal isn’t for justice to be done while I’m still far away,” said Hernández, who is now living in Spain. “For me, justice would mean being back in the United States.”

At a minimum, those affected by Trump’s campaign of mass deportations said congressional hearings can establish a definitive historical record of everything that’s happened since Trump resumed office.

“Those hearings alone are not going to change what happened,” Toczylowski said. “But they are the beginning of making sure that it never happens again.”

Legal observers wearing yellow vests remained outside the ICE building following the detentions.

text:
This week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed to U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), top Democrat of the House Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and U.S. Representative John Garamendi (D-CA-08) that it will not use ships, including training vessels or private foreign ships, for deportations.

This confirmation comes after Carbajal and Garamendi sent a letter demanding the agency abandon its proposal to use maritime vessels for mass deportations. The Congressmen sent the letter following New York Times reporting that revealed DHS considered using ships for mass deportations and identified Cal Poly Maritime Academy’s training ship, the Golden Bear, as a possible deportation vessel.

“While this commitment from DHS is a major victory for the Central Coast and congressional oversight, our work is not done. We must continue to hold the Trump Administration accountable for its extreme immigration enforcement and mass deportation agenda,” said Rep. Carbajal, the top Democrat on the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee and a Senior Member of the Armed Services Committee. “When Congressman Garamendi and I spoke out against the Trump administration’s plan to use maritime vessels—including the Cal Poly Maritime Academy’s Golden Bear—for deportations, they had no choice but to back down. This is a major win for accountability, but we cannot let up. I will continue pressing DHS for answers, closely monitoring its actions, and pushing back against policies that undermine due process and put people’s safety and rights at risk.”

“When Congressman Carbajal and I said that Donald Trump, Markwayne Mullin, and ICE will never use the Golden Bear or any ship for their mass deportation agenda, we meant it,” said Rep. Garamendi. “Today, I’m proud to announce the Department of Homeland Security has confirmed that it will not use any ship, including training vessels or private or foreign ships, for deportations. This isn’t the final step; we will continue to use our oversight powers to make sure Trump’s DHS keeps its word. I’m glad to stand with Congressman Carbajal on this issue, and I will continue to stand with him and every member of Congress to hold the Trump Administration to account.”

The Department of Homeland Security’s response can be found HERE.

Carbajal and Garamendi’s original letter can be found HERE.

Background

Carbajal is a leader in fighting the Trump administration’s extreme immigration policies.

In October 2026, Carbajal visited the Santa Maria ICE facility — marking his third visit since 2025 — as part of his ongoing investigation into the recent surge in ICE activity on the Central Coast. In the same month, the Congressman demanded a full investigation into the October 21 detention and injury of 20-year-old Erik Zepeda, a U.S. citizen and Santa Maria High School student with disabilities who was tackled, restrained, and questioned by ICE agents while walking to school. Zepeda was hospitalized and underwent surgery for wrist injuries sustained during the wrongful detainment.

Carbajal visited the Adelanto ICE processing facility in May 2026 to meet with detainees, three of whom are Central Coast constituents. The Congressman also assessed conditions in the facility and inquired about the reported deaths of detainees.

Carbajal is a co-sponsor of the No Secret Police Act, which would require law enforcement officers and agents of DHS engaged in border security and civil immigration enforcement to clearly display identification and insignia when detaining or arresting individuals and to ban them from using home-made, non-tactical masks.

Gov. Kathy Hochul says she wants answers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and contractor Akima Infrastructure Protection LLC about a detention facility under construction in Batavia.

The governor's office, along with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and Department of Health, is calling on ICE and Akima to explain their plan to ensure the safety of those incarcerated at the facility, which could, reportedly, house up to 100 women in tents, as winter weather approaches.

"The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) and New York State Department of Health (DOH) write jointly to seek information relating to Akima Infrastructure Protection LLC (Akima)’s construction and anticipated operation of a tent detention facility on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Buffalo Service Processing Center (BSPC) in Batavia, New York," a letter states. "To date, DEC and DOH have not received any information or outreach from the federal government or Akima about this facility. We understand from public reporting, however, that the facility may be used to detain up to 100 women and will employ numerous staff. Because aspects of this facility’s construction and operation may implicate DEC’s and DOH’s regulatory authority over environmental and public health issues, we request additional information about the project."

Hochul adds that the state has never received any information from the federal government or Akima about the project.

According to the governor's office, the state is seeking information on "how the site will operate in response to serious concerns about the facility's potential human rights, environmental and public health impacts."

ICE and Akima have until Wednesday, Nov. 25, to respond.

text:
A federal judge this week struck down a Department of Homeland Security rule that would have capped admission periods for international students and exchange visitors at four years, a decision welcomed by universities and international education groups.

The decision keeps a longstanding policy known as “duration of status” in place. That policy allows students on F-1 visas and exchange visitors on J-1 visas, including researchers, to remain in the US for the duration of their programs. If enacted, the DHS rule would have instead required students who needed more than 4 years to complete their programs to apply for an extension, with no guarantee it would be granted. That change would have burdened PhD students, who often need more time to complete their programs. A 2025 analysis by AIP’s statistics team found that about 97% of international PhD recipients in physics and astronomy took more than four years to finish.

This week’s decision follows a cascade of recent legal activity. DHS’s final rule was published in July but was blocked by US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor on Sept. 14, one day before the rule was due to go into effect. The government appealed that decision, but later asked the court to pause the appeal for 30 days while Saylor considered the case’s merits. The First Circuit granted the request to pause the appeal on Nov. 13. A few days later, on Nov. 16, Saylor found that DHS had acted unlawfully and set aside the rule in full. The government may now separately appeal this decision, but filing an appeal alone will not put the rule into effect.

NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, and a group of other higher education and labor organizations led the legal challenge against the DHS rule and welcomed Judge Saylor’s ruling.

“With this ruling, the judge has sent an unequivocal and resounding message: the longstanding Duration of Status policy is retained. This outcome underscores the importance of defending international students through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy,” said Fanta Aw, NAFSA’s executive director and CEO, in a news release.

DHS exceeded its authority and inadequately justified changes

In his Nov. 16 opinion, Judge Saylor said DHS had exceeded its statutory authority by attempting to restrict which academic programs international students could pursue, stating that the purpose of the F-1 visa class is to “permit, and indeed encourage, foreign students to pursue educational opportunities in the United States.”

Most international students are in the US on F-1 visas. The DHS rule would have barred F-1 graduate students from changing majors during their programs. It also would have prevented students who completed a US program in F-1 status after Sept. 15, 2026, from obtaining or maintaining that status through another program at the same or a lower level. Judge Saylor said the restrictions could effectively bar students from pursuing joint degrees. He also noted that DHS itself acknowledged legitimate reasons for pursuing another degree at the same or a lower level, such as earning an MBA after a JD.

“Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage. The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program,” Saylor wrote, explaining his reasoning for vacating DHS’s rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. Saylor also found DHS’s rule to be arbitrary and capricious because the agency did not appropriately weigh the costs and benefits of the changes, or adequately justify how they would support the agency’s stated aim of reducing immigration fraud and improving national security, among other reasons.

However, Seddighzadeh said that tracking the flights that way had become “an incredibly laborious process” at more than 70 ICE flights a day, and that the monitor’s work had “increased threefold since last year, reaching over 2,000 ICE flights per month”.
The complaint, filed in Washington DC federal court, alleges CSI “remains the contractor responsible for brokering nearly all ICE Air flights for the Administration”.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has agreed to pay the private contractor CSI Aviation up to $305.7m without competitive bidding on top of existing larger contracts and changed an existing agreement so that it can keep aircraft off public flight-tracking websites, federal contracting records show.

The change in September was to “add LADD”, the name of a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) program that prevents planes from appearing on some tracking websites. It may further inhibit monitoring of ICE flights, including flights to third countries, by immigrant and civil rights advocates.

On 31 October ICE also signed a new order with CSI worth up to $1.28bn to keep running its charter flights for another year in a deal that will also see CSI’s staff draw up the lists of people put on its deportation and transfer flights. Under ICE’s own handbook and the original terms of the agreement, supplying those lists was the agency’s job.

Neither the staffing deal, posted to a federal procurement website in July, nor the September contract change on flights have previously been reported in detail. The revelations show that despite protests and political reversals, the Trump administration’s ongoing deportation program is continuing to provide windfalls to private companies.

Angelina Godoy, director of the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights, told the Guardian that she was “alarmed” by the contract, including the apparent intention to remove ICE flights from tracking websites.

“There is no legitimate reason to remove such flights from tracking systems; the only reason to do so is to seek further secrecy for the agency’s operations.” Godoy added, “It’s an affront to democracy and the rule of law for any government to be secretly shuttling people across the globe with no effective oversight or accountability for such operations.”

The Guardian contacted DHS, ICE and CSI Aviation for comment.

The staffing deal covers “up to 140 dedicated flight coordinators” at ICE field offices and air operations hubs, working “18 hours a day, 7 days a week”, according to a justification signed on 16 July by ICE’s head of contracting, Albert Dainton. The document says CSI is “the only source capable” of the work, citing its “proprietary systems” and “integrated flight tracking and manifest management systems that are interoperable with ICE’s operational platforms”. With options, the deal runs to March 2029, just after the scheduled end of Donald Trump’s term.

The justification says “increased operational demands now require these services”, and that “ICE field offices face challenges due to competing priorities and limited staffing”. The coordinators, it says, will “reduce administrative burdens on ICE personnel”.

These increased demands are apparently enough to induce DHS to disregard its own operational rules and to overturn the terms of previous contracts.

Under the original terms of the agreement, published by DHS in 2025, the government was to give CSI “a manifest containing the names of all passengers for each flight prior to departure”. ICE’s own air operations handbook assigns the work to agency staff. Its 2023 edition says ICE’s air removal coordinators are “responsible for reviewing and allocating seat requests, preparing flight manifests” in an agency system, the T-8 charter application.

CSI staff already had sweeping access to ICE data systems according to legal documents. In a sworn declaration filed in January in the US court of federal claims, where CSI unsuccessfully challenged a separate DHS contract, the company’s senior vice-president for government services, Richard DeLucia, said its personnel “have full access to ICE’s data systems to input data and verify manifests on every mission”. He said “the current program has evolved to capture more administrative functions for ICE ERO and to unburden ICE Officers so they can continue field operations”.

The same documents suggest a revolving door between the agencies and contractors. DeLucia said 19 of CSI’s more than 300 employees came from immigration agencies, “mostly recent retirees from ICE and CBP”, and that they handled “Immigration paperwork verification for all migrant domestic transfers and international removal missions”.

“We pride ourselves on hiring the best ICE personnel after they have left active duty to continue to bring a high level of continuity to our deportation system,” he wrote.

The September change adds LADD to the contract management section of the agreement, according to the federal award record. In aviation, LADD is the FAA’s Limiting Aircraft Data Displayed programme, under which aircraft owners and operators can keep their planes off public flight-tracking websites. The planes still broadcast their positions; the block changes what the websites display.

One flight-tracking site, FlightRadar24, reportedly received blocking notices under the programme for more than a dozen aircraft in March 2025, including planes often used for ICE deportations and transfers. The 2024 law behind the programme provides for blocking “upon request of a private aircraft owner or operator” for “the noncommercial flights of the owner or operator”. In May, 40 House Democrats wrote to the FAA citing “reports that ICE has misused” the programme “to shield deportation flights from public and congressional scrutiny”, and said that use was “out of the scope of this program”, the Guardian reported.

In an email, the New Jersey Democratic congressman Rob Menendez, one of the letter’s signatories, told the Guardian “ICE operates in near-secrecy, evading congressional oversight and making it almost impossible for families, their lawyers, and our casework teams to locate their loved ones.”

Menendez added that Democrats have “known for months that the Trump Administration has been abusing its ability to hide flights from public view. It was never intended to let ICE hide deportation flights from public scrutiny. That’s why we led over 30 of our colleagues in demanding answers from the FAA back in May, but the Administration continues to stonewall us.”

Menendez warned: “When Democrats take back the Majority next year, we will launch aggressive oversight into these secret flights and end ICE’s private flight secrecy once and for all.”

Fetaine Seddighzadeh of Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, one of the nonprofits that tracks ICE flights, told the Guardian in an email that “since late September, all ICE Air aircraft that previously showed visible tails became blocked on FlightAware and Flightradar24”, and that as of 5 November “the vast majority” of ICE flights could no longer be followed by their callsigns either. “With the absence of posted flight plans, we no longer know where removal and domestic shuffle flights are headed until the flight path is complete,” she said.

LADD binds commercial trackers such as Flightradar24 and FlightAware that use FAA data, but it “does nothing even against a casual observer, since many other aircraft trackers, including OpenSky or ADS-B Exchange, do not use FAA data and rely purely on crowdsourced ADS-B data which shows the aircraft”, said Martin Strohmeier, a board member of the OpenSky Network who researched aviation privacy at the University of Oxford. “Many charter aircraft operators put their aircraft on the list for one reason or another,” he said.

However, Seddighzadeh said that tracking the flights that way had become “an incredibly laborious process” at more than 70 ICE flights a day, and that the monitor’s work had “increased threefold since last year, reaching over 2,000 ICE flights per month”. Real-time tracking, she said, “may provide an early – and sometimes the only publicly visible – clue that a transfer or deportation is underway”.

“LADD blocks are the Trump administration’s latest attempt to further obscure its cruel deportation campaign,” Seddighzadeh said, calling it “this opaque and lawless system that has systematically violated due process, separated families, and uprooted thousands of people’s lives from communities across the country”.

The $1.28bn order was placed under a 2024 framework agreement that ICE awarded to CSI after receiving seven bids. However the staffing deal was not competitive, according to procurement records. Nor, reportedly, was a $562m order for flights that ICE placed with CSI in February 2025.

Rival bidders contested the framework agreement. In February 2025 one of them, Classic Air Charter, challenged CSI’s award at the US court of federal claims, after what its complaint called “five rounds of bid protest litigation”, arguing that ICE had evaluated CSI’s bid wrongly and allowed the company to “cure the defects in its quotation”. ICE staff then recommended terminating CSI’s award and cancelling the solicitation, a decision that government lawyers told the court belonged to the deputy homeland security secretary. ICE terminated the agreement in April 2025 “due to a protest at the Court of Federal Claims”, according to the federal award record.

In May ICE moved to reinstate it. Internal ICE emails released to the ACLU of Colorado after it sued under the Freedom of Information Act (Foia) show the request queued for approval at the top of DHS. “The ICE Air reinstatement was added back to the list as awaiting S2 approval (though I hear it’s actually S1 now for this one),” an ICE contract specialist wrote on 14 May 2025. S1 is DHS shorthand for the secretary, then Kristi Noem, whose office had to approve contracts worth more than $100,000.

A tracker of items awaiting the secretary’s approval still listed the reinstatement as “In Review” on 5 June. On 12 June ICE told the court it was “working to implement a proposal that would result in the voluntary dismissal” of the protest. Classic Air Charter dropped its challenge on 24 June. The federal record dates the reinstatement 25 June.

The Guardian contacted the ACLU of Colorado for comment.

Noem’s successor, Markwayne Mullin, rescinded the requirement for the secretary’s sign-off on contracts over $100,000 in April this year, as the Guardian previously reported. Dainton approved the staffing deal in both of the justification’s approval roles, as ICE’s advocate for competition and as its head of contracting.

The expanding relationship between DHS and CSI comes as the contractor faces a lawsuit over its role in flights that took Venezuelan men to a prison in El Salvador in March 2025. The Guardian reported on the commencement of that suit in July. The complaint, filed in Washington DC federal court, alleges CSI “remains the contractor responsible for brokering nearly all ICE Air flights for the Administration”.

On 12 November CSI asked the court to dismiss the case and to move it to Texas. In its filing, the company argued that “ICE (not CSI) had responsibility for the ‘manifest containing the names of all passengers for each flight’ (ie, identifying persons to be removed)”, citing the same contract clause.

In a sworn declaration filed alongside, CSI’s vice-president for government services, Andrew Talbott, said “ICE, not CSI, determined which individuals would board the planes”. CSI also argued that the complaint “does not allege that CSI was aware of the J.G.G. proceedings or that this Court’s orders were communicated to CSI”.

Godoy, the Center for Human Rights director, said ICE already had “considerable problems” with “putting people onto flights despite federal court orders having been issued prohibiting their transfer or deportation”.

“This would almost undoubtedly get worse if there were also private companies involved in the decisionmaking process, who would have to be notified by ICE of court rulings,” she said. Contractors, she added, “typically argue that Foia does not apply to them”.

text:
WASHINGTON—The U.S. Supreme Court today granted the government’s request to reverse an appeals court decision that had allowed a legal challenge to the Department of Justice policy silencing immigration judges to proceed in federal court. It also denied the cross-petition for certiorari filed by the National Association of Immigration Judges (NAIJ), which had argued that federal employees should be permitted to challenge broad prior restraints on their speech in federal court without first having to go through cumbersome and potentially futile administrative proceedings. The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University represents NAIJ.

“It’s disappointing that the Court failed to take this opportunity to make clear that public servants can go directly to court to challenge broad restrictions on their speech,” said Alex Abdo, litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute. “Forcing public employees to wade through cumbersome and potentially futile administrative proceedings before challenging prior restraints allows unconstitutional censorship to persist. Now more than ever, we need the insights of the nation’s immigration judges and other public employees to understand the work of our government.”

In 2020, the Knight Institute filed this lawsuit on behalf of NAIJ, challenging an Executive Office for Immigration Review policy that prohibits immigration judges from speaking publicly in their personal capacities about immigration or the agency that employs them. A district court dismissed the case in 2023, holding that the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 requires such claims to proceed through administrative review.

In June 2025, the Fourth Circuit revived the case, expressing concern that recent actions by the Trump administration may have undermined the agencies charged with hearing federal employment claims—the Office of Special Counsel and Merit Systems Protection Board—and that they may no longer be operating as Congress intended. But the court also held that, if that system is functioning as Congress intended, immigration judges would be required to challenge the policy through that administrative process rather than in federal court.

In February, the Knight Institute filed a cross-petition for certiorari asking the Court to consider that question. The cross-petition was filed after the government petitioned the Court in December 2025, asking it to reverse the Fourth Circuit’s ruling.

“We’re disappointed by today’s decision and by the Court’s failure to address the significant free speech concerns at the heart of this case. However, this litigation is far from over,” said Holly A. D’Andrea, president of the National Association of Immigration Judges. “The case has been remanded to the Fourth Circuit, and NAIJ will continue fighting to protect the free speech rights of immigration judges, to seek meaningful review of the Executive Office for Immigration Review’s speech policies, and to ensure that immigration judges may engage in public discourse on immigration matters in their personal capacities. Justice cannot endure when judges are intimidated into silence, nor can a nation remain free when the rule of law is subordinate to the whims of political ambition.”

NAIJ is a nonpartisan, nonprofit voluntary association of federal immigration judges. Its members have long participated in public conversations and events about immigration law, including through teaching, training, and community engagement.

Read today’s decision here.

Read more about the lawsuit, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, here.

Lawyers on the case include Ramya Krishnan, Alex Abdo, Xiangnong (George) Wang, and Jameel Jaffer of the Knight First Amendment Institute, and Victor M. Glasberg of Victor M. Glasberg & Associates.

text:
WASHINGTON—The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University today filed a cross-petition for certiorari with the U.S. Supreme Court, asking it to review a First Amendment challenge to a federal policy that forbids immigration judges from speaking publicly about immigration law and policy and the federal agency that employs them. The cross-petition asks, specifically, that the Court take up the question of whether federal employees challenging prior restraints on their speech must pursue their claims in front of administrative agencies, without any guarantee of eventual judicial review. The cross-petition comes after the government’s petition, which was filed late last year and which asks the Court to review a different aspect of the ruling by the court of appeals.

“Federal employees shouldn’t have to go through a cumbersome administrative process to challenge sweeping prior restraints on their speech,” said Ramya Krishnan, senior staff attorney at the Knight First Amendment Institute. “The Supreme Court should make clear that public servants can get immediate relief from gag orders by challenging them directly in court.”

In 2020, the Knight Institute filed the lawsuit on behalf of the National Association of Immigration Judges (NAIJ) challenging an Executive Office for Immigration Review policy that imposes an unconstitutional prior restraint on the speech of immigration judges. The district court dismissed the case in 2023, holding that the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) requires NAIJ to raise its claims administratively before seeking judicial review. In June of last year, the Fourth Circuit revived the legal challenge, expressing concern that the agencies charged with hearing federal employment claims—the Office of Special Counsel and Merit Systems Protection Board—may no longer be operating as Congress intended. The government’s petition, filed on December 23, challenges this determination. In the portion of its ruling that NAIJ’s cross-petition challenges, the Fourth Circuit went on to say that, if the CSRA is operating as intended, NAIJ’s members would need to challenge the prior restraint on their speech through the CSRA’s scheme of administrative review.

“The gag order that this administration has imposed on the speech of immigration judges is brazenly unconstitutional,” said Alex Abdo, the litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute. “Federal employees have unique insights to offer on the operation of government, and that is particularly so for immigration judges, who have a front row seat to the ongoing upheaval of our immigration system.”

Late last year, the Fourth Circuit denied the government’s petition for rehearing en banc. On December 19, the Supreme Court rejected the government’s request to stay the effect of the appeals court decision pending further proceedings before the Court. On December 23, the Trump administration filed a petition for certiorari, asking the Supreme Court to summarily reverse the Fourth Circuit’s ruling requiring further consideration of whether the CSRA is operating as Congress intended. In addition to the cross-petition filed today, NAIJ will oppose the government’s petition by March 2.

The NAIJ is a nonpartisan, nonprofit voluntary association of federal immigration judges. For years, members of NAIJ regularly spoke at conferences, guest lectured at universities and law schools, participated in immigration-law trainings, and spoke to local community groups, all in their personal capacities.

Read today’s cross petition for cert here.

Read more about the lawsuit, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, here.

Lawyers on the case include, in addition to Krishnan andAbdo, Xiangnong (George) Wang and Jameel Jaffer of the Knight First Amendment Institute, and Victor M. Glasberg of Victor M. Glasberg & Associates.

text:
A federal judge has struck down a Trump administration rule that would have imposed fixed limits on how long international students and exchange visitors could remain in the United States, preserving longstanding immigration protections for foreign nationals pursuing education and training.

The ruling, issued Monday, Nov. 16, by U.S. District Judge Dennis Saylor in Massachusetts, invalidated a Department of Homeland Security regulation that sought to replace the existing duration-of-status system with fixed periods of admission.

The decision affects individuals holding F-1 student visas, J-1 exchange visitor visas and I visas for representatives of foreign news media, along with their eligible dependents.

Under the longstanding system, qualifying international students are generally permitted to remain in the United States for the duration of their approved academic programs, provided they maintain their immigration status and comply with applicable requirements.

The administration's regulation would have replaced that arrangement with fixed admission periods, generally capped at four years, requiring affected individuals to seek extensions from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services if additional time was needed.

The changes raised concerns among universities, international education organizations and students about additional administrative requirements and potential disruptions to academic programs.

In his ruling, Saylor determined that the Department of Homeland Security exceeded its legal authority by introducing restrictions inconsistent with Congress' intent in establishing the affected visa programs.

The judge also found that the regulation violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the federal law governing how agencies develop and implement regulations.

The lawsuit was brought by a coalition of higher education and labor organizations, including the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the American Federation of Teachers and the United Auto Workers.

The organizations challenged the rule after its introduction earlier this year, arguing that the changes would undermine international education and create unnecessary obstacles for foreign students and scholars.

The court had previously postponed the regulation's effective date in September while the legal challenge proceeded.

Monday's decision vacates the rule nationwide, allowing colleges and universities to continue operating under the previous duration-of-status framework.

The ruling is particularly relevant to Caribbean nationals studying at U.S. universities, including institutions across Florida, which have longstanding educational connections with the region.

Students enrolled in lengthy degree programs, research placements and exchange opportunities could have faced additional immigration procedures under the proposed restrictions.

However, the decision does not eliminate existing visa requirements. International students must still maintain their immigration status, comply with school reporting requirements and follow applicable rules governing employment and academic enrollment.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision, leaving open the possibility of further legal proceedings.

For now, the ruling preserves the existing system and removes the immediate prospect of fixed admission periods for affected international students, exchange visitors and foreign media representatives.

Dive Brief:

A federal judge on Monday struck down a U.S. Department of Homeland Security rule seeking to cap international student visa stays at four years.

Calling the rule arbitrary and capricious, U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor said DHS had violated the Administrative Procedure Act and overstepped its authority. Saylor had paused enforcement of the rule in September, just before it was set to take effect.

DHS appealed the judge’s temporary injunction in September, but the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals paused the proceedings earlier this month ahead of Saylor’s final ruling at the Trump administration’s request. DHS did not immediately respond to questions Tuesday about next steps.

Dive Insight:

DHS published the rule in July, arguing it was needed to protect national security and prevent visa fraud. International students would have been able to seek extensions on their visas, but the decision would have been at federal officials’ sole discretion.

The rule would have changed long-standing policy permitting foreign students to stay in the U.S. for as long as it takes to complete their academic studies.

Several higher ed groups and unions, including the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and the American Federation of Teachers, sued the agency in August over the regulations.

Saylor handed the plaintiffs an early win when he temporarily blocked the visa cap from taking effect. Writing that they were likely to succeed in their case, the judge flagged that the rule could be abused by the Trump administration.

“It is not difficult to imagine how that system might be abused to punish those whose viewpoints or research are disfavored by the officials making the decision — or, indeed, punish disfavored institutions,” Saylor said in his Sept. 14 order.

He repeated those concerns Monday, describing the student visa process DHS sought to set up as an “unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system.”

Saylor further said DHS failed to weigh “less burdensome” options.

The DHS rule would have done more than limit student visa stays. Some international students would have been barred from changing their field of study or transferring colleges. And they could not come to the U.S. to pursue an academic degree at the same or a lower level than a degree they already possess.

For example, an international student who holds a law degree would effectively be banned from pursuing a master’s degree in the U.S., Saylor said.

“Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” he said. “The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority” to undermine the student visa program.

The judge’s decision may not put the case to bed, as the Trump administration could still appeal it. The continued uncertainty comes as new data shows a decline in international enrollment in the U.S.

text:
As immigration enforcement increases across the Bay Area, the high-profile arrests of two women tied to local universities have tested campus administrations. Observers say their responses could offer a model for how such institutions can stand by people facing detention and the risk of deportation.

When a University of San Francisco nursing professor was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at her home in Lodi in September, and a UC Berkeley business student was detained in late October at San Francisco International Airport, leaders at both universities mobilized within hours to connect the women with legal aid and rally support for their release.

One legal analyst said it could signal an increase in universities’ willingness to stand up to the Trump administration, which has canceled international student visas, attacked diversity policies, slashed research funding and accused campuses of tolerating antisemitism.

“I think most universities have been profiles in cowardice up until now, on this matter and others, trying to stay underneath the radar so that they don’t put in jeopardy the hundreds of millions of dollars they get in federal grants,” said Deep Gulasekaram, an expert in immigration and constitutional law at the University of Colorado Law School. “Perhaps this is an indication that universities have realized that they have some ability to push back.”

When UC Berkeley student Paula Albornoz Hernández, 23, was arrested by ICE at San Francisco International Airport on Oct. 30 as she was heading to Oregon for a weekend getaway, the chancellor’s office sprang into action within hours, according to the lawyer who petitioned a federal judge for her release from detention.

Gina Daly, UC Berkeley’s associate vice chancellor in charge of governmental relations, said the university developed protocols a decade ago for what to do if ICE arrested a student or staff member.

“The good news is those protocols worked,” she said. “We were able to mobilize very, very quickly and get her the support she needed. And within a very short amount of time, we were able to get her released so that she could continue her studies.”

U.S. District Judge Dena Coggins ordered ICE to release Albornoz Hernández and, after nine days of detention, she went home. But De Bremaeker told KQED his client is still struggling with trauma and health issues from the time she was locked up. And her pending asylum claim must now be made in immigration court, where ICE will argue for her deportation, instead of in a non-adversarial interview with an asylum officer.

Fry-Bowers was on vacation but immediately reached out to the campus provost’s office. By the end of the day, the USF law school had connected Lawani’s family with an attorney and, soon after, the university enlisted the help of her U.S. representative, Josh Harder, and other members of the California Congressional delegation.

But Lawani, the director of a master’s program with 230 students and who Fry-Bowers described as a “phenomenal colleague” and beloved professor, could not be found in ICE’s online detainee locator for three days — during which she was moved repeatedly from state to state. She was eventually able to phone a relative from the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, where she has now been detained for two months.

Her absence has left an enormous hole in the USF nursing school, Fry-Bowers said.

“It’s a crater like a bomb went off,” she said. “We already are strapped. I mean, there’s a nursing faculty shortage … So to take somebody who has leadership responsibilities to the extent that Ann has out of the school suddenly? It’s been a nightmare.”

Attorney Natalia Vieira Santanna noted that Lawani has a valid work permit and “has always functioned inside of the law.” She said the university has aided Lawani’s case by providing evidence showing the harm her detention is causing the community.

“It’s the first time that one of my clients gets such an outpouring of support and a lot of it is thanks to the University of San Francisco,” Vieira said. “They are doing a lot of the outreach to make the public aware of what’s happening.”

USF, a Jesuit school, has planned vigils to pray for Lawani on Wednesday morning at both its San Francisco and Orange County campuses. Meanwhile, a petition to ICE for her release has garnered nearly 43,000 signatures, and a GoFundMe campaign has so far raised nearly $110,000 for her legal and family expenses. Last week, USF President Salvador Aceves sent a letter to the university community describing the administration’s work “behind the scenes” to push for Lawani’s release.

However, with the federal courts swamped by thousands of habeas petitions from the growing ranks of detained immigrants, a judge has yet to rule on whether Lawani must be released.

Even if she is, Lawani still faces a real risk of deportation. Though the government is barred from sending her to Nigeria, it could try to deport her to a different country. Such “third-country removals” were extremely rare in the past, but since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, more than 25,000 people have been sent to countries where they may have no ties or legal standing. The U.S. Supreme Court is set to hear arguments next month as to whether such removals are legal.

In a statement to KQED, the Department of Homeland Security called both women “illegal aliens,” citing the fact that each overstayed her initial visa “in defiance of our laws.” However, neither woman appears to be unlawfully present in the U.S. Albornoz Hernández has a pending asylum application and Lawani has lawful presence under the grant of withholding of removal. Both have valid work permits issued by the government.

“I also mentioned that it would be good to look into those protocols because unfortunately they have now been really stress-tested, and that I was impressed with the level of support and cooperation,” he said.

In addition to having the resources to provide legal aid and the institutional heft to mobilize support from elected officials, Gulasekaram said universities have another advantage: a public platform to speak up on behalf of people like Lawani and Albornoz Hernández who ICE has arrested.

“[Trump administration officials] like Stephen Miller would have you believe that these removals are all directed at dangerous criminals. But these two cases are exactly the opposite: one’s a nursing professor, the other’s a student at UC Berkeley,” he said. “They’re significant contributors to American civic and economic life. And one of the things that universities can do is really showcase that.”

Most of the thousands of California immigrants arrested by ICE do not have access to the kind of resources that large institutions can bring to bear. That’s been on the mind of Fry-Bowers, who said her ethical training as a nurse and a dean at a Jesuit institution is rooted in the values of justice and human worth.

“My priority right now is Ann, but this is so much larger than Ann,” she said. “Whether it’s Ann’s case or the thousands of other cases that don’t have somebody fighting for them, they’ve been made invisible and locked away. I don’t know that there’s a greater injustice and a greater infraction toward human dignity.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Congressmen John Garamendi (CA-08) and Salud Carbajal (CA-24), two senior members of the House Armed Services Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, that it will not use ships, including training vessels or private foreign ships, for deportations.

The confirmation follows a letter the two sent to the agency demanding as much. Their demands came after The New York Times reported that DHS was considering using ships for mass deportations and identified Cal Poly Maritime Academy’s training ship, the Golden Bear, as a possible vessel.

“When Congressman Carbajal and I said that Donald Trump, Markwayne Mullin, and ICE will never use the Golden Bear or any ship for their mass deportation agenda, we meant it,” said Congressman Garamendi. “Today, I’m proud to announce the Department of Homeland Security has confirmed that it will not use any ship, including training vessels or private or foreign ships, for deportations. This isn’t the final step; we will continue to use our oversight powers to make sure Trump’s DHS keeps its word. I’m glad to stand with Congressman Carbajal on this issue, and I will continue to stand with him and every member of Congress to hold the Trump Administration to account.”

“While this commitment from DHS is a major victory for the Central Coast and congressional oversight, our work is not done. We must continue to hold the Trump Administration accountable for its extreme immigration enforcement and mass deportation agenda,” said Rep. Carbajal, the top Democrat on the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee and a Senior Member of the Armed Services Committee. “When Congressman Garamendi and I spoke out against the Trump administration’s plan to use maritime vessels—including the Cal Poly Maritime Academy’s Golden Bear—for deportations, they had no choice but to back down. This is a major win for accountability, but we cannot let up. I will continue pressing DHS for answers, closely monitoring its actions, and pushing back against policies that undermine due process and put people’s safety and rights at risk.”

Garamendi and Carbajal’s initial letter is the latest oversight action addressing President Donald Trump’s misuse of the military for his mass deportation agenda.

In December 2025, Congressman John Garamendi (D-CA-08) and U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) released a report detailing the Trump administration’s diversion of funds and resources from the Department of Defense (DoD) to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for immigration enforcement.

In January 2025, after discovering that military planes from Travis Air Force Base were used to deport undocumented immigrants, Congressman Garamendi demanded answers from the DoD. After Garamendi pushed back, DHS and the DoD later moved away from using military aircraft for deportations.

In February 2025, Garamendi demanded answers about the Trump administration’s attempt to divert much-needed medical personnel to the Guantanamo Bay detention facility. After the letter was sent, the military canceled its orders.

In May 2025, after plans were floated to turn Travis into a mass migrant detention center, Garamendi and Representative Mike Thompson (D-CA-04) pushed back. DHS later dropped its plan to turn the military base into a detention center.
