text:
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee demanded Wednesday that President Donald Trump’s sons, closest advisers, and top administration officials - including Vice President JD Vance - preserve documents and provide additional information related to what he alleges is corruption and misconduct, teeing up what is likely to be a fierce fight next year over congressional efforts to investigate Trump.

The dozen notices were issued by Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) and lay out his early investigative priorities for when Democrats take control of the House next year. Garcia is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee in the new session, and he appears to be aiming squarely at the president’s inner circle for potential probes into the Trump family’s business dealings, what he alleges are pay-to-play schemes within the Trump administration, federal immigration policy and the release of the Epstein files.

“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”

Some of the letter recipients could not immediately be reached for comment Wednesday. The Trump administration has previously disputed accusations of misconduct.

The letters come days after a federal prosecutor threatened a possible criminal investigation of Garcia, arguing that he was abusing the oversight process to target associates of the president. On Monday, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, told Garcia to preserve documents related to his “intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their constitutional rights.”

White House counsel Will Scharf issued a similar admonition to Garcia last week, accusing congressional Democrats - who began discussing possible investigations of the administration even before their wins in the midterms - of “abusive and capricious threats,” and noting that “unlawful subpoenas” could “warrant further investigation.” The White House has already sought legal opinions that could shield the Trump administration from participating in any congressional investigations.

A spokesperson for Garcia did not respond to questions about those warnings and whether he would comply with Reitz’s records retention request.

In an interview with The Washington Post last week, Garcia described Scharf’s letter as an intimidation tactic.

“We’re not going to be intimidated, and the president’s not going to stop us from investigation,” he said. “This is all political. It’s very clear.”

At the top of Garcia’s list Wednesday were the president’s sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump. In letters to them, Garcia said the committee may investigate their cryptocurrency venture World Liberty Financial, which has faced criticism for selling a major stake to Emirati investors shortly before Trump’s 2025 inauguration, among other deals.

Garcia wrote to the Trump sons that they appear to have pursued business enterprises to “personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale,” while “businesses seeking contracts or preferential treatment from your father’s Administration seem to profit from their association with you.” He ordered them to preserve relevant records.

Trump Jr. has pushed back on scrutiny of his family’s business dealings, arguing at a summit hosted by Axios on Tuesday that it was unfair to expect him to “sit in a corner, suck my thumb, and wait, you know, eight years, in this case, 12 years, until we’re out of the political game.”

Garcia also lobbed a complaint at Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and close adviser. The lawmaker said in a letter that the House Oversight Committee could look for potential conflicts of interest with investments that Kushner - who runs a private equity firm - has made across the globe as he serves as a peace negotiator for the Trump administration in the Middle East and Ukraine.

“These ​allegations ​have ​it ​exactly ​backwards. Jared ​Kushner has ​always ​acted ​in ​the ​best ​interests ​of the United States,” Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Kushner, said in a statement. “Any suggestion that he has used ​his public ​service for personal financial gain is ​categorically false.”

In interviews with The Post, Garcia has repeatedly said one of his main goals as the leader of the Oversight Committee will be investigating Trump’s use of the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in his crackdown on illegal immigration.

To that end, among those who received notices from Garcia on Wednesday was Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff and the architect of Trump’s immigration agenda. Garcia wrote to Miller asking him to preserve his communications related to his “role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending” a mass deportation campaign that Garcia called lawless and inhumane.

The Oversight Committee has led the congressional investigation into files related to the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In a letter to Vance on Wednesday, Garcia suggested that work will accelerate in the Democratic majority.

The lawmaker requested that Vance provide more information by Dec. 2 about White House Situation Room meetings he reportedly participated in last year to, Garcia writes, “undermine public interest in the Epstein files and avoid scrutiny of President Trump.”

In a comment last year to the New York Times, which first reported on the meetings, a White House spokeswoman said Trump was innocent in all matters related to Epstein and noted that the administration had released thousands of pages of documents from the files.

Garcia also demanded in a letter Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche fulfill existing requests from the committee related to the Epstein files that the lawmaker said the Justice Department has so far refused to comply with. These include sharing information about the botched release of the files under a law passed by Congress last year and the decision to transfer Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a minimum-security prison.

During his confirmation hearing this summer, Blanche defended the department’s handling of the Epstein files and said any errors in their release were unintentional and quickly fixed.

Garcia additionally signaled plans to investigate former Trump administration officials, sending letters on Wednesday to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former ambassador to Greece; former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles; and former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi L. Noem, and her former DHS senior adviser Corey Lewandowski.

The CEO for the Trust for the National Mall, Catherine Townsend, was also sent a letter Wednesday related to private donations for the White House ballroom project. Two prison officials, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Federal Prison Camp Bryan Prison Warden Tanisha Hall, were sent requests to preserve records related to the continuing Epstein investigation.

Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

Criticism from within the coalition

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

text:
During an appeals process, the Trier Administrative Court ruled that following a criminal conviction, a man from Afghanistan could be subject to deportation to his country of origin.

In a recently published judgment, judges dismissed the man's legal challenge against his deportation order upon completing his prison sentence.

The assailant was found guilty of attacking his wife with a knife, which almost cost her life.

In upholding the order, the court classified the offense as a sufficiently severe instance to establish legal grounds for the man qualifying as a "particularly serious case of public interest for expulsion" under German residence law, pointing to the extreme level of violence involved in the attack.

The city of Trier is particularly sensitive to the issue of violent crimes committed by migrants and refugees following a deadly attack in the city earlier this year, which was also perpetrated by an Afghan national.

Read Also

German court confirms removal motion against Afghan asylum seeker classed as 'extremist'

Court judgement: Afghan continues to be 'threat to society'

Citing the severity of the victim's injuries, the administrative court concluded that there remains a "considerable danger" that the man may commit further violent acts.

Moreover, the ruling noted that the underlying motive of the assault demonstrated a "misogynistic attitude" which the court said was incompatible with Germany's free and democratic basic social order.

The Trier judges said that the ruling was furthermore intended to serve as a deterrent for others, signaling that such violent crimes can result in deportation.

Read Also

Afghanistan: ICC unseals warrants against several Taliban figures for violations of women's rights

Details of criminal conviction for violent attack on wife in 2019

The original case relates to a 2019 ruling by the Trier Regional Court, in which the Afghan national was sentenced to six years in prison for causing grievous bodily harm after stabbing his wife 18 times, leaving the woman severely injured.

The court determined at that time that the attack had been motivated by jealousy, with court findings stating that the man had struggled to accept his wife's efforts to integrate more actively into German society, including attending German language courses and going to a gym.

Prior to completing his prison sentence in 2025, the immigration office in Trier issued a deportation order against the Afghan.

The man subsequently appealed the decision before the administrative court — the higher legal instance in charge of assessing instances of such challenges.

Following the latest ruling against him, the Afghan national can yet seek to appeal the Trier Administrative Court's decision at a higher court.

Read Also

Germany deports 40 Afghans amid continued criticism from rights groups

Assailant found to be unrepentant

In his appeal, the Afghan applicant argued that he should be allowed to remain in Germany on family grounds, noting that he has five children living in the country.

While the court acknowledged these ties, it ruled that protecting potential future victims and safeguarding the general public outweighed his personal interests.

The man reportedly had also refused to enter psychological therapy to come to terms with his offense while in custody.

Read Also

Five years of Taliban rule, displacement, migration, deportation and a human rights crisis

Broader context of deportations to Afghanistan

Deportations from Germany to Afghanistan however remain contentious due to the human rights situation in the country since its takeover by the Taliban in 2021.

Deportations of non-criminal Afghans remain generally suspended in Germany as part of standard asylum and migration practices.

However, on a case-by-case basis, individuals convicted of particularly serious criminal offenses and those who are classified by German security agencies as potential threats to public safety can be sent back to Afghanistan as part of growing efforts to prevent violent acts by immigrants.

text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is demanding information from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a Virginia-based construction company about a new tent immigration detention facility set to house women.

In letters released Wednesday by Hochul, two New York state agencies are pressing for information on the soft-sided facility in Batavia, New York.

The site is an addition to the Buffalo Service Processing Center, which is the largest immigration detention center in New York and currently only holds men.

According to the letters released by Hochul, the tent facility in New York is set to house up to 100 women. The detention center is being constructed by the firm Akima Infrastructure Protection amid the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.

In the letter, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and the state's Department of Health pointed to federal laws to argue that ICE failed to coordinate or conduct proper environmental consultations and public notifications before construction began.

The New York state agencies requested a response by next week to questions about facility conditions, medical care, food and construction.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In documents previously released by New York lawmakers last month, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a letter the contract supports the Buffalo area through "the expansion and provision of detention services for illegal aliens."

Mullin said in his letter that the tent facility is expected to cost about $8.7 million.

The letters released by Hochul on Wednesday follow concerns raised by lawmakers and immigrant advocates about conditions at other soft-sided facilities.

The facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," a soft-sided detention center in Florida, was closed earlier this year following lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers. When the closure was announced, Florida and ICE officials said the facility was meant to be temporary.

An inspector general report in September found that some detainees at the Florida facility were confined to small metal enclosures, presenting "significant risks" to their health and safety.

The largest immigration detention center in the U.S., Camp East Montana in Texas, is also a soft-sided facility. Human rights organizations and advocacy groups have raised concerns and have filed lawsuits alleging detainees face medical neglect, a lack of adequate food and water, and prolonged confinement in windowless tents.

"Federal oversight agencies have documented unsanitary conditions, gaps in medical services, and deficiencies with clean water access at tent immigration detention facilities in Texas and Florida," wrote the commissioners of the two New York agencies.

name: Policy
title: ICE Has $91 Billion Left for Mass Deportation. Can Congress Stop It?
description:
As of October 2026, ICE has $91 billion remaining from both reconciliation bills to spend on mass deportation between now and 2029.
Of that amount, ICE directly received $75 billion, with $29.8 billion specifically for immigration enforcement (including hiring), and another $45 billion for immigration detention.
What Can Congress Do About ICE’s Unspent $91 Billion and Other Unobligated Immigration Enforcement Funds?
Refuse Future Funding Immigration enforcement expansion usually comes with ongoing and continued annual costs.
Conclusion If Congress does not take back, restrict, or redirect these funds, ICE and CBP can keep expanding immigration enforcement in the years ahead.
text:
Overview

Just a decade ago, U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement’s annual budget was less than $6 billion. But today ICE is the highest funded U.S. law enforcement agency with over $28 billion per year at its disposal from 2025 through 2029. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 and the Secure America Act of 2026 have transformed the United States’ immigration enforcement agencies, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Border Patrol, by funding them at unprecedented levels, with nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars to spend by September 2029. This funding came with almost no reporting or other meaningful oversight and outside of the usual appropriations process that typically funds federal agencies.

While this unprecedented level of funding has driven dramatic increases in widespread and aggressive immigration enforcement nationwide, recently published federal spending data reveals that the Trump administration has not spent most of the funding from these two bills. As of October 2026, ICE has $91 billion remaining from both reconciliation bills to spend on mass deportation between now and 2029. CBP has $45.6 billion remaining from both bills.

One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025

Signed into law by President Trump in July 2025, OBBBA was a reconciliation bill — a budget bill not subject to a 60-vote filibuster in the Senate — that provided the Department of Homeland Security $170.7 billion for immigration and border enforcement activities. Of that amount, ICE directly received $75 billion, with $29.8 billion specifically for immigration enforcement (including hiring), and another $45 billion for immigration detention. This left ICE with funding roughly three times its most recent annual appropriated budget.

While ICE planned to spend most of these funds by the end of Fiscal Year 2026, the agency has billions remaining to expand its mass deportation agenda.

According to data recently published by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), as of September 30, 2026, ICE has “obligated” (committed to spending or already spent) $17.1 billion of the money it received in OBBBA—less than a quarter of its total funding. This leaves the agency with $57.6 billion of the total $75 billion it received in the OBBBA in 2025 for further increases in enforcement and detention.

CBP has committed to spending or has spent a larger proportion of its OBBBA funds. After receiving $65 billion, it has obligated $42 billion as of September 30, 2026. This means CBP has $22.6 billion in OBBBA funds remaining.

Of the money ICE has already spent, $10.5 billion (61 percent) has gone to detention facilities, $2.6 billion (15 percent) to transportation and removal operations, and another $1.9 billion (11 percent) to hiring and human resources. This has included directly purchasing at least seven detention facilities from private prison companies, hiring approximately 12,000 new ICE officers, increasing the number of deportation flights, and purchasing new surveillance technologies. These allocations underscore that the agency’s priority continues to be advancing President Trump’s mass deportation agenda with an emphasis on maximizing the number of arrests, detentions, and deportations.

ICE’s OBBBA spending plans also demonstrate that the agency intends to frontload most of its remaining OBBBA money, with plans to spend 86 percent of the money it received in 2025 between Fiscal Years 2025 and 2027. In FY 2026 alone, the agency had planned to spend $15.7 billion for constructing and expanding detention facility capacity.

While ICE’s spending plans state that the agency would spend approximately $39.9 billion in OBBBA funds in FY 2026, it had only obligated $17.1 billion by the end of the fiscal year. This means that, while ICE is not spending the funds as quickly as it had planned, it still has tens of billions of dollars it can use to expand immigration enforcement and detention into the last two years of the Trump administration.

Secure America Act of 2026

Signed into law in June 2026, the Secure America Act used the congressional reconciliation process to fund ICE and parts of U.S. Customs and Border Protection due to a Congressional impasse in the annual appropriations process. In total, the bill provided $69.5 billion through September 30, 2029. This adds to the $170.7 billion DHS already received in OBBBA, which also lasts through September 2029. Like the OBBBA, the Secure America Act gives immigration enforcement agencies an unprecedented level of funding, with no meaningful reporting requirements or other oversight measures.

The Secure America Act was drafted to provide ICE and CBP funding even if Congress failed to pass an appropriations bill for DHS, as happened for FY 2026. As a result, if Congress fails to provide any regular appropriations for ICE and CBP in future years, the Secure America Act will make up for that loss of funding. However, should Congress pass any regular appropriations bill for ICE or CBP in FY 2027 through 2029, the Secure America Act funding would still be available.

As of September 30, 2026, budget documents published by OMB indicate that ICE has used very little of these Secure America Act funds, with $33.4 billion remaining. Most of what it has spent has gone to personnel and operational costs. Similarly, of the $26 billion provided to CBP in the bill, $23 billion remain. Currently, neither ICE nor CBP has released a spending plan to show how they plan to use this money.

What Can Congress Do About ICE’s Unspent $91 Billion and Other Unobligated Immigration Enforcement Funds?

Congress cannot “cancel” money that has already been spent alone. While it has several tools to rescind, freeze, or redirect immigration enforcement funding, all these tools would also require President Trump to sign new legislation, which is unlikely given his support of the prior reconciliation funding. These options may also depend on whether the money has already been obligated or spent.

However, Congress can also refuse to provide additional annual appropriations to these agencies and conduct robust hearings and oversight of the ways they are currently spending reconciliation dollars.

Congress can substantially reduce ICE’s ability to use remaining funds through several mechanisms:

Rescissions

Congress can pass a rescission bill canceling unobligated balances. In other words, any funding not yet legally committed to detention or surveillance contracts, hiring, or operations, could be rescinded. In the past, Congress has used rescissions to take back previously appropriated funds; for example, after Congress provided roughly $80 billion to the Internal Revenue Service in 2022 to increase tax enforcement, bills passed in 2024 and 2025 rescinded over $41 billion of that funding.

A future Congress with sufficient votes could do something similar and target specific ICE hiring, detention, transportation, surveillance, or infrastructure accounts. In practice, this is the cleanest method for recovering billions of unspent dollars. However, a rescission bill does require a final signature by the president and could be subject to a veto. Therefore, the success of any rescission bill likely rests on the ability of Congress to attach the rescission to another must-pass bill.

Annual Appropriations Riders

Even if money remains available to the immigration enforcement agencies from OBBBA and the Secure America Act, Congress can attach limitations in DHS appropriations bills that apply to the dollars the agency received through those prior reconciliation bills. For example, it could prohibit the use of funds for new detention contracts, cap detention capacity to a set number of beds, prohibit hiring beyond current staffing levels, prevent use of funds for certain types of enforcement operations, and restrict transfers between accounts so that Congress can assert more control over how and where the agencies obligate dollars. This process does not reduce funding, but it can limit its use and scope.

Repeal or Amend the Original Bills

Congress could enact new legislation repealing portions of the OBBBA and Secure America Act. For example, it could terminate multi-year funding authorities, reduce agency staffing levels, eliminate entire enforcement programs, and convert mandatory funding into discretionary funding through annual appropriations. However, legislation of this nature would be challenging politically as it requires entirely new legislation outside the reconciliation funding process and would require both 60 Senate votes to avoid a filibuster and a signature by the president.

Refuse Future Funding

Immigration enforcement expansion usually comes with ongoing and continued annual costs. Congress could use its power of the purse via the appropriations process to halt future appropriations for the immigration enforcement agencies as it did in FY 2026. This would mean halting future funding for detention operations, additional hiring, and reducing or zeroing out transportation and removal operation budgets. While this would not recover ICE’s unobligated dollars, it could shrink enforcement capacity over time.

Oversight and Investigations

Congress can use its oversight powers to slow or halt the expansion of the immigration enforcement system. Congressional committees with jurisdiction over the federal immigration enforcement agencies can require expenditure plans, hold investigative hearings on money spent, demand audits by the Government Accountability Office, investigate contracting and procurement practices, and even condition future funding on oversight compliance requirements. Aggressive and consistent oversight could significantly delay major expansions or expenditures from the agencies.

Given that Congress structured much of the recent reconciliation funding as mandatory spending available over multiple years, a new Congress would likely need either a rescission package targeting unobligated balances, a new reconciliation bill reducing mandatory funding, and/or appropriations restrictions that prevent expenditures of remaining funds.

Conclusion

If Congress does not take back, restrict, or redirect these funds, ICE and CBP can keep expanding immigration enforcement in the years ahead. With ICE still holding tens of billions of dollars through September 2029, we can expect more detention facility construction and purchases, including additional facilities bought directly from private prison companies, and more people held in detention. We can also expect continued hiring beyond the approximately 12,000 new officers already brought on, more deportation flights and removal operations, and expanded surveillance technologies. Taken together, these investments could drive more arrests, detentions, and deportations nationwide.

text:
The 2026 Midterm Elections resulted in a sweeping victory for the Democratic Party, with Democrats projected to hold a significant majority in both the House and Senate beginning in 2027. A “blue wave” has seen resounding Democratic victories across the country, as Democrats won by significant margins even in states and districts that have strongly supported Republicans in recent election cycles, including Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, and Mississippi.

In response to the historic losses suffered, members of the Trump administration and Republican leaders were vocal in expressing where blame should fall. Many have drawn attention to the U.S. conflict in Iran and its impact on the economy as driving factors in alienating the working class from the GOP.

Vice President J.D. Vance posted a detailed response to the midterm results on X emphasizing the impact of the Iran War. He said bluntly, “The reason we lost is the war.” He added, “To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be.” Senator Ted Cruz echoed Vance’s sentiments, saying, “Tariffs have made everything too expensive and the Iran war has dragged on too long.” Cruz continued, “It should have been brief, decisive and over. It needs to end.”

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis was among the most vocal Republican leaders during the midterm cycle, and he joined other party leaders in emphasizing the impact of the Iran war. DeSantis said, “We just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact.”

With Republicans vocally opposing Trump’s actions in Iran, the Trump administration—in response to the midterms—has experienced some inner turmoil with several high-profile resignations. The resignation of Chief of Staff Susie Wiles headlined a list of departures from the administration that included White House Deputy Chief of Staff Richard Walters, Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, and Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon.

President Trump announced that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles would be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump ally and an architect of the administration’s immigration policy. Trump commented on Miller’s appointment, saying, “I wanted to make a change. I think Susie’s done a very good job, great job, but I just wanted to make it. Stephen’s been great. And we have got to make moves.”

With Democrats set to have control over the legislature for the rest of Trump’s term, Miller’s appointment is seen by many as the elevation of a trusted advisor who can help advance the administration’s agenda in key areas without congressional approval. These areas of focus include policy on immigration, tariffs, federal spending, and housing costs.

In an interview with Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes,” President Trump expressed his thoughts on the midterm results and provided more details regarding the administration’s next steps.

When asked for his political analysis of the results, Trump said, “Well, number one, I was not on the ballot … I think if I was on the ballot, it would’ve been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love [voters had for me].” He also acknowledged the grievances of voters, saying, “There seems to be a dislike for Israel. So you have that. You have the war itself. You have the gas prices. And I think those are the primary reasons.”

Trump also reflected on the impact of his administration’s immigration policy, and how it might change going forward. He said, “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Notre Dame students commented on the results of the midterm elections and what they believe the next steps for the Republican Party should be.

In an interview with the Rover, a Notre Dame graduate student attributed the results of the midterms to a “crisis of confidence in the Republican Party because of the failure of the administration and Congress to deliver on their campaign promises of no new wars and mass deportations.” He added, “The older generation appears to be losing their grip, while younger generations are beginning to feel their electoral power.”

Ethan Simmons, a sophomore from Knott Hall, told the Rover, “I do not wish that our Congress and electorate migrate leftward, but the failures of our present administration to fulfill its promises of mass deportations, exposure of corruption, and abstention from international conflict do necessitate a transformation of the Republican Party that can only happen as a consequence of these elections.”

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Bexar County commissioners passed a new resolution Tuesday signaling further opposition to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement presence in South Texas, though it wasn’t clear if any concrete action might come of it.

The mostly Democratic members of the court had already passed a resolution in March voicing opposition to the plan to turn an East Side warehouse off Loop 410 into an ICE processing facility.

Tuesday’s resolution, though, specifically mentions opposition to other federal leases and contracts: leases at Brooks for “the purpose of immigration-related legal offices and hearings,” an ICE lease of a building in the 3500 block of Crosspoint, and a $382 million contract with the private security company hired to renovate the East Side warehouse to also transport ICE detainees throughout Texas.

The resolution appeared to piggyback off the City of San Antonio’s federal lawsuit over the planned warehouse conversion, which the city claimed had apparently skipped over an environmental review process required under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The city confirmed last week it was in discussions with the federal government about a deal to pause the warehouse project while environmental reviews are conducted. However, there hasn’t been any word since then about a deal being finalized.

The resolution states support for the city’s legal actions and “demands Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) and all information and alternatives proposed from relative federal authorities on federal immigration enforcement initiatives in Bexar County.”

Precinct 4 Commissioner Tommy Calvert, who represents the area around the East Side warehouse, pushed for the resolution, which he said was “very similar” to the one commissioners passed in March.

“It just outlines other facilities that may not have gone through the NEPA process and puts our opposition on record,” Calvert said.

Larry Roberson, the civil division chief for the Bexar County District Attorney’s Office, said the city attorney’s office is “really great” at keeping county legal staff involved “and knowing how we can help and when we can help.”

He also confirmed with Calvert the intention would be for him to return to commissioners court before pursuing anything on the county side.

Calvert told KSAT, “I can’t comment at this time” when asked if the resolution to the county actually filing something in court.

Precinct 3 Commissioner Grant Moody, the lone Republican on the commissioners court, was the lone vote against Tuesday’s resolution, as he was against the one in March.

text:
The Trump administration is being sued over a new federal housing rule that could force some U.S. citizens living in mixed-status families to choose between losing housing assistance and living apart from relatives who are not eligible for the aid.

The lawsuit challenges a Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule published November 12 that changes how citizenship and immigration status are verified for people living in federally assisted housing. The rule is scheduled to take effect December 14. The plaintiffs are asking a judge to postpone that date and block enforcement of the rule in the Central District of California while the case proceeds.

Public Counsel, Kendall Brill & Kelly LLP and Bird Marella LLP filed the lawsuit on Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California against the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and HUD Secretary Scott Turner. The plaintiffs are three Los Angeles County residents and two tenant organizations, People Organized for Westside Renewal, or POWER, and Union de Vecinos.

Read More on News

For decades, mixed-status families have been allowed to live together in federally assisted housing, with assistance based only on family members who qualify. HUD has also allowed other household members to decline to claim eligible immigration status under a provision known as "do not contend."

The new rule eliminates that option and expands verification requirements. It generally requires family members to establish U.S. citizenship or an eligible immigration status. Plaintiffs argue the change will effectively end ongoing prorated assistance for many mixed-status households, leaving families with the choice of separating or losing their housing assistance.

"No family should have to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads. Yet HUD’s rule would force precisely that choice on families across the country, including U.S. citizen children who could lose their homes because of their parents’ immigration status. Congress did not require this. HUD chose it," Amanda Mangaser Savage, strategic litigation counsel at Public Counsel, told Newsweek.

Newsweek has contacted HUD for comment via email outside of office hours.

The HUD rule is one of several moves by the Trump administration to tighten immigrants' access to government assistance and expand the potential immigration consequences of using public benefits. The administration has implemented the public charge rule, giving immigration officers greater discretion to consider benefits including Medicaid, food stamps, and housing assistance when reviewing some green card applications. The changes have come alongside increased immigration enforcement and a campaign encouraging people in the country illegally to self-deport.

About 79,300 people, including roughly 36,000 eligible children, live in mixed-status households receiving HUD assistance, according to HUD figures cited in the lawsuit.

HUD estimated that maintaining the same level of housing assistance under the rule would require an additional $311 million to $385 million, according to the court filings.

“This new HUD rule would push thousands of mixed-status families, including U.S. citizen children, out of their homes,” David Alpert, Kendall Brill & Kelly LLP attorney, said in a statement shared with Newsweek. “Our clients are among them."

One plaintiff, identified as M.R., is a U.S. citizen with cerebral palsy who has lived in public housing since age 1 and relies on his family for support. His parents and sister, a DACA recipient, cannot establish HUD-eligible immigration status, according to the complaint. The lawsuit says the family could lose its home or M.R. could be separated from relatives who help care for him.

A second plaintiff, J.L., lives with a mother, stepfather and two brothers. J.L. and the brothers are U.S. citizens, while the parents do not have HUD-eligible immigration status, according to the filing. The family has lived in public housing for about 15 years and similarly faces losing assistance or separating if the rule takes effect, the complaint says.

Families that continue allowing an ineligible household member to live in the home could also lose housing assistance for at least two years under the rule. The rule also requires housing authorities and certain property owners to report household members they determine are unlawfully in the country to the Department of Homeland Security.

The case could have particular consequences in Los Angeles, where the plaintiffs live and the two organizations operate. The complaint cites a shortage of about 486,000 affordable homes for lower-income renters in Los Angeles County and a homeless population of about 73,040. It says the fair market rent for a two-bedroom apartment is $2,964 a month and estimates a household would need to earn $57 an hour to afford that rent without becoming rent-burdened.

“Los Angeles is home to some of our nation’s largest populations of mixed-status families, and the HUD rule would disproportionately threaten our most vulnerable communities—especially children—by putting their housing stability at risk simply because of their parents' immigration status,” Alexander H. Tran, counsel at Bird Marella, said in a statement.

The lawsuit argues that HUD exceeded its authority and violated federal housing law and the Constitution. The plaintiffs say Congress intended to allow eligible members of mixed-status families to receive reduced assistance and that HUD failed to adequately consider the risks of displacement, family separation and homelessness.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to block the rule before it takes effect on December 14 and ultimately declare it unlawful and set it aside.

text:
WASHINGTON -

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is set to appear Wednesday at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game as travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.

The hearing in front of the House Homeland Security Committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats. But it comes as the U.S. has faced a series of cyber and technology problems that have left Americans feeling vulnerable.

The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm drubbing of Republicans to grill the Cabinet official who is key to President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda. Two others expected to face questioning are FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.

Here is a look at likely topics at the hearing:

Mullin is likely to be asked about the ground stop and cyber threats

Mullin, whose department includes the agency tasked with protecting the country’s cyber infrastructure, was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

During a news conference Friday with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at the White House, he pushed for more funding for the aging air traffic control system while also assuring the public that the government was not seeing any signs of a deliberate cyberattack.

The Trump administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

But there also has been a string of other technology issues across other government agencies and private companies that have rattled Americans.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft suffered an outage that lasted for hours, severely impacting services, including Outlook, Teams and artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. The company said it was due to a technical issue that arose during an upgrade.

The banking giant Chase and the airline carrier United both experienced technology outages, while an internal network used by the National Security Agency to communicate classified information went offline Tuesday after what the agency described as routine maintenance.

During an interview Monday on Fox News Channel, Mullin, a former senator from Oklahoma, again sought to reassure Americans after the string of cyber problems, saying he could say with “98%” certainty that they weren’t the result of a cyberattack.

But Mullin could face questions about an agency that falls under his department’s purview that is supposed to play a central role in the federal government’s response to cyber incidents. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

But CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick to lead the agency withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it languished for months in the Senate.

CISA also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the federal government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

The secretary has faced scrutiny over his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday to watch the LSU-Texas game.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

Mullin said during an interview on CNBC that the airways had been open for 21 hours by the time his flight took off.

“We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time,” Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Mullin, whose department includes Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, will likely also face questioning over the Republican president’s immigration agenda at a time when Democrats are vowing rigorous oversight of everything from immigration detention contracts to the use of force by ICE officers.

Trump has indicated he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions over how easily compromise could be reached on the issue.

Mullin took over from ousted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March after the killing of two American citizen protesters in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

The suit cites reporting by CT Insider columnist Dan Haar about the June 4 raid.

"A free society can’t tolerate secret police who illegally hide who they are and what they do as they terrorize communities and rip apart families," Lentini said in a statement. "The law is clear that public records belong to everyone. Serious questions have been raised about ICE’s activities, and we deserve answers, not more examples of how lawless these agencies have become under Donald Trump.

"My questions are simple: Who bought these patches, who authorized their use, and what are the rules for DHS agents pretending to be press? It shouldn’t take a federal lawsuit to get answers," the statement said. "A law-abiding agency shouldn’t have any problem answering them, but, unfortunately, this is ICE."

It's unclear what organization the men wearing "MEDIA" patches were with. An ICE spokesperson told Haar at the time that, "ICE does not reveal the identities of third party media, or ERO officers embedded on operations," referring to ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations.

Instances in which members of federal law enforcement posed as members of the news media have drawn criticism, out of concern that it could threaten the trust placed in journalists.

In a 2007 operation, an FBI agent posed as an Associated Press journalist to help identify a teen hacker sending bomb threats to his high school in Washington. The ruse came to light years later, prompting the AP to file a lawsuit and a review by the Justice Department's inspector general.

"Impersonating the media is an extreme move used only in edge cases, like undercover operations where the subterfuge is absolutely necessary. Even then, DOJ and FBI, by policy, require each instance to be approved by senior leadership after an extensive review, calling it a 'sensitive circumstance,'" Lentini's lawyer, Kel McClanahan, said.

The lawsuit, which was filed last week and names Lentini as plaintiff, stems from FOIA requests that he filed with ICE, the DHS privacy office and Customs and Border Patrol on July 13.

Lentini is listed as a lawyer on the case along with McClanahan.

The suit said the "relatively narrow" FOIA requests were to determine whether the individuals seen during the Danbury raid "may have been ICE agents mislabeling themselves as members of the media." It said the requests also were intended to learn whether the Homeland Security agencies involved in immigration enforcement "had developed policies or taken other steps to further a practice of agency personnel mislabeling themselves as members of the media."

Lentini's FOIA request asked for any "multimedia agreement" between DHS or any of its agencies and any multimedia production company in effect on the day of the raid in Danbury, the lawsuit said. The request also asked for information on any DHS purchases of "Velcro patches" reading "MEDIA" or "PRESS;" records showing when ICE, CBP or other DHS personnel can identify themselves as media or press; and "records about or referencing the use of vest patches labeled 'MEDIA' or 'PRESS' by ICE agents, CBP agents, or other DHS personnel," the suit said.

The lawsuit says ICE failed to acknowledge the request for 42 days, then sent a notice saying the request “does not reasonably describe the records sought in a way that allows ICE to conduct a focused and reasonable search.”

The suit said Customs and Border Patrol acknowledged Lentini's request on July 15 and sent a message saying the records he sought were not under the agency's purview. The agency administratively closed the request, the lawsuit said. Lentini filed an appeal, which the lawsuit said CBP has not acknowledged.

The lawsuit said DHS acknowledged receiving Lentini's request, but did not respond further.

The suit asks the court to order the agencies to release the requested records at no charge.

text:
London, United Kingdom – The seven asylum seekers were on the runway, their plane bound for Rwanda from a military airport in southern England.

It was mid-June 2022.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded in Uganda

list 2 of 3Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda

list 3 of 3Why are five EU countries reviving plans to deport migrants to Rwanda?

end of list

They were being sent thousands of kilometres away to a country they had never visited and with little idea of what awaited them.

But after much legal wrangling, a ruling from the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) stopped their deportation minutes before the flight was due to take off.

British immigration lawyer Alasdair Mackenzie, who was involved in the case, said the people being deported – among them Iranians, Iraqis, an Albanian and a Vietnamese citizen – were terrified.

“A lot of them were in an absolutely desperate state,” he told Al Jazeera. “They felt terrified as they were going to a place they didn’t know, being shunted around like packages. Rwanda is a very repressive country. There were concerns that asylum seekers would not be able to speak up or protest about their conditions.”

Four years later, European governments are preparing to revive the idea.

Germany, Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands announced plans on Monday to establish a deportation centre in Rwanda for people whose asylum claims have been rejected. The proposal is part of a wider European push to increase removals by transferring rejected asylum seekers to “return hubs” in countries with which they have no previous connection.

Rwanda has pledged independent monitoring and the involvement of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. It has also pushed back against concerns from rights groups. On Tuesday, after 47 organisations decried the proposal and warned that Rwanda does not respect international human rights standards, Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said: “Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country.”

Rwandan investigative journalist Samuel Baker Byansi, who now lives in an undisclosed location in Europe, said of the new plans: “This partnership buys their silence.”

In 2022, Byansi was investigating Rwanda’s suspected military activities in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his colleague John Williams Ntwali. He said he received warnings that they both could be arrested or killed.

“I received a tip from credible sources that me and my colleagues would be subject of arrest or elimination. I had a way to leave the country, so I did. John died months later,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ntwali officially died in a reported road accident, but Byansi and human rights monitors have questioned the circumstances surrounding his death.

Byansi fears the migration deal will give the Rwandan government another way to deflect international scrutiny.

President Paul “Kagame puts Western governments in a position where they cannot hold him accountable.”

Kagame, Rwanda’s leader since 2000, has been praised for overseeing the country’s economic transformation after the 1994 genocide. But his government faces persistent accusations of repression.

The UN and other organisations have repeatedly accused Rwanda of supporting the armed group M23 in its war in the eastern DRC. In October, the United States announced sanctions against Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence over its “destabilising activities”.

In October, a prominent critic of the Rwandan government was found decapitated outside the Ugandan capital, Kampala.

Amnesty warns of ‘real danger’

Amnesty International argued that transferring asylum seekers and migrants to a country with such a record risks leaving them with little protection or ability to challenge their treatment.

“Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible, and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” the rights group said.

Some are concerned about the potential to monitor the treatment of people after they are deported.

Tineke Strik, a Dutch member of the European Parliament, visited Rwanda in September to inspect facilities in Kigali that could be used to house Europe’s rejected asylum seekers.

Rwandan officials presented the proposal as a mutually beneficial arrangement, telling her the people who arrive could remain in the country and eventually receive residency or citizenship.

“The authorities were pitching the scheme as a win-win,” Strik told Al Jazeera. “… But it was not possible for us to verify their claims as there are no [domestic] NGOs expressing criticism.”

Strik also tried to establish the whereabouts and wellbeing of people recently deported to Rwanda by United States President Donald Trump’s administration but was unable to obtain details.

“It made me convinced how impossible it will be for European governments to check on what is happening over there.”

Rwanda has previously been used as a destination for deported asylum seekers. From 2013 to 2018, Israel sent thousands of Eritrean and Sudanese citizens to the country. Many reportedly subsequently left Rwanda or were deported elsewhere.

The United Kingdom’s proposed arrangement with Kigali in 2022 accumulated estimated costs of $940m but resulted in just four voluntary transfers before the Supreme Court ruled it unlawful. The Labour government abandoned it in 2024, the same year the party won a general election and returned to power.

The European proposals would apply to people whose asylum claims have been rejected, rather than potentially all unauthorised arrivals.

But lawyers involved in the earlier British scheme remain concerned about the consequences of sending people to a country where they may struggle to challenge their treatment.

In 2018, Rwandan police fired on several Congolese refugees protesting against food cuts in the country’s west. Twelve died in an incident that has added to concerns about the protection available to vulnerable refugees and migrants already living there.

Kigali has nevertheless defended its role as a potential destination for deported asylum seekers and migrants.

Rwanda hosts large numbers of refugees, predominantly from neighbouring DRC and Burundi. Interior Minister Biruta described Rwanda’s policies as “progressive” because they allow people to work and launch businesses.

Dissent from Spain’s Sanchez to a Dutch politician: Deal ‘will not work’

The proposals have also exposed divisions within Europe over how far governments should go to deter irregular migration.

While Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner defended the initiative as “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the scheme has no “future or humanity”. French President Emmanuel Macron questioned the idea in June. “I’m not sure that these are the fundamental principles on which our Europe was built, and I don’t believe it’s effective either,” he said.

Asylum applications in the European Union lodged in the first half of 2026 fell by 17 percent compared with the same period a year earlier, reaching their lowest level since 2021.

“Europe could invest much more in establishing a smoother cooperation with countries of origin,” Strik said. Return hubs are expensive, apply to few people, carry a high reputational risk “and will not work”, she said.

Further details of the Rwanda scheme are expected in early 2027, and an initial pilot project at this point is expected to involve about 100 people.

Aside from the human rights concerns, Mackenzie, the immigration lawyer, questioned the theory that return hubs would act as a deterrent.

“People don’t set off and cover thousands of miles across land and sea with the expectation that they are going to be sent back. To the extent that they are aware of these policies, they are prepared to take the risk because the economic or political conditions in their home countries are so dire.”

text:
A gavel rests on a block atop a judge’s bench in an empty courtroom. Photo: Shopify Partners / Burst

(The Center Square) — New Jersey is taking the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to federal court, claiming it has refused to turn over information about immigrants being held at its Delaney Hall ICE detention facility.

The lawsuit , filed in U.S. District Court Tuesday by Attorney General Jennifer Devenport, alleges that DHS and The GEO Group, Inc. — a private company that operates the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility — have failed to respond to subpoenas seeking information about the treatment of detainees.

In a lawsuit, Davenport accused GEO Group and DHS of "stonewalling" the state's investigation "into a serious and troubling pattern of alleged civil rights violations" in the privately run facility.

"Despite being a private corporation doing business in New Jersey and operating Delaney Hall on property it owns within New Jersey, GEO Group refused to comply with the subpoena, claiming that it would need authorization from DHS under DHS’s internal housekeeping regulation," Davenport, a Democrat, wrote in the 31-page complaint.

GEO Group declined to comment on the lawsuit, referring to questions about the legal challenge to Homeland Security. A DHS spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Homeland Security has repeatedly rejected claims by New Jersey officials and advocacy groups that migrants are being mistreated in the facility and in a previous statement said ICE "is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments."

Delaney Hall has become the latest flashpoint in opposition to President Donald Trump's crackdown on immigration since a group of detainees allegedly went on a hunger strike to protest conditions inside the facility.

The privately-run 1,000-bed facility was rocked by protests earlier this year with often violent clashes between protestors and ICE agents, prompting criticism from the Trump administration. Dozens were arrested by federal, state and local police, including Newark Mayor Ras Baraka.

Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill has repeatedly called on ICE to shut down the facility, citing a lack of access to the facility during a recent visit and the deaths of at least three detainees over the past year.

title: Immigrants have generated a fiscal surplus in the United States for the past 124 years
description:
Of the $14.6 trillion in immigrant fiscal surplus, 86 percent has accrued since 1965 and the creation of the modern Great Society welfare state,” says the study.
A better policy would be based on the premise that immigrants bring fiscal and economic benefits to the country, the study says.
Congress should return to the presumption of openness and reauthorize peaceful immigrants to come to the United States legally,” the authors argue.
In 2023, immigrants had an employment rate —the share of people employed relative to the population— 14 percentage points higher than that of U.S.-born Americans.
By contrast, between 1994 and 2023 immigrants used between 18% and 25% fewer benefits.
text:
One of the most frequently used arguments by the Donald Trump Administration to justify its campaign against migrants is that they take advantage of public funds, harming Americans. Multiple studies have shown the opposite. The most recent one, published Tuesday by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank in Washington, D.C., finds that immigrants have a net positive impact on the U.S. economy. “Immigrants have paid more in taxes to every level of government than they have received in government benefits every year since 1900,” states David J. Bier, one of the co-authors.

According to the study, immigrants have reduced federal, state, and local government deficits every year for the last 124 years by a cumulative $14.6 trillion. As a share of gross domestic product (GDP), the immigrant surplus was more than twice as fiscally beneficial in 2023 as in 1913, before the modern welfare state and individual federal income tax, reads the report.

“In real inflation-adjusted terms, the immigrant surplus in 2023 was more than 53 times larger than in 1913: $585 billion versus $11 billion. Of the $14.6 trillion in immigrant fiscal surplus, 86 percent has accrued since 1965 and the creation of the modern Great Society welfare state,” says the study.

Titled “Immigrants’ Historical Effects on Government Budgets: 1900–2023,” the paper attempts to calculate allocations of government spending to immigrants and natives for each year of the 20th century to show how this fiscal benefit has changed over time, notes Bier. The study concludes that immigration has never been as positive, both fiscally and economically, as it is today.

The analysis highlights that the biggest difference from past eras is that today’s migrants are much more productive —and therefore pay more taxes per capita— than those in 1913, producing a larger net fiscal surplus. “When immigrants come to America and work, they help make the country a wealthier and more prosperous place. Congress should reform outdated laws that restrict immigration based on the false premise that immigrants are economically harmful,” the authors David Bier and Julián Salazar say.

Passing reform of a broken immigration system is one of the issues the new Congress resulting from the November 3 midterm elections will face. When it is sworn in on January 3, Democrats will hold majorities in both chambers. In the days after the midterms, several Democratic lawmakers voiced support for using that majority to pass a pathway to legalize undocumented migrants who have been living and working in the U.S. for years.

Since Trump returned to the White House, many of these workers have lost their legal resident status and have been targeted in arrests and deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The administration blames undocumented migrants for straining public finances, but in reality these workers pay taxes and cannot access any federal benefits.

Since 1776, some 130 million immigrants have arrived in the United States. According to the research, many people believe that while immigration benefited the country in the past, the welfare state has removed —or at least reduced— that benefit because of the cost of government services and payments to immigrants.

However, although public spending has grown over the years, it has not reduced the fiscal benefit migrants provide, because tax revenues have grown as well. In the early 20th century the government established new taxes —including income taxes and Social Security contributions— that have offset the increase in welfare spending over the last century.

In 2023, fewer than 4% of applicants for legal permanent resident cards (the green card) were approved. A better policy would be based on the premise that immigrants bring fiscal and economic benefits to the country, the study says. “Prior to 1921, more than 98% of immigrant applicants were approved to receive permanent residence. That system better reflected American traditions and economic reality. Congress should return to the presumption of openness and reauthorize peaceful immigrants to come to the United States legally,” the authors argue.

They work more and earn less

Migrants earn lower hourly wages, but generate higher total income per capita than natives because, for more than a century, they have been more likely to work. In 2023, immigrants had an employment rate —the share of people employed relative to the population— 14 percentage points higher than that of U.S.-born Americans. The share of the immigrant population in its prime working years is typically higher than that of the U.S.-born population. In almost every year of the 20th century and the early 21st, the average immigrant paid more in taxes than the average U.S.-born person. By contrast, between 1994 and 2023 immigrants used between 18% and 25% fewer benefits.

Bier and Salazar contradict Milton Friedman, who said that “free immigration was a good thing before 1914, and free immigration is a bad thing today.” “Milton Friedman failed to consider that the worse the fiscal situation of the United States, the more beneficial new immigrants become.,” they say in response to the famed economist.

title: “We Remain In This Nightmare”: Another Letter From the Hell of ICE Detention | The Nation
authors: smccroskey, Robert Hunt, Sara Bennett, Maryam Tahmasebi, Tobita Chow, Janos Marton, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com
description:
And, while there are many horrors in this life of detention, the warping of time has felt especially cruel.
I, too, have been violently cut off from my life outside these detention walls.
I am acutely aware of the pain that children are experiencing in this prison of family detention.
Taking it away, to me, is one of the many unforgivable sins committed towards children in detention.
Change will require laws that prevent the government from stripping people of their lawful immigration status without meaningful due process and that establish meaningful judicial oversight of immigration detention.
text:
How do you keep track of time when it does not move linearly—when days last forever and decades seem to go by in a flash?

I used to think about this as a child. Waiting all day for the hour of cartoons I could watch on TV felt endless, but entire summers were over in the blink of an eye.

These days, I’m feeling the nonlinear passage of time—but for very different reasons.

It is now over seven months since my son, my husband, and I were detained and locked in ICE detention, despite having no criminal records, settled immigration status with valid permanent residency, and no charges of any personal misconduct. (You can read more details about our case in the piece I wrote for The Nation in August.) My son and I are still detained in the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, while my husband remains separated from us, detained in the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall. And, while there are many horrors in this life of detention, the warping of time has felt especially cruel.

Over seven months. Two hundred and twenty days. Over half a year. Every one of them lived, endured, and marked by harm. In whatever scale I put these numbers, they feel surreal and terrifying. This has been, without doubt, the longest traumatic experience of our lives, and it has felt like an eternity—more than seven months of absolute hell.

Every day I think about my kind, soulful son’s childhood slipping through his fingers. I think about the months of his precious life that his father has missed. Teenage years are full of growth and new experiences, but for the last seven months, my son—a minor who has done absolutely nothing wrong—has been denied that most basic right: the right for a child to have a normal, happy life. He spent his birthday in this horrible place. He has been robbed of the high-school experiences that his friends are having. And he has been separated from his father for over half a year.

I, too, have been violently cut off from my life outside these detention walls. I taught hundreds of undergraduate students and dozens of graduate students every semester. I miss teaching even more than I miss wearing normal clothes or reading books on my phone. I haven’t been able to teach any of my undergraduate classes or my graduate courses for two semesters now. I still don’t know what happened to one of my PhD candidates, who was very close to defending her proposal. My husband has been similarly torn from his own professional academic world.

If you are wondering whether daily life here becomes normal or tolerable, the answer is no. It absolutely does not. There is not a single day that goes by that I don’t have to take a deep breath just to force myself to keep breathing. There is not a single day that I don’t rage, or that I don’t miss my husband—who can only hear our voices once every two weeks for 10 minutes. Not a single day that I don’t need to force my face into submission so as not to let my son know how I truly feel.

Yet, along with the pain, there is resolve. I am a trauma-informed psychologist. This place or the circumstances can’t take that away from me. Every day, I put on my community psychologist hat and do everything in my power, using all the tools in my toolbox, to help other families. To find ways to witness, observe, and break down the incompetent, cruel systems and the dehumanizing policies around us. To help the community that I now live within. Every day, I am also sustained by my extraordinary friends who hold my grief, hold space for my anger, and never leave me alone.

Hanging over this nightmare is one still-unanswered question: why? Who has benefited from this cruelty? Who has profited from the baseless accusations still being hurled around about me and my family? What has been gained by decimating the normal lives of two educators and their child?

And we are far from alone. I am acutely aware of the pain that children are experiencing in this prison of family detention. I see the devastation in their eyes every single day—the sadness, the fear, the distrust, the defeat.

It feels like being stabbed in the heart again and again. But even with horrors abundant and repeating every day, there are instances that stay with you for far longer and cut far deeper than you expected. One happened recently in the so-called “library.” There was a child who looked to be around 5 years old. His mother was trying to write a letter. But she kept being interrupted by her child asking, over and over again, when they were going back home.

The pain I felt in that moment stayed with me for many days. Home. Such a simple, unattainable concept for many. For children, it is a foundational part of their psychological development. It is the cornerstone of their sense of safety and belonging. Taking it away, to me, is one of the many unforgivable sins committed towards children in detention. The mother said nothing in response to the child’s pleas. I know why she kept her face blank and kept typing. What do you even say? How do you explain to a 5-year-old that home is most likely never going to be the same—that there is no going back?

Ad Policy

After I wrote my Nation piece in August, I received so many kind responses from people of conscience who heard my plea and responded by reaching a hand out and amplifying our voices. Now I am writing this just under a week after the midterm elections—and, once again, I have been heartened. It was beautiful to see that, across the country, people voiced their disdain for the horrible ICE practices that led to the imprisonment of me, my family, and everyone else detained with us. It was inspiring to see so many people across the country express their opposition to the dehumanization and brutalization of law-abiding people, including lawful permanent residents.

But we are all still here, locked away. The murky immigration laws that allowed all of this to happen are still on the books. We all remain in this nightmare. My family and I are still experiencing unending, unendurable misery created by lies and smear campaigns and executed by a system that we have no power to fight against. What I dream of these days is the same dream I have had all through this ordeal: freedom for my family and a normal, safe life where my child can go to school, and my husband and I can go back to writing and teaching. This, however, is not only about me and my family. I am here with so many other people, and nothing in our day-to-day lives has changed. Nor will it if the pressure stops. No one can go home now and think that we are done because of an election. We are nowhere near the finish line.

Change will require laws that prevent the government from stripping people of their lawful immigration status without meaningful due process and that establish meaningful judicial oversight of immigration detention. It will happen when there are clear laws that prohibit the detention of children and separation of families, ending the horrific trauma inflicted upon thousands of people with zero criminal background every day. Shutting down one detention center, such as Dilley, without changing the laws only means families are being separated and tormented in a different place. No elected official can kick this trauma out of their backyard thinking it will go away. As long as the root cause is not addressed, this can happen in any state or any city, and it can be far worse. The collective psyche can’t hide from this.

There is so much work that needs to be done to repair the broken systems that made these atrocities possible. There is so much work that needs to be done to create better policies that prevent a repeat of any of this. While hope is now possible, healing demands far more than that. Healing sometimes needs opening the wounds and bearing the hurt of looking closely at what has happened. Healing needs us to mourn what we have lost collectively and demands commitment to the healing process.

The scale of damage is vast. The state of our immigration policies is an open wound that we can no longer afford to ignore. This is not pain experienced only by immigrant families, or witnessed only by those of us living through it. It is our collective pain. Regardless of where we live, or whether we have personally contributed to or experienced these injustices, we are all affected by their consequences. And the solution must also be collective. We must acknowledge what is happening, allow ourselves to feel the weight of it, and decide that we do not want to live in a country that treats children this way. We do not want children to be intentionally traumatized or to know the pain of losing their homes and the security of belonging. And with that decision comes action to change policies, systems, and laws.

Now, with people having elected representatives to act on their behalf, it is time for those representatives to act. We need them to put their bodies on the line. We need them to come to Dilley, to witness what is happening, to hear the families, and to advocate for those who cannot make their voices heard. Don’t forget about us. Don’t stop fighting until we are all, collectively, free.

title: Immigrant legal providers start state budget asks early, push Hochul to give them $200M to ... - AMNY
description:
$20 million would specifically be dedicated to serving unaccompanied minors facing deportation.
Funding that in its entirety would take more than this $200 million, but ICARE says this state budget money would be a “good first step” to effectively doing so.
Hochul’s office declined to directly respond to questions from amNewYork regarding whether the governor would agree to this $200 million ask and where funding for immigration-related legal services would be on her list of budget priorities.
