text:
The Immigrant Children Advocates’ Relief Effort (ICARE), a group of legal advocates working to expand access to legal representation for immigrant children facing deportation in New York City, made the request to Hochul on behalf of its coalition, which includes public interest firms such as the Legal Aid Society and Kids in Need of Defense, alongside other groups, like the Vera Institute of Justice and the New York Immigration Coalition.

That $200 million would support immigrants of all ages statewide, funding social services and beginning to bridge the gap that leaves approximately 22% of people and 32% of unaccompanied minors without representation, according to July data from the Vera Institute of Justice. $20 million would specifically be dedicated to serving unaccompanied minors facing deportation.

There are currently over 1,000 minors without parents or legal guardians on ICARE’s waiting list for representation and about 11,600 across the state in removal proceedings, said Sierra Kraft, the group’s executive director.

When unaccompanied minors have an attorney representing them, they are at least 100 times more likely to win their case, meaning that without this money, children who have valid legal arguments to remain in the U.S. will be displaced.

“This is about fairness and due process. We have seen young people and immigrant communities under attack, and without representation, kids are nearly guaranteed to lose their case without a qualified lawyer in their corner helping them out and crafting legal arguments on why their safety is at risk,” Kraft said. “A lot of kids have viable forms of relief in the court. They should be provided an attorney and not be expected to represent themselves.”

ICARE’s also pushing Hochul to actively support the passage of and sign both the Access to Representation Act (ARA) and the Building Up Immigrant Legal Defense (BUILD) Act, which would establish a Right to Counsel program – or guaranteed representation – to all immigrants in deportation proceedings who can’t afford it. Funding that in its entirety would take more than this $200 million, but ICARE says this state budget money would be a “good first step” to effectively doing so.

Hochul’s office declined to directly respond to questions from amNewYork regarding whether the governor would agree to this $200 million ask and where funding for immigration-related legal services would be on her list of budget priorities. A spokesperson highlighted her previous support for funding this type of representation, including her $7.25 million in emergency funding for immigrant legal providers earlier this year.

“Governor Hochul will review all legislation that passes both houses of the state legislature, and details of the Governor’s Executive Budget Proposal will be released in January,” Hochul’s office said in a statement. “The Governor has committed millions of dollars to provide legal services for vulnerable immigrant children and is committed to working with the legislature to keep New Yorkers safe.”

The funding ask comes as Trump’s federal government cut off contracts for immigrant legal providers over the summer and has continued to escalate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) action targeting immigrants and people of color across the country and in New York City.

ICARE says it sees the $200 million request broken into three categories: $90 million just to sustain current statewide immigration-related legal and social service programs, then an additional $60 million to address new deportation demands and $50 million to strengthen the infrastructure behind providing its legal services and building long-term capacity.

That $200 million would be more than double the $74.2 million the coalition received from the state for this type of representation last year. Increasing complexity in immigration cases is driving the need for more money, Kraft said.

More habeas corpus petitions must be filed quickly to get people out of detention and prevent them from being flung to another state where lawyers can’t reach them and asylum applications are being dismissed and denied at higher rates, meaning there’s a more frequent need to file appeals on them. All of that contributes to why the group says it needs at least $90 million – over $15 million more than it received from Hochul’s office last year – to keep its level of representation in deportation cases steady.

“The cost of delivering services continues to increase,” Kraft said. “Because each case is far more complex than it used to be, the money that was received last year won’t be enough. There needs to be an increase in funding for legal service providers to be able to offer and deliver the same services and meet the increasing need.”

The group of immigration legal services providers will also be seeking additional funding from the city during the upcoming budget cycle to continue filling the current gap in representation for those facing deportation.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is laying the groundwork for long-promised investigations of the Trump administration that will launch with the new Congress in January.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control, sent letters directing members of President Donald Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. It’s an early step toward undertaking investigations of the Republican president and his administration.

The letters released Wednesday cover a wide range of potential investigations, including alleged financial conflicts involving Trump’s family, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein.

“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”

Targets of the letters include two of Trump’s sons, Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law.

The White House has repeatedly pushed back at the investigative ambitions outlined by Democrats, with officials saying they are willing to engage on oversight inquiries that they see as legitimate but not ones assessed as politically motivated.

The president is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

The letters offer an early glimpse of how Democrats plan to use their newly won congressional majority to scrutinize Trump and his administration. As favorable election results rolled in for Democrats on election night, Garcia posted a two-word warning on social media: “Lawyer up.”

The preservation notices do not compel recipients to turn over documents, but they signal the investigations that Democrats intend to pursue once they gain control of the committee and its subpoena power in January.

Before the midterms, Garcia outlined several areas Democrats would scrutinize, including the administration’s handling of the Epstein investigation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and potential financial conflicts involving Trump’s family.

The letters to Kushner and Trump’s sons Eric and Donald Jr. seek to preserve documents related to alleged conflicts of interest and their business dealings. Garcia also sent notices to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over separate allegations of misconduct and financial conflicts.

The letters to Vance and Blanche focus on the administration’s handling of files related to Epstein, including allegations by Democrats that White House officials sought to conceal information and manage the political fallout from the investigation.

The White House has warned Garcia and other Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration may open them up to investigations from the Justice Department.

Last week, White House counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Garcia that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The investigative powers of Congress are well established, inherent in its constitutional authority as a check on the other branches of government. Modern U.S. history is filled with congressional investigations and their aftermath, from the Watergate investigation to the 9/11 attacks to Republicans’ more recent look into Democratic President Joe Biden’s family.

The association said judges are not prevented from personally discussing subjects from immigration court procedure to their own experiences as judges.
Why Immigration Judges Are Going to the Supreme Court The immediate question for the Supreme Court is not whether the DOJ policy is a First Amendment violation.

text:
Immigration judges are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene in a yearslong First Amendment fight over a Department of Justice (DOJ) policy that restricts what they can say publicly about immigration and the federal agency that employs them.

The National Association of Immigration Judges (NAIJ) filed a petition Tuesday, asking the justices to review an appeals court ruling that prevents the group from challenging the policy directly in federal district court, instead directing judges toward the federal government's civil service review system.

The judges contend that route may never lead to judicial review and that forcing them to wait while the policy remains in place creates an immediate First Amendment injury by chilling speech before it even happens.

Read More on U.S.

"When the government places a prior restraint on the expression of public employees, they should be able to go to court to challenge that restraint immediately," Ramya Krishnan, senior staff attorney for the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, which brought the lawsuit, told Newsweek. "With immigration policy, at the center of national debate, it's more important than ever that the public hear what immigration judges have to say."

Newsweek reached out to the DOJ for comment via email Tuesday afternoon.

What Are Immigration Judges Barred From Saying?

Immigration judges are employees of the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), which falls under the DOJ's responsibility.

The challenged policy treats speech concerning agency policies, programs or subjects directly related to judges' official duties as official-capacity speech. The petition says that effectively prohibits judges from speaking in their personal capacities about immigration or EOIR.

Before the restrictions began in 2017, under the first Trump administration, judges regularly spoke at conferences, taught at universities and law schools, and participated in immigration law training, subject to approvals and disclaimers making clear they were speaking personally, the petition said.

The association said judges are not prevented from personally discussing subjects from immigration court procedure to their own experiences as judges.

"The result is to deny the public access to important insights from those with direct knowledge of how the immigration system operates," the petition said.

"Judges do not turn in their right to free speech when they put on the robe," Holly A. D’Andrea, president of the National Association of Immigration Judges, said in a press release. "Our country was designed to be governed by public reason, not private silence. Silencing judges deprives the public of a key perspective on the rule of law."

Why Immigration Judges Are Going to the Supreme Court

The immediate question for the Supreme Court is not whether the DOJ policy is a First Amendment violation. Instead, the justices, should they decide to hear the case, would need to decide whether immigration judges are even allowed to take their constitutional challenge directly to federal court.

The case was initially brought July 1, 2020, when the Knight Institute filed a lawsuit on behalf of the NAIJ, challenging the policy.

The district court where the case was filed turned the case away, citing the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute, which prevents unions—in this case, the NAIJ—from using that system to deal with a complaint. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals backed that decision.

After that, in 2022, the NAIJ was formally decertified as the judges' bargaining representative on the case, meaning the original reason for the federal district court turning the case away no longer existed. The Fourth Circuit then vacated its previous decision.

However, the case faced another block in federal court in 2023: the Civil Service Reform Act. That legislation says that the judges would need to go through the DOJ's own complaint system and this is why the appeal has been taken to the Supreme Court.

"Even if they did eventually get judicial review, that judicial review wouldn't be meaningful, because judges are being chilled right now," Krishnan said. "And any relief they got through judicial review at the end of the day under the scheme would come too late to remedy the ongoing and irreparable harm to their First Amendment rights."

The Supreme Court has already intervened in this case, in May, when it granted the government's petition and summarily reversed the Fourth Circuit's judgment. The justices, however, did not resolve the underlying free speech issue or the jurisdiction issue being brought up now.

Judges Warn of a 'First Amendment Black Hole'

"The Fourth Circuit’s conclusion threatens to create a First Amendment black hole—allowing each new administration to impose prior restraints on the speech of federal employees without any guarantee of judicial review of those restraints," the petition read.

The plaintiffs argue that the federal government could "categorically forbid federal employees from engaging in even private speech about gun rights, health care, vaccines, university admissions, or the war in Gaza—and judicial review of these brazenly unconstitutional policies would come only with the blessing of an agency official, and only after protracted and futile administrative proceedings."

All of these concerns stem from the path identified by the Fourth Circuit. An employee could submit a complaint to the Office of Special Counsel, but reaching the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)—which adjudicates complaints—depends on the Special Counsel deciding to pursue corrective active, meaning it is not guaranteed at all.

Between fiscal years 2020 and 2025, the petition said, only one MSPB appeal was lodged, the petition said.

Why the Case Could Reach Beyond Immigration

While the case is about immigration judges and their rights, the petition argues that the restrictions could affect a wide range of federal employees wishing to speak about gun rights, healthcare, vaccines and more.

If the Supreme Court does grant the appeal and forces the case to be heard in federal district court, the wider DOJ policy could then be challenged.

"If the Supreme Court does grant certiorari on this question, and were to decide in our favor, then that means that the district court, in our case, could finally reach the merits of our First Amendment claims, which are strong, and hold that this policy is unconstitutional and prohibit the agency from enforcing it against judges who speak publicly about immigration law and policy," Krishnan said.

title: Landlord seeks dismissal of Glenwood Springs lawsuit over ICE facility - Post Independent
description:
Florida-based JG Housing Solutions filed a motion to dismiss Friday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
“JG Housing Solutions has filed a motion to ask the federal district court to dismiss the City of Glenwood Springs’ lawsuit against it.
According to JG Housing Solutions’ motion, the city’s lawsuit alleges that ICE detained 27 people at the facility between May 22 and Aug. 4, 2026, after the special use permit had been revoked.
“JG Housing Solutions has no control over the federal government or any of its actions at any of its leased facilities.
“JG Housing Solutions should not be caught in the middle of this controversy – it has done nothing wrong,” Bryan said.
text:
The owner of a Glenwood Springs property leased to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is asking a federal judge to dismiss the city’s lawsuit over detention operations at the facility, arguing the city is attempting to hold a private landlord responsible for the actions of the federal government.

Florida-based JG Housing Solutions filed a motion to dismiss Friday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. The company argues that the city cannot use its zoning regulations to interfere with federal immigration enforcement at its property at 100 Midland Ave.

Christopher Bryan, an attorney with Garfield and Hecht representing JG Housing Solutions, said the city’s legal dispute should be directed at the federal government rather than his client.

“JG Housing Solutions has filed a motion to ask the federal district court to dismiss the City of Glenwood Springs’ lawsuit against it. The reason is simple: JG Housing Solutions is a private landlord, and the dispute the City is raising is with the federal government,” Bryan said in an email to the Post Independent Tuesday.

The city, however, maintains that its lawsuit is a matter of enforcing local land use regulations against a private property owner.

“The city has followed fair, impartial, and standard practices to resolve issues and have taken the same steps toward resolving issues in this process as it would have with any other entity. This lawsuit is just about enforcing violation of the city’s Land Use Code with a private property owner, regardless of the building’s tenant,” the city said in an emailed statement to the Post Independent.

The dispute dates back to April, when the Glenwood Springs Planning and Zoning Commission revoked a special use permit that had allowed ICE to detain people at the property for up to 12 hours.

The permit was issued to the federal government in 2004, before the city’s zoning regulations changed in 2018 to prohibit detention facilities.

According to Law360, a legal news publication covering litigation and court proceedings , the city revoked the permit after obtaining records showing ICE had met or exceeded the detention limit 10 times in May and August 2025.

According to JG Housing Solutions’ motion, the city’s lawsuit alleges that ICE detained 27 people at the facility between May 22 and Aug. 4, 2026, after the special use permit had been revoked.

The Glenwood Springs City Council voted in August to pursue legal action over the continued detention operations.

Glenwood Springs filed its lawsuit Sept. 25 in Garfield County District Court, alleging that ICE continued using the property as a detention facility after the special use permit was revoked. According to the city’s complaint, as summarized in JG Housing Solutions’ motion to dismiss, the city’s Land Use Code has prohibited detention facilities since 2018.

JG Housing Solutions moved the case to federal court Oct. 26 before filing its motion to dismiss Nov. 13. The company argues that the city cannot use its zoning authority to indirectly regulate federal immigration enforcement by pursuing legal action against the landlord.

In its motion, JG Housing Solutions argues that the city cannot use its zoning authority to indirectly regulate federal immigration enforcement by pursuing legal action against the landlord. The company cites the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause and the doctrine of intergovernmental immunity, which generally protects federal operations from state and local interference.

The motion also argues that federal law gives the federal government authority to determine where immigration detainees are held, overriding conflicting local restrictions. JG Housing further contends that the federal government is a necessary party to the lawsuit but cannot be joined because of sovereign immunity, which generally prevents lawsuits against the federal government without its consent.

Bryan said JG Housing Solutions purchased the property with a preexisting federal lease allowing the government to use the space for its agencies and lawful federal operations. The federal government has leased space at the property since 2003.

He also said the company had no ability to challenge the city’s decision to revoke the special use permit because the federal government, not JG Housing Solutions, held the permit.

“JG Housing Solutions has no control over the federal government or any of its actions at any of its leased facilities. The federal government has not addressed the City of Glenwood Springs’ complaints, and the City has not sued the federal government. Instead, the City sued JG Housing Solutions, the property owner,” Bryan said.

The motion argues that an order preventing JG Housing Solutions from leasing the property for detention operations would conflict with its existing federal lease. The company maintains that it cannot direct ICE’s operations or remove the agency from the property.

Rather than pursuing the landlord, Bryan said the city could seek assistance from Colorado’s congressional delegation, offer to purchase the property or pursue legal action against the federal government.

“Suing a small, family-owned business that simply owns the commercial property will not give the City the relief it seeks, because JG Housing Solutions has no authority over how the federal government uses the space,” Bryan said.

The city’s lawsuit seeks a court declaration that leasing the property for detention operations violates its Land Use Code, an order prohibiting JG Housing Solutions from continuing that use and penalties of $1,000 per day until the alleged violations stop, according to the motion.

JG Housing Solutions is asking the judge to dismiss the lawsuit with prejudice for failure to state a legally sufficient claim or, alternatively, without prejudice because the federal government is a required party that cannot be joined.

Bryan maintained that his client has complied with the terms of its lease and should not be held responsible for the federal government’s activities.

“JG Housing Solutions should not be caught in the middle of this controversy – it has done nothing wrong,” Bryan said.

The city declined to comment further on the pending litigation.

“A ruling has not yet been rendered. No additional comments from city officials will be shared at this time,” the city said in its emailed statement.

The motion remains pending in federal court.

text:
Each month, Take the Fifth blog compiles and analyzes key statistics from the opinions issued by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. These monthly snapshots offer useful insights into the inner workings of the Court, the relative success of various appeals, and broader trends in how the Fifth Circuit disposes of its docket. Following is Take the Fifth’s look at October 2026.

The Big Picture: 178 Opinions

The Fifth Circuit released 178 total opinions in October 2026, 23 fewer than in September and continuing to calm back down from August’s unusual peak of 258.

Of the October 2026 opinions, 38 were designated for publication (a 21.3% publication rate), while the remaining 140 were unpublished, and therefore lacking in precedential authority.

Where the Appeals Are Coming From

The Northern District of Mississippi was the only district with a perfect affirmance rate in October, though on a sample of just 1 decision—a full affirmance.

The Northern District of Texas led as the source of the most Fifth Circuit decisions, originating 47 total opinions in October. Of those, 41 were full affirmances or appeal dismissals, 1 was a partial affirmance/partial vacatur or reversal, 2 were full reversals, 2 were full vacaturs, and 1 was a denial of a motion.

The Western District of Texas followed with 42 dispositions: 37 full affirmances or dismissals, 1 full reversal, 2 full vacaturs, 1 order granting rehearing en banc, and 1 published denial of rehearing en banc. The Southern District of Texas produced 32 dispositions, including 28 full affirmances or dismissals, 1 partial reversal, 1 full reversal, 1 full vacatur, and 1 denial of a motion.

The remaining districts rounded out October’s docket: the Western District of Louisiana (13 dispositions, including 12 full affirmances or dismissals and 1 grant of a motion), the Southern District of Mississippi (9, including 1 full reversal and 1 full vacatur), the Eastern District of Texas (8, including 1 full reversal and 1 denial of a motion), the Eastern District of Louisiana (7, including 1 partial reversal, 1 full vacatur, and 1 published denial of rehearing en banc), and the Middle District of Louisiana (2, consisting of 1 full affirmance and 1 full reversal). On petitions for review of Board of Immigration Appeals orders, 15 were denied or dismissed and 1 was granted. On petitions for review of other agency actions, there was 1 grant of rehearing en banc.

What the Appeals Are About—And Who They Benefit

As always, criminal appeals dominated the docket, accounting for 77 of the 178 opinions. Of those, 75 resulted in full affirmances or dismissals and 2 were full vacaturs. The bottom line: 75 dispositions favored the prosecution; 2 favored the defendant. That roughly 97.4% government-win rate in criminal cases continues to drive the Court’s overall affirmance numbers.

In immigration cases, the government fared nearly as well. Seventeen of 19 dispositions favored the government (including 1 full affirmance, 15 BIA petition denials, and 1 denial of a motion), while only 2 favored the immigrant (1 full reversal and 1 grant of a BIA petition). Prisoner suits followed the same pattern: both dispositions (2 full affirmances or dismissals) favored the government defendants.

The commercial-civil docket (including insurance disputes) offered little relief for appellants in October: out of 24 dispositions, only 4 favored the plaintiff (16.7%), with 20 favoring the defendant. That docket included 19 full affirmances or dismissals, 2 full reversals, 1 full vacatur, 1 published denial of rehearing en banc, and 1 denial of a motion. Civil rights and constitutional claims (non-prisoner suits) yielded 17 dispositions, with 14 favoring the defendant and 3 favoring the plaintiff; along with 11 full affirmances or dismissals, that category produced 1 partial reversal, 1 full reversal, 2 full vacaturs, 1 published denial of rehearing en banc, and 1 order granting rehearing en banc.

In employment and labor-law cases, 10 of 14 dispositions favored the employer, while 4 favored employees; the category included 11 full affirmances or dismissals, 1 partial reversal, 1 full reversal, and 1 order granting rehearing en banc. Qualified immunity cases were light in October, with just 2 full affirmances, both favoring the government defendant. Bankruptcy cases likewise produced 2 full affirmances, both favoring the creditor.

Habeas corpus and other post-conviction relief cases offered no bright spots for petitioners: all 5 dispositions (4 full affirmances or dismissals and 1 motion denial) favored the government. Personal torts, by contrast, showed a perfect split, with 3 dispositions favoring the defendant and 3 favoring the plaintiff across 4 full affirmances, 1 partial reversal, and 1 full vacatur.

Other categories in October: environmental law/toxic torts (1 affirmance and 1 grant of a motion, both favoring the defendant), products liability (1 affirmance, favoring the defendant), maritime law (1 affirmance, favoring the defendant), social security (1 affirmance, favoring the government’s denial of benefits), class action (1 full vacatur, favoring the defendant), administrative law (1 affirmance and 1 full reversal—1 favoring each side), and international law (1 full reversal, favoring the plaintiff).

Does Oral Argument Matter?

The data continues to suggest that it does, at least for appellants. Among the 34 decisions in orally argued cases, the full-affirmance rate was just 61.29% (counting full affirmances and denials of petitions for review of agency orders, and excluding rehearing and motions orders). Those 34 decisions included 18 full affirmances, 2 partial affirmances/partial reversals or vacaturs, 6 full reversals, 4 full vacaturs, 1 published denial of rehearing en banc, 2 grants of rehearing en banc, and 1 denial of a BIA petition. In all, 11 of the 34 orally argued dispositions (32.4%) favored civil plaintiffs or non-state parties, compared to 23 favoring the defendant/state.

In the 3 cases where oral argument was initially granted but later withdrawn, the full-affirmance rate was 100% (2 full affirmances and 1 denial of a BIA petition), and all 3 dispositions favored the defendant/state—a reversal of August’s unusually appellant-friendly results in this category, though on a very small sample. Typically, the oral-argument-withdrawn cases hover at an affirmance rate between orally argued and no-oral-argument cases, but this small sample size from October skewed that normal picture.

In the 141 cases never ordered for oral argument, the full-affirmance rate soared to 95.59%, and only 10 dispositions favored the civil plaintiff/non-state party. Those decisions included 117 full affirmances, 13 denials of BIA petitions, 1 partial reversal, 1 full reversal, 3 full vacaturs, 1 published denial of rehearing en banc, 1 grant of a BIA petition, 3 denials of motions, and 1 grant of a motion. The takeaway for practitioners remains consistent: if, as an appellant, you get oral argument, your odds of a favorable outcome improve meaningfully.

How Much Law Is Being Made?

Of the 38 published opinions, only 18 were full affirmances or other denials of appellate relief (17 full affirmances and 1 denial of a BIA petition), for a published-opinion affirmance rate of just 47.4%. The rest included 2 partial affirmances/partial reversals or vacaturs, 6 full reversals, 4 full vacaturs, 2 grants of rehearing en banc, 2 published denials of rehearing en banc, 3 denials of motions, and 1 grant of a motion. In contrast, the 140 unpublished opinions showed a 95.7% full-affirmance rate (134 of 140, counting 120 full affirmances or dismissals and 14 denials or dismissals of BIA petitions). The pattern remains clear: when the Court makes new law, it’s much more likely to be doing something other than simply affirming.

Who Was Doing What on the Court?

Judge Smith was the busiest judge of October, participating on panels issuing decisions in 43 cases. Judge Higginson and Judge Duncan (37 panel decisions each) followed, with Judge Jones close behind at 35.

On the writing side, Judge Higginson was the busiest attributed author with 8 opinions (majority, concurring, and dissenting combined), followed by Judge Ho with 6. Judges Richman, Ho, and Oldham shared the lead in separate concurrences, with 2 each. Judges Haynes, Ho, and Oldham each authored 3 dissenting or dubitante opinions, with Judge Haynes adding another dissent without opinion.

The Court issued 147 per curiam opinions (138 unpublished), though 5 of those designated “per curiam” were accompanied by separate concurrences or dissents, making them not true per curia “by the court.” Judge Smith also led in participation on panels issuing published opinions (18 panels), followed by Judge Higginson (15), and Judges Southwick and Engelhardt (11 each).

Among senior-status judges, Judges Davis (13 panels issuing opinions), King (11 panels), and Higginbotham and Clement (10 panels each) carried the heaviest participation loads. On the lighter end among active-status judges, Judge Graves had the lightest production at 16 panel decisions, not counting Chief Judge Elrod (14 panels), who carries the administrative load of being Chief.

Conclusion

Most decisions in October, as always, were unanimous, with 15 dissents and 7 concurrences out of 178 opinions. For practitioners, the key takeaways from October are: (1) the gap between argued and non-argued cases was stark, with a 61.29% full-affirmance rate in orally argued cases compared to 95.59% in cases never ordered for argument, so securing oral argument remains one of the clearest markers of a live appeal; (2) the criminal docket’s roughly 97.4% government-win rate (75 of 77 dispositions) means criminal appellants should continue to calibrate expectations accordingly; and (3) the Court ordered rehearing en banc twice in October and issued published opinions that affirmed only 47.4% of the time, a reminder that when the Court chooses to make law, the outcome is far less predictable than the overall affirmance numbers suggest.

text:
The ACLU of South Carolina, North Carolina, and Georgia has filed a class action lawsuit against federal immigration authorities.

The lawsuit alleges that ICE is unlawfully re-detaining immigrants who had previously been released from custody.

Attorneys claim this new practice reverses a former policy and violates the Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable seizures.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of South Carolina has joined ACLU affiliates in North Carolina and Georgia in a federal lawsuit challenging the re-detention of immigrants who previously had been released from immigration custody.

The ACLU chapters in the three states, along with Foley Hoag LLP, filed the 61-page class action lawsuit Nov. 12 against federal immigration authorities. The lawsuit alleges immigrants in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia face unlawful re-detention by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Atlanta field office.

According to the lawsuit, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) previously exempted individuals who had been released from immigration custody from being re-detained, unless there had been a change in their circumstances. The practice was called the "Changed Circumstances Policy."

The lawsuit alleges DHS now allows the re-detention of immigrants, including in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia — which are all covered by the Atlanta ICE field office.

The result of the policy switch has been "immediate and drastic," according to the lawsuit.

"Individuals have been re-arrested and re-detained without warning while appearing for their routine ICE check-ins," the lawsuit states.

Attorneys in the case represent four plaintiffs living in North Carolina and Georgia who previously were detained by ICE and later released from immigration custody. Some were detained again years after their initial detention, according to the lawsuit.

Neither DHS nor ICE have responded to a Greenville News request for comment.

The lawsuit alleges that DHS offered no explanation for the change in policy and that the change causes irreparable harm to the plaintiffs and immigrants. It also argues the practice violates the Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable seizures.

Attorneys for the plaintiffs are asking the court to determine that the re-detention policy is unconstitutional.

In a statement, ACLU SC Staff Attorney Sarah Schreiber said that South Carolinians shouldn't have to live in fear that their family or neighbors will be thrown back into detention.

“We are proud to stand with our fellow ACLU affiliates to defend our clients and the rule of law against these egregious and unjustifiable abuses," Schreiber stated.

text:
A federal judge has dealt a substantial legal blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to tighten immigration rules for international students, exchange visitors, and foreign journalists. On November 16, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts invalidated a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule that would have replaced the longstanding “Duration of Status” system with fixed periods of authorized admission.

The ruling in *Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, marks a major victory for the international students and American universities that challenged the administration’s restrictions.

U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV found that DHS had exceeded its statutory authority by imposing certain academic restrictions and had not adequately justified its broader regulatory changes under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The court vacated the rule in full, rather than simply delaying its implementation. As a result, the existing Duration of Status framework remains in force unless the ruling is stayed or overturned on appeal.

Understanding the Duration of Status System

For decades, international students admitted to the United States in F-1 status have generally been permitted to stay for the Duration of Status, often referred to as D/S.

Under this system, students may remain in the country while enrolled in an authorized academic program, as long as they maintain their immigration status and follow the applicable regulations.

Unlike many other nonimmigrant categories, F-1 students are not typically given a specific expiration date for their authorized stay when they are admitted.

Instead, their permission to remain depends on continued compliance with requirements, including maintaining a full course of study, keeping their Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) records up to date, and observing relevant employment restrictions.

This approach reflects the realities of higher education, where research commitments, dissertation work, changes in academic focus, or other valid circumstances may extend the time needed to complete a program.

However, Duration of Status does not grant an unlimited right to remain in the United States. Students must continue to satisfy immigration requirements, and completing an academic program generally begins a limited grace period, unless the individual qualifies for another authorized activity or immigration benefit.

It is also important to distinguish visa validity from immigration status. An F-1 visa stamp may expire while a student remains in lawful F-1 status within the United States. The visa stamp generally determines whether a person may seek admission, while the authorized period of stay is determined separately.

What the Trump Administration’s Rule Would Have Changed

On July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a final rule titled Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media.

The rule proposed a fundamental overhaul of how the United States administers the F, J, and I nonimmigrant classifications.

Under the proposed system, international students generally would have been admitted for fixed periods of no more than four years, even if their academic programs required more time to complete.

Students who needed to remain in the United States beyond their authorized admission periods would have had to file formal applications for extensions of stay with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

The rule also proposed limits affecting academic mobility, including changes to educational objectives, transfers between institutions, and enrollment in additional academic programs.

Foreign media representatives with I status also would have been subject to fixed admission periods, replacing the existing duration-based framework.

DHS said the changes would strengthen immigration oversight, improve fraud detection, and enable the government to periodically reassess whether foreign nationals remained eligible for their respective immigration classifications.

The administration contended that the existing system allowed some foreign nationals to stay in the United States for extended periods without adequate individualized immigration review.

Why the Federal Court Rejected the Regulation

Judge Saylor’s November 16 decision addressed both flaws in DHS’s rulemaking process and the limits of the agency’s authority under federal law.

The Administrative Procedure Act requires federal agencies to provide reasoned explanations for regulatory decisions, consider key aspects of the issues before them, and respond reasonably to significant objections raised during the rulemaking process.

The court concluded that DHS had not met these requirements.

Specifically, the court found that DHS had not adequately assessed the costs and benefits of replacing Duration of Status with fixed periods of admission.

The government also failed to explain sufficiently why existing monitoring systems could not address the concerns it had identified.

One key consideration was SEVIS, the federal database through which educational institutions report information about international students and exchange visitors.

Instead of adequately considering whether improvements to SEVIS could achieve its objectives, DHS adopted a more burdensome approach that required additional immigration applications and government adjudications.

The court also questioned whether the proposed restrictions were consistent with the purposes of the F-1 classification established by Congress.

Judge Saylor stressed that Congress created the student visa program to support legitimate educational opportunities in the United States.

The court determined that certain restrictions on academic progress and educational choices exceeded DHS’s lawful regulatory authority.

As Judge Saylor explained:

“The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program.”

The decision thus involved more than a disagreement with the administration’s immigration priorities. The court concluded that the regulation failed to comply with established legal requirements governing federal agency action.

A Legal Dispute That Began Before the Rule Took Effect

The November ruling came after months of litigation involving educational associations, universities, and labor organizations.

On August 18, 2026, a coalition led by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and NAFSA: Association of International Educators filed a lawsuit challenging the regulation.

The plaintiffs maintained that the rule would disrupt academic programs, create significant administrative costs, and weaken the United States’ ability to attract international talent.

On September 14, Judge Saylor issued a nationwide preliminary injunction barring the regulation from taking effect.

The government appealed that preliminary ruling to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on September 30.

While the preliminary appeal was still pending, however, the district court continued to address the merits of the case.

On November 16, the court entered summary judgment for the plaintiffs, rejected the government’s competing motion, and vacated the regulation under 5 U.S.C. § 706.

The distinction has legal significance. A preliminary injunction typically offers temporary relief while litigation is ongoing. By contrast, a final judgment vacating a regulation eliminates the rule’s legal effect, subject to further appellate proceedings.

What the Decision Means for International Students

The immediate effect is that international students can continue to rely on the existing Duration of Status framework.

For F-1 students, the November decision does not establish a new four-year limit on admission or require an application to USCIS for an extension solely because their academic programs last longer than four years.

Students pursuing doctoral degrees, undertaking extended research, or completing other legitimate educational requirements therefore retain the flexibility provided by current immigration regulations.

The decision also preserves the existing regulatory framework for eligible school transfers, changes in academic programs, and additional educational programs.

Students must still comply with all applicable immigration requirements, including maintaining valid SEVIS records, securing any required school authorization, and following employment restrictions.

The ruling does not end USCIS oversight, bar enforcement against students who violate their status, or guarantee approval of future immigration benefits.

For J-1 exchange visitors, the decision likewise prevents the new fixed-admission system from taking effect. However, J-1 participants must continue meeting program-specific requirements, including authorized program dates and any applicable two-year foreign residence obligation.

Foreign journalists in I status also benefit because the rule’s proposed admission restrictions have been vacated.

Implications for OPT, STEM OPT, and Future Employment

The ruling also has significant implications for international students preparing to move from academic study into the workforce.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the 24-month STEM OPT extension continue to provide eligible F-1 students with important opportunities to gain practical experience related to their fields of study.

The vacated regulation did not broadly eliminate OPT. However, its fixed admission periods and added procedural requirements could have made the transition from academic study to practical training and later employment-based immigration categories more difficult.

By maintaining the existing Duration of Status framework, the court’s decision removes these specific proposed obstacles.

Nevertheless, the ruling does not bar DHS from seeking separate regulatory changes to OPT, STEM OPT, or other employment authorization programs through legally valid procedures.

Students considering H-1B employment should continue to follow developments involving the H-1B program, cap-gap protections, employment authorization, and changes in immigration status.

Current Status: November 17, 2026

As of November 17, 2026, the legal position is settled: the July 2026 DHS fixed-admission regulation has been vacated, while the preexisting Duration of Status framework remains in effect.

The government had appealed the September preliminary injunction. On November 13, the First Circuit paused the appellate proceedings for 30 days, allowing the district court time to issue its final decision.

After the November 16 judgment, the earlier appeal may be moot because the final judgment has replaced the preliminary injunction.

The Trump administration may separately appeal the final ruling and request a stay of the vacatur. Filing an appeal, however, would not by itself reinstate the regulation.

At the time this article was published, the reviewed sources did not show that an appellate court had stayed or reversed the November 16 judgment.

The administration could also propose a revised regulation that addresses the court’s objections, but any replacement would have to meet applicable statutory and administrative-law requirements.

Broader Implications for U.S. Immigration Policy

The decision comes as concerns grow about the competitiveness of American higher education.

The Institute of International Education’s Open Doors 2026 report indicates that U.S. institutions enrolled approximately 1.15 million international students in the 2025–2026 academic year. Recent enrollment data also point to declining demand, especially among new international students.

International students support university finances, scientific research, technological innovation, and the wider U.S. economy.

Advocates of stricter immigration controls maintain that stronger screening and periodic reviews are needed to preserve program integrity and address national security concerns.

Universities and immigration advocates, by contrast, argue that the government already has extensive monitoring and enforcement powers, and that further administrative hurdles could deter qualified students from studying in the United States.

Judge Saylor’s decision does not prevent DHS from intensifying immigration enforcement. Instead, it underscores that federal agencies must remain within the authority Congress has granted them and provide sufficient legal and factual grounds for major regulatory changes.

Conclusion

The November 16, 2026, ruling stands as one of the year’s most significant judicial developments in international student immigration policy.

By setting aside the Trump administration’s fixed-admission regulation, the federal court has maintained the longstanding Duration of Status framework for eligible international students and exchange visitors, while blocking the implementation of further restrictions on academic mobility.

The decision offers immediate, meaningful certainty for students, universities, and employers.

However, the case may proceed through the federal appellate courts, and further regulatory efforts remain possible.

International students should continue to maintain their immigration status, consult with designated school officials, and follow developments that may affect their academic and career plans.

Ultimately, the ruling underscores a significant constraint on executive immigration policymaking: although the federal government has broad authority to regulate nonimmigrant admissions and enforce immigration laws, its actions must align with congressional intent and comply with federal administrative la

title: What the First Democratic Attorney General In a Generation Could Mean For Texas
description:
For nearly three decades, the Texas Attorney General’s office served as one of the conservative legal movement’s most powerful institutions.
A little over a quarter-century ago, the Texas Attorney General’s office was a relatively quiet state agency.
That began to change under John Cornyn, who in 1998 became the first Republican elected attorney general in Texas since Reconstruction.
The election of Johnson as the state’s next attorney general is going to change all of this in a hurry.
During the administrations of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, Texas saw what an ambitious attorney general can accomplish.
text:
For nearly three decades, the Texas Attorney General’s office served as one of the conservative legal movement’s most powerful institutions. It challenged Democratic presidents in court, developed legal theories that reshaped national debates, and cultivated a generation of conservative lawyers who would go on to occupy influential positions in the federal judiciary and Congress.

Now, for the first time since 1998, a Democrat is preparing to take office. The incoming administration of Nathan Johnson, a former state lawmaker, will have the opportunity to put these resources to a different use: defending workers, students, and reproductive freedom rather than challenging the protections they rely on, and using the state’s legal power to protect Texans from abuses by government and private interests alike.

A little over a quarter-century ago, the Texas Attorney General’s office was a relatively quiet state agency. Its work largely consisted of collecting child support and defending the state in court. That began to change under John Cornyn, who in 1998 became the first Republican elected attorney general in Texas since Reconstruction. During his tenure, Cornyn established the office of the Texas Solicitor General, a specialized team of appellate lawyers responsible for representing Texas in state and federal courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Cornyn was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2002, but his decisions created the infrastructure that Greg Abbott would use to transform the office into a vehicle to advance conservative causes. Abbott, who served for 12 years before being elected governor in 2014, gave the Texas Solicitor General, now-Senator Ted Cruz, a straightforward mission: “Look across the country. If there are conservative principles we can fight and defend, if we can make a difference defending the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, go do it,” Cruz recalled in 2019.

When President Barack Obama entered the White House in 2009, Texas became a central antagonist in efforts to block his administration’s agenda. Under Abbott, the state filed more than 30 lawsuits against the Obama administration in six years, challenging the Affordable Care Act, federal environmental regulations, and immigration protections for undocumented young people.

Abbott’s successor, Ken Paxton, took this strategy even further. In 2020, Paxton asked the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn election results in four states that Donald Trump had lost. The Court rejected that request, but in the years that followed, Paxton’s office filed dozens of challenges to President Joe Biden’s policies on immigration, the environment, and healthcare. Paxton also continued to fight to invalidate the Affordable Care Act and to restrict protections for LGBTQ people.

Under the leadership of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, the Texas Attorney General’s office became especially adept at manipulating the federal court system to ensure that its lawsuits landed before sympathetic judges. For example, the Northern District of Texas does not randomize case assignments, and instead uses smaller divisions run by a single judge. Therefore, litigants can file in these single-judge divisions and be almost guaranteed they will get a conservative judge of their choice.

Then, after some Northern District judge inevitably rules in its favor, the Texas Attorney General’s office gets to defend those decisions at the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, the most conservative federal appeals court in the country. From there, appeals go before the conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court. This pipeline has helped fast-track some of the most consequential challenges to federal law and policy, turning cases that begin in Texas into national precedent.

But the office’s influence extends beyond the lawsuits it brings. It has also served as a pipeline for conservative lawyers looking to join the ranks of the federal judiciary. According to a Texas Tribune investigation, nine federal judges appointed by Trump between 2018 and 2020 had previously worked in the Texas Attorney General’s office, including Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho, Andrew Oldham, and Kyle Duncan.

The election of Johnson as the state’s next attorney general is going to change all of this in a hurry. As a native Texan, I believe the new attorney general should use the office’s authority to change how the state exercises power and whom it protects. That means looking beyond the cases the office can bring or defend, and recognizing its influence over the conduct of state agencies and the relationship between government and the people it serves. This is a substantially different conception of the attorney general’s role: using the office’s considerable resources to hold government officials accountable, confront abuses of corporate power, and defend the rights of Texans.

That responsibility begins with the office’s own use of state power. First, Johnson should abandon Paxton’s efforts to pursue out-of-state physicians who provide abortion medication to Texans. He should also withdraw the office from its agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that authorizes state employees to perform certain federal immigration-enforcement actions—like assisting in investigations, apprehension, and detention—under ICE supervision. And where Paxton challenged federal protections for LGBTQ students, Johnson should take advantage of the state’s legal resources to defend students against discrimination, not to perpetuate it.

Furthermore, Johnson should take a different approach to economic and environmental protections. Under Paxton, the office sued to block expanded federal protections that would have made more than four million additional workers eligible for overtime pay. Paxton also challenged federal methane regulations requiring oil and gas companies to monitor leaks and reduce emissions—rules the EPA estimated would prevent approximately 58 million tons of methane emissions from entering the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038.

Johnson should stop using the office’s resources to undermine worker protections and reasonable environmental standards. Instead, the office should focus on ensuring labor compliance in emerging industries, protecting immigrant workers, and fighting misclassification of workers as independent contractors—deceptive practices that affect Texans in blue-collar or service-sector jobs. And in a state where oil and gas production touches nearly every corner of the economy, the office should take seriously its responsibility to protect communities from unlawful pollution, contamination, and other practices that put their health and property at risk.

During the administrations of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, Texas saw what an ambitious attorney general can accomplish. But the measure of this new administration should not be how many of Paxton’s cases it abandons or how dramatically it departs from his politics. It should be whether Texans can feel the difference in how their government treats them. Whether workers can count on the state to pursue employers who steal their wages. Whether communities can hold polluters accountable. Whether civil rights mean something when government agencies violate them. And whether the state’s lawyers work for those who have too often been left to fend for themselves.

Texas does not need a less ambitious attorney general. It needs one willing to be ambitious about the right things—and most importantly, for the people.

title: Inhumane ICE detentions must stop with this 8-year-old's case - MS NOW
authors: Autumn Brewington, Rep. Mike Levin, Ja’han Jones
description:
I had one of those core-shaking moments recently, watching footage of three federal immigration agents taking an 8-year-old boy into custody.
Trump also expressed a willingness to work with Democrats on immigration reform.
That same week, an 8-year-old boy from Haiti went with his uncle to a scheduled immigration appointment in San Diego.
Last week I posed questions for the president and his chief of staff: What exactly did taking this 8-year-old boy accomplish?
I struggle to imagine a more fundamental test of those principles than how we choose to treat an 8-year-old child.
text:
Some moments in life make you question how we arrived at where we are. I had one of those core-shaking moments recently, watching footage of three federal immigration agents taking an 8-year-old boy into custody.

After almost two weeks, the boy has been reunited with his family. We should not look away from the trauma he experienced or the risk of other children experiencing similar horrors.

Now consider what President Donald Trump was saying just one day after the boy was taken into custody.

In the wake of the midterm election results, the president made a rather extraordinary admission on “60 Minutes”: The immigration enforcement actions of his administration may have gone too far, he said. Trump also expressed a willingness to work with Democrats on immigration reform.

Those words might have offered hope for genuine progress — had Trump not announced Stephen Miller, the architect of his aggressive immigration policies, as his new chief of staff hours after the interview.

That same week, an 8-year-old boy from Haiti went with his uncle to a scheduled immigration appointment in San Diego. The child, a third grader at Fay Elementary School, has lived with his uncle’s family since his father was deported last year. Instead of returning home after the appointment, this child was seemingly restrained and escorted away by not one, not two, but three Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers.

Three federal agents to take a third grader into custody? This scene should be unimaginable in America.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson cited federal anti-trafficking law and questions about legal guardianship when media outlets and officials sought to know how the department justified separating the child from the relatives who had been caring for him since his father’s deportation. According to that same spokesperson, ICE transferred the boy to the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

I cannot fathom the fear, confusion and trauma this child experienced. I struggle to understand how anyone could watch that footage and conclude this was necessary. And this young boy is not the only child whose life has been upended by the Trump administration’s inhumane immigration enforcement actions. Thankfully, this boy’s story appears to have a happy ending, but for so many others that is simply not the case.

Alongside my colleagues in the San Diego congressional delegation, I’ve demanded answers from the departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services about the boy’s safety, his detention and the justification for the agents’ actions.

But that’s my response as a legislator. As a human being, I find myself confronting questions that are simpler to ask and far harder to answer: When did we as a country become so willing to let fear and resentment overcome basic human decency? When did we begin treating empathy as a weakness rather than an obligation we owe one another? And what does it say if we no longer question whether what is done in our country’s name reflects the values we claim to hold?

Our immigration system is broken. But the notion that we must sacrifice our humanity or decency to reform it, or that Democrats and Republicans cannot solve this together, is categorically false.

More articles

Before we’re Republicans or Democrats, we’re human beings. Our disagreements are real, but they need not obscure fundamental truths. It is on our shared common ground that we can begin to reform our immigration system.

Rep. Maria Salazar, a Republican, and Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Democrat, and I worked together last summer to introduce the Dignity Act, the most comprehensive immigration and border security reform bill in decades.

Our legislation would create a pathway to legal status for undocumented immigrants already living in the United States and strengthen our border security; it would protect Dreamers, those who hold Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) holders. Our legislation would also address visa backlogs.

It’s not perfect, but our bill demonstrates something that ought to be self-evident: We can secure our borders without abandoning our values or losing sight of the people whose lives are affected by them.

Meaningful immigration reform begins with recognizing the human consequences of the policies we choose to enforce. Last week I posed questions for the president and his chief of staff: What exactly did taking this 8-year-old boy accomplish? Did three armed federal agents taking a third grader into custody make our borders any more secure? Did separating him from his family make Americans safer?

So far, I have not heard answers that justify what happened.

For all our disagreements, surely Americans can agree that the power of government comes with an obligation to exercise basic human decency.

The promise of America has always rested on our willingness to recognize when we have fallen short of our ideals and to relentlessly work toward a more perfect union.

I struggle to imagine a more fundamental test of those principles than how we choose to treat an 8-year-old child.

title: Court challenge pending over state driver's license ban to legal immigrants - GreenevilleSun.com
description: As Ukrainians and other non-U.S. citizens with valid federal work permits living in Tennessee await the results of a court challenge in December, they remain unable to renew their driver’s
text:
As Ukrainians and other non-U.S. citizens with valid federal work permits living in Tennessee await the results of a court challenge in December, they remain unable to renew their driver’s licenses.

Included are Ukrainians living legally in Greene and surrounding counties.

A court order issued last week extends a temporary restraining order blocking a recent abrupt change in state policy while the legal challenge brought by the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and other groups is pending in court.



Tennessee is turning down applications for driver’s licenses from immigrants who are authorized by the federal government to work and live in the United States, “a policy shift that could strip thousands of longtime license-holders of the ability to legally drive, according to immigration attorneys and advocates,” the Tennessee Lookout earlier reported.

Yaroslav Hnatusko, a co-founder of the Restore Ukraine volunteer organization and an East Tennessee State University graduate, expressed concern as the issue plays out in the legal system.

“Unfortunately, every single Ukrainian under Temporary Protected Status has been denied in driving license renewal. This is not just specific to East Tennessee, but across the entire state,” he said in an email.

“In the meantime, many other states already accommodated this situation,” Hnatusko said.

Hnatusko said that when the Russian invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, “Tennessee and East Tennessee provided refuge for many Ukrainians and were an extremely hospitable state. For some reason, the state is making our home state a very unwelcoming place.”

The Tennessee Driver Services Division is now overseen by the state Department of Safety and Homeland Security.

“Ukrainians in East Tennessee who have attempted to renew their licenses say DMV officials have turned them away without further guidance, and they hope that state-level changes can help them restore their driving privileges,” Hnatusko said.

Without changes in the license application system, “Ukrainian community members will struggle to get to work, attend school, go to church, buy groceries, visit the doctor or make it to appointments with immigration officials. In regions with limited public transportation, these tasks are even more difficult. Driving without a license could lead to criminal charges, jeopardizing an immigrant’s TPS status even further,” he said.

The court challenge “is one step forward. Ukrainians are now expecting official notice from Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security that TPS holders can renew their (driver’s licenses),” Hnatusko said.

Northeast Tennessee “has around 200 Ukrainian families who were affected,” he added.

Other Ukrainians living in East Tennessee have also voiced concern, including Washington County resident Iryna Marton.

“Ukrainians who came to Tennessee to find safety and rebuild their lives want to continue working, supporting their families, paying taxes, and contributing to their communities. When people cannot renew their driver’s licenses because of uncertainty surrounding federal documentation, they can lose access to the very things that allow them to remain self-sufficient. We are asking Tennessee to provide a practical, lawful temporary solution.” Marton said in an email.

A homeland security spokesperson cited state law that requires applicants for the temporary licenses to provide documentation that establishes a specific period of lawful status in the United States, but “The employment authorization card does not,” according to Tennessee Lookout.

The National Immigration Law Center, TIRRC and a Nashville law firm filed a lawsuit on Oct. 30 challenging the new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security. Six immigrants are also plaintiffs in the legal action.

The Chancery Court filing states the “sudden change” by TDOS “is causing widespread confusion, anxiety, and fear.”

“Without the ability to legally drive, plaintiffs risk losing their jobs and income and encountering significant hardships in raising their U.S. citizen children and providing for their families’ basic daily needs,” the filing states.

According to TIRRC, for many years, TDOS issued temporary driver’s licenses to Tennesseans who could show they had permission from the federal government to be in the country.

“TDOS routinely accepted work permits and other federal government documents as proof of a person’s legal stay in the U.S. for a period of time,” a TIRRC news release states.

Under the new rule, TDOS only issues driver’s licenses to certain non-U.S. citizens who can present a valid visa, I-94, I-94W, or a temporary green card.

The lawsuit argues that TDOS made the change “without following proper legal steps, overstepped its authority, and failed to give the public a chance to provide input,” according to TIRRC.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” Peter McGraw, Legal Deputy Director of the National Immigration Law Center, said in the news release.

“TDOS issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them,” McGraw said.

The lawsuit asks the court to block the new rule and require TDOS to return to its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

“Regardless of where they were born, Tennesseans rely on the ability to drive in order to work, care for their families, and access the basic needs of life — groceries, medical appointments, their children’s education. The plaintiffs in this action, like so many others across the state, have found their lives upended by the state’s abrupt rule change, which was implemented without warning or explanation. This is why we are taking legal action. All Tennesseans expect to be treated fairly before the law, and expect their own government to follow it too,” Spring Miller, TIRRC Senior Legal Strategy director, said in the news release.

Requests for comment from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security by The Greeneville Sun were not returned.

A Dec. 8 hearing date in the case has been set in Davidson County Chancery Court.
