text:
On November 16, the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted summary judgment to a coalition of higher education and labor organizations and vacated in its entirety the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS Final Rule that would have replaced “duration of status” with fixed admission periods for F, J, and I nonimmigrants.

The longstanding duration-of-status framework remains in effect. Colleges and universities nationwide may continue to admit, enroll, and advise F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors under the regulations and procedures that applied before the Final Rule, regardless of whether they were plaintiffs in Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. US Department of Homeland Security, No. 1:26-cv-13799-FDS (D. Mass.).

However, the decision remains subject to appellate review, leaving a question open about whether colleges and universities have secured a lasting victory or merely won this round.

Background

On July 17, DHS published a Final Rule titled “Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,” 91 Fed. Reg. 44976. The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15. Among other things, it would have:

Replaced duration-of-status admission with fixed admission periods tied to the length of a student’s or exchange visitor’s program, generally subject to a four-year maximum ;

Required F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors who needed additional time to seek an extension of stay through US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), with approval left to the agency’s discretion and generally without an administrative appeal ;

Restricted academic mobility for F-1 students , prohibit ing graduate-level students from changing educational objectives and, generally, transferring institutions during their programs, subject to limited exceptions, and preventing students from beginning a new program at the same or a lower academic level than a previously completed program ;

Reduced the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 days to 30 days ; and

Limited most I nonimmigrants (foreign information media representatives) to admission periods of no more than 240 days, with a shorter period for certain individuals holding passports issued by the People’s Republic of China.

The coalition of higher education and labor organizations that challenged the rule included the Presidents’ Alliance, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, and several other labor organizations.

On September 14, Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV issued a preliminary injunction postponing the rule’s effective date under Section 705 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The court concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their claim that the rule was arbitrary and capricious. Preliminary relief prevented DHS from implementing the rule while the litigation proceeded, leaving the existing regulatory framework in place nationwide.

The government appealed the preliminary injunction to the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. The parties subsequently returned to the district court on cross-motions for summary judgment.

The court’s decision

On November 16, the court granted the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment and denied the government’s cross-motion. It concluded that the Final Rule was unlawful on two independent grounds: it was arbitrary and capricious under the APA, and its restrictions on F-1 academic mobility exceeded DHS’s statutory authority.

The rule was arbitrary and capricious

The court adopted its earlier analysis from the preliminary injunction decision, concluding that DHS failed to satisfy several fundamental APA requirements. Specifically, DHS failed to:

Conduct a reasoned assessment of the rule’s costs and benefits ;

Establish a rational connection between the rule and its stated objectives of preventing fraud and protecting national security ;

Meaningfully consider less burdensome alternatives that could address the agency’s concerns; and

Provide adequate responses to significant public comments raising substantial concerns about the rule’s effects and implementation.

The court was particularly critical of DHS’s reliance on fraud and national security concerns to justify replacing a longstanding system with fixed admission periods and discretionary extensions. It found that DHS had not adequately explained how requiring an immigration-status review after four years would prevent the types of misconduct it identified, or why the proposed system was preferable to less disruptive alternatives.

DHS failed to account for existing SEVIS tools

The November 16 decision also addressed a specific deficiency in DHS’s consideration of alternatives: its failure to evaluate whether enhanced use of SEVIS could address the agency’s stated concerns.

The court noted that schools participating in the F-1 and J-1 programs already operate under extensive reporting and recordkeeping obligations. Designated school officials (DSOs) and responsible officers (ROs) must provide accurate, complete, and timely information about students and exchange visitors, including changes in academic status and program participation. Schools and program sponsors risk losing their certification or designation if they fail to meet those requirements.

The court also identified several ways DHS already uses SEVIS information to detect potential fraud and abuse. Those efforts include prosecuting “pay-to-stay” schemes, reviewing SEVIS records for potential violations, and running the names of more than one million students through the National Crime Information Center.

DHS argued that SEVIS is a school reporting system, not an immigration-status adjudication system. The court found that explanation insufficient. DHS had not adequately explained how an unreviewable, discretionary renewal process after four years would meaningfully improve fraud detection, or why its benefits would outweigh the substantial costs of abandoning the existing framework.

At a minimum, the court concluded that DHS should have evaluated the costs and benefits of enhancing SEVIS against those of the Final Rule. Its failure to do so provided further support for the conclusion that the rule was arbitrary and capricious.

The rule exceeded DHS’s statutory authority

The court also resolved a question it had reserved at the preliminary injunction stage: whether the Final Rule’s restrictions on academic mobility were consistent with the F-1 statute, 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(F).

That statute defines the F-1 classification to include bona fide students who are qualified to pursue a full course of study and seek to enter the United States temporarily for that purpose. DHS argued that its regulatory authority permitted it to define the types of academic programs that could qualify as an appropriate “course of study.”

The court rejected that interpretation. Relying on Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. US Department of Homeland Security, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), the court explained that although Congress delegated authority to DHS to regulate the time and conditions of nonimmigrants’ stay, those requirements must be reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 visa classification.

The court concluded that the Final Rule’s academic restrictions did not meet that standard. Among other things, the rule would have effectively restricted students from:

Completing extended programs of study, including PhD programs;

Pursuing joint graduate degrees;

Changing their academic concentrations; and

Pursuing a second degree at the same or a lower academic level, including an MBA after completing a JD

The court emphasized that the F-1 program exists to permit and encourage foreign students to pursue educational opportunities in the United States. Restrictions that prevent bona fide students from pursuing legitimate academic programs are not reasonably related to that purpose.

The court vacated the entire Final Rule

Finally, the court rejected DHS’s request to remand the rule to the agency without vacating it. The court explained that vacatur is the standard remedy under the APA and that there was no basis to depart from that remedy here. The existing regulatory framework had been in place for decades, and the Final Rule had never taken effect.

Accordingly, the court vacated the Final Rule in its entirety under 5 U.S.C. § 706.

What this means for your institution

Continue operating under duration of status. The existing regulatory framework remains in effect for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors. Institutions may continue to admit, enroll, and advise students and scholars under the rules and procedures that applied before the Final Rule. The new fixed admission periods and USCIS extension-of-stay process do not apply.

Academic pathways remain available. Institutions may continue to support PhD timelines, joint and dual degrees, changes in academic concentration, transfers, and additional degrees at the same or a lower academic level under existing regulations. These options remain subject to applicable F-1 eligibility, program requirements, and SEVIS reporting obligations; the decision does not eliminate those requirements.

Maintenance of status. Despite this decision, DHS has signal ed an increased focus on maintenance of status, and we expect to see that continue in adjudications of change of status cases for students seeking to transition to other nonimmigrant and immigrant visa statuses, including H-1B. Institutions should remind students of the obligations and requirements of their statuses and the potential for violations to impact their future status options.

Maintain existing SEVIS compliance. The court’s discussion of SEVIS reinforces the importance of the reporting and recordkeeping obligations already imposed on schools and exchange visitor sponsors. Accurate and timely reporting remains essential to maintaining institutional certification and program designation. The decision does not reduce those obligations; it underscores that DHS failed to adequately consider the existing system and potential enhancements to it as alternatives to the Final Rule.

Communicate the changes carefully. Institutions should ensure that international student and scholar offices, admissions personnel, academic leadership, faculty hosts, and affected students understand that the Final Rule has been vacated and that the preexisting duration-of-status framework remains controlling.

Looking ahead

On November 13, the First Circuit placed the government’s appeal of the September 14 preliminary injunction in abeyance for 30 days, while the district court resolved the merits. That appeal may now become moot because the preliminary injunction has been superseded by the final judgment. DHS may separately appeal the November 16 decision and seek a stay. An appeal alone would not automatically reinstate the vacated rule.

Nonetheless, the court’s application of the “reasonably related” standard from Washington Alliance may have implications beyond the duration-of-status rule. In particular, its analysis may inform future challenges to DHS restrictions affecting F-1 students’ academic and practical training opportunities, including the separately pending challenge to the now-enjoined Curricular Practical Training (CPT) broadcast messages.

The merits of the CPT litigation present distinct legal questions, including whether DHS may impose new eligibility requirements through agency guidance without notice-and-comment rulemaking and whether its interpretation is consistent with the existing CPT regulation. The November 16 decision does not resolve those questions, but its discussion of the statutory purpose of the F-1 classification may provide useful context as the court considers DHS’s authority to restrict students’ educational and practical-training opportunities.

text:
President Donald Trump gave his base a shock Sunday, telling

60 Minutes” he’s having second thoughts about his hardball approach to immigration enforcement.

Asked how immigration affected the Republican Party’s midterm performance, he told interviewer Ross Douthat, “I think I got an A-plus for closing up the border.”

But then he said the verdict was mixed, adding: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation or breaking of the law: that was that they came into the country illegally.”

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” he concluded when pressed by Douthat.

“That hurt me.”

Yet two years ago, Trump’s promises to reverse the flood of illegal immigration unleashed by Joe Biden helped him win reelection — and win every battleground state to boot.

And as dismal as last Tuesday’s results were for the GOP, exit polls show voters trusted Republicans more than Democrats on immigration, 45% to 43%.

Republicans were a solid majority — 57% — of those who rated immigration enforcement “crucial” to how they voted.

Those core Republicans won’t reward the president, or the party, for going weak.

But Trump sent another signal shortly after the midterms that ought to reassure immigration hawks when he announced Stephen Miller, a staunch restrictionist, would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

MAGA wasn’t wiped out in last week’s Democratic tsunami — just as Trump wasn’t swept out of public life by the 2020 election.

He knows how to make a comeback, and that’s what he’s planning here.

But it’s a dangerous gambit:

Trump wants to soften his image, and the Republican Party’s, but he has to do it without capitulating to the Democrats, who have not changed a whit since the Biden years.

A smart strategy will be to put the Democrats on the defensive, forcing them to choose between American workers or the companies that employ cheap illegal labor.

If workplace immigration raids trigger bad publicity, there are gentler-seeming yet just as effective ways to go after the boardrooms instead, with high fines and indeed prison terms for executives who break the nation’s immigration and labor laws.

The corporate crooks who profit from illegal immigration aren’t so easily defended by the open-borders left, and if the administration goes after them, it will show voters who is really on the side of American workers — and who’s in bed with big business.

Republicans win when they’re the populist party, as Trump’s reelection and last week’s midterm debacle both illustrated: All the policies Republicans champion have to be framed in populist terms, and the party can’t afford to be seen as corrupt or too tight with Big Tech.

The GOP also can’t afford to seem cruel or racist, and despite what his enemies say about him, Trump has more often than not succeeded in talking about immigration enforcement in ways that appeal to citizens of all ethnic backgrounds.

Midterm voters had qualms about ICE’s enforcement tactics, but Americans still want secure borders, and they want illegal immigrants who commit crimes to be the first to be deported.

The Trump administration can put productive pressure on the Democratic Congress, daring legislators to cut off the forms of enforcement that remain overwhelmingly popular.

Trump today is in the same position Bill Clinton was in after the 1994 midterms, when Democrats suffered an historic wipeout that cost them both the House and Senate.

Clinton looked like he’d be a dead man going into his 1996 reelection battle, but he outmaneuvered the new Republican Congress in the test of wills over the 1995 government shutdown, and voters gave him credit, too, for working with Republicans to pass welfare reform.

He was easily reelected.

Trump won’t be on the ballot in 2028, but the Trump party will be. Republican chances in the next election heavily depend on what the president does from here on out.

He can’t simply trust Democrats to make good on an immigration deal: Ronald Reagan learned that the hard way when he agreed to an amnesty in 1986 on the promise that Democrats in Congress would legislate stronger enforcement.

But Trump can force Congress to make hard choices between legal workers and lawbreaking employers, and he can speak in conciliatory tones even as he puts Democrats in a position of having to reveal their radicalism.

Immigration has always been a winning issue for Trump. Now he needs to make it one for his party as well.

text:
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.

Mohamed Yusuf, 51, suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma.

“It was an incredibly brutal attack,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Tuesday.

She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday.

Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation.

Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said.

The court filing said Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1am on Saturday. His brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like the name Mohamed.

“He was apparently pulled out of the car and was standing there when Patel drove over him and might have circled back and driven over him again,” Moriarty said.

Uber ‘horrified’

Patel’s parents called police for a wellness check after he arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior”, according to the court filing.

When the officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.

Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was”, the filing says.

Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.

Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, that it has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.

Rights advocates have raised concerns about rhetoric against Somali Americans by US President Donald Trump and his allies, and condemned his immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

title: Courts are unhappy with Customs and Border Protection seizing Americans' phones
authors: Matthew Petti, Jacob Sullum, Reem Ibrahim, Josh Pauzé
description:
Legal pressure is building up against Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for its practice of seizing American citizens' electronics without a warrant.
Before it could decrypt the data, Lattarulo sued the government.
The government claims that it seized Lattarulo's phone as part of an investigation into Georges Cote for illegally employing foreigners.
Burroughs ordered the government not to decrypt Lattarulo's data while the case is being litigated.
Although the courts have historically given the government a lot of deference at the border, CBP and other DHS agencies may be overstaying their welcome.
text:
Legal pressure is building up against Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for its practice of seizing American citizens' electronics without a warrant. Last week, Judge Leonie M. Brinkema ruled that the agency was improperly hiding what it did to nurse Muhammad Numaan Imam's electronics. A few days later, Judge Allison D. Burroughs ruled that CBP was likely retaliating against lawyer Andrew Lattarulo by searching his phone.

For years, CBP has claimed the absolute authority to look through all travelers' electronic data as part of its routine search for contraband at the border, where Fourth Amendment privacy protections don't apply. If travelers don't consent to give up their passwords, then agents can simply seize their devices. But the Supreme Court appears interested in hearing a challenge to the electronic border searches, and lower courts also seem increasingly annoyed with the border agency's attitude.

Lattarulo co-owns the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which takes on both personal injury and immigration cases. Last year, while returning from vacation, he passed through CBP preclearance in Aruba, which allows travelers to "cross" the border before stepping onto a plane to America. But at the domestic terminal in Boston Logan International Airport, three CBP officers and a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent pulled Lattarulo aside to seize his phone. The DHS mailed back Lattarulo's phone after downloading all of his data. Before it could decrypt the data, Lattarulo sued the government.

The government claims that it seized Lattarulo's phone as part of an investigation into Georges Cote for illegally employing foreigners. Burroughs, the judge, was not impressed with that explanation. She believes that the DHS is punishing Lattarulo for speaking out on immigrants' rights. After all, law firm partner Audai Cote—who actually oversees employment compliance at the firm and who had received a request for information from the DHS three days earlier—passed through the same airport on the same day with no issue.

The government "provided no evidence that searches of cellphones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here," Burroughs wrote in a ruling on Friday. "The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual."

Burroughs ordered the government not to decrypt Lattarulo's data while the case is being litigated. She didn't immediately rule on Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claims, but suggested that the government overstepped its bounds there, too. "Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo's border crossing (or, more broadly, the government's interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government's border search," she wrote.

At least the government gave a reason for searching Lattarulo. Imam, a psychiatric nurse practitioner from Virginia, has no idea why the CBP seized his electronics last month. CBP officers at Washington-Dulles International Airport told Imam that he had been "flagged" for unnamed reasons during his return from a family vacation to Turkey. They demanded his phone passwords, and Imam said that he legally couldn't hand them over, because his phone had communications with patients and case management software.

"Your lawyer cannot do anything. We are the authorities at the border," one of the officers told Imam before seizing all of his family's electronics, according to the lawsuit.

Imam sued, and the CBP immediately mailed back the electronics, without ever explaining what they were looking for. Brinkema, the judge, ordered the CBP to explain what it did to those electronics before sending them back. The agency is now fighting to keep its answers sealed from both the public and Imam himself, arguing that they involve sensitive information about law enforcement tactics.

"Nearly all of the information the defendants claim is privileged concerns what CBP does when it seizes electronic devices, which the government has routinely disclosed on the public record in other cases," Brinkema wrote in her Tuesday ruling. "That the government has equipment they use to attempt to access and copy the data contained on cellphones and laptops should be of no great surprise to anyone, much less to those who may have something to hide."

She gave the agency one more chance to demonstrate—by Tuesday this week—why she shouldn't unseal most of the information. A day before the deadline, CBP asked for a two-day extension because "this Court's order requires coordination across multiple components of the Department of Homeland Security regarding sensitive law enforcement matters."

Although the courts have historically given the government a lot of deference at the border, CBP and other DHS agencies may be overstaying their welcome. Some of the government's pretexts for hassling travelers have been a little bit too thin, and the government's attempts to avoid giving information make it seem evasive. Trying to seize lawyers' correspondence also raises attorney-client privacy issues beyond the Fourth Amendment—not to mention making a victim out of people that judges are far more likely to identify with.

text:
GEO Group, the private prison company that runs the Delaney Hall Detention Facility in New Jersey as one of dozens of immigration detention centers it operates nationwide, has for months failed to comply with a subpoena issued by New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, a new lawsuit says.

The allegation is laid out in a lawsuit filed Tuesday by Davenport that seeks to compel the company to comply, if a judge deems that it violated the law by failing to respond.

According to the complaint, the New Jersey attorney general's office issued a subpoena to GEO Group in August as part of a probe into the medical treatment ICE detainees are receiving at Delaney Hall. The state is investigating potential civil and constitutional rights violations after at least three people have died at the facility during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

GEO Group failed to comply with the subpoena, claiming that it needed permission from the Department of Homeland Security to do so, the complaint says. Although the state attorney general's office does not believe the company needs DHS' authorization to comply, the AG's office says it has repeatedly asked DHS to do so, according to the complaint.

"These repeated inquiries have been met with silence. Not only has DHS failed to authorize the production of any information, but it has refused even to confirm whether it will or will not authorize GEO Group to produce responsive material," the complaint says.

In a statement, Davenport's office said the failure to comply with the subpoena amounts to "a pattern of stonewalling any efforts to examine conditions inside Delaney Hall."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement, "ICE is regularly audited and inspected by external agencies. ICE is committed to transparency, and the Delaney Hall detention facility complies with all required state and local laws. All detainees are provided with proper meals, quality water, blankets, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers."

text:
A young man brought to a San Francisco emergency department earlier this year by immigration enforcement agents was terrified. His family did not know where he was, and he did not know when he would see them again.

Dr. Francesco Sergi, a resident physician at the University of California, San Francisco who helped care for the man, said medical staff were able to contact his relatives and let them know he was alive and in the hospital. But other patients in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody have not been so lucky, Sergi said, with agents preventing them from contacting family or attorneys, and medical staff having to negotiate with ICE agents to protect patients’ rights.

Sergi was among more than 50 doctors, nurses and immigrant rights advocates who rallied outside a University of California Board of Regents meeting at UCSF in Mission Bay Tuesday morning, demanding that university leaders adopt systemwide policies to better protect patients in ICE custody.

Although state and local laws restrict immigration enforcement in hospitals, ICE agents can still accompany people who are already in their custody to medical appointments under California Senate Bill 81, enacted in September 2025.

But healthcare workers on Tuesday demanded that the UC Board of Regents establish clearer rules to protect staff and patients:

Requiring staff to ask agents to leave during medical exams;

Ensuring patients can communicate with family and lawyers;

Verifying that patients can get follow-up care before they are sent back to detention.

According to Sergi, the UCSF resident physicians participating in Tuesday’s rally have, between them, cared for about 10 patients in ICE custody at San Francisco hospitals over the past year. In some encounters, he said, ICE agents have refused to leave examination rooms, prevented patients from contacting family members or attorneys and pressured doctors to discharge patients before a safe medical discharge plan was in place, he said.

Without clear institutional rules, “a lot of folks are just unsure what to actually do in these contexts,” Sergi said.

Debate over hospital safeguards

Dr. SatKartar Khalsa, a fourth-year emergency medicine resident at San Francisco General Hospital, and a regional vice president of the resident physicians’ union, said existing UC policies largely address cases in which agents enter hospitals to search for someone, rather than when ICE agents bring patients who are already in their custody.

Khalsa said agents have sometimes refused their requests to leave examination rooms, requiring negotiations before they could privately treat patients.

“You can feel it in the air, in the whole floor and the whole hospital when ICE is with a patient,” Khalsa said in an interview on Monday. “It just creates so much fear.”

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for UC Health wrote, “UC is committed to providing safe, compassionate care to every patient, regardless of immigration status.”

The statement says that UC has adopted the California Attorney General’s September 2026 guidelines as systemwide policy, which require hospitals to protect patient information and direct staff to notify administrators and consult legal counsel when immigration agents request access to facilities, patients or medical records.

“Care for patients who arrive in law enforcement custody follows the applicable hospital or clinic procedures,” the statement reads.

The Attorney General’s guidelines address several issues raised by the residents, including patient privacy, communication with family members and attorneys and discharge planning. They direct healthcare workers to request that agents leave during examinations and report refusals to hospital administrators or legal counsel.

But the UC statement did not specify how individual hospitals have implemented those provisions, or whether staff have been trained on them.

The union that represents UC resident physicians has proposed an eight-page “model policy” that would require all hospital staff to ask ICE agents to leave during medical examinations, facilitate confidential communication with relatives and lawyers and prevent ICE agents from making medical decisions for patients.

The proposal goes further than the Attorney General’s guidelines in some respects, requiring written assurances that patients will receive medications and follow-up care before they are returned to immigration detention.

Under the proposal, ICE would have to identify the medical provider responsible for a patient’s subsequent care and provide written assurances that prescribed medications, equipment and follow-up treatment would be available.

The Attorney General’s guidelines require hospitals to make reasonable efforts to confirm that immigration facilities can meet patients’ medical needs, but provide for escalation and documentation when safe discharge cannot be verified. Neither the guidelines, nor the proposed policies, establish how hospitals could compel detention facilities to deliver promised care after patients are transferred.

Statewide push for patient protections

Elsewhere in California, healthcare workers have already pushed for stronger protections for patients.

Los Angeles County hospitals, including L.A. General Medical Center, adopted new policies in March governing the treatment of patients in immigration custody, including protections for patient privacy, and the right to communication with family members and lawyers.

Highland Hospital in Oakland has protocols directing staff to ask immigration agents to leave during medical evaluations, although healthcare workers there have raised concerns that the protocols aren’t being followed consistently.

Some UCSF nurses at Tuesday’s rally, who declined to give their names, also expressed fears for the safety of healthcare workers, citing the case of Ann Lawani, a nurse and professor at the University of San Francisco, who remains in ICE custody following her September arrest at her home in Lodi.

The consequences of ICE presence at hospitals and clinics extend beyond the patients who are already in ICE custody, Khalsa said. They described treating other patients who had put off seeking medical attention for dangerous conditions because they feared being reported to immigration authorities.

“I’ve had several patients that have delayed seeking care because of misconceptions that their presence would be reported to ICE or to the police,” Khalsa said.

They described diabetes patients who required intensive care after they went without insulin, and others whose untreated high blood pressure caused organ damage.

Khalsa and Sergi emphasized that they haven’t witnessed an ICE raid at a hospital, and that patients, no matter their immigration status, should not be afraid to get medical treatment.

“We really want to set limits so that all of our patients can feel safe when they’re accessing care,” Sergi said.

title: ICE Agents Pepper-Spray Pregnant Woman and Throw Her on the Ground
description:
As ICE agents forced their way into her sister-in-law’s vehicle, claiming that she was transporting strangers, Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera Alvarado, started recording.
Moments later, ICE agents can be seen throwing her to the ground on her stomach, and cuffing her hands behind her back.
It’s no secret that ICE agents across the country practice excessive force, warrantless searches and arrests, racial profiling, and wrongful detentions.
This isn’t even the first time an ICE agent has used excessive force on a pregnant woman.
During the agency’s sweeping enforcement operation in Minneapolis earlier this year, ICE agents violently restrained a woman, dragging her through the snow and pinning her face down as onlookers shouted that the woman was pregnant.
text:
A U.S. citizen was pepper-sprayed and thrown on the ground by federal immigration agents on Sunday, even after she warned them that she was pregnant.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade and some of her family members were monitoring federal immigration agents’ activity outside Stanislaus County Jail in Modesto, California, when ICE blocked her sister-in-law Monica Alvarado’s vehicle. As ICE agents forced their way into her sister-in-law’s vehicle, claiming that she was transporting strangers, Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera Alvarado, started recording.

In a video shared with ABC News by Vargas Andrade’s attorney, Patrick Kolasinski, agents can be seen also trying to arrest Vargas Andrade, but she pulls away. One agent is seen deploying pepper spray toward her. “She’s pregnant with child,” her husband can be heard saying.

Moments later, ICE agents can be seen throwing her to the ground on her stomach, and cuffing her hands behind her back.

Vargas Andrade was taken by ICE and detained for several hours before being released, her attorney told ABC News. She visited a hospital, where doctors determined that her baby was unharmed. One other person who was riding in Alvarado’s car was detained by ICE.

ICE has accused Vargas Andrade of assaulting ICE officers, which she denies. So far, no charges have been filed against her.

It’s no secret that ICE agents across the country practice excessive force, warrantless searches and arrests, racial profiling, and wrongful detentions. This isn’t even the first time an ICE agent has used excessive force on a pregnant woman. During the agency’s sweeping enforcement operation in Minneapolis earlier this year, ICE agents violently restrained a woman, dragging her through the snow and pinning her face down as onlookers shouted that the woman was pregnant. Not to mention, many pregnant women in ICE detention suffer from abuse and medical neglect.

Texas GOP Representative Beth Van Duyne thinks that the release of the new iPhone—not a cyberattack—could be responsible for the slew of network outages that have afflicted the U.S. in the month of November.

“We’re getting reports that Apple is now the latest in the list of disruptions after we saw banking and Microsoft, the ground stop.… What is your reaction, and can you give us any more information on the cause of some of these?” Newsmax’s Bianca de la Garza asked Van Duyne, who worked for the Department of Housing and Urban Development in the first Trump administration before being elected to Congress.

“I understand it too. I was on a plane on Friday night and got grounded, and I got sent back, and the next three flights got canceled. So I’m right up there with you,” Van Duyne replied. “People are rightly to be concerned. It seems like there’s a lot of communication missteps that have happened in the last five days.… Let’s not make it seem as if it’s a bigger deal than it is.

“Is it just happens to be happening to Microsoft, and then to Apple? Was it something bigger than that? Is it the fact that we’ve got so many people now that are using, you know, AI, and we don’t have the data capacity to be able to keep up with it?” Van Duyne continued. “They just came out with a new iPhone. What kind of drag is that causing? There could be a lot of causes for it—I would just prepare not to assume it’s the worst.”

Van Duyne’s rambling assertions are baseless, as people using a new iPhone or asking ChatGPT to make them a grocery list should have little to no impact on massive networks that millions of Americans were using every day with few issues before last week. The possibility of a cyberattack is a reasonable question to raise when multiple large banks, Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Security Agency, and several other technology services have all experienced outages in the past few days. A new iPhone entering the market is not.

Whatever the issue was, it appeared to be widespread across multiple products and platforms. People on social media reported problems using their Apple Pay and accessing their iCloud accounts. Apple’s system status webpage showed there were also issues with AppleCare, Apple Business, and the App Store. At Apple stores in New York City and Chicago, employees told NBC News that they had been unable to complete sales or make appointments.

Charles Schwab, a financial services company, said it had resolved an issue that temporarily downed its website Tuesday, just one day after major banks such as JP Morgan Chase and Bank of America were hit by outages.

Gmail also appeared to experience an outage Tuesday, according to Downdetector, which tracks problems with widely used technology platforms.

Last week, Microsoft Outlook, Workday, and the Federal Aviation Administration all had mysterious service outages. On Monday, major banks experienced problems. Earlier Tuesday, the system that the National Security Agency uses for internal communications also went down.

If people are looking to the Trump administration for answers, they may want to look elsewhere. Speaking on Fox News Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he was 98 percent sure that these outages weren’t the results of cyberattacks, but rather than provide answers, he simply spun his own theories. And days after the national aviation ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that he still doesn’t have any “clarity” on what caused the problem.

A proposal from the Census Bureau could exclude as many as 38 million people from the population count, a new report from the Coalition on Human Needs finds.

The Commerce Department, which runs the census, put forward a new rule in September that would change how people are counted for the 2030 census. This would erase most noncitizens from the population count for the first time in the survey’s history.

Under this potential new rule, instead of someone’s “usual residence” being the place where they “live and sleep most of the time,” it would instead be defined as the place “consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records.”

This would exclude not only most noncitizen immigrants but people with an annual household income lower than a certain federal threshold, who are not required to file federal income taxes. People who don’t file taxes make up a staggering 11.5 percent of the population, according to the report: around 38 million people.

Previously, Republicans have tried to exclude immigrants from the population count, contending that Democrats benefit from counting noncitizens because their states tend to have larger immigrant populations. If a large number of immigrants were excluded from the count, this would also affect the distribution of the Electoral College.

But this proposal would impact tens of millions of people independent of immigration status.

In addition to the 38 million people who don’t file taxes, the Coalition on Human Needs report found that as many as 30 million people “had no matching addresses between the IRS records and the 2020 Census.” Altogether, the proposal risks missing a whopping 20 percent of the U.S. population.

“Overall, this proposal is so broken, you can’t even tell which 20 percent of the country is going to be left out,” Christopher Kang, executive director of the Coalition on Human Needs, told Talking Points Memo.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked for $50 billion after the Federal Aviation Administration spontaneously grounded thousands of planes on Friday and disrupted many more flights, painting the enormous cash allowance as the necessary solution to the agency’s alleged infrastructure woes. But the fine print of that request, which was made public Tuesday, has raised some eyebrows.

A joint letter signed by the FAA, the office of the president, and the Transportation Department breaks down the budget request into multiple line items. It includes $10 billion to improve or entirely reconstruct five air traffic control centers, and another $10 billion for constructing or improving up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.

The letter also reinforces requests laid out by Senator Eric Schmitt in September, when the Missouri Republican floated a $30 billion FAA investment that included $10 billion to “modernize” air traffic control systems (including $7.2 billion to automate work stations and common platforms, and $2 billion for cloud computing), $10 billion for other airport improvements, and another $10 billion to update terminals at “high-impact transitional hub airports.”

It was not clear if the round numbers were based on actual cost estimates, or if Duffy was pitching the massive budget request as a shot in the dark. PBS Newshour’s Lisa Desjardins highlighted the odd price tags, noting that one bullet-pointed necessity in the letter—a $2 billion Air Traffic Route Control Center—would cost about as much as a Navy missile destroyer.

She also questioned why the administration would prioritize expenditures on airports if the situation affecting the nation’s air traffic control system was as severe as described.

text:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this month in San Diego has been released, according to an advocacy group and the boy's school.

"School leadership, and counselors had a meeting with the student when he returned to school this morning to ensure he had all the supports he and his family needed, and then he went off to class," the San Diego Unified School District said in a statement.

Haitian Bridge Alliance, which had advocated for the boy's release, said it welcomed the development.

"An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love—not in immigration detention," said Guerline Jozef, executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, in a statement. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry."

The Department of Homeland Security previously confirmed that ICE agents placed the child in federal care on Nov. 5 after he attended a check-in appointment with a man the agency said claimed to be the boy's uncle.

Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy, a third grader, has been living with relatives since his father was deported in 2025. In August of this year, following a legal victory for the Trump administration, some 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S. lost Temporary Protected Status, stripping them of deportation protections and work permits.

Advocates recorded and documented the moment when the 8-year-old was escorted by at least one ICE agent inside the Edward J. Schwartz building in San Diego, with Haitian Bridge Alliance saying the detention left the boy's cousins "in tears."

DHS said at the time that the agents designated the child an unaccompanied minor because "the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor."

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," DHS added.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement is an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services that is responsible for housing minors who lack a valid immigration status and who are taken into custody without their parents or legal guardians.

Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a previous statement that "when parents are taken into custody by ICE, they are not provided an opportunity to return home to see their children or to be able to transfer guardianship."

"ICE just incarcerated then deported without taking into account the wellbeing of the children left behind," it said.

title: DACA Update: Texas Attorney General Election Creates Uncertainty Regarding DACA Work Benefits
description:
Quick Hits DACA work benefits in Texas could depend on decisions by the incoming Texas attorney general to continue or withdraw from ongoing DACA litigation.

However, the Fifth Circuit Court limited potential remedies, including the termination of DACA work benefits, to the State of Texas.
(Please see our earlier article, “DACA Expected to Reopen: What Employers Need to Know About the Latest Legal Shift.”) The Texas Attorney General Election and a Review of Pending Litigation Texas voters recently elected Nathan Johnson as the state’s next attorney general, with the new attorney general entering office in January 2027.

text:
Quick Hits

DACA work benefits in Texas could depend on decisions by the incoming Texas attorney general to continue or withdraw from ongoing DACA litigation.

A federal judge’s decision on DACA termination in Texas remains pending, and the federal judge could issue a decision before the new Texas attorney general takes office, which could lead to further appeals.

Texas’s incoming attorney general has promised to review ongoing litigation involving Texas and has not confirmed continuing or withdrawing from ongoing DACA litigation, creating some uncertainty on continued or terminated DACA work benefits in Texas.

Where the DACA Litigation Stands With the State of Texas

In 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that DACA program protections against deportation and authorizing work benefits were unlawful. However, the Fifth Circuit Court limited potential remedies, including the termination of DACA work benefits, to the State of Texas. Right now, the litigants are awaiting a U.S. district judge’s implementing order on the final scope of DACA termination, which would implement the circuit court’s ruling in a final decision. (Please see our earlier article, “DACA Expected to Reopen: What Employers Need to Know About the Latest Legal Shift.”)

The Texas Attorney General Election and a Review of Pending Litigation

Texas voters recently elected Nathan Johnson as the state’s next attorney general, with the new attorney general entering office in January 2027. In public interviews, Johnson has promised a thorough review of ongoing litigation involving the State of Texas. He has confirmed an intent to strictly scrutinize ongoing “showpiece” litigation in the Texas Attorney General’s Office that he would consider not in the state’s interest to continue. However, the attorney general–elect has not identified specific areas of litigation or specific lawsuits that will receive higher scrutiny in making future litigation decisions.

Until Texas Attorney General–Elect Johnson confirms an intention to continue or withdraw from Texas’s ongoing litigation requesting DACA program termination, the timing of a final decision involving continued or terminated DACA work benefits will be uncertain. The attorney general–elect may withdraw Texas from ongoing DACA litigation, or, if the federal judge issues a decision on DACA’s termination before the new attorney general takes office, the new attorney general may not continue the litigation on appeal. While Texas’s future litigation posture is uncertain at present, it is unlikely that the attorney general–elect would continue federal litigation requesting DACA termination.

Looking Ahead

A federal judge’s ruling on the scope and terms of the DACA program’s termination could have an immediate impact on Texas workforces. While a decision to terminate DACA work benefits could be stayed pending appeal or motion for reconsideration, the ruling could be given immediate effect and require prompt action by Texas employers related to their employees who are DACA beneficiaries. Texas employers should remain aware that Texas’s litigation position could change next year, depending on the new attorney general’s decision to continue or withdraw from the DACA litigation. As a result of the recent election, a final resolution on DACA work benefits for Texas employees could take some time.

For now, Texas employers may want to consider the following:

continuing to accept unexpired employment authorization documents (EADs) held by DACA recipients (Category (c)(33));

tracking EAD expiration dates and reminding employees to apply for renewals 120 to 150 days prior to expiration; and

monitoring the litigation involving DACA termination, as a ruling terminating DACA work benefits could require immediate action by employers.

Ogletree Deakins’ Immigration Practice Group will continue to monitor developments and provide updates on the Immigration and Texas blogs as additional information becomes available.

title: ICE making unlawful warrantless arrests in Virginia, lawsuit says - The Virginian-Pilot
description:

He is one of six people and a Virginia immigrant-services organization suing the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, accusing federal immigration officers of making unlawful arrests across the state.

text:
A Newport News man said he was driving to work when federal immigration officers stopped his car and handcuffed him.

He said the officers never asked about his immigration status or showed him a warrant. He was taken to an ICE office in Norfolk.

He is one of six people and a Virginia immigrant-services organization suing the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, accusing federal immigration officers of making unlawful arrests across the state.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in federal court in Alexandria, argues ICE has routinely made arrests without warrants and without determining whether the people being detained were likely to flee before officers could obtain one. Federal law allows immigration officers to make warrantless arrests only when they have probable cause to believe someone is in the country illegally and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

The complaint alleges that ICE has abandoned safeguards meant to ensure officers make that determination on a case-by-case basis. DHS did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit.

“ICE agents are arresting people first and assuming they’ll figure out a reason to justify it later, flagrantly ignoring federal law that’s been in place for decades,” said American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia Senior Supervising Attorney Sophia Gregg.

The Newport News man, Alvaro Alvarez Flores, said the encounter happened July 13. After officers stopped him, he showed them a valid Virginia driver’s license. When asked where he was from, he said Mexico.

He told officers his sister and brother-in-law, both of whom are U.S. citizens, lived nearby. But he was handcuffed and taken to the Norfolk ICE office after officers drove around with him for about two hours.

During the drive, the complaint alleges, an officer read license plate numbers of passing vehicles over the radio. After receiving names from the database, the officer reportedly rejected some drivers because their names did not sound Hispanic. The officers eventually stopped another vehicle and detained its occupants, who also appeared to be Latino, according to the lawsuit.

Another plaintiff, Britney Ramirez Corona, an 18-year-old U.S. citizen from Norfolk, said she was detained while trying to retrieve a vehicle after an earlier immigration arrest. She repeatedly told officers she was a U.S. citizen and had identification in her wallet, the complaint says.

The lawsuit describes several other arrests in Virginia, including people who were detained while driving or attending community events.

At the center of the case is an ICE policy issued in January by then-acting Director Todd Lyons. The plaintiffs argue the policy broadly defines when someone is likely to flee, allowing officers to make warrantless arrests without considering individual circumstances such as family, employment and ties to the community.

The complaint also says ICE moved away from safeguards established in 2021 after an earlier lawsuit challenging warrantless arrests.

The plaintiffs are seeking class-action status and asking a judge to block the agency from continuing the alleged practice. The complaint cites a separate report estimating that ICE made more than 15,000 arrests in Virginia since January 2025.

Emma Rose Brown, emma.brown@virginiamedia.com

Reed College participated in the successful legal challenge through the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration.
“This decision is a victory for international students, for Reed, and for higher education across the country,” said Reed College President Audrey Bilger.

text:
Reed College joined a successful legal challenge to a federal rule that would have imposed new restrictions on international students and scholars.

By Sheena McFarland

November 17, 2026

A federal court has struck down a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule that would have imposed new limits on how long international students and exchange visitors could remain in the United States. Reed College participated in the successful legal challenge through the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration.

The US District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the rule in its entirety, preserving the longstanding “Duration of Status” framework that allows international students and exchange visitors to remain in the country for the duration of their academic programs or exchange activities, provided they maintain their immigration status.

The rule would have replaced that framework with fixed admission periods of no more than four years, requiring students whose programs extended beyond their authorized stay to apply for extensions. It also would have restricted students’ ability to transfer institutions, change educational objectives, or pursue additional programs of study.

“This decision is a victory for international students, for Reed, and for higher education across the country,” said Reed College President Audrey Bilger. “International students are vital to the intellectual and cultural life of our campus. They bring perspectives, experiences, and ideas that challenge assumptions, deepen learning, and strengthen our entire community. We are at our best when we welcome talented students and scholars from around the world and give them the freedom and stability to pursue their education.”

Reed participated in the lawsuit as a declarant through the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a coalition of US college and university leaders that Reed joined in 2018. The coalition argued that the rule would create uncertainty and administrative burdens for international students and institutions, disrupt academic plans, and make it more difficult for US colleges and universities to attract international talent.

The court found that DHS had acted arbitrarily and capriciously by failing to adequately assess the rule’s costs and benefits, justify its changes, consider less burdensome alternatives, or meaningfully respond to public comments. The court also ruled that restrictions on academic studies exceeded DHS's statutory authority.

The decision builds on Reed's ongoing advocacy for international students and scholars. In April 2025, Reed joined 86 institutions and associations in supporting an amicus brief in AAUP v. Rubio, challenging federal actions involving visa revocations, detentions, and deportations of noncitizen students and scholars.

The latest ruling preserves a framework that provides international students with greater stability as they pursue their education and underscores Reed's commitment to an academic community strengthened by the exchange of ideas and perspectives from around the world.

The other organizations that filed the challenge alongside the Presidents’ Alliance in the challenge are NAFSA: Association of International Educators; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts; the American Federation of Teachers; Graduate Labor Organization, AFT Local 6516; the International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America; United Auto Workers Local 2322; and the NewsGuild-CWA. The plaintiffs are represented by McDermott Will & Schulte.

More information about the ruling is available on the Presidents’ Alliance website.

text:
A battle is raging between local activists and the tiny town of Hudson over ICE detention facilities, highway signs and marching bands.

Back in October, members of the No Concentration Camps in Colorado group cleaned up a stretch of Highway 52 just outside Hudson. The group was acting under the Colorado Department of Transportation’s (CDOT) Adopt-A-Highway program. The idea was simple: clean up a portion of the highway a few times a year and have a sign with the group’s name plastered on it just a few miles from a proposed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center.

Hudson fired back quickly, trying to stop CDOT from putting up the sign. Tensions rose for a few weeks, and CDOT ultimately sided with the group, but the war is still ongoing in the town of around 2,000 residents.

It raises the almost-impossible question: What the hell is going on in Hudson?

Adoption application

Jeff Akkerman and a couple of dozen other members of No Concentration Camps in Colorado spent all day on Oct. 24 cleaning up sections of Highway 52 and Interstate 76 outside Hudson. According to Akkerman, it was a plain affair. They stayed quiet, cleaned and left. The wait for the group’s highway signs commenced.

When he received an email directly from CDOT, his heart sank. It said his and the group’s efforts were worthless. The department revoked the adoption and claimed that the volunteers had broken Rule 4 of the Adopt-A-Highway program, according to emails obtained by Westword.

“While performing activities on right-of-way, the method, manner, and appearance of the participants will not in any way distract, disrupt, or adversely affect traffic,” reads the rule. “Participants may not display messages, carry banners, or advertise their business affiliation or cause.”

But Akkerman was confused. The group had discussed ad nauseam that they could not break any rules or do anything to disrupt drivers while cleaning the roadsides.

“We weren’t going to have any signs or protests or anything. And so I was like, ‘Did somebody do something without knowing?’ I didn’t think they would,” he says.

Then it clicked. The email notifying him of the broken rule was sent on Oct. 22, but he didn’t read it until after they did the work on Oct. 24. So Akkerman received the email two days before the group even went out to clean. He filed a Colorado Open Records Act request for any CDOT correspondence on the issue. He received a collection of emails between Hudson officials and the state department.

On Oct. 21, Hudson Town Councilmember and Mayor Pro-Tem Don Post asked if it was allowed to have “political messaging” on state-sponsored road signs. Town Manager Bryce Lange also claimed that the group’s name was a political statement on its own, according to the emails.

“What options, if any, does the Town have to formally object to the wording or request reconsideration?” Lange asked CDOT.

Councilmember Matt Cole then emailed CDOT on Oct. 22, writing verbatim:

“We have found out that couple spots of hwy 52 was adopted by a group. This group is a group or the group of protestors that have been costing problems in Hudson protesting the I.C.E detention center. One of my biggest concerns is them out there with protest signs while they are doing their clean-up events. Which I believe is against CDOT policy. And the Cdot blue adopts Signs they show on a FB page I believe would give a bad political view of local government and cdot supporting them, which should not be the case.”

CDOT responded for a few emails, talking as if the group had (or planned to) clean up with protest signs, breaking the aforementioned rule.

Akkerman theorizes that CDOT had misunderstood Cole’s email, believing the group to have already broken the rules (two days before, mind you). But he questions how the email was written in the first place.

“If you read (Cole’s) email, I don’t know if this was intentional on his part or not; there are some really interesting spelling and other kinds of mistakes,” Akkerman tells Westword. “So it could have just been a mistake in the tenses that he used, or it could have been intentionally malicious, trying to make it sound as though we had already done so… CDOT read that, thought we had done so, and so they contacted me and let me know that our agreement had been canceled.”

But CDOT had made another mistake. The department reached back out to the group and said Adopt-A-Highway locations cannot be in areas with speeds of 65 mph or higher. The spot the group had cleaned and adopted was above that, so it was canceled again. But CDOT eventually came back around at the beginning of November, retracting the cancellation over “breaking policy” and allowing the adopted sign to be put in a slower section of Highway 52.

“CDOT’s been really helpful, to be honest with you,” says Dorian Gray, founder of No Concentration Camps in Colorado. Yes, his name is a pseudonym.

He continues: “The person who was handling it was out of town, so a different person grabbed it, all sorts of stuff. And I mean, I also don’t fault CDOT for listening to and believing elected members of municipal governments. It seemed like the Hudson Town Council member was aware and communicating that they were filing a complaint, but that we weren’t out there until the 24th.”

CDOT tells Westword that it “briefly paused” the agreement to look into the concerns raised by the Hudson councilmembers. CDOT officials talked to the group and clarified their intentions, going forward with the adoption on a safer portion of the highway from mile markers 29 to 31.

“CDOT cannot interfere with which organizations partner with Adopt A Highway, regardless of the cause, as long as they are in compliance with CDOT policies,” a representative with the department told the town.

But even with the mess-up, the question still remains: Why are Hudson officials so against the group?

Now here’s your sign

No Concentration Camps in Colorado and Hudson’s rocky relationship stem from last summer. Gray started the group after the ACLU released information regarding ICE’s planned expansions under the Big Beautiful Bill. Gray then created a list of demands for Governor Jared Polis regarding limiting ICE expansion. He went to local organizations and got around 35 nonprofits to sign the demand letter.

That was just the start of No Concentration Camps in Colorado — a sort of guerrilla group that does extensive research into ICE, including a map of all “black sites,” or extended holding cells, in the country.

“I think that the rule of law should be followed,” Gray says. “I think other people, any American who believes in our Constitution, should take issue with the extrajudicial practices of ICE and the extrajudicial practice of administrative detention in general, where a person is not being charged with any crime, doesn’t have a sentence to serve, and is just being put in prison.”

The group caught wind of Hudson’s ongoing plan to create a 1,200-bed immigration detention facility at the former Hudson Correctional Facility, which was once a prison for the Alaska Department of Corrections. According to a lawsuit filed by the Colorado Attorney General’s Office against ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the government signed a five-year contract worth more than $500 million with the GEO Group to renovate and operate the site on July 9. It’ll be known as the Big Horn facility.

GEO Group is the same private prison corporation that runs the Aurora ICE facility. You know, the one that the Attorney General’s office sued over its alleged failure to comply with a state public health order after a tuberculosis outbreak at the facility in August.

The group began protesting town council meetings over a year ago. They pleaded with the council to vote against the zoning of the facility. The area is currently zoned industrial, and the town must vote on an exemption to rezone it for incarceration. The town has not opted to go against the facility.

“At a recent council meeting, they blamed us for costing them $40,000,” Akkerman says. “And the only thing I can think is that it’s covering all the police officers — the extra police officers that they’ve been hiring to harass us.”

Akkerman claims that the town has closed off benches outside the town hall and increased police activity, especially after adding local activist marching band, Notes of Dissent, to the mix.

Notes of Dissent plays music outside the town hall to raise awareness of the issue. They even march down streets, passing out fliers and playing music to let residents know what is going on.

“That first protest, I think, did stir some anxiety in the town council because there was such an overwhelming number of people. It got a little rowdy, frankly. People were banging on the glass,” says Allie Chilton, a member of the protest band. “They have been forced to be more transparent about what’s playing out. Now they haven’t actually taken any action to stop it, but there have been some small victories and some small indications that they’re listening.”

Furthermore, the Attorney General’s Office filed a lawsuit against DHS and ICE requiring an environmental impact assessment before the contract could go forward. Nonprofit Together Colorado also sued the department over the zoning changes, claiming GEO Group would need to hold public hearings before changing the zoning to allow incarceration.

“Let’s be honest about this,” DHS said in a statement to 9News back in September. “This isn’t about the environment. It’s about trying to stop President Trump from making America safe again. The left didn’t care about the mountains of litter that illegal aliens dumped on ranches and riverbeds during Biden’s border crisis. They’re feigning concern now because they want those same illegal aliens to stay forever — and vote here as well.”

Akkerman theorizes that Hudson officials may also have a direct conflict of interest.

“Mayor Joe Hammock works at a prison in Denver, and a long time ago he worked at the prison in Hudson,” he says. “Now he has a much longer commute. We think maybe he wants to work right there in town, in his backyard, instead of having to drive down to Hudson again.”

Westword reached out to Hudson officials regarding the facility, next steps and potential conflicts of interest. They did not respond.

“It highlights a microcosm of just what corruption in the United States looks like: how the interests of private prisons leech their way into everything, even small local politics in Hudson, Colorado, which seems so innocuous, so inconsequential to the rest of the world,” Gray says.

Gray continues that private prison companies come into small towns and promise them new jobs and increasing tax revenue. He calls the detention centers “pain factories.”

“The second they stop making money, they’re gone,” he says. “And if anybody thinks that these migrant detention centers are meant to be long-term at this capacity, then I don’t think they understand what deportation is. It’s not sustainable.”

The fight continues

It hasn’t just been protesting at town council meetings, though. Both Akkerman and Gray say they have been trying to integrate themselves with the community, canvassing to speak to residents and even holding diaper and food drives for residents.

The group has heard some feedback that they’re outsiders, just coming in to disrupt the little town, so they’ve been allegedly making an effort to help out.

“This facility is going to impact a lot more people than just Hudson,” Akkerman says. “We’re not telling them how to micromanage their little town of Hudson, but this facility has very far-reaching impacts. And them saying that we’re not residents of Hudson and that it shouldn’t be our issue is kind of silly to say that. It does impact lots of people.”

And how have the residents felt? Are they on their side?

“The divides are very real,” Gray says. “There are a lot of people who feel like they have nothing better to do. Sometimes they even know this is immoral, but if it’s between doing something immoral and putting food on the table, then they’re going to choose to feed their families.”

He says others have been afraid to speak out, even providing statements for them to read to the council on their behalf.

Still, the group believes this is a humanitarian issue, not just a Hudson issue, so they continue to fight against the facility.

“It’ll be easier to stop before it becomes fully functional, but the fight continues regardless of whether we’re able to lobby the government of Hudson to stop it before it opens,” Chilton says. “We all work together, but we are stretched thin, and we need more people to get involved, and all it requires is showing up and plugging in.”

text:
State officials say federal authorities have not answered questions about a $31.8 million contract tied to the warehouse.

State officials are accusing federal immigration authorities of stonewalling their requests for information about a planned detention center in Roxbury. State officials have threatened further court action if the situation doesn’t change.

The Department of Homeland Security, which bought a 470,000-square-foot warehouse off Route 46 in February, agreed to halt all conversion work at the site and conduct an environmental assessment under the National Environmental Policy Act after the state and Roxbury sued to block the project.

But state officials say recent actions by DHS, including processing detainees in the warehouse parking lot and signing a $31.8 million contract for the site with a Tennessee-based firm, have raised questions about whether the agency is complying with the agreement.

“Defendants may not commit resources to work that would convert the warehouse site into a detention center without first conducting the required environmental reviews,” state Attorney General Jennifer Davenport wrote in a nine-page joint status report filed Nov. 16 in U.S. District Court.

“But if defendants have already committed resources to converting the facility, then any forthcoming [environmental assessment] will be mere window dressing for a decision that has already been made — subjecting plaintiffs to a wide range of infrastructure, environmental, and public health harms without the required review,” Davenport wrote.

In a brief reply, attorneys from the Department of Justice wrote that federal officials hired the firm to maintain the property, design ICE’s preferred plan for converting the warehouse into a detention center, and conduct the environmental review.

Federal officials told state and local officials that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to renovate the warehouse for some level of detention capacity, among other uses, in accordance with the court order.

Immigration authorities are still working on fulfilling the state’s request to review the contract in time to submit a court-mandated status report, according to the status report.

The filing means that the state and federal governments remain deadlocked over the controversial proposal to build a detention center that would house somewhere between 500 and 1,500 detainees in the Morris County town.

Questions also remain about whether DHS is complying with a May court order barring work to convert the warehouse into a detention center until an environmental review is completed and state and local officials have a chance to challenge the findings.

After the order was issued, federal officials told the court that DHS had decided not to pursue a detention center on the property, which the government bought for $129.3 million. But two weeks later, the agency reversed itself and said administrators had not yet decided what they wanted to do.

Roxbury, a Republican-dominated town, joined the state’s March lawsuit to block the project after residents and activists raised concerns about the proposed detention center. The suit accused ICE officials of ignoring federal laws requiring environmental reviews and consultations with state and local governments before moving ahead with plans.

Some residents and activists have pushed township officials to do more. Protesters disrupted last week’s Roxbury Township Council meeting and called on officials to do more to stop the detention center. One activist accused council members of doing only the minimum necessary to enforce the court order. Mayor Shawn Potillo defended the township’s response, saying local officials oppose the project and are fighting it in court.

Under a May consent order, ICE said it would do only basic maintenance and security work until the environmental review is complete and the other conditions of the order are met.

But ICE officials later admitted that agents from its Newark Enforcement and Removal Operations Field Office brought 14 undocumented immigrants to the warehouse on two occasions after raids in Dover and Ledgewood. The activity stopped only after the field office director told underlings to end the practice.

State and local officials have repeatedly asked to review the multimillion-dollar contract, as well as information about ICE’s activities at the site. State officials first requested a copy of the contract Nov. 6 and sought additional clarification Nov. 10. Federal officials agreed to provide it, but state officials had not received the contract when the status report was filed.

The defendants, including ICE, DHS and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have yet to answer other questions about the contract and their activities at the warehouse, according to the attorney general.

Federal attorneys disputed the state’s characterization of their response, saying they answered an initial request for information about the contract within three hours.

“Although defendants have denied holding individuals inside the warehouse and have represented that they will no longer use the warehouse site in connection with enforcement actions, they still have not answered questions plaintiffs raised more than three weeks ago about how long and where the detainees were held at the site,” Davenport wrote.

The attorney general said the state may seek a court conference if federal officials fail to provide the contract or answer questions about whether they are complying with the May order. But she said there’s no need to set a new court schedule for a possible renewed preliminary injunction motion until federal officials finish the environmental review.

“The parties can propose a schedule for future proceedings, including any renewed preliminary injunction motion, if and when an [environmental assessment] is completed,” Davenport said.
