On October 5, 2026, the Association of American Universities (AAU), Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM) filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in response to the two SEVP broadcast messages the agency sent in late August, which suddenly and without explanation, changed the eligibility requirements for F-1 Curricular Practical Training (CPT) that the federal government had endorsed for more than 35 years. See both SEVP emails and more details about the impact of these messages in ISSO news. The lawsuit essentially claims that SEVP was effecting regulatory-level changes without following the standard federal rulemaking process.

On November 6, 2026, a hearing on the plaintiffs’ motions for stay and preliminary injunction was held, the court heard from both parties and took the oral arguments and written filings under consideration.

On November 17, 2026, the court granted both the motion for a preliminary injunction and the motion for stay of agency action in accordance with the following order:

The plaintiffs’ motion for a stay pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 705 is GRANTED. SEVP’s Broadcast Messages of August 12, 2026, and August 24, 2026, are STAYED, such that those broadcasts may not be enforced or applied pending judicial review.

The plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction under Federal Rule Civil Procedure 65(a) is GRANTED. The defendants, as well as their agents and anyone acting in concert or participation with them, are ENJOINED from implementing, enforcing, or otherwise carrying out the new interpretation of CPT eligibility set forth in SEVP’s Broadcast Messages of August 12, 2026 and August 24, 2026 as to the plaintiffs and each of their members, including their members’ employees and students, both prospectively and with respect to conduct and approvals that occurred prior to the issuance of those broadcasts.

This ruling also referenced the email disclaimers, which state that broadcasts are not “a rule or a final action by SEVP” and “may not be relied upon to create any right or benefit” as such language is not dispositive—particularly where the guidance adopts a concrete interpretation of a regulation, with immediate consequences, and contains “commands” and “orders” which are contrary to established approach and that “SEVP cannot escape judicial review under the APA by simply including these disclaimers”.

What’s Next:

Both forms of judicial relief are preliminary and do not constitute a final resolution of the litigation. The ISSO will continue to follow the progress of the litigation and update the community.

The ISSO team will continue to collaborate with academic stakeholders, the Office of General Counsel to draft and disseminate updated guidance for program directors to consider when effecting academic curricular changes that involve training requirements such as practicums, clinical rotations, internships and/or other experiential training opportunities.

text:
Some countries in the European Union, the EU, which have long struggled with illegal immigration issues, have agreed to a plan to establish a “refugee deportation hub” in Rwanda, Africa. They aim to create temporary facilities to accommodate immigrants whose entry to Europe has been denied, but concerns about human rights violations have also been raised.

The governments of Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece, and the Netherlands held a press conference in Vienna, Austria, on the 16th, local time, announcing, “We have decided to establish a ‘repatriation center’ in Rwanda to deport immigrants whose asylum applications have been rejected.” At this facility, immigrants can choose to return to their home countries, settle in Rwanda, or move to a third country where they have legal residency status.

Amid growing anti-immigration sentiment in countries ahead of elections, the five governments are being evaluated for taking preemptive measures. In 2025, the five countries received 206,500 asylum applicants, accounting for over 30% of the EU’s total. However, out of the 491,950 immigrants ordered to leave the EU last year, only 135,460 were actually deported outside the EU.

The pilot facility will initially accommodate 100 people. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen stated, “This measure will be a game-changer in combating illegal immigration,” adding, “It will dismantle the business models of human traffickers and restore control over our borders.” So far, 19 out of the 27 EU member states have expressed support for the establishment of such repatriation facilities, while France and Spain oppose the plan on humanitarian grounds.

The press conference was also attended by Vincent Biruta, Rwanda’s Minister of Home Affairs. He stated, “We will provide a ‘second chance’ to those who do not have the right to stay in Europe.” The five governments plan to pay Rwanda for the relocation costs. Rwanda is interpreted as aiming to gain diplomatic and economic benefits, such as various investments and aid, by cooperating with Western countries.

However, 47 European human rights organizations have called for the withdrawal of the plan, stating, “This is about establishing a ‘refugee camp’ in Rwanda, a country with ongoing human rights abuse controversies.” Amnesty International’s Austrian branch criticized, “Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible,” adding, “A dark era that severely violates human rights is approaching.” France’s Le Monde commented, “This marks a departure from the ‘principles of hospitality and protection,’ which have been Europe’s ideal since World War II.”

Legal controversies may also arise. The UK signed an agreement with Rwanda in 2022 to send illegal immigrants to Rwanda. However, the following year, the UK Supreme Court ruled it illegal, stating, “Rwanda is not a safe third country for immigrants, and there is a risk they could be transferred to countries where they face persecution again.”

The New York Times (NYT) reported, “European politicians are under pressure to present solutions to the immigration issue,” adding, “The pressure is intensifying as hard-right forces are capitalizing on the public’s fears regarding immigration.”

text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) led a group of Democrats in a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Director David Venturella urging them to release the Guerrero-Germán family from the Dilley Detention Center.

Joining Congresswoman Escobar (in alphabetical order) are Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-7), Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (IL-4), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Al Green (TX-9), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Summer Lee (PA-12), Stephen Lynch (MA-8), Christian Menefee (TX-18), Emily Randall (WA-6), Linda Sanchez (CA-39), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Juan Vargas (CA-52), and Representatives-Elect Leticia Gutierrez (TX-9) and Katy Padilla-Stout (TX-23).

The full letter can be found here or below:

Secretary Mullin and Acting Director Venturella:

I am writing with an urgent plea regarding Michell Germán and her family, who are currently being held at the South Texas Family Residential Center, also known as Dilley Detention Center (Dilley), in Dilley, Texas.

The Guerrero-Germán family, originally from Venezuela, have been residents of El Paso, Texas for several years after being paroled into the United States and pursuing an asylum determination. Parents Pablo Jose Guerrero-Pimentel and Dolores Emilia Zarraga-Colina, along with daughters Michell Germán and her 11-year-old sister were detained on October 22, 2026 in El Paso. The family was apprehended by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) during what ICE referred to as “targeted enforcement arrests” in a statement to local news outlet KVIA. In that same statement, ICE claims that neither parent has “documentation to remain in the U.S. legally”.

However, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, a lawyer for the family, shared in a statement to El Paso Matters that the family is in “valid immigration proceedings, has a lawyer and work permits, and no criminal record”. The detention has impacted the entire family and “traumatized” the two girls.

Michell is a star student at El Paso High School, where she’s enrolled in the school’s Center for Career and Technology Education Program studying cosmetology. Social and outgoing, Michell is a member of the Tigerettes, the school’s dance team, has a part-time job, and volunteers with seniors in the El Paso community. Earlier in the schoolyear, Michell was part of the school’s Homecoming Parade and crowned Lady-in-Waiting.

During her time at El Paso High School, Michell has created a close-knit community of friends who clearly value her and her family. Classmates share that Michell is reliable and trustworthy, and that shows up for her friends. In an interview with El Paso Matters, a friend describes Michell and her family as “incredible people” with good hearts.

When Michell was unable to join her classmates in being honored at Senior Night as a result of being detained by ICE. When her name was called to step out onto the football field at the school stadium, her friends carried a poster of her onto the field to cheers and applause from classmates and families in the stands. Michell should have been on the field among her friends, but was instead sitting over 500 miles away, in detention at Dilley.

Dilley Detention Center was closed in 2024, but reopened in 2025 by the second Trump administration as they began detaining families as part of the President’s mass deportation campaign. In a ProPublica article titled “The Children of Dilley” and published on February 9, 2026, mothers and children detained at Dilley shared several concerns about the conditions at the facility. Parents and children shared instances of mold and worms in food, and drinking water that made people feel ill. Mothers shared that conditions at the facility are so dire, that some children developed suicidal ideation and attempted self-harm. Parents and children alike described insufficient medical care at Dilley, including children with medical complaints frequently experiencing delays, dismissals, or lack of follow-up from on-site medical staff.

I urge you to release Michell German and her family from Dilley Detention Center. They should be allowed to continue pursuing their asylum case at home in El Paso, where they will be able to better communicate with their legal team and prepare for any upcoming court dates or hearings pertinent to their case.

text:
Former Venezuelan boxing champion Jorge Linares is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement after immigration authorities detained him Sunday in El Paso, Texas, according to Linares and his legal counsel.

“I’m being held by ICE in El Paso, Texas. What a crazy situation,” the former boxer wrote on X.

US Border Patrol agents and ICE officers arrested Linares at El Paso International Airport, an ICE spokesperson confirmed to CNN, describing him as “a foreign national in the country without legal immigration status, arriving from Venezuela.”

According to ICE, Linares entered the country October 26, 2023, on a permit for a temporary stay and “remained in the country beyond the authorized period.” He will remain in custody “pending deportation proceedings.”

Wilner & O’Reilly, the law firm representing Linares, confirmed his detention, saying in a statement he “is authorized to be in the United States and has cooperated fully with immigration authorities.”

“We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration cases follow established procedures, and those procedures take time,” his lawyers added.

Born in Barinitas, Venezuela, the 41-year-old Linares retired from boxing in 2023 following a distinguished career spanning more than two decades, during which he held world titles in the featherweight, super featherweight and lightweight divisions. A significant portion of his career was in Japan.

News of his detention emerged Monday. “I can confirm that my friend Jorge Linares, a former WBA world champion, is in ICE custody,” said Gilberto J. Mendoza, president of the World Boxing Association.

Mendoza noted Linares’ case is being handled by immigration attorneys and that he remains “in constant contact” with the athlete’s family.

“As president of the WBA, I will always support our champions — both inside and outside the ring. Stay strong, Jorge,” Mendoza added.

text:
Dutch OnlyFans model and Instagram influencer Vera Dijkmans, who was arrested at Newark Airport in New Jersey earlier this month, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after she failed to appear at an immigration court hearing in May, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed to NL Times. By missing that court hearing, the judge in charge of the case ordered her to leave the United States, and she will remain in custody until she is deported, DHS said.

Dijkmans, 29, was arrested last Wednesday at Newark Liberty International Airport and has remained in custody since then at a New Jersey detention center that has drawn criticism over poor conditions. Hundreds of detainees staged a hunger strike there this spring, citing poor treatment.

DHS confirmed that Dijkmans was granted the temporary, but extended B-2 tourist visa for her stay in the United States beginning August 2024, adding that "she was placed into removal proceedings" a year later. Her case was brought before an immigration judge on May 26, but Dijkmans was not in court and was not represented by an attorney. "She received due process and will remain in ICE custody pending removal," DHS stated.

Dijkmans missed the letter informing her of the hearing about the change in status, and the removal hearings “because she was traveling," her mother told RTL earlier. Her family confirmed she held a B-2 tourist visa, which does not give permission to work in the U.S. She then began the process of applying for a Green Card, which grants permanent residency and a right to work.

"To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States," DHS said in response. Her arrest was during a "targeted enforcement operation" at the Newark Airport on Nov. 11. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport," DHS said in a statement.

The immigration service has not alleged illegal employment. While in the U.S., Dijkmans created content for her accounts and was filmed with prominent UFC fighters, including Alex Pereira.

She has nearly six million Instagram followers and has claimed she earns millions of dollars annually on OnlyFans, a platform where creators are able to share explicit content with subscribers.

The agency said it was not the first time that she had a run-in with authorities at the country's border, facing an earlier accusation stemming from a flight into Houston. "In March 2019, U.S. Customs and Border Protection arrested Dijkmans and she was removed from the country after attempting to illegally enter through George Bush Intercontinental Airport," DHS said in a statement.

The Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is providing consular assistance to Dijkmans. The spokesperson told ANP the ministry cannot comment on the substance of the matter and does not want to "interfere in the legal proceedings of other countries, just as we would not tolerate that the other way around."

Those in the United States without proper documentation or authorization can use the U.S. government's CBP Home App to confirm they will self-deport. In doing so, they get 3,000 dollars and a free flight out of the country, DHS claimed. This also preserves more opportunities to return to the United States later, as opposed to an arrest and court-ordered deportation that makes it much more difficult to enter the U.S. again, the agency said.

text:
The announcement of a partnership between five EU countries and Rwanda to set up the first return hub outside the bloc has sparked controversy across Europe.

Although the final deal is still under negotiation, growing criticism has emerged over Rwanda’s human rights record. Furthermore, the planned deportations from the five participating countries — Austria, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece — to Rwanda, which are expected to begin in 2027, could face legal challenges before European courts.

“I see neither future nor humanity in it,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said in an interview when asked about the initiative, in an indirect swipe at the five member states involved in the project.

The proposed partnership concluded in Vienna on Monday would establish the EU’s first return hub outside the bloc, with the facility expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those transferred to Rwanda would be free to move around the country and would be expected to integrate into Rwandan society and the local labour market.

Many members of the European Parliament strongly condemned the political agreement, citing both the risk of abuses in Rwanda and the prospect of migrants being stranded in a country with which they have no ties.

“It is particularly disturbing that the fate of human beings is entrusted to a country burdened by documented allegations of serious violations of fundamental rights,” said Italian MEP Marco Tarquinio of the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group.

Similar concerns were voiced by other MEPs, including Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of Renew Europe, who questioned the rationale behind the agreement in an interview with Euronews’ flagship programme, Europe Tonight: “If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked.

The European Parliament has previously taken a hard line on Kigali. It called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, over alleged war crimes and the occupation of territory in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by Rwanda’s defence forces.

Humanitarian organisations also voiced their opposition. In a joint statement, a total of 45 NGOs described the partnership as a “cruel measure” that pushes migrants into further insecurity.

Rwanda's human rights record in question

Rwanda has sought to establish itself as a partner for Western countries looking to relocate migrants beyond their borders, although previous agreements of this kind have faced significant challenges.

In 2018, Kigali backed out of an agreement with Israel to accept refugees deported against their will, while a deal to transfer asylum seekers from the United Kingdom was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court because of Rwanda’s poor human rights record.

In 2025, Kigali agreed to accept 250 migrants from the US under a deal with President Donald Trump’s administration but has so far relocated only a few of them.

According to an Amnesty International report, in all these cases Rwanda failed to show it could guarantee fair procedures and adequate protection for people transferred from another jurisdiction.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta dismissed the criticism in response to a question from Euronews at the conference on Tuesday.

“Human rights in Rwanda are respected for everyone, and specifically for the migrants who choose to come to our country,” he said, describing his country’s integration policy as “one of the most progressive” because it allows refugees to work.

Biruta defended Rwanda’s long experience with migrants. He pointed out that Kigali currently hosts more than 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers and has run a transit centre for people evacuated from Libya since 2017.

“Which other country has come forward to propose a solution for those refugees? We were the only ones,” he said.

text:
A federal judge has tossed a Trump administration rule that would have limited how long many international students could remain in the United States, and required some to seek government approval to finish their studies.

U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Massachusetts vacated the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule on Monday, finding it was “arbitrary and capricious” and exceeded the authority Congress gave the agency. The ruling prevents the new restrictions from taking effect.

The rule would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” system for people on F, J and I visas. That system generally allows international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists to remain in the U.S. while they continue to comply with the conditions of their status.

Read More on Education

Under the Trump administration rule, most F and J visa holders would instead have been admitted for a fixed period of no more than four years. Those who needed additional time, including students in longer degree programs, would have needed to apply for an extension. The rule also imposed new limits on students changing programs or pursuing certain additional degrees.

The rule was issued by DHS in July and was scheduled to take effect in September. A group of higher education organizations and labor unions sued in August, and Saylor temporarily blocked the rule in September while the case proceeded.

On Monday, Saylor, a George W. Bush appointee, sided with the groups challenging the rule, finding that DHS had not properly justified the changes.

He said the agency failed to properly weigh the costs and benefits or show why concerns about fraud and national security required the new restrictions.

The rule would also have restricted some students from pursuing long programs such as PhDs, joint degrees or certain additional degrees. Saylor said those limits conflicted with the purpose of the F-1 student visa program.

“Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity—providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States—that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” Judge Saylor wrote. “The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program.”

Saylor noted that the current system had been in place for decades and the new rule had never taken effect.

'Rampant Abuse of Our Immigration System'

The administration argued the changes would allow immigration officials to check visa holders more regularly and help combat fraud and national security risks.

Adam Klein, co-founder of Globali.ai and a former senior DHS official, told Newsweek, “This is particularly important for doctoral students, researchers, and others whose academic programs do not necessarily fit within a fixed timetable.”

Klein added: “DHS has a legitimate interest in identifying students who violate their status or use educational programs improperly. But requiring students who are otherwise complying with the law to seek repeated government permission to continue their studies does not necessarily improve fraud detection."

DHS General Counsel James Percival wrote in a post on X, "Come on a student visa, take one class per semester, and stay here for decades. According to Judge Dennis Saylor, ICE must permit this rampant abuse of our immigration system."

The lawsuit was brought by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, American Federation of Teachers, Graduate Labor Organization, The NewsGuild-CWA, United Auto Workers, and UAW Local 2322.

The groups argued the rule would harm students and schools.

The government has appealed F. Dennis Saylor IV’s earlier ruling blocking the rule. That appeal remains pending.

Declining Enrolment

A fall 2026 survey by the Institute of International Education found that international student numbers at responding U.S. colleges and universities fell 9 percent in the 2026-27 academic year, including a 15 percent drop among graduate students and a 15 percent decline in new international enrollment.

Among institutions reporting declines, 88 percent cited the visa application process as a factor, while 70 percent pointed to travel restrictions and 60 percent said students were choosing to study in other countries.

Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said in a press release, "The harmful consequences of the current administration’s policy actions and efforts are already evident in the significant declines in international student enrollment and interest we are witnessing. If implemented, this rule would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses."

Jon Schleuss, president of The NewsGuild-CWA, said in a news release, “International journalists working in the United States have been on pins and needles waiting for a decision in this case, and we are thrilled that Judge Saylor struck down the Trump administration’s rule."

text:
An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”

The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.

The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.

A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.

The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.

ICE Goons Accused of Throwing Pregnant Woman to the Ground

ICE agents have been accused of pepper-spraying a pregnant U.S. citizen before forcing her face-down onto the ground and handcuffing her.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, had been protesting against federal immigration officers outside a jail with her husband, Adolfo Talavera Alvarado, and her sister-in-law, Monica Alvarado.

Her husband captured the disturbing confrontation on camera as agents attempted to detain the mom of two, who is 12 weeks pregnant, with one apparently using pepper spray before officers wrestled her onto her stomach.

“She’s pregnant with child,” Talavera can be heard shouting as the agents restrain his wife.

“This was something I never expected, especially from ICE agents, and knowing that I’m a United States citizen,” Vargas Andrade told KCRA3. “I was using all my rights to protest and to record and show everybody in the world what was going on, but unfortunately this did happen.”

While Vargas Andrade’s unborn baby was unharmed, she said the ordeal on Sunday was particularly frightening because she had previously suffered two miscarriages.

“Being pregnant, my first thought was my baby, my kids, what was going to happen,” she said. “I got scared,” Talavera told the Guardian. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”

The incident in Modesto, California, started when ICE officers stopped a vehicle driven by Monica, who had offered a ride to a man leaving the Stanislaus County Jail.

According to Vargas Andrade’s attorney, Patrick Kolasinski, agents entered the vehicle and detained the passenger, prompting Vargas Andrade and her husband to start filming.

She subsequently accused an agent of backing into her before other officers intervened. “We bumped,” she told CBS Sacramento, disputing that she had assaulted an officer. “That’s when everything started,” she added. “They started holding my hands with my phone in my hand. I was trying to still go around. That’s when another agent maced me and dropped me to the floor.”

Despite her American citizenship, Vargas Andrade was taken to an immigration enforcement facility in Stockton, California, where she remained for several hours before being released without charges, Kolasinski said.

She was later checked out at a hospital, where doctors established that her baby had not been harmed.

Her treatment follows other allegations involving federal immigration officers and American citizens.

In January, Brandon Sigüenza, 32, described how ICE personnel allegedly smashed his car windows and used pepper spray before detaining him for eight hours while he monitored immigration operations in Minneapolis.

That same month, Minnesota police chiefs raised concerns about immigration agents targeting off-duty officers of color. One female officer was allegedly surrounded by ICE vehicles and confronted by armed agents, one of whom reportedly knocked her phone away when she tried to record the encounter.

“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

The Department of Homeland Security has been contacted for comment.

title: The Supreme Court's Emergency Coalitions - by Adam Feldman - Legalytics
description:
The contrast points to a recurring difficulty in interpreting the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions.
Departures from appointing-party expectations An appointing-party comparison reveals a pattern that gets lost when emergency decisions are described simply as Republican or Democratic victories.
The executive-action emergency cases appear considerably more polarized than the Supreme Court’s merits docket when both are viewed as a whole.
Both comparisons point to less agreement in the executive emergency cases, particularly during the first term.
Where this leaves us The Court’s emergency decisions reveal more than the number of applications a president wins.
text:
When the Supreme Court rejected President Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from the administration’s overall emergency-docket record. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. The administration had lost, but the disagreement extended well beyond the familiar ideological split.

Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay. No other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the denial.

The contrast points to a recurring difficulty in interpreting the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions. The same conservative majority can produce several different coalitions, sometimes depending on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. Meanwhile, some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, while others have varied considerably. The identities of the president and the legal issue frequently move together, making them difficult to disentangle.

The prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. This installment turns to the individual justices. Its working sample covers federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decision events after removing six verified out-of-scope or single-justice dispositions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 events, respectively. Justice-level denominators can be smaller because of tenure, participation, or mixed positions.

There is an important qualification throughout: the Court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis uses coded alignment, assigning a justice to the Court’s disposition unless an express position or other evidence indicates otherwise. That produces a measure of apparent agreement, presuming that justices who do not speak also do not dissent.

Share

Different presidents, different justice-level records

The most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact—or grant it relief—barely moved.

Thomas and Alito present a different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%. Gorsuch’s rates were 83%, 54%, and 84%, while Kavanaugh’s were 78%, 67%, and 79%. Barrett aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Her three eligible Trump I observations are too few to establish a useful historical baseline.

The liberal justices show the opposite general movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the Court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

The figure above makes the distinction particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple conservative-versus-Democratic-president framing might suggest. The chart prints the underlying numerators and denominators because several justices did not serve for all three periods and some decisions cannot be assigned a straightforward binary position.

These numbers invite explanations, but they do not establish a cause. A president defending an environmental rule presents a different legal question from one seeking permission to remove an independent-agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

The issues that unite and divide the justices

Immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in ten of eleven immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and eleven of thirteen under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in ten of ten eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and twelve of thirteen under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of thirteen.

This is a particularly revealing sequence. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates, but separated more frequently when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most Trump II positions. The category covers different immigration rules, however, and the results should not be mistaken for comparisons of identical legal questions.

Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a division within the conservative majority. In ten eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine. Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.

The Court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete explanation for part of this split. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. The policy setting was similar, but the agencies and statutory grants of authority were different. The votes reflected those distinctions.

This figure puts the issue patterns in the same visual frame. The first three rows compare immigration across administrations; the remaining rows show Biden’s health litigation alongside Trump II personnel and foreign-affairs disputes. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all four, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett. The latter sample is particularly small, but its differences are worth following in the individual cases.

Subject matter therefore helps explain how the justices separate, even if it cannot fully explain why. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision. Aggregate presidential support rates combine those considerations into a single number.

Departures from appointing-party expectations

An appointing-party comparison reveals a pattern that gets lost when emergency decisions are described simply as Republican or Democratic victories. Under Biden, Roberts supported the federal executive in 26 of 36 eligible events (72%), Barrett in 25 (69%), and Kavanaugh in 24 (67%). Thomas did so in fourteen (39%), and Alito in seventeen (47%). These are all Republican appointees, yet their treatment of the Democratic administration varied considerably.

During Trump II, the same differences appear in reverse. Roberts’ coded position departed from the administration’s in ten of 38 events, while Kavanaugh’s did so in eight and Gorsuch’s in six. Thomas and Alito were each coded as opposing the administration in three. Among the liberals, Kagan supported Trump’s executive position in nine of 38 events, Sotomayor in six, and Jackson in three. The liberals thus differ even when the administration’s broad policy direction might seem to predict nearly uniform opposition.

Supporting a Democratic administration’s position in a case may be consistent with a conservative interpretation of statutory authority; denying a Republican administration’s application may reflect the traditional requirements for emergency relief. More importantly, the absence of a publicly recorded dissent does not establish an affirmative vote against the president. None of Thomas’ or Alito’s three coded anti-Trump II alignments was an expressly documented anti-administration position.

A clearer view of these departures comes from cases in which the justices actually explained their positions. During Biden, Barrett joined the Court’s three liberals to dissent from the stay of the EPA’s Good Neighbor Plan in Ohio v. EPA. She criticized the Court’s decision to intervene in a technically complex regulatory dispute on a thin emergency record. Her agreement with the liberals defended the administration’s regulation, but the rationale focused on administrative law and the standards governing emergency intervention.

The practical question is whether the justices who depart most often from appointing-party expectations tend to depart together. Their pairwise relationships suggest a recognizable structure, with one exceptionally cohesive conservative pairing and several others that shift when the underlying legal questions change.

The coalitions inside the conservative majority

Thomas and Alito agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decision events. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both publicly expressed positions favoring more relief for the administration than the Court granted or would otherwise provide. In Trump v. Kingdom, they were the only two justices who publicly indicated that they would grant the government’s application. The order did not identify the other justices’ votes, so its silence cannot be treated as an affirmative recorded vote by each of their colleagues.

Other pairings are nearly as cohesive. Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 eligible Trump II events (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 comparable events (97%). The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

The foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. The disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. The Court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported the intermediate outcome. Describing Gorsuch or Kavanaugh as opposing the executive because they dissented from part of the Court’s order would invert their actual positions: they wanted more relief for the government.

In Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the Court’s denial of relief, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds. The groupings were different, as were the legal questions.

The evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. It does not support a single sequence moving from the most to the least supportive of presidential power. Justices who agree in one field can separate in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines

The three liberal justices also exhibit meaningful differences. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 eligible events (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 coded events; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single unit in every emergency dispute.

Their publicly registered dissents differ as well. After grouping related applications into independent events, Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 events, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement. That distinction reflects what the record discloses, not necessarily a different unrecorded vote.

Some of the most revealing coalitions cross the Court’s usual ideological divide. Barrett’s dissent with all three liberals in Ohio v. EPA was a fully documented shared position. During Biden, Gorsuch and Jackson jointly dissented from emergency intervention in the Title 42 litigation in Arizona v. Mayorkas; Sotomayor and Kagan also indicated that they would deny the application, although they did not join Gorsuch’s opinion. The justices reached the same requested disposition through different reasoning.

Trump II produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined specified portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the entire disposition.

These examples highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is important. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for different reasons (we see it with concurrences all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. The emergency docket makes these relationships difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

Is the emergency docket less consensual than the merits docket?

The executive-action emergency cases appear considerably more polarized than the Supreme Court’s merits docket when both are viewed as a whole. Comparing the six conservatives with the three liberals, the analysis measures the share of eligible conservative–liberal justice pairings that ended up on the same side of a decision. Each nine-justice case can contribute eighteen pairings. This is a measure of agreement across ideological blocs, rather than a count of unanimously decided cases.

For the 2024 term, cross-ideological pair agreement was 68% on the argued merits docket and 20% in the Trump II executive-action emergency sample after excluding Trump v. CASA, an argued emergency application that appears in both sources. For the 2025 term, the corresponding percentages were 61% and 42%, excluding the similarly overlapping Cook decision. Both comparisons point to less agreement in the executive emergency cases, particularly during the first term.

The picture changes once unanimous merits decisions are removed. The Court resolved 27 of the 60 argued merits cases in the 2024 term without dissent and 25 of 57 in the 2025 term. Each unanimous decision contributes agreement across every eligible conservative–liberal pair, making the full merits docket look more consensual than its contested cases. With unanimous cases excluded, cross-ideological agreement in the merits sample falls to 41% in 2024 and 30% in 2025. The executive-action emergency rates remain 20% and 42%. In the later term, the ordering actually reverses.

Share

The last figure shows why the comparison group changes the conclusion. The 2024 emergency sample remains much more divided than contested merits cases, but the 2025 emergency sample does not. The estimates also rest on relatively few independent emergency decisions—21 in the first term and ten in the second once the overlapping argued applications are removed. Their pairwise observations share underlying cases and cannot be treated as independent votes for statistical purposes.

The uncertainty extends beyond sample size. Unlike a merits opinion, an unsigned emergency order may disclose only a dissent or no votes at all. Restricting the emergency comparison to orders with publicly recorded disagreement lowers observed cross-bloc agreement in both terms, but does not produce a truly equivalent dataset: unrecorded emergency positions are still inferred, whereas merits votes are ordinarily available. Nor are the case populations matched by legal subject. Immigration, executive removal, national-security, and spending disputes occupy a greater share of the emergency sample than of the full argued merits docket.

The data do not establish that the emergency procedure itself causes greater ideological division. They establish a narrower and still significant fact: the particular set of executive-action emergencies examined here often produced sharply divided coded coalitions, and the size of the gap with merits decisions depends on whether the benchmark includes unanimous cases.

The justice-level patterns require less speculation. Roberts’ stable aggregate record, the cohesion of Thomas and Alito, the shifting alliances of the remaining conservatives, and the different degrees of liberal opposition recur across the data. Their exceptions often become understandable only when the legal issue and requested remedy are placed alongside the presidential identity.

Where this leaves us

The Court’s emergency decisions reveal more than the number of applications a president wins. They show a conservative majority whose members often agree but separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines. The issue comparisons help explain why these configurations change: immigration, public health, removal authority, and federal spending present different questions even when the same president is asking for relief.

The comparison with the merits docket reinforces the need for apples-to-apples when looking at these two types of subsets. Executive-action emergencies are less consensus-prone than the merits docket overall in the periods examined, but the distinction becomes less uniform when the comparison is limited to contested merits decisions. The stronger finding lies in the relationships among the justices themselves—and in how much of those relationships the justices choose to reveal when acting without a full merits opinion.

text:
Monroe County commissioners have sued to invalidate Stinesville's immigration enforcement agreement with federal authorities.

The lawsuit questions whether local police chiefs can enter such agreements without approval from elected officials.

Commissioners argue the dispute is about procedural authority, not immigration policy.

Monroe County commissioners have filed a lawsuit seeking to invalidate Stinesville's agreement with federal immigration authorities, alleging local officers have already exercised powers granted under what they contend is an invalid agreement, including transporting individuals from the Monroe County Jail.

In the lawsuit, filed Nov. 10, 2026, in Monroe Circuit Court, commissioners asked that a judge declare as void Stinesville’s agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and prohibit Stinesville’s law enforcement officers from exercising powers granted under the agreement.

The case could have implications far beyond Stinesville. Across Indiana and other states, local law enforcement agencies have increasingly entered agreements allowing officers to assist federal immigration authorities. Commissioners are asking a judge to determine whether police chiefs and town marshals can enter those agreements on their own or whether they first require approval from elected officials, a ruling that could affect how similar agreements are authorized elsewhere.

County commissioners have filed the suit against Stinesville; its town marshal, Shane Pittman, who signed the agreement on behalf of the town; and Todd Rokita, Indiana's attorney general, who concluded that police chiefs and town marshals may enter such agreements without approval from city councils or town boards. The lawsuit asks a judge to reject that interpretation and follows warnings from Rokita's office that local officials who discourage participation in the program could face penalties under state law.

Commissioners contend the dispute is about process, not immigration policy. They argue that requiring approval from elected officials “does not prohibit participation” in the federal program but simply determines who has authority to enter such agreements on behalf of a municipality.

The lawsuit alleges that Pittman signed the agreement, called a 287(g), when he was deputy marshal on Jan. 30, 2026, without authorization from or a vote of the Stinesville Town Council. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security signed the agreement Feb. 10.

"Stinesville officers have conducted stops under the agreement in unincorporated Monroe County and transported individuals from the Monroe County jail," commissioners said in the suit. "These activities affect County jail operations, territorial law-enforcement interests, financial exposure, interlocal, and insurance interests."

The lawsuit also states that on Oct. 6 Rokita sent the Stinesville Town Council an advisory letter concluding Stinesville’s police chief could execute the agreement with ICE without town council approval. Rokita in the letter also warned that "county action discouraging continued participation" would violate state law and that his office could pursue civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.

Commissioners pointed out that other Indiana towns, including Waterloo and Andrews, publicly approved agreements before their police officials signed them, and that the Claypool Town Council suspended its marshal on July 21 after he entered an agreement with federal immigration officials without town council approval.

While the Stinesville Town Council voted Nov. 10 to ratify the agreement, commissioners plan to argue in an amended filing that the vote did not cure what they contend was a defective approval process because the agreement had already been signed and implemented. They maintain the dispute is about whether elected officials, not police officials acting alone, have authority to commit municipalities to such partnerships.

A spokeswoman for Rokita's office said via email Friday that the attorney general had not yet been served with the lawsuit.

"We will evaluate it when we receive it, and we will continue to oppose and fight any, and all efforts by Monroe County to interfere with immigration enforcement activities in Indiana," the statement read.

Pittman and Stinesville Town Board President Scott McGlocklin did not reply to emailed inquiries. They had not filed a response to the lawsuit. No hearing has been set.

text:
Coalition calls on UC leadership to protect immigrant patients and health care workers through strong, enforceable systemwide policies

SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Today, resident physicians and nurses from across the University of California, alongside community members, rallied outside the Board of Regents Meeting. The coalition is demanding that UC get Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) out of its hospitals and establish clear, systemwide protections for patients and health care workers.

The rally coincides with hundreds of emails that were sent to the Board of Regents and UC President Milliken reiterating the need for a comprehensive policy and protocol. The email action is cosponsored by CIR/SEIU, the California Immigrant Policy Center, California Nurses Association, and UAW 4811.

These actions are part of a growing campaign to ensure UC hospitals remain places of healing, dignity, and confidential medical care for everyone, regardless of immigration or custody status.

Currently, the lack of clear, consistent protocols and staff training for situations involving patients in immigration enforcement custody at UC Health facilities creates confusion, safety risks, and the potential for violations of patients’ rights. Health care workers need clear guidance to protect patient privacy, uphold legal rights, and provide appropriate medical care.

“As doctors, the well-being of the people we serve is our utmost priority. The presence of immigration enforcement in our hospitals undermines our ability to provide care and impedes patients from receiving proper, dignified treatment. UC must take action now to protect patients and staff,” said Dr. SatKartar Khalsa, CIR-SEIU regional vice president.

The presence of immigration enforcement officers in health care settings can interfere with medical examinations and treatment, compromise patient confidentiality, and undermine trust between patients and providers. Patients in immigration custody may face barriers to contacting family, accessing support services, and participating in decisions about their care. health care workers also report fears of unsafe working conditions, racial profiling, and retaliation for advocating for their patients.

"Nurses demand that our hospitals must be places of healing and safety and completely off limits to any sort of ICE or federal immigration agent presence," said Jamile Cabacungan, a medical-surgical-telemetry RN at UCSF Stanyan Hospital. "From the start of this cruel and unnecessary deportation program, nurses have been educating ourselves and our patients to know and exercise our rights, and we even sponsored state legislation to keep ICE out of our hospitals. Our employer UC must step up and proactively do everything possible to support us and our ability to provide safe care to our patients and communities."

The coalition has specific demands which essentially call on UC leadership to:

Protect patient privacy and dignity by limiting ICE access to patient care areas and safeguarding confidential patient communications.

Uphold patients’ rights and continuity of care, including access to certified medical interpreters, family notification, surrogate decision-makers, social services, legal support, and safe disposition planning.

Protect health care workers from racial profiling and retaliation for advocating for immigrant patients.

Establish clear protocols and staff training for responding to immigration enforcement activity in hospitals.

Ensure transparency and accountability, including information about federal immigration agents’ visits to UC hospitals over the past year.

Meet with union representatives to address health care workers’ concerns and develop effective protections.

At a minimum, the coalition is urging UC to adopt the updated California attorney general guidelines, with stronger protections modeled on comprehensive immigrant rights policies. These protections must include practical protocols, staff training, clear lines of responsibility, and accountability for implementation.

The coalition will also deliver formal public testimony at the UC Board of Regents meeting on Nov. 18, urging UC leadership to address these concerns and commit to systemwide protections. The rally follows coordinated phone and email actions calling on the university to take immediate action.

UC RNs also detail problems with staffing and A.I.

In addition to their concerns about immigration, UC nurses on Nov. 17 also detailed problems they are experiencing within the UC medical system over chronic understaffing and inappropriate staffing, as well as encroachment of artificial intelligence (A.I.) on their nursing practice.

At many of its facilities, including the UCLA campuses and UCSF, management’s failure to staff enough nurses routinely leads to extremely long emergency department wait times, holding patients in emergency department spaces, such as hallways, where they should not be placed, and unsafely reassigning nurses outside their units of expertise -- a practice known as “floating.”

UC nurses also oppose the giant health system’s rollout of untested and unregulated artificial intelligence into their workplaces without their input or agreement. “Nurses are not inherently against new technology, but we know when our employers are actually using technology to deskill, displace, and override our judgment,” said Lee Reinerston, an emergency department RN at Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland. “Hospitals want to remove real human nurses from the bedside because it ultimately cuts costs and boosts their profits. Some of this A.I. is untested or tested unreliably, it is unregulated and not verified to be effective. What has been proven time and time again to be effective is safe RN staffing. Nurses provide the skills, experience, intuition, judgment, and hands-on care that can never be replaced by an algorithm, software, or robots.”

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has renewed a lawsuit against the city of Houston over Mayor John Whitmire's recent executive order limiting how police interact with federal immigration authorities, but the mayor vowed to fight the state in court.

Attorneys in Paxton's office on Friday filed a motion for summary judgement in a case originally brought earlier this year in Fort Bend County, arguing Whitmire's Nov. 6 executive order violated Senate Bill 4, which prohibits cities and counties from declining to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.

"The good news is that with the election results, with the governor-elect, the attorney general - SB 4 is not their priority," Whitmire said after a Tuesday morning groundbreaking on a new adoption center for the city animal shelter.

Joe Jaworski, an attorney and former Democratic candidate for attorney general, said he couldn't see any path for Paxton to win the case before his time is office is up. It would take 21 days to set a hearing for the motion and, in all likelihood, incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson would dismiss the case on his first day in office, Jaworski said.

Paxton is proceeding with the case against Houston despite having dropped other high-profile cases since the election, Jaworski noted.

"It feels like some of the MAGA warriors are undaunted and, while they can, sending out signals to the base to see who's still there," he said.

Travis Fife, an attorney for the Texas Civil Rights Project, echoed that.

"Paxton should enjoy his vacation to Fiji and leave Houston to the clear will of its voters," Fife said.

The city's policies on immigration have become a central conflict at City Hall ever since President Donald Trump's administration added 700,000 civil "administrative" ICE warrants to a national police database last year at the outset of his immigration crackdown.

Whitmire for months turned back calls to restrict the police department's interactions with ICE, citing the risk of angering Gov. Greg Abbott, Paxton and other state leaders. Then, in April, the city council passed an ordinance limiting HPD's cooperation with ICE – only to quickly rescind it after Abbott threatened to pull $114 million in public safety grants from the city.

Paxton also sued the city. That case had sat dormant since late April until Paxton's new court filing Friday.

"These repeat violations show that both branches of Houston's municipal government seek to curtail HPD's cooperation with ICE and handcuff the freedom of individual officers to assist federal authorities," state attorneys wrote in Friday's court filing.

READ MORE: Whitmire orders HPD to limit ICE contacts after Democrats’ midterm election sweep

While the state's new Democratic leaders don't take office until January, Whitmire in announcing his executive order this month said he'd be willing to take the risk now of angering the outgoing Republican leadership.

The order says HPD will contact ICE "only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants." Previously, officers were instructed to call ICE anytime they came across someone with an administrative warrant and wait "a reasonable amount of time" for an ICE agent to reach the scene – a directive that sometimes led officers to wait more than an hour.

That policy had been negotiated with Abbott's office after the council showdown in April. Under that policy, Houston police handed 17 people to immigration authorities from July through September, according to city data.

Another 13 people were charged with crimes and transferred to the Harris County jail, where they are likely to be released to ICE. That group would not be affected by Whitmire’s executive order.

READ MORE:Inside the collapse of Houston’s ICE policy

Immigration advocates have questioned whether that policy violated the U.S. Constitution by directing officers to detain people based solely upon civil warrants and not criminal charges.

Three council members in the days after Whitmire's executive order proposed codifying his changes into city laws. The mayor said Tuesday he is concerned that effort would violate Senate Bill 4, the same measure on which Paxton's lawsuit is based.

The council members as of Tuesday morning had not heard back from the city legal department on whether or not the measure was "lawful" and could progress toward a council vote.

One of the authors of that ordinance, Council Member Alejandra Salinas urged the mayor to fight Paxton's office in court.

"Ken Paxton is yet again trying to bully Houston into abandoning protections for our immigrant neighbors and families," she said. "Earlier this year, we urged the city to defend our original immigration ordinance in court, and now we have another opportunity to get this right."

TEXAS — Walking on a well-used hiking trail of what is considered the “crown jewel” of the National Wildlife Refuge System, Denisse Carreon recalls visiting the same path with her grandfather decades ago.

“I would come here when I was young with my grandpa,” Carreon said.

On the U.S.-Mexico border near the city of Alamo, the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge is a 2,088-acre federal preserve — long considered sacred and protected ground.

“When I was in high school as part of the National Honor Society, we actually built a trail,” Carreon said.

Established in 1943, the natural refuge offered protection of migratory birds, butterflies and other wildlife species native to the Rio Grande Valley. Now, recently placed orange ribbon survey stakes inside the federal preserve signal that Carreon’s special place as a child will be torn down in the name of border security.

Spectrum News has learned through attorneys representing contractors that new U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) wall plans will spare a levee where border wall was initially planned, but wall construction will continue as marked by new stakes parallel to the levee.

“We’re following the judge’s order,“ said Spencer Construction attorney Ruben Pena. “The judge ordered us to stop so we agreed. CBP said you can stop but there is more wall to be built.”

In July, a lawsuit filed by the Hidalgo County Irrigation District tried to stop the building of border wall through the preserve. Before the lawsuit was filed this summer, wall construction through the preserve began. U.S. Magistrate Judge Juan Alanis issued a restraining order for Spencer Construction, LLC and Royal Concrete Products, LLC to halt further work and damage to the levee owned by Hidalgo County.

The construction companies and CBP then decided to establish a new path off the levee to continue construction.

Staring at the new stakes planted about 50 feet below the levee, Carreon said, “there’s no need for a border wall.”

The latest CBP data released earlier this month shows more than 90 miles of new border walls have been built during President Donald Trump's second term. CBP reports that 388.2 miles of wall barrier on the border is planned, and 90 miles of new wall is slated for the RGV.

Carreon says the new Congress must work together to stop the Trump administration’s promise to erect as much wall as possible.

“We need all of congress, republicans and democrats and independents to all protect Santa Anna. Enough is enough. Ya basta,” Carreon said.

text:
East Lansing could soon accept a large federal grant to upgrade its security cameras, but the grant appears to come with conditions that conflict with East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and diversity, equity and inclusion programming.

The city has been awarded and could accept a $472,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Justice, or DOJ, that pays for upgrades for up to 350 security cameras. The city’s cameras are a decade old and the new cameras will have better image quality and motion detection, according to the staff report.

However, the grant comes with a series of conditions. One condition states recipients “may not prohibit, or in any way restrict, any government entity or official from sending to, receiving from, maintaining, or exchanging information regarding citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, of any individual with components of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or any other federal, state or local government entity.”

Another condition says that by accepting the grant, recipients certify they do not operate diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The grant also stipulates recipients must comply with all presidential memoranda and executive orders.

The East Lansing City Council could accept the grant funding by approving the consent agenda at its meeting Tuesday night, a possibility that has some residents concerned about East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and other stances. East Lansing officials say accepting the grant would not force any policy changes and the city is asking the DOJ to remove the conditions. East Lansing’s mayor said if the federal government tries to challenge or revoke the funding, the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed.

Residents are concerned that accepting the grant contradicts the city’s current sanctuary city status. The resolution declaring East Lansing a sanctuary city states that in a manner consistent with state and federal law, city officials will not actively collaborate with federal agents solely for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration law.

Further, East Lansing employs a DEI director.

“I have grave concerns that by accepting this grant money, that the city is committing to cooperating with the U.S. Department of Justice when it comes to immigration enforcement,” said Karen Hoene, chair of the city’s Human Rights Commission. “This is very concerning considering the fact that we are a sanctuary city and we have City Council members that have committed to remaining a sanctuary city.”

Hoene said that the City Council placing the resolution to accept the grant funding on the consent agenda, which is usually passed without discussion, is “sneaky” and feels like a “MAGA move.”

But city officials say the grant does not force it to change any of its operations. Councilmember Mark Meadows said the city’s policy is that officials do not communicate with federal officials on immigration enforcement, except in cases where federal law requires it. He said this will continue to be how the city operates.

Meadows said conditions the grant places are illegal and courts have ruled cities don’t have to comply with these regulations. He said the federal government cannot force municipalities to assist in federal immigration enforcement.

“It’s just another example of Trump’s administration trying to, I guess, create law that doesn’t exist,” Meadows said. “That’s how we’ve approached it.

“If they want to yank the grant, then they’ll have the opportunity to yank the grant. But we haven’t changed anything,” he continued. “We’re accepting it. If we get the money, they can order us to return the money. We’ll deal with that at that point in time.”

Mayor Erik Altmann said in a call on Tuesday that the city believes the conditions are unenforceable due to injunctions and court rulings. He pointed to a two-page memorandum that was added to the City Council agenda at some point on Tuesday after residents had reached out to East Lansing Info about the grant conditions.

The memorandum from Interim City Manager Annette Irwin, dated Nov. 18 – which is tomorrow – asks that the conditions referencing DEI, immigration enforcement and executive orders be removed. The memo argues that the conditions are not enforceable.

Altmann said accepting the grant does not change the city’s policies and the plan is to continue operating in the same way. He said he does not know how the federal government will respond.

“The problem is that we are in completely uncharted territory here,” Altmann said. “I have no idea because nobody can predict what the Trump administration is going to do on a given day.”

If the federal government does seek to challenge or revoke the funding, Altmann said the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed.

“That is a conversation we will have to have, not just at the council level but at the community level if we get to that point,” he said.

“We have a bunch of people writing to us at the City Council account saying basically ‘don’t take a half-million-dollar grant,’” Altmann continued. “There’s probably a lot of other people in the community who say ‘You better take a half-million-dollar grant.’”

Senators Cortez Masto and Rosen have repeatedly called for more stringent oversight of prediction markets.

text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) joined Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif) in calling out Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig for the agency’s decision to prohibit prediction markets from geofencing, allowing prediction markets to continue operating in all 50 states and on Tribal lands.

This CFTC decision undermines Nevada’s state gaming laws applicable to sports event contracts listed on prediction markets, which were upheld by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in August, and similar state and Tribal restrictions in Michigan, California, and Washington. Both Senators from each of these states joined the letter.

“Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws…. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation,” wrote the Senators.

“We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws… The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved,” they continued.

Senators Cortez Masto, Schiff, and Rosen were joined by Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

The full text of the letter can be found here.

Senators Cortez Masto and Rosen have repeatedly called for more stringent oversight of prediction markets. The Senators have previously called on the CFTC to prohibit prediction markets incentivizing physical injury, death, or war; raised the alarm about offshore prediction markets allowing people to bet on wildfires; and pushed the CFTC to do more to combat insider trading in prediction markets. They have also urged Selig to abstain from intervening in pending litigation involving prediction markets. Cortez Masto is a co-sponsor of the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act, which would prohibit CFTC-registered entities – like Polymarket and Kalshi – from listing any prediction contracts that resemble a sports bet or casino-style game.
