Daily News

Immigration agents' seizure of lawyer's phone…

Fourth Amendment

Immigration agents' seizure of lawyer's phone at airport appears retaliatory, judge finds

A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at the Boston Logan International Airport in September 2025.

U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the District of Massachusetts also found that federal agents likely violated the First Amendment rights of Andrew Lattarulo, a co-owner of the law firm Georges Cote in Massachusetts. Lattarulo runs an Instagram account featuring videos explaining immigrants’ rights and critiquing federal immigration policies.

After agents seized Lattarulo’s phone without a warrant and downloaded a copy of its contents, they returned the phone. The government has claimed that the seizure was part of an investigation into his firm for potentially employing unauthorized immigrants.

Lattarulo’s lawsuit alleges that agents targeted him because of his advocacy and seized information that included confidential communications with his clients.

Burroughs’ ruling mandates that federal officials preserve all copied cellphone data without accessing it as litigation continues, according to a story by Law.com.

description:

The EU law enabling return hubs outside the bloc states that only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards are respected” are eligible.

Al-Sahlani pondered the feasibility of Rwanda returning migrants to their countries of origin, questioning how Rwanda would be able to carry out such returns when European countries themselves had struggled to do so.

text:
In the first edition of Euronews' new flagship show, Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones brought viewers the latest analysis of the stories making headlines over the weekend and on Monday.

Jones opened the programme with the latest EU developments on migration, as five countries - Greece, Denmark, Germany, Austria and the Netherlands - announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants, with the first pilot centres expected to be operational by mid-2027.

Our correspondent Vincenzo Genovese, reporting from Vienna, said it marked an unprecedented move in EU migration policy, with the bloc sending irregular migrants to a country with which they have no previous connection - a move compared to Donald Trump's approach in the US.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the agreement a "game changer," saying it would help European countries regain control and remove incentives for illegal migrants.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, the first facility will accommodate around 100 people. The hub would consist of open facilities rather than closed deportation centres, and migrants would be free to move around the country. The goal is to give them the chance to integrate into local society and the labour market.

The EU law enabling return hubs outside the bloc states that only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards are respected” are eligible.

Rwanda has a questionable track record on human rights. However, Rwanda's minister of the interior, Vincent Biruta, said the country was ready, had good experience in dealing with migrants and would respect fundamental rights.

Legal challenges could emerge when deportations begin next year, as happened with the UK-Rwanda agreement.

On Monday, Frederiksen added that she had a strong feeling that other countries would join the scheme.

Nineteen of the twenty-seven EU governments support the deportation plan. Only France and Spain have made clear their opposition to it. Italy already has its own agreement with Albania.

THE DEBATE

MEPs Charlie Weimers and Abir Al-Sahlani discuss Rwanda

Jones hosted Swedish MEP Charlie Weimers, a Member of the European Parliament since 2019 and part of the European Conservatives and Reformists group, and Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of the Renew Europe Group, who has also been an MEP since 2019, to debate the Rwanda "Return Hub."

Weimers said he agreed with Frederiksen, adding that he thought the policy was a "game changer." Noting that "every system" starts small, he said it would be successful if it led to further steps in the future to address migration policy in the EU.

Al-Sahlani pondered the feasibility of Rwanda returning migrants to their countries of origin, questioning how Rwanda would be able to carry out such returns when European countries themselves had struggled to do so.

“If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked, citing concerns over Rwanda's dependence on development aid and security concerns, as well as other unanswered questions.

Weimers calls deal a 'deterrent'

Meanwhile, Jones challenged Weimers over the cost-effectiveness of the proposed centres, citing Italy’s Albania scheme, which is costing Italian taxpayers €670 million over five years while handling only 0.3% of illegal arrivals into Italy. But Weimers described the new deal as being intended as a "deterrent" to those considering illegally migrating to Europe.

Al-Sahlani also criticised the growing influence of far-right narratives on European migration policy, arguing that governments were failing to use existing legislation and tools effectively.

The Renew Europe Group MEP further accused political leaders of portraying refugees as a threat and making them scapegoats for wider societal problems. She also warned that migration debates were increasingly driven by emotion rather than facts, fuelled by the misuse of statistics, selective truths and fabricated stories that vilify people seeking refuge.

Don't forget to join us tomorrow at 6 p.m. for the latest analysis of Europe's top headlines.

text:
As many as 38 million people could be left out of the population count, independent of immigration status, if the Census Bureau finalizes its proposed rule to redefine how it identifies where people live.

That’s according to a new report from the Coalition on Human Needs using the Census Bureau’s own data.

The Coalition on Human Needs is an organization made up of of public interest groups and think tanks, including the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, United Way, AFSCME, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, that advocates for policies that would benefit low-income populations.

“It became very clear that if you’re trying to tie being counted in the census to whether or not you have an address in your tax record that matches, that if you don’t file taxes in the first place, you won’t be counted,” Christopher Kang, executive director of the Coalition on Human Needs, told TPM.

The Census Bureau did not respond to a TPM request for comment.

The Commerce Department on September 9 proposed a new rule that sought to make foundational changes to the 2030 census, a change that could erase most noncitizens from the 10-year census count for the first time in the survey’s history.

The proposed rule would try to accomplish the exclusion of immigrants in part by using tax records as an indicator of a census participant’s “usual residence.” While the Census Bureau has used federal administrative records like tax data to fill in information gaps on past decennial censuses, using the records as the primary means of determining where a person lives is unprecedented.

Previously, the census defined a person’s usual residence as where a person “live[s] and sleep[s] most of the time.” Under the new rule, the census would narrow that definition to the place “consistent with, and evidenced by, their tax records.”

Though the Constitution mandates that a state’s congressional representation reflect “the whole number of persons in each State,” Republicans have long sought to shift political power from blue states to red states by excluding immigrants from the population count used to determine representation. Republican activists contend that Democratic states tend to benefit politically from larger immigrant populations, an argument that was the basis for a lawsuit filed by Alabama ahead of the 2020 census. (It was dismissed in 2021.) Excluding immigrants from the count used for congressional representation would also impact the Electoral College.

It’s part of an overall effort by the Trump administration to increase Republican power by manipulating all aspects of the democratic process, of a piece with its push to redraw congressional districts that favor Republicans (which backfired during the midterms) and its unfounded claims about various forms of alleged voter fraud.

The proposal drew sharp and immediate rebuke from data policy experts, various kinds of advocacy groups, states, localities and tribal nations. Now, citing the Census Bureau’s own research, the Coalition on Human Needs report found that a whopping 11.5% of the population doesn’t have “any IRS” forms.

People with an annual household income lower than a certain federal threshold are not legally required to file federal income taxes. That could include gig workers who make less than $20,000 and don’t reach 200 transactions, and other kinds of self-employed small business owners. There’s an additional tax form that people who receive Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program, or a certain block of SSI benefits might have filed, but vagueness in the Census Bureau’s seismic proposal makes it unclear which forms will be used.

And since the Bureau’s rule only specifies utilizing “e.g., tax returns, W-2 forms,” it’s even unclear what kind of taxed workers could be at risk of exclusion under the proposal.

The report also found that Census Bureau research showed as many as 30 million people “had no matching addresses between the IRS records and the 2020 Census.” Taken together with the 38 million people who do not file federal income taxes, the Coalition of Human Needs report calculated that this proposal risks undercounting around 20% of the entire population, regardless of immigration status.

“Overall, this proposal is so broken, you can’t even tell which 20% of the country is going to be left out,” Kang said.

Of the nearly 150,000 comments submitted on the Bureau’s proposed rule, the overwhelming majority — 88% — opposed the rule, according to data from a coalition of data policy organizations and experts called Hands Off Our Census. Most comments opposed the parts of the Bureau’s rule that would eliminate the collection of race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, and that would exclude most noncitizens. But the proposal’s unprecedented changes to where the decennial census counts people brought opposition even from within the federal government, TPM reporting found.

Before the proposed rule was published, officials from the Treasury Department pushed back on the proposal and suggested that the Commerce Department — under which the Census Bureau falls — use tax information only for “corroborating evidence of an individual’s residence.” Treasury advised that “no particular tax record is controlling, and the evidentiary weight assigned to such information should reflect the purpose, timing, and reliability of the particular data element.” Commerce ignored the guidance.

“I think it’s important to put this proposal in context of everything else that is going on in the administration,” Aravind Boddupalli, senior research associate in the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, told TPM. “The overall picture is pointing to the use of the tax system for services beyond tax collection and tax enforcement towards other priorities such as immigration enforcement.”

If filed, tax returns are not legally required to record a person’s home address because they’re designed to ensure the IRS can contact filers, not for the census purposes of enumeration.

“Fundamentally, there would always be an undercount of how many people show up on our tax system,” Boddupalli said.

The Census Bureau has long used administrative records in its data collection, said John Iselin, associate director of economic analysis at the Yale Budget Lab. But use of the records have to be cognizant of their limits.

“There are real cases where because of the complexity of that matching process…you might not be able to make that match work,” Iselin told TPM. “And all those would mean that real information about someone that might be found through a decennial census process would be missed.”

text:
Quick Hits

DACA work benefits in Texas could depend on decisions by the incoming Texas attorney general to continue or withdraw from ongoing DACA litigation.

A federal judge’s decision on DACA termination in Texas remains pending, and the federal judge could issue a decision before the new Texas attorney general takes office, which could lead to further appeals.

Texas’s incoming attorney general has promised to review ongoing litigation involving Texas and has not confirmed continuing or withdrawing from ongoing DACA litigation, creating some uncertainty on continued or terminated DACA work benefits in Texas.

Where the DACA Litigation Stands With the State of Texas

In 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that DACA program protections against deportation and authorizing work benefits were unlawful. However, the Fifth Circuit Court limited potential remedies, including the termination of DACA work benefits, to the State of Texas. Right now, the litigants are awaiting a U.S. district judge’s implementing order on the final scope of DACA termination, which would implement the circuit court’s ruling in a final decision. (Please see our earlier article, “DACA Expected to Reopen: What Employers Need to Know About the Latest Legal Shift.”)

The Texas Attorney General Election and a Review of Pending Litigation

Texas voters recently elected Nathan Johnson as the state’s next attorney general, with the new attorney general entering office in January 2027. In public interviews, Johnson has promised a thorough review of ongoing litigation involving the State of Texas. He has confirmed an intent to strictly scrutinize ongoing “showpiece” litigation in the Texas Attorney General’s Office that he would consider not in the state’s interest to continue. However, the attorney general–elect has not identified specific areas of litigation or specific lawsuits that will receive higher scrutiny in making future litigation decisions.

Until Texas Attorney General–Elect Johnson confirms an intention to continue or withdraw from Texas’s ongoing litigation requesting DACA program termination, the timing of a final decision involving continued or terminated DACA work benefits will be uncertain. The attorney general–elect may withdraw Texas from ongoing DACA litigation, or, if the federal judge issues a decision on DACA’s termination before the new attorney general takes office, the new attorney general may not continue the litigation on appeal. While Texas’s future litigation posture is uncertain at present, it is unlikely that the attorney general–elect would continue federal litigation requesting DACA termination.

Looking Ahead

A federal judge’s ruling on the scope and terms of the DACA program’s termination could have an immediate impact on Texas workforces. While a decision to terminate DACA work benefits could be stayed pending appeal or motion for reconsideration, the ruling could be given immediate effect and require prompt action by Texas employers related to their employees who are DACA beneficiaries. Texas employers should remain aware that Texas’s litigation position could change next year, depending on the new attorney general’s decision to continue or withdraw from the DACA litigation. As a result of the recent election, a final resolution on DACA work benefits for Texas employees could take some time.

For now, Texas employers may want to consider the following:

continuing to accept unexpired employment authorization documents (EADs) held by DACA recipients (Category (c)(33));

tracking EAD expiration dates and reminding employees to apply for renewals 120 to 150 days prior to expiration; and

monitoring the litigation involving DACA termination, as a ruling terminating DACA work benefits could require immediate action by employers.

Ogletree Deakins’ Immigration Practice Group will continue to monitor developments and provide updates on the Immigration and Texas blogs as additional information becomes available.

Flights for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement have resumed at Dallas Love Field Airport, according to activists with No Love For ICE Air.

Though Love Field officials could not confirm if Signature Aviation, the private airline that contracted with ICE , was continuing its services for the federal agency, “they have communicated their intention to restart operations” after a roughly month-long pause, an airport spokesperson told KERA.

The spokesperson said in a written statement that the decision to contract with any federal, state, or local entities is up to an aviation company’s discretion.

“DAL does not have an approval, oversight, or facilitation role in federal immigration enforcement operations at FBOs, nor can it speak on behalf of the businesses,” the statement said.

Signature Aviation halted ICE flights on Oct. 1, which activists shared at a press conference early last month.

John Putnam, with the group No Love for ICE Air, said activists documented a deportation flight at Love Field on Oct. 27. KERA reached out to Signature Aviation but did not hear back.

“This airport should be for travel, for sports teams, for people visiting their families and things like that,” Putnam said. “And because of Signature Aviation’s choice to allow ICE to operate these flights, it’s a place where people get very cruelly deported… So we’re very frustrated and sad.”

description:

Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C.
Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.
On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.
The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided.
text:
On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

***

Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

Section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”

As for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, said fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”

The Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

But a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

The 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

***

If the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

That is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process issue. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

Rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

text:
Former Department of Justice Civil Rights division head Harmeet K. Dhillon said Monday that a federal investigation into a Harvard Law School visiting professor accused of firing a pellet gun near a Brookline synagogue was never completed because the professor left the country before the FBI could interview him.

Dhillon also defended her public comments following the incident, despite synagogue leaders previously saying they did not believe it was motivated by antisemitism.

Dhillon made the remarks at a fireside chat — titled “Civil Rights and the Rule of Law: DEI, Free Speech, and the Trump Administration” — with the HLS Federalist Society, moderated by the chapter’s Vice President of Speakers and second-year law student Tasha D. Dambacher.

Carlos Portugal Gouvea — a Brazilian citizen — was arrested after allegedly firing two shots outside Temple Beth Zion in Brookline on the eve of Yom Kippur in October 2025, damaging a car window. Though he told police he was “hunting rats,” he was later charged with illegally discharging a pellet gun, disorderly conduct, disturbing the peace, and vandalizing property.

“It is my job as the head of the civil rights division to investigate potential hate crimes, and we have opened up many investigations into potential hate crimes that ultimately don’t resolve and don’t result in prosecutions,” Dhillon said. “This person self-deported before an investigation could be concluded, before the FBI could interview him.”

The Law School placed Gouvea on administrative leave, and he subsequently pled guilty in Nov. 2025 to one charge — illegally discharging a pellet gun — and had the other charges dismissed as part of a plea deal. Gouvea was required to pay $386.59 in restitution to the individual whose car window he broke with a pellet and six months of pretrial probation.

After federal immigration authorities arrested Gouveva following the revocation of his J-1 visa, the Department of Homeland Security said he voluntarily left the country rather than being deported.

Synagogue leadership previously said they did not believe the incident was antisemitic event, citing information from Brookline police that said Gouvea “was unaware that he lived next to, and was shooting his BB gun next to, a synagogue or that it was a religious holiday.”

At the time, Dhillon wrote on X that she was “on it” and “Do NOT mess with houses of worship or people of faith in our country. Not on this watch.”

Get The Crimson in your inbox.

Asked during the question-and-answer period whether her comments had harmed the reputation of the Trump administration, Dhillon said she did not regret them.

“First of all, your premise at the beginning was leaders of the temple, ‘did not believe that he knew,’” Dhillon said. “I don’t know how they are reading the mind of this professor or know that.”

“I will not apologize for opening up investigations into and condemning antisemitic violence wherever I find it,” she added. “Let me tell you, people have died in attacks on houses of worship in this country, including in the last two years. It is a zero tolerance policy, and I’m proud of that effort.”

Before the question-and-answer period, Dambacher said Dhillon would not be able to “speak about anything about pending litigation against Harvard.”

Dhillon’s talk came after she resigned from her post at the Justice Department on Nov. 5, just two days after the midterm elections. She wrote in an email to division staff that she had informed President Donald Trump in early October of her plans to return to private practice.

CBS reported that Trump wanted to fire Dhillon after her Oct. 18 appearance on “60 Minutes,” expressing concerns that she hadn’t been forceful enough in her explanations to defend the administration’s election integrity efforts.

Advertisement

During her talk, Dhillon said her biggest accomplishment “was changing the personnel at the civil rights division.”

“The second is the radical concept that the Civil Rights division exists to protect the rights of all Americans, and not just a subset of Americans who were the initial and appropriately designed protectees of the civil rights laws, because we had a lot of discrimination in our country when we started the Civil Rights division in 1957,” she added.

Dhillon became one of the Trump administration’s leading figures in its campaign against diversity, equity, and inclusion programs — suing states to obtain voter rolls, launching investigations into universities over alleged civil rights violations in programming and admissions practices, and pursuing restrictions on transgender athletes in women’s sports.

“There will always be a need to keep pressure up on these institutions because it is human nature to, well I won’t say it’s human nature to discriminate,” Dhillon said, “but I will say that there have been decades of people who made their careers around diversity initiatives.”

text:
Senate Republicans Scramble to Install Russ Vought’s Deputy in Key Legislative Role

At Talking Points Memo, we’ve covered closely a somewhat obscure agency called the Government Accountability Office. With just weeks left before the new Congress, Republicans are scrambling to bring the agency under Donald Trump’s control.

The reasons why this is important are a bit wonky for the 8:00 a.m. hour, but stick with me.

Unlike executive branch agencies, the independence of which the Trump administration and the Supreme Court have thoroughly gutted, the GAO is outside of the president’s control. It is an independent agency within the legislative branch. One of its primary areas of focus is the way in which funds appropriated by Congress get spent. That’s a topic on which — from DOGE to the decimation of USAID to Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought’s impoundments — the administration has gotten particularly, uh, creative, and done it’s greatest damage.

GAO has a track record of calling out these decisions, at times flatly describing Vought’s maneuvers as illegal. It is even empowered to sue over how the White House implements Congress’ spending decisions, and is one of the only entities with standing to do so.

For the better part of a year, the agency has been without a permanent director. Earlier this month, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee chair Rand Paul (R-KY) somewhat ominously scheduled a hearing for a nominee after not engaging with the vacancy for months.

On Monday, the White House made official who that nominee would be: it is seeking to pervert the agency’s purpose by installing a deputy to — you guessed it — Russ Vought in the role of director. Eric Ueland, a longtime Republican staffer and, now, Trump’s pick to head GAO, is the second-in-command at Vought’s Office of Management and Budget.

GAO directors serve 15-year terms, and so whatever happens here could long outlast Trump and even his movement.

To put it more explicitly, Trump — helped by pliant Republican senators — is seeking to make an executive branch official the director of one of the last remaining, functional watchdog agencies with power to check his executive branch.

Democrats, of course, slammed the decision.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress,” said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray (D-WA), who will lead the panel next year.

“Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO,” Murray said in a statement.

Experts who closely watch the appropriations process are pessimistic that Ueland will be blocked, but I’m not sure the fight is entirely over. Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) objected to the nominee yesterday evening.

Other Republicans who have critiqued the Trump administration’s steamrolling of Congress, including Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and, yes, the outgoing Susan Collins (R-ME), might not love this choice. Perhaps there will be a fight. We’ll be watching closely.

Programming Note

At some point in the next several days, I’m going to have a second kid. We don’t know when this will happen. (We’re happy she avoided the week of Nov. 3.) But when it does, possibly as early as tomorrow, The Brief will pause until early to mid-December.

Bill Cassidy’s Regrets Over His RFK Vote Reach New Heights

Sen. Bill Cassidy’s (R-LA) plot arc is now complete. The doctor-turned-senator once showed some spine in 2021 when he voted to convict Trump over the Jan. 6 insurrection. But in Trump’s second term, and despite his clearly well-founded misgivings, Cassidy provided the key vote to let RFK Jr. sit atop America’s public health agency.

Cassidy seemingly immediately regretted the decision, and began needling Kennedy from the Senate floor. That attracted two Republican, Trump-aligned primary challengers, both of whom won more votes than Cassidy in 2026 and one of whom will now replace him early next year.

With his days in office dwindling, Cassidy went all out over the weekend and called on Trump to replace Kennedy. “If I were president, I would choose someone else because there needs to be accountability for higher healthcare costs, more measles deaths, losing elimination status, and no progress on processed foods,” he told host Margaret Brennan.

Of course, there was a moment to stop Kennedy, and this is not it.

Tabs

Last week and into the weekend, some of the more extreme figures in reactionary politics gathered at a Christian nationalist conference outside Dallas to figure out what a post-MAGA movement would look like. Alex Jones, Nick Fuentes, and a host of Christian nationalist pastors spouting antisemitism and urging the repeal of the 19th Amendment all shared the stage. And while they aspire to play a big role in the next presidential campaign, this movement isn’t yet quite ready for primetime, Madeline Peltz writes for TPM.

A plan by Trump’s Census Bureau to rely on tax data as it seeks to exclude immigrants from the decennial count stands to miss tens of millions of Americans, TPM’s Layla A. Jones writes.

Josh Marshall wonders if the timing of this intelligence emerging in the press has something to do with the post-election attempts in Israel to form a governing coalition that excludes Benjamin Netanyahu.

James Comer (R-KY), the attack-dog head of the House Oversight Committee, made his name launching countless congressional investigations that seemed largely aimed at providing material for Fox News. With Republicans now in the minority, he is pivoting, per NBC News — to run for governor of Kentucky.

Its Jensen Huang, sadly mounting a Napoleonesque attempt at a comeback, backed by President Trump and various other Silicon Valley figures. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said. title: ICE arrests continue at sensitive locations in Massachusetts despite PROTECT Act
description:
Maura Healey introduced the PROTECT Act last winter, amid violent incidents involving ICE in Minnesota and public protests.
LUCE said that's exactly what ICE is doing right now, especially in Massachusetts courthouses.
Governor Healey signed the PROTECT Act to keep ICE out of schools, daycares, hospitals, nursing homes and courthouses and keep people safe.
According to law enforcement training materials for the PROTECT Act, enforcement of the law belongs to the Attorney General's office but not to local police who "have no authority to enforce the act."
It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be.
text:
A father was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in front of his children in Boston and immigration advocates said where it happened suggests federal agents could be violating the PROTECT Act, a new law in Massachusetts.

Speaking through a translator, a Boston mom told WBZ-TV how her husband was detained by ICE in front of the couple's 5-year-old and 4-year-old. It happened in early November as the father of three and native of Honduras was preparing to bring their two youngest children to the Gardner Pilot School in Allston.

"His mother-in-law called me saying that he was detained and that the children, our children, were inside of the car crying," the woman said. She did not want to share her name for this interview. She said the arrest happened a short distance from the school, but not on its property.

Immigration advocates for the LUCE Immigrant Justice Network of Massachusetts are calling attention to stories like this one as they say ICE is violating new state legislation, called the PROTECT Act, aimed at keeping agents away from schools, daycares, healthcare facilities, and courthouses.

"What we really need right now from the state leaders is their leadership to implement the PROTECT Act because having a law on the papers doesn't mean it's going to happen in reality," said Pietra Adami, the workers' rights coordinator for the Brazilian Women's Group and LUCE.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey introduced the PROTECT Act last winter, amid violent incidents involving ICE in Minnesota and public protests. Asked how it would be enforced at the time, Healey said, "don't bring the fight."

LUCE said that's exactly what ICE is doing right now, especially in Massachusetts courthouses. Between November 3 and November 12, security systems at Massachusetts courts have recorded 22 arrests by ICE.

In response to the alleged PROTECT Act violations, a spokesperson for the governor's office released a statement saying, "We are closely monitoring reports of ICE activity in Massachusetts communities, including at courthouses. Governor Healey signed the PROTECT Act to keep ICE out of schools, daycares, hospitals, nursing homes and courthouses and keep people safe. We are in touch with the Attorney General's Office and evaluating our options."

According to law enforcement training materials for the PROTECT Act, enforcement of the law belongs to the Attorney General's office but not to local police who "have no authority to enforce the act."

An ICE spokesperson told WBZ that federal law supersedes state law and that, "The Supremacy Clause makes it clear that sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement."

"ICE does not conduct planned operations targeting churches or other areas such as schools, hospitals, or polling locations to execute arrests. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement. While we understand the sensitivity of these locations, if an active public safety threat endangered these locations, offenders may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"The ability of law enforcement to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense. It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be. It is also safer for our officers and the community. These illegal aliens have gone through security and been screened to not have any weapons."

A request for comment was not returned by the Attorney General's office.

The Boston mom whose husband remains in ICE custody at the Plymouth County Correctional Facility wants some sort of relief for her family. She said her husband has no criminal history and has been in the United States since 2013. He now has a pending asylum claim.

"We are not criminals. We came here to this country to work with this honesty and everything that's happening right now, it's affecting us, deeply," she said.

text:
European governments have the right to tighten their migration policies but must not undermine their commitments to human rights, Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has told Euronews.

Berset rejected suggestions that Europe was facing a migration crisis or that the right to asylum was becoming politically unsustainable, insisting that governments could reconcile tougher immigration controls with their international obligations.

“Human rights are human rights for everybody or for no one,” he said.

Berset stressed that European human rights legislation did not prevent governments from deporting migrants who had no legitimate right to remain, pointing out that the European Court of Human Rights had upheld some expulsions while ruling against others.

He also insisted that plans to establish so-called return hubs outside the European Union had to meet European human rights standards. "Can they be compatible with European human rights standards? We need to prepare this well and have a proper discussion about it," he said.

His remarks come as five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish a return hub for rejected asylum seekers.

Berset expressed regret that preparations appeared to have taken place without continuing earlier discussions initiated at the Council of Europe.

He warned that respect for the rules-based order, which he described as essential to ensuring stability, peace and predictability, must also underpin Europe’s approach to migration.

text:
The latest in a series of viral Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in San Diego is prompting requests for policy changes in the city.

Last Friday’s ICE arrest involved a man and his teenage daughter.

Video captured from a home security camera showed an unmarked vehicle pull in front of a truck before colliding with it in San Diego’s Oak Park neighborhood.

Monica Ortega, 18, comes into view and raises her hands as she approaches the vehicle. Her father, Alan Ortega Meneses, is inside the truck. An ICE agent rushes around the car and pushes her to the ground while approaching her father’s vehicle.

She gets back up and walks forward. The officer turns around, points and shouts commands at her, then pushes Ortega back to the ground and pulls out a gun. First he aims it at the vehicle, and then at her.

The agent then switches to a taser, and Ortega is handcuffed by two men while screaming. She said her 11-year-old sister watched from nearby.

“I was just crying, I couldn't comprehend what was going on,” she told KPBS over the phone. “My neighbors and my community cleaned my wounds. They came out with a first aid kit and cleaned me up.”

The interaction with ICE was posted online by activist and social media influencer Arturo Gonzalez. Ortega described her interaction with the San Diego Police Department, who later showed up to the scene.

“While the officer came, he just went straight up to me … as I was answering he just walked away midway, and I just remember my heart dropped,” she said. “Because (I thought) this one person who is supposed to be here to protect and serve us is not caring and rolled his eyes at me and walked away.”

In a statement regarding the incident, the San Diego Police Department (SDPD) said it “received a call for service from an unknown male … regarding a two-vehicle collision with possible injuries in the 3900 block of 58th St.”

The department said officers were on scene for just under half an hour.

“Approximately five officers and a sergeant responded to the scene," the SDPD statement read. "The incident with federal agents occurred prior to SDPD arrival, and federal agents were no longer on scene when officers arrived."

The incident occurred in Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera’s district. He met with Ortega’s family and her neighbors on Saturday.

“Trust is being eroded. I heard this in response to Friday's events. The ICE officers were wearing vests that said ‘police,’” Elo-Rivera said.

Now he’s called on Mayor Todd Gloria to issue city directives in response to the ICE arrest.

Elo-Rivera wants the San Diego Police Department's presence to be publicly disclosed in these incidents. He’s seeking a published report within three business days each time the agency responds to a scene where federal immigration agents are present.

He also wants the department to help families find their loved ones after an ICE arrest.

“The ask is very simple," Elo-Rivera said. "It's to communicate publicly about why they were there, how long they were there, what they did there so folks can know that they were not working alongside ICE to rip families apart and cause havoc in our city.”

Staff from the Mayor’s office said they committed to implementing both requests during Monday's city council meeting.

The City Council adopted an ordinance last year in an effort to limit cooperation between SDPD and federal agents carrying out the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Elo-Rivera publicly accused San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl of lacking transparency around the issue in recent weeks. In response, Wahl pledged more frequent reports to the City Council when officers are called to a scene involving federal immigration agents.

In a statement regarding the arrest, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said, “On November 13, 2026, ICE arrested Alan Ortega Meneses, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico, during a targeted enforcement operation in San Diego, California.”

The statement also said that Meneses’ daughter interfered with officers and repeatedly ignored their commands to move out of the way.

“After physically attacking officers and reaching for an officer’s gun, she was detained. At the same time, Meneses drove his vehicle into a government vehicle and then initiated an attempted (a) vehicular assault on officers as well. After refusing to comply with orders and being observed reaching under his seat, officers relied on their training to safely control the situation and place Meneses under arrest,” the DHS statement said.

Ortega disputes that account of events.

DHS also claimed Meneses has an extensive criminal history. KPBS did not find San Diego Superior Court records matching his name to the alleged crimes in time for publication.

title: Europe's Rwanda return hub raises serious human rights concerns – a migration researcher explains
description:
Human rights organisations have warned against hubs in Rwanda – with Amnesty International calling them potential “black holes” for human rights.
The flawed thinking Governments have said that return hubs will break the smugglers’ business model.
As Europe’s leading intergovernmental human rights organisation, the Council of Europe, has noted, it has also meant outsourcing border control to countries with a documented history of serious human rights violations.
The centres have drawn heavy criticism from Italian courts and human rights organisations.
With a future hub in Rwanda, questions remain unanswered: who is responsible if someone’s rights are violated there, the EU country or the host?
text:
When I met Chadi, a young Tunisian man recently deported from Italy after crossing the Mediterranean by boat, he was already planning his next attempt: “They brought me here, but I’m not planning on staying.”

His story is worth keeping in mind given that five EU governments – Denmark, Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands – have announced that Rwanda will host Europe’s first “return hub”. This will be a migrant deportation centre, where people whose asylum claims have been rejected, but who cannot yet be sent home, will be held or resettled. The first transfers are planned for 2027, starting with a pilot of around 100 people.

Human rights organisations have warned against hubs in Rwanda – with Amnesty International calling them potential “black holes” for human rights. Indeed, Rwanda is a troubling choice.

Its president, Paul Kagame, was re-elected in 2024 with 99% of the vote. UN experts say Rwanda exercises significant control over the M23 rebels in neighbouring Congo, the brutal conflict’s leading perpetrators of sexual violence. While in 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled Rwanda unsafe for asylum seekers. So how will Europe guarantee the rights of people it sends there?

Rwanda has also done this before. From 2013, Israel sent Eritrean and Sudanese asylum seekers there under secret deals. Many had their documents taken and were smuggled onward, some all the way to the Mediterranean.

The flawed thinking

Governments have said that return hubs will break the smugglers’ business model. Research points the other way.

A major study based on interviews with more than 80,000 migrants and 450 smugglers found that tougher borders without legal routes increase demand for smugglers. My own research shows that smugglers often work hand in hand with the very authorities Europe pays to stop them.

The UK government has said it will watch the scheme “with interest” and has not ruled out joining.

When asked why France wasn’t part of the group of five, President Emmanuel Macron said simply: “I have never seen a return hub in a third country operate.” He’s right. Return hubs are sold as an innovation, but the logic behind them – outsourcing migration control to countries outside Europe – is not new.

It’s called externalisation and it has been part of European policy for three decades. In that time it has proved ineffective, expensive and corrosive to international law.

As Europe’s leading intergovernmental human rights organisation, the Council of Europe, has noted, it has also meant outsourcing border control to countries with a documented history of serious human rights violations.

Human rights abuses

I’ve conducted fieldwork across North and West Africa for more than a decade, particularly in Tunisia, Libya and Mauritania.I have interviewed hundreds of migrants, and following these deals and their consequences on the ground.

In 2023 the EU struck a €1 billion (£860 million) deal with Tunisia, the so-called Team Europe deal. Most of the money was loans and budget support for Tunisia’s struggling economy, but at its core the deal was about border control.

Since then, violence and arbitrary detention have increased in an already authoritarian and repressive country, where being a Black, undocumented migrant is itself a risk. The same template was rolled out to Mauritania and Egypt in 2024. When I was in Mauritania earlier this year, I saw the same pattern repeating.

Offshoring asylum has been tried before. Denmark first proposed a Rwanda-style scheme in 2021. The UK went further, signing one, before courts blocked it and Keir Starmer scrapped it in 2024, having spent roughly £700 million to send four people to Rwanda, all voluntarily.

Today’s hubs differ in one way: they are for people whose claims have already been rejected in Europe, not for processing claims abroad. But the concerns remain the same.

Expensive and fragile

One country hosts a return hub: Albania, which struck a 2025 deal with Italy to convert its Gjadër centre into exactly that. The centres have drawn heavy criticism from Italian courts and human rights organisations.

Albania itself has signalled that the arrangement won’t survive past 2030, when it expects to join the EU. That is the crux of the matter: deals like this are not a stable foundation for long-term policy. They can unravel whenever the political weather changes in the partner country.

Rather than treating these experiences as a warning, the EU is doubling down. With a future hub in Rwanda, questions remain unanswered: who is responsible if someone’s rights are violated there, the EU country or the host? And once someone arrives, how do you stop them from leaving?

The many people on the move I have met over the years are rarely discouraged by being returned, pushed back, intercepted or deported. It only makes their journeys longer, more expensive and more dangerous. As Chadi told me: “They can return me as many times as they want, but I will keep trying.”

text:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was placed in federal custody after an immigration check-in in San Diego earlier this month was reunited with his family on Nov. 16.

His return, confirmed by Democratic U.S. Rep. Juan Vargas of California and Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, came nearly two weeks after federal officers took the third grader from the uncle who had been raising him. The detention drew swift backlash from his school district, local officials and members of Congress, who wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. demanding his release.

"My heart breaks thinking about what he endured," Vargas said in a statement. "I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place. I have serious questions about how this was handled, and I will be pushing the Administration for answers."

The child, who has not been identified by name, is among the children caught up in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with thousands detained alongside their parents, placed alone in federal shelters or left behind when a parent was deported.

The Department of Homeland Security did not address the child's release in a statement to USA TODAY and referred further questions to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), the Health and Human Services agency that cares for migrant children who are without a parent or legal guardian. DHS has said it took the child into custody and labeled him an unaccompanied minor "out of an abundance of caution" after his uncle "could not establish legal guardianship."

ORR said it does not discuss individual cases and is required by law to care for any child DHS refers to as unaccompanied.

"Family reunification is the goal for every child," the agency said in a statement. "Placement decisions are based on each child’s safety and best interests."

'Did not want to break the law'

The third grader had lived in the United States since 2019, Jozef said. Since his father’s deportation to Mexico in March 2025, he had been staying with his uncle and cousins in City Heights, a San Diego neighborhood that for decades has been a first home for refugees and immigrants from Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia.

He lost his protection from deportation this summer, after the Supreme Court allowed the administration to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians. Months later, a letter arrived summoning him to appear before U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

His uncle took him to the federal building downtown because he "did not want to break the law," according to the San Diego Unified School District, which later recounted the episode in a letter to federal officials. A volunteer who monitors immigration check-ins recorded what followed.

In the video, three armed officers lead the child, dressed in a pressed white button-down, away from the ICE field office and into an elevator. His uncle, who had been listed in school records as the child's authorized caregiver, went home without him.

'His freedom should never have required a public outcry'

To take the child into custody, officers relied on a 2008 anti-trafficking law that requires the government to place unaccompanied migrant children in ORR's care.

That law has increasingly been applied to children like him. For years, ORR shelters housed mostly children who had crossed the southern border alone. But as immigration enforcement has pushed deeper into the country’s interior, the shelters have taken in a growing number of kids separated from the relatives raising them in the United States, attorneys and advocacy groups say.

At Fay Elementary, the district sent crisis counselors to help his classmates cope with his absence. Meanwhile, his advocates were trying to find him.

For days, his family did not know where he was being held. Vargas, along with Reps. Sara Jacobs, Mike Levin, and Scott Peters and Sens. Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, pressed the administration to confirm the child's whereabouts and explain how it planned to reunite him with his family.

The answer came when the child was released. On Nov. 16, Vargas said the child had been held at a facility in Texas, and thanked "everyone who demanded freedom and justice for this child."

Measured against the agency’s current standards, his stay was brief. Children released from ORR custody in October had spent an average of 185 days in its care, according to agency data, compared with 30 days in fiscal year 2024. On an average day that month, the agency held about 1,740 children.

Advocates attribute the longer stays largely to stricter vetting of relatives and guardians who seek to take children in. The administration has added identity and income requirements and begun sharing sponsors’ information with ICE – changes ORR says are meant to protect children "from trafficking and exploitation."

Beyond ORR’s shelters, immigration enforcement has reached thousands of other children. More than 8,000 children were arrested and detained by immigration authorities from January 2025 to July 2026, according to data from the Deportation Data Project, which analyzes federal enforcement records.

For the child, at least, the separation is over. He is back with the uncle and cousins who raised him.

"An 8-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love — not in immigration detention," Jozef said. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry."

text:
The White House has ordered federal agencies to obtain approval before employees agree to testify before Congress, giving President Donald Trump's legal and legislative affairs teams control over requests for testimony as Democrats prepare to investigate his administration after taking control of both chambers in January.

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the directive November 16, 2026, requiring executive departments and agencies to secure clearance from both the White House Office of Legislative Affairs and the Office of White House Counsel before any employee agrees to appear before a congressional committee.

The one-page memorandum, sent to agency general counsels, describes the requirement as an established White House consultation process. Scharf also announced that additional instructions governing other interactions with Congress would follow.

Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections and have pledged investigations into Trump's administration, his family's business dealings, immigration enforcement, the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and other government activities. Their incoming committee chairs will have the authority to call witnesses, demand documents and issue subpoenas.

The directive follows a separate warning Scharf sent to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee when the new Congress convenes. In a November 9 letter, Scharf accused Democratic lawmakers of threatening investigations that could exceed their constitutional authority and warned that certain actions could amount to criminal misconduct.

Scharf cited Supreme Court decisions requiring congressional investigations to serve a legitimate legislative purpose rather than punish political opponents. He also warned that issuing unlawful subpoenas could warrant further investigation by the executive branch.

Garcia rejected the warning, asserting that Congress derives its investigative authority from Article I of the Constitution and operates independently of the White House. Democratic lawmakers have maintained that their planned investigations fall within Congress's responsibility to oversee federal agencies and government spending.

A White House official defended the administration's position, saying it would resist investigations considered politically motivated and baseless.

Federal law protects government employees' ability to provide information to Congress. Under 5 U.S.C. § 7211, federal employees have the right to communicate with lawmakers and congressional committees without interference or denial of that right.

The executive branch has asserted a competing authority to supervise employees' official communications. In a 2004 legal opinion, the Justice Department concluded that senior agency officials could restrict employees from providing certain information to Congress, relying on presidential authority to oversee the executive branch and protect privileged government communications.

That opinion arose from a dispute involving federal health officials and congressional requests for government cost estimates. The Justice Department rejected a broader interpretation of employee disclosure protections advanced by the Congressional Research Service, which had argued that agency officials generally could not prevent employees from supplying information to lawmakers.

Congress can compel testimony through subpoenas, although the executive branch may challenge those demands or assert executive privilege over certain information. Such disputes can lead to negotiations, contempt proceedings or federal court challenges.

Scharf's new memorandum requires approval before an employee agrees to testify but leaves the criteria for granting permission, response deadlines and procedures for handling congressional subpoenas unresolved. Agencies receiving testimony requests will now have to seek White House clearance before committing employees to appear.

text:
The 8-year-old Haitian boy who ICE detained in San Diego nearly two weeks ago has been reunited with his family, advocates with Haitian Bridge Alliance said on Monday.

The boy, a third grader at Fay Elementary School in City Heights, was taken into federal custody on Nov. 4. Video recorded by volunteer observer Karen Pohl at the federal building shows three armed federal agents walking the boy away from ICE’s field office and into an elevator.

That video spread, sparking outrage and protest, and reaching national coverage. Last Thursday, protesters, many of them carrying signs, called for the released of the boy outside the Edward J. Schwartz federal building in downtown San Diego, where ICE holds its offices.

Now, new signs saying "welcome home" decorate the office of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, which worked to bring him back to his family. The organization, the boy and his family all said they are happy to be back together after a difficult wait.

While in federal custody, the boy was taken to a facility in Texas, the organization said.

"The aunt was literally crying, and she said, 'I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.' They haven't been able to sleep because of that," said Guerline Jozef, of the Haitian Bridge Alliance. "The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him. They are able to, you know, rub his head and show how much they missed and love him," Jozef said.

The boy previously had Temporary Protected Status and was living with his uncle after his father was deported last year. ICE called the family for a check-in and said the uncle couldn’t establish legal guardianship, so they took the child into custody for his safety, the agency said.

Congressman Juan Vargas represents the family and intervened with the federal government to secure the boy’s release.

"The people that I was able to talk to, some that I knew pretty well, I said, 'Well, what are you guys doing?' And they were saying, 'Well, you know, they just look at numbers and that’s what they’re looking at right now. They’re trying to get numbers," Vargas said.

The boy told NBC 7 he loves Haitian food and he hoped to have that for dinner Monday night. He said he's looking forward to returning to school, where his favorite class is P.E., this week.

authors: Damon Root, Liz Wolfe, Ted Carpenter, Reem Ibrahim, Charles Oliver
description:

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court's current term has been a bit lacking so far when it comes to high-profile cases. I don't mean to imply any lack of important cases—indeed, just last week the Court heard oral arguments in a major case about holding federal officials to account for constitutional rights violations—rather, what I mean is that we haven't really yet seen the kind of headline-grabbing legal disputes that capture national attention and send political activists into overdrive.

But that may be about to change. On Friday, the justices agreed to hear arguments in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a case arising from the Trump administration's unilateral executive suspension of asylum protections for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. Much like last term's big showdown over tariffs, the key question in this case is whether President Donald Trump is guilty of wielding authority that properly belongs to a different branch of the federal government. At the very least, a SCOTUS fight over immigration and presidential overreach in the waning age of Trump has the makings of a blockbuster case.

Under federal immigration law, persons who are unlawfully present in the United States are subject to removal proceedings. At the same time, federal law also says that such persons may attempt to obtain relief from removal by seeking asylum, or by seeking withholding from removal, under either the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) or the Convention Against Torture, on the grounds that they would face persecution or torture if deported.

The Trump administration, however, asserts that it may unilaterally suspend the asylum and withholding from removal protections for persons who unlawfully crossed the U.S.-Mexico border. According to a January 2025 presidential proclamation, "the President's inherent powers to control the borders of the United States, including those deriving from his authority to control the foreign affairs of the United States, necessarily include the ability to prevent the physical entry of aliens involved in an invasion into the United States, and to rapidly repatriate them to an alternative location."

In April 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected this executive argument. "Our task is to determine whether Congress has granted the Executive the authority to remove foreign individuals present in the United States without adhering to the removal procedures or providing the substantive removal protections that Congress prescribed in the INA," the appellate court said. "We conclude that the INA's text, structure, and history make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts."

It is that loss before the D.C. Circuit that the Trump administration has now persuaded the Supreme Court to review.

In addition to reviewing the statutory question decided by the D.C. Circuit, it is possible the Supreme Court may also wade into the underlying argument over what counts as an "invasion" for constitutional purposes, as Trump's assertion of "inherent" executive power in this case rests on Trump's view that the president is doubly empowered to act in this manner because an "invasion" is occurring at the southern border. That view from Trump is a version of the oft-heard argument that normal constitutional limits on the president should be weakened or even removed when the president is acting in the name of foreign affairs or national security.

My guess is that the Supreme Court will avoid this constitutional minefield and stick to the safer grounds of statutory interpretation. But an outbreak of broader constitutional conflict is possible.
