text:
It is a less visible aspect of President Donald Trump’s immigration offensive. But more than 60 people have died behind the walls of immigration detention centers since the Republican returned to the White House for a second term.

Medical neglect, physical abuse, excessive punishment, lack of food, filth, contaminated water and a system of mistreatment designed to pressure undocumented people to accept deportation. The list of alleged human rights violations at the over 170 jails run by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its contractors is extensive.

As the number of detained migrants rises, the Trump administration has minimized oversight of these facilities and has at times left verification of conditions to the very multimillion-dollar companies that operate them. Democrats, who will regain control of Congress in January, have pledged to step up scrutiny of ICE jails and put an end to abuses.

Democrats have faced obstacles carrying out surprise inspections of these centers and have had to turn to the courts to defend their right to enter without prior notice. That has been the stage for another prolonged showdown between the Trump administration and its congressional opponents. The conflict worsened when the government shut the doors to lawmakers by adopting a policy requiring visits to be requested several days in advance. That requirement, which is no longer in force, limited their ability to see firsthand what was happening in these facilities.

“We’ve heard horrific stories: people not receiving medication, not enough food, and the list goes on,” California Congressman Robert García said in October. García is poised to chair the House Committee on Oversight and Reform. After the Democrats’ decisive midterm victory, the Long Beach representative vowed to put the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) — and in particular ICE agents, whom he says he has documented for more than 1,000 abuses — and the facilities that hold migrants under increased scrutiny.

In early October, García visited, with other Democratic lawmakers, one of the centers with the highest death tolls during Trump’s second term: Adelanto, in California’s high desert. The four deceased at the facility were Mexican. Upon entering, the congressman was surprised to hear administrators repeat the president’s narrative. “They told us that most people at Adelanto had criminal records, when we know that is not true,” he said.

Weak government oversight

Another detention center expected to face increased scrutiny starting in January is Eloy, Arizona, where at least two migrants have died since early 2025. Representative-elect JoAnna Mendoza, whose district includes that facility, is also calling for stricter oversight.

“We need clear audits in the detention centers,” Mendoza told EL PAÍS in an interview in August. “Some of these centers are audited by private companies. How can we be sure those audits aren’t being falsified? We need oversight of all this,” she insisted.

Nearly two years into Trump’s immigration offensive, oversight mechanisms for ICE jails have weakened. A report published two days after the midterms by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent agency that works for Congress, notes that, through last June, two of the four entities charged with inspecting those centers had reduced their visits or had stopped them altogether.

ICE’s own Office of Detention Oversight (ODO) decreased the frequency of its reviews. The Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman ceased inspections due to budget cuts and a significant reduction in staff. The other two entities, which maintained their activities unchanged, are the ICE-dependent Institutional Health Services Corps (IHSC) and the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General (OIG).

The GAO report cites a March 2025 memorandum approved by the then–acting ICE director that formalized reduced regularity of ODO inspections and expanded self-inspection mechanisms. The measure aimed to reduce administrative burdens on private operators of the centers. In other words, the companies themselves would be responsible for monitoring.

However, the GAO report warns that the lack of inspections by government officials makes it difficult to identify “deficiencies in their facilities, including those related to the health, life, and safety” of detained migrants.

In a statement sent to EL PAÍS, a DHS spokesperson said ICE is subject to periodic audits and inspections by external bodies to ensure its centers meet standards. The spokesperson also said migrants in its custody receive three meals a day, potable water, clothing, access to showers, personal hygiene items, and comprehensive medical care.

“ICE enforces stricter detention standards than most U.S. prisons,” the spokesperson said, without directly addressing the warnings from members of Congress that there would be greater scrutiny.

A profitable business

Immigrant incarceration has become a lucrative business. During fiscal years 2025 and 2026, ICE received more than $45 billion allocated exclusively to immigration detention. The agency also expanded its network of facilities: it operated 128 in April 2025 and 172 last April, a 34% increase. Meanwhile, it holds about 67,000 people in custody, a 71% rise compared with the start of Trump’s second term.

The equation is simple for ICE contractors: more occupied beds means more money. GEO Group, operator of about 20 immigration detention facilities — including Adelanto — currently houses roughly 20,000 migrants in its centers. After the midterms, the publicly traded company celebrated a financial milestone: it announced year-to-date revenue had surpassed $2 billion, a figure it had not reached since it began operating in 1984.

The tie between GEO Group and Trump goes beyond the multimillion-dollar donations the company has made to the president’s campaigns and to political organizations that support his movement. Three officials who have held prominent posts in the current administration were on its payroll. Before becoming attorney general, Pam Bondi worked as a lobbyist for GEO Group. David Venturella, the current acting ICE director, was a company executive for 11 years. And Tom Homan, Trump’s border czar, was a paid consultant to one of its subsidiaries.

Another company that has benefited from aggressive immigration raids is CoreCivic, which has also made multimillion-dollar contributions to Trump. The company earned an additional $1.5 billion from the sale of two California jails to ICE — one in San Diego and another in California City — both sites flagged by allegations of mistreatment and abuse. The federal agency agreed that CoreCivic would continue to operate the facilities while the contracts remain in effect.

“Big corporations and billionaires have profited from every human being sent to these horrible facilities across the country,” Congressman Robert García said in October.

GEO Group did not respond to a request for comment from this outlet. A CoreCivic spokesperson, however, said in a written statement that the company has worked with the federal government for more than 40 years under administrations of both parties. “We have always welcomed oversight of our work, and that has not changed,” the spokesperson said.

The case of Ulises

Holding ICE contractors accountable is not easy. Laura Murchie, an attorney with Disability Law United, compares that struggle to David versus Goliath. “It takes a whole team of lawyers to try to get GEO Group and CoreCivic to answer for their actions,” she told EL PAÍS. “It’s difficult for affected people, and even for the lawyers handling their cases, to get them to assume responsibility,” she added.

In July, Murchie launched a legal battle against both companies, ICE, DHS, and the Trump administration. She represents Ulises Peña López, a Mexican immigrant with special needs who, according to a lawsuit filed in the Northern District of California, was the victim of “a violent arrest” by ICE agents in Sunnyvale in February 2025.

The complaint alleges ICE officers took Ulises to a secluded alley where they beat him until he lost consciousness, requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Paramedics rushed him to a hospital, but before he recovered, federal agents took him into custody. He spent six months detained in GEO Group and CoreCivic facilities before being deported in October of that year to Mexico, his native country. He now lives there, separated from his wife and young daughter.

“During his detention, the necessary accommodations for his disabilities were not made. As a result, he continues to suffer harm primarily stemming from the mistreatment he endured while in custody,” Murchie says.

The aftermath has affected Ulises’s daily life and employment prospects: in Mexico he is now limited to part-time work. In California he earned a living in construction.

“After the violent arrest he suffered loss of vision and hearing, as well as numbness and paralysis on the right side of his body, affecting his mobility. He needs a cane to walk and suffers severe headaches,” the attorney explained.

The lawsuit seeks compensation for the physical and emotional damages Ulises suffered. His return to California is not among the remedies requested in the case, because, his lawyer explains, they consider that a lost battle. Murchie acknowledges the litigation will be an uphill struggle, largely because of the power and influence of ICE contractors. “We are talking about multibillion-dollar companies,” she stresses.

text:
The Council of Europe's (CoE's) Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) last week published updated standards setting out the human rights requirements for detaining migrants, asylum seekers and other foreign nationals under immigration legislation.

You can download the 42-page standard here.

Drawing on more than 36 years of CPT monitoring visits to CoE member states, including the UK, the standard sets out 13 areas of guidance, covering the prevention of ill-treatment, detention safeguards, accommodation, material conditions, staffing, healthcare, the treatment of vulnerable people, security measures and accountability. It also addresses the prevention of self-harm and suicide, independent monitoring, complaints procedures and contingency planning.

The CPT identifies the following guiding principles:

Immigration detention must:

be used only as a measure of last resort;

be non-punitive;

be subject to accountability mechanisms.

Persons in immigration detention must:

be protected from ill-treatment;

be afforded fundamental safeguards;

be held in suitable premises, with decent conditions;

have their health needs and vulnerabilities addressed.

While the Committee acknowledges that states have the right to control their borders and determine their immigration policies, it stresses that these powers must be exercised in accordance with international human rights obligations, including the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment and the principle of non-refoulement.

Immigration detention should be used only as a last resort, the CPT says, stressing that irregular entry for the purpose of seeking asylum is not in itself an unlawful act and does not constitute a ground for detention.

It states: "18. When a permissible ground for detention is identified following an individual assessment, authorities should first consider less intrusive alternatives to detention, particularly for persons with specific vulnerabilities. These alternative non-detention measures may include various restrictions on movement which fall short of detention, such as community supervision, regular reporting, or assignment to a specific residence.

"19. Bearing in mind that immigration detention should only be used as a measure of last resort, the detention of asylum seekers should be even more exceptional. Under international refugee law, irregular entry for the purpose of seeking international protection is not in itself an unlawful act and does not constitute a ground for detention. In those instances where there are exceptional reasons for depriving an asylum seeker of their liberty, these reasons should be fully documented. Furthermore, asylum seekers should preferably be held separately from foreign nationals who have not applied for international protection."

The CPT also calls on states to provide adequate legal and procedural safeguards, stating: "16. Procedural safeguards – such as the provision of decisions in writing and in a language and form which the persons understand, timely and effective access to legal assistance throughout the procedure, the right to be heard in person by the decision-making authority, access to interpretation, the right to receive a written, reasoned decision, the possibility to appeal, and the automatic suspensive effect of the appeal – are essential to preventing violations of Article 3. The process should ensure confidentiality, provide an objective analysis of the human rights situation in the receiving country, and include an individual assessment of the prima facie risk of ill-treatment in the event of removal of the person concerned."

On legal assistance, the standard clarifies: "25. The right of access to a lawyer applies from the outset of detention and continues throughout the entire period of deprivation of liberty. It includes assistance with matters relating to detention, residence, and removal, as well as the right to confidential communication with a lawyer and to have legal counsel present during official interviews.

"26. The right of access to a lawyer includes access to free legal aid for persons who cannot afford the services of a private lawyer. Detained persons should be informed of available providers and legal counselling schemes should be established, where possible, with in-person, telephone, or video call duty lawyer systems. Authorities should cooperate with relevant Bar Associations to effectively guarantee this right.

"27. Effective access to a lawyer also requires the removal of barriers, including disproportionate restrictions on mobile phone, telephone, and internet use. Lawyers should be enabled to consult personal files and have prompt and effective access to their clients, including any meetings required prior to judicial hearings or official interviews, with the assistance of an interpreter provided free of charge, if requested by the person or by staff. Administrative requirements should not be unnecessarily burdensome, such as unduly limiting the frequency or duration of legal consultations."

The CPT said the updated guidance is intended to help member states prevent ill-treatment and ensure that all foreign nationals deprived of their liberty are treated with dignity and held in humane conditions consistent with the administrative nature of immigration detention.

Emphasising the need for humane and decent conditions, the Committee said its visits had repeatedly identified overcrowded and unsuitable detention facilities, poor material conditions, prolonged detention and restrictive regimes.

name: Policy
title: What do Democrats' sweeping midterm wins mean for Trump's ICE crackdown?
description: Despite House and Senate majorities, Democrats face a battle to enact legislation – but they have the power to conduct tough new oversight
text:
Despite House and Senate majorities, Democrats face a battle to enact legislation – but they have the power to conduct tough new oversight

The Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” wins gave them strong majorities in both chambers of Congress, new governors’ mansions and power in some unexpected places. Voters dealt a stunning rebuke to Donald Trump – and his ruthless deportation campaign and violent ICE raids across the country were among the key issues that cost Republicans support. But what will Democrats do about the immigration crackdown?

The US Congress theoretically has the ability to force many changes on ICE through legislation, such as taking away funds, restricting detention centers and mandating a focus on migrants with violent records – after Trump’s pledges to target “the worst of the worst” actually turned into mass arrests of people without criminal records and even of people with legal papers.

Democrats have said such things as, “We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities [have] killed individuals … assaulted individuals… incarcerated individuals” (Mississippi Representative Bennie Thompson , likely to chair the House homeland security committee), and “We will rip ICE apart” (incoming US Senator of Minnesota Peggy Flanagan ).

But even with House and Senate majorities, enacting legislation will face steep odds without Republicans on board, considering presidential veto power and the Senate filibuster, which requires at least 60 votes to move bills forward.

And not everyone in the Democratic caucus is on the same page. Leaders are initially proposing more modest guardrails, banning masks for ICE officers and requiring body-worn cameras in the field.

In practice, one of the clearest unilateral powers Democrats will have next year is that of greater oversight, conducting investigations to expose the faults of the Trump administration’s immigration policy.

Democratic-led congressional committees will be able to issue subpoenas, and they already plan to call in homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin , new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller , border czar Tom Homan and former border patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino for questioning in public.

They may also hold hearings in cities where they can present evidence of agency misconduct, while continuing congressional visits to ICE detention facilities to check on conditions there and increase public exposure.

Meanwhile, they could consider impeachment . It is unclear whether the US constitution allows for someone like Miller, as chief of staff, to be impeached. But if Democrats lead a second attempt to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth – and especially if they succeed in removing him from office – it could curtail Miller’s authority by putting other impeachable officials directing immigration enforcement, such as Mullin, on notice that they could lose their jobs if they follow any White House advice to act lawlessly.

Democrats, both sitting and incoming, are now pushing for comprehensive immigration changes to a system that both parties have long agreed is “broken”, but Congress has not had the will to reform top to tail, balancing security measures at the US-Mexico border with helping immigrants already in the US.

Sufficient bipartisan unity is hard to come by. Republicans largely oppose what they call “amnesty” – giving people in the country unlawfully the chance to legalize their status. Some progressive Democrats, meanwhile, denounce crackdowns on the border and restrictions on seeking asylum that contradict international law.

Yet more targeted fixes may be on the table. Some 81% of Americans endorse a citizenship pathway for undocumented immigrants who came to the US as children, also known as “Dreamers”, according to a recent Gallup poll. Even the Trump administration has indicated renewed openness to this idea since the midterm drubbing.

Lawmakers may be able to get agreement to reinstate temporary protected status (TPS), a program allowing work permits and protection from deportation for nationalities in the US who are unable to safely return to their home countries, especially for Haitians and Afghans . The administration has ended TPS for roughly a million people across more than a dozen nationalities.

Legislation could even create a pathway to a green card for TPS holders, something that does not exist now.

However, once again, with Trump threatening to become “ Mr Veto ” it’s unclear how he and Senate Republicans will proceed.

DHS, which oversees immigration enforcement and many immigration benefits in the US, has received about a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding during Trump’s second term alone. Taxpayers’ money designated for ICE soared and it is now the highest federally-funded US law enforcement agency.

That includes a roughly $70bn cash infusion in June, meant to bankroll the department through the end of Trump’s presidency. Democrats say they plan to make efforts to claw back or withhold at least some of that funding through legislation once they control Congress.

Very unlikely. The slogan “abolish ICE” became a political liability for Democrats as Americans turned on undocumented immigrants when unauthorized border crossings rose sharply under the Biden administration and Trump and his Maga white nationalist ranks started calling them an “invasion”. Even to many mainstream US voters the notion that you should entirely abolish ICE – like defunding the police – stood for the left being too soft on law and order.

Despite the backlash that Republicans are now feeling given the perceived cruelty of Trump’s mass deportation campaign and ICE violence on the streets, an ideological divide among progressive and more moderate Democrats would probably preclude closing down the agency.

The re-elected centrist Democratic congressman Henry Cuellar, representing a Texas-Mexico border district, last Wednesday said simply: “I’m not going to abolish ICE.”

Although immigration enforcement is broadly a federal responsibility, state and local governments have been deeply involved in recent years – especially through cooperation between police and sheriffs’ departments and ICE, whether because of what’s called 287(g) agreements or other collaborative policies.

Texas, in particular, saw a political earthquake, where Democrats flipped a US Senate seat, the governorship, the attorney general’s office and the state House of Representatives.

This followed decades of Republican dominance statewide and increasingly draconian immigration enforcement. Texas’s laws and policies have required local law enforcement to work with ICE and state penalties have criminalized people who unlawfully crossed the border with Mexico.

Leadership in states that swung heavily blue now have the opportunity to back off such aggressive tactics, likely leading to fewer ICE arrests, less depletion of immigrant-heavy workforces, and the potential for communities to rebuild trust with local law enforcement.

Democrats are now set to hold all 10 of the House seats along the almost 3,000 miles of the US-Mexico border and the four border governorships – California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas – for the first time since 1979, as well as four states’ top legal offices. Hard-right Texas governor Greg Abbott, for example, outgoing after 12 years, unilaterally bussed migrants to Democratic-led cities and spent an estimated $11bn militarizing the Tex-Mex border with the extreme project, “ Operation Lone Star ”. Now Democrats will examine what they can and wish to unwind.

Democratic state leaders could help reinstate policies that help immigrants, such as access to in-state college tuition for undocumented students, after those were gutted in some states amid federal collusion in Trump’s second term.

They could also join lawsuits challenging Trump-era policies, and cities, counties and states that are suddenly on the same side of the political debate could pool resources to fight legal battles against the federal government instead of against each other .

The label “sanctuary city” has somewhat gone out of vogue in recent years. But in a similar vein, Democratic city and county leaders, as well as state legislatures, may devise new laws and strategies to block cooperation with ICE, at least when it comes to immigrants who do not pose a public safety risk.

For federal congressional seats that have flipped in favor of Democrats, immigrants may discover a new ally. Congressional offices often help their constituents – including noncitizens – contact federal agencies, get answers from the government and sometimes find solutions. That can mean finally receiving a work permit stuck in limbo, helping a family member overseas with their visa processing or getting a loved one out of detention.

Ultimately, the president and his subordinates have given no signs that policies will be easing - and they plan to continue deportations.

Despite Trump telling 60 Minutes after the midterm losses that maybe immigration enforcement was “too tough” , he appointed the ferociously anti-immigration zealot and longtime ally Miller as his chief of staff shortly after that interview was recorded.

While Democrats can shine a spotlight on excesses and racist attitudes and act as a buffer, more transformational change will probably have to wait to see if a Democrat – particularly a progressive – wins the White House in 2028.

title: More barriers for migrant minors in the US: a shelter prevents a child from seeking legal help ...
description:

They have also found federal shelters where organizations were not allowed to provide legal help for new cases.
text:
A nine-year-old migrant held at a youth shelter in Texas tried to call an information hotline to understand what could happen at his hearing before an immigration judge. Shelter staff did not allow him to connect to that number. Desperate, he called his mother, who lives in California, and asked her for help. The mother then contacted the organization that created the hotline to support detained minors; she told them about the obstacles her son was facing in obtaining basic information. Only after that did the child receive a call from that organization: they explained how the court process works, what his rights are, and even determined that he had a strong asylum case.

“That contact did not happen because the child dialed; it happened because his mother did,” Eduardo Martínez, a legal advocate for the Pro Bono Asylum Representation Project in South Texas (ProBAR), tells EL PAÍS. “What’s worrying is that not every child in a detention center has a family member or sponsor who can act as an advocate for them.”

The line the child tried to reach is called Orientation and Resources for Youth in Detention, DORY for short. ProBAR created it to support migrant minors held in federal custody without their parents or legal guardians. It was established just after July 31, when the Trump administration ended a long-standing funding contract that for years had allowed about 100 organizations to represent more than 20,000 children for free in their immigration proceedings since 2003.

When the helpline began operating in August, ProBAR was receiving calls from 11 youth facilities. But by September, Martínez says, calls were coming from only two centers. And although they had access to fewer shelters, Martínez says the number of calls did not drop: “More children were calling because, as we’ve been seeing, their immigration hearings are being moved up.”

Activists say what happened to this nine-year-old is just one more barrier among many the federal government is putting in front of minors so they cannot defend their cases or seek help in a timely way. Organizations have argued that there can be no due process if migrant children and teenagers in government custody do not understand the system they face, the penalties and offers they receive, the court terminology used, and the consequences.

The federal office that holds custody of the minors, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), disputes the organizations’ claims. In an email it said it is meeting “its legal obligations” and “is not acting in any way that would discourage a minor from seeking appropriate legal protection.”

Only in October did the government announce the creation of a division it describes as independent — though it is run by the same federal agency that holds custody of the children — that will be responsible for defending unaccompanied minors. There are still few details on how it will operate.

Of the more than 56,000 cases involving unaccompanied minors resolved so far in 2026, 55% never had legal representation before an immigration court, according to a data analysis by the Vera Institute of Justice, a nonprofit research group. That figure represents a seven percentage-point increase from 2025 and a 17 percentage-point increase from 2024.

An “avalanche of harm”

Since January 2025, when Trump began his second term, the president has sought to remove federal funding for legal support programs for migrant minors.

At the same time, he has reduced existing legal protections designed to safeguard minors in immigration proceedings: one measure taken in April 2025 was to summon children in ORR custody to immigration courts, when previously they were brought only after being reunified with their parents or sponsors.

By July of that year, in violation of federal law, border agents began asking migrant children whether they wanted to “self-deport,” and shortly after, those in federal shelters started receiving letters urging them to abandon their cases and return to their home countries in exchange for a cash payment in dollars.

Shaina Aber is executive director of the Acacia Center for Justice, the nonprofit that received federal funds and distributed them to 100 organizations for the defense of minors. She estimates that two in ten children in Trump administration custody have lost their pro bono lawyers because the programs that supported them were closed and that four of those programs have shut down. The federal funding cuts have left minors more vulnerable to additional measures being rolled out.

Acacia’s director says that since July they have learned of children with pending or approved petitions before the Department of Homeland Security who have received removal orders from immigration judges; they have encountered minors whose cases were dismissed without them being heard in court; they have identified children pressured to abandon their applications in exchange for $3,000, and when they asked for time to consider the offer, that time was denied. They have also found federal shelters where organizations were not allowed to provide legal help for new cases.

She recounts the case of a child in Arizona without a lawyer whom an immigration judge gave only two options: voluntary departure or deportation. “The child broke down crying and said he was afraid to return to his country. The judge issued an order of removal,” Aber says. When attorneys from one of the organizations in Acacia’s network tried to contact the child the next day to offer legal help to appeal the decision, he had already been deported.

The National Immigration Law Center (NILC) brought a suit in a federal district court in Maryland on behalf of children represented by organizations in several states and won. They argued that multiple federal agencies were “illegally dismantling the rights of unaccompanied minors seeking help.”

Among the cases supporting the lawsuit were dozens of summonses to appear at hearings with less than 24 hours’ notice and, in some instances, a single lawyer had to be in more than one of those hearings at the same time. That left many children — including victims of violence who were in shelters and had limited access to their attorneys — without the opportunity to properly prepare for their interviews.

NILC says that in one of those cases a girl who had been hospitalized for a heart condition was forced the next day to undergo a hours-long asylum interview about her claim: it was based on sexual abuse she suffered in her country of origin.

In a press release, NILC reports that the girl asked to end the interview because she felt pain in her chest: “She was crying while holding her chest. And instead of ending the interview, the official insisted she continue. Only after subjecting the minor for hours to severe mental and emotional distress did the official agree to reschedule the interview.”

For Aber, all of the above “makes it clear that the government is trying to limit minors’ access to representation as well as their ability to access the legal system.” She views the sum of the measures taken by the government over two years as “an avalanche of harm inflicted on hundreds of children.”

authors: PHILIPP JENNE and GEIR MOULSON The Associated Press

The aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said alongside officials from the other European countries and Rwanda's interior minister.
She predicted that "many other European countries" would join in.
"Offshore deportation centers are the latest cynical expression of the EU's drive to shift its responsibilities to other countries," Human Rights Watch researcher Clementine de Montjoye said in a statement.
Amnesty International Austria asylum and migration expert Aimée Stuflesser said in a statement that "today's disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past."
text:
VIENNA -- A group of European countries announced on Monday that they aim to set up a "return hub" in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year, a move they hope will also deter more people from coming.

The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren't legally able to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central plank of that effort.

The plan by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands, which have spearheaded negotiations with non-EU countries, drew immediate criticism from human rights groups.

The aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said alongside officials from the other European countries and Rwanda's interior minister.

"I think this will be a game changer making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. "We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration."

She predicted that "many other European countries" would join in. Her immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, said the plan is to have a fully negotiated agreement with Rwanda "within the next few months."

Officials were vague about how many migrants might be sent to Rwanda, but emphasized the plan's deterrent effect.

"The most important number is the number that we will never see because hopefully they will not start their journey to Europe," Frederiksen said. "So this is a milestone."

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said his country would give a "second chance" to people who have no right to stay in Europe. He said that those who arrive will be offered the opportunity "to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference."

Asked how Rwanda would guarantee refugees' human rights, he said Rwanda would bring on board organizations such as the U.N. refugee agency and "there will be an independent monitoring mechanism."

Human rights groups have criticized plans to deport migrants to facilities in third countries, arguing that European nations can't guarantee their rights will be respected there. European officials insist that the new hubs would abide by European and international law.

"Offshore deportation centers are the latest cynical expression of the EU's drive to shift its responsibilities to other countries," Human Rights Watch researcher Clementine de Montjoye said in a statement. "Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

Amnesty International Austria asylum and migration expert Aimée Stuflesser said in a statement that "today's disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past."

The U.N. refugee agency said it only supports the possible use of return hubs in line with human rights standards, and as a way to help returns of people whose claims for asylum were denied after a full and fair assessment.

UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh said the agency was involved in "constructive discussions" with the five EU countries "to provide advice on the compliance of the return hub process with international human rights law standards." No agreement with the countries has been signed.

Information for this article was contributed by Jamey Keaten of The Associated Press.

text:
On 16 November 2026, a US federal judge struck down the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.

The US District Court for the District of Massachusetts found that the rule was “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedure Act. In legal terminology, an arbitrary and capricious act is defined as one that is “lacking a rational basis, ignoring the facts and evidence, or based on whim rather than law or reason.”

The judgement means:

The decades-long D/S framework remains intact;

The rule insisting on fixed admission periods, extension-of-stay requirements, and restrictions on academic mobility will not come into effect.

Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, responded to the ruling:

“Today’s ruling is a clear and important victory for international students and scholars and the colleges and universities that welcome them. Preserving Duration of Status gives students greater certainty as they pursue their education and allows institutions to support their academic progress without arbitrary hurdles and unnecessary barriers. The harmful consequences of the current administration’s policy actions and efforts are already evident in the significant declines in international student enrolment and interest we are witnessing.”

The challenge made by US international education and business sectors succeeded

The court’s decision represents an important win for the coalition of educational and business organisations that challenged the final rule in the summer. Represented by Paul Hughes, partner at McDermott Will & Schulte, this coalition includes NAFSA: Association of International Educators; the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM); the American Federation of Teachers (AFT); Graduate Labor Organization, AFT Local 6516 (GLO); International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW); United Auto Workers Local 2322; and the NewsGuild-CWA.

Dr Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, stated:

“With this ruling, the judge has sent an unequivocal and resounding message: the longstanding Duration of Status policy is retained. This outcome underscores the importance of defending international education through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy.”

How did the court come to its decision?

NAFSA writes: “The court held that the rule was arbitrary and capricious because DHS failed to appropriately weigh its costs and benefits, justify the changes based on its stated fraud and national security concerns, consider less burdensome alternatives, or adequately respond to significant public comments. The court further emphasized that DHS failed to meaningfully consider improvements to the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) as an alternative to imposing a costly new system.

The court also held that the rule’s restrictions on academic studies exceeded DHS’s statutory authority because they were not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 student visa program. As the court explained, ‘The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program.’”

What does it mean for international students and institutions?

As a result of the 16 November ruling, international students will continue to enjoy the benefits of the Duration of Status (D/S) system – principally the ability to remain in the US for the duration of their academic journey. They remain able to transfer from one institution to another and to enrol in additional programmes without automatically needing a visa extension. If they do require an extension, they will go to the Designated School Official (DSO) as usual rather than having to apply to an immigration authority with no knowledge of their case.

US colleges and universities – which have been rocked by the DHS’s efforts to abolish D/S – will find some relief because the administrative burden of adapting student supports, databases, legal protections, communications to stakeholders, enrolment management, etc. to the final rule will end, at least for now. However, many have already faced staff, student, and agent distress and mounting costs related to the real chance that the final rule would remain in place.

It is widely expected that the US government will appeal the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts’ decision to preserve D/S.

A win for international students and American research vitality

Robert J. McCarron, president and CEO of the Association of Independent Colleges & Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), stated:

“We are pleased that the court vacated the entire Duration of Status rule as arbitrary and capricious and reiterated in its ruling that the “nature and purpose” of the F-1 visa is to permit, and indeed encourage, international students to pursue educational opportunities here. International students add to the vibrancy of our campuses, drive innovative research, and support the Commonwealth’s economic vitality.”

Randi Weingarten, president of AFT, added:

“Today’s final order will have resounding impacts for generations of scientists and scholars from every corner of the globe that make America the worldwide leader in cutting-edge research. The Trump administration’s proposed limits on how long international scholars have to complete their studies were arbitrary and hostile. We stand united with our 420,000 higher education members, international and American alike, so they can continue to pursue difficult questions, challenge conventional wisdom, publish findings without political interference and make US colleges and universities the envy of the world."

text:
European governments have the right to tighten their migration policies but must not undermine their commitments to human rights, Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has told Euronews.

Berset rejected suggestions that Europe was facing a migration crisis or that the right to asylum was becoming politically unsustainable, insisting that governments could reconcile tougher immigration controls with their international obligations.

"Human rights are human rights for everybody or for no one," he said.

Berset stressed that European human rights legislation did not prevent governments from deporting migrants who had no legitimate right to remain, pointing out that the European Court of Human Rights had upheld some expulsions while ruling against others.

He also insisted that plans to establish so-called return hubs outside the European Union had to meet European human rights standards. "Can they be compatible with European human rights standards? We need to prepare this well and have a proper discussion about it," he said.

His remarks come as five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish a return hub for rejected asylum seekers.

Berset expressed regret that preparations appeared to have taken place without continuing earlier discussions initiated at the Council of Europe.

He warned that respect for the rules-based order, which he described as essential to ensuring stability, peace and predictability, must also underpin Europe's approach to migration.

text:
Takeaways

DOL proposes overhauling PERM practices, including longer recruitment periods, expanded advertising requirements, and closer alignment with employers’ ordinary hiring practices.

Certain layoffs within two years before filing would bar PERM applications; later layoffs would trigger notification and job-offer obligations.

Current requirements remain in place while rulemaking proceeds.

The proposal does not impose changes immediately. There will be a 60 day notice-and-comment period prior to release of a final rule.

The proposed rule is expected to draw considerable interest from businesses and various interest groups, potentially resulting in a high volume of public comments submitted. DOL must consider those comments and meaningfully address significant issues raised in any final rule. Consequently, the final rule could substantively differ from the proposal.

Expanded Recruitment Requirements

The proposal would replace mandatory print newspaper advertising and the employer’s existing recruitment framework with requirements centered on electronic recruitment.

Generally, employers would need a state workforce agency job order, employer website advertising where applicable, advertising on job search websites, and recruitment through a job fair, campus event, or school placement office under the proposal. Social media advertising would be required where customarily used for comparable positions.

Under the proposal, most required advertisements would run for at least 90 calendar days, or longer where the employer’s customary recruitment practices require. The advertisements would need to end 30–60 calendar days before filing a PERM labor certification.

Employers would also need to use recruitment channels and application procedures comparable to those used for similar non-PERM positions. Advertisements would disclose wages and additional job details, and a signed recruitment report would accompany the application.

Restrictions Following Layoffs

Under the proposal, employers could not file PERMs if they have laid off U.S. workers in the same or similar occupation within the relevant area of intended employment during the preceding two years, up from the current six months.

Covered layoffs after filing would trigger notice to DOL, and USCIS if an immigrant petition is pending, within five business days, along with obligations to offer the sponsored position to affected workers and document outcomes. These obligations would generally continue through Form I-140 approval. Restrictions would also reach certain placements at other employers that have conducted layoffs.

Schedule A, Continuing Notice Obligations

The proposal would eliminate the Schedule A route currently used for professional nurses, physical therapists, and certain workers of exceptional ability, requiring affected employers to undertake individualized labor certification.

Notices of filing would begin within 10 business days before filing and generally remain available through I-140 approval, including at applicable third-party worksites.

Employer Considerations

Employers should assess how longer recruitment periods, layoff history, and coordination among recruiting, HR, and immigration teams could affect sponsorship plans.

DOL proposes applying the new framework to applications filed on or after the 90th day following publication of a final rule. Beginning recruitment under the current requirements would therefore not necessarily preserve those requirements for a later filing.

Jackson Lewis attorneys are monitoring implementation of any updated PERM regulation. If you have questions about the potential changes to PERM filings, please reach out to our team for help.

title: 5 countries announce plan to deport failed asylum-seekers to Rwanda - POLITICO
description:
VIENNA — Five European Union countries plan to open a deportation hub in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said Monday.
The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU.
In a statement Monday, the U.N. organization confirmed it had received a request from Rwanda to support EU return hub arrangements.
“We are already exploring other partner countries, and I think other European countries will participate as well,” Frederiksen said.
Frederiksen also pushed back against human rights concerns in the partnership with Rwanda.
text:
VIENNA — Five European Union countries plan to open a deportation hub in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said Monday.

“If people without the right of residence in the EU cannot be removed, our entire asylum system is made a mockery of. And we are not going to allow that,” Stocker said.

Stocker, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and government ministers from those two countries plus the Netherlands, Germany and Greece announced the plan at a press conference. The ministers stopped short of confirming they had cemented a deal, but said the hub would become operational during 2027.

There are still some “technical things” that have to be “sorted out,” Frederiksen said. “But the framework, the idea and the partnership is now in place.”

A reform of EU legislation adopted earlier this year made it possible for countries to negotiate deals to set up such deportation centers — as long as they comply with fundamental rights obligations.

The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU.

The countries said they intend to target adults without children, and specifically people who don’t cooperate — or whose home countries don’t collaborate — in the deportation process.

“For me, today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system; a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens. To put it very short, it needs to be a democratic decision who can enter and who can stay in our societies,” Frederiksen said.

Staying in Rwanda

The five countries want to set up a reception center with the capacity to register and process 100 people at a time. Rejected asylum seekers who decide to stay in Rwanda rather than return to their country of origin would be given a residence permit and support to find a job and learn the language.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said he expected few would opt to stay, but insisted that those who do “are not going to be kept in a camp … they’ll be integrated in our society.”

“Those transferred to Rwanda will have the opportunity to settle, integrate into Rwandese society and build a new future,” said Dutch Foreign Affairs Minister Tom Berendsen.

When sending migrants to Rwanda, their protection would remain a “key priority,” he said. The partnership would also have to meet the principle of non-refoulement, which forbids countries from forcing people to countries where they might be under threat, as well as other principles of international and European law, Berendsen added.

Rwanda has “considerable experience in hosting refugees” and a “strong track record of working with international organizations, including the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees(UNHCR),” the Dutch minister said, adding that the five countries want to continue working with these organizations.

It’s not yet clear whether the IOM will be involved. In a statement Monday, the U.N. organization confirmed it had received a request from Rwanda to support EU return hub arrangements. “IOM has indicated that it can support in principle, provided its mandate and international standards can be upheld,” the organization said.

Civil society groups are not convinced.

In a joint reaction, 47 human rights, civil society and trade union groups warned that European authorities had previously reported “torture in detention, arbitrary arrests and impunity within the security services” in Rwanda, as well as a “real risk” of refoulement.

EU countries’ partnership “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” they wrote in a call on the EU to protect human rights.

“I think we need to go beyond the existing cliché,” Biruta said on Monday. Rwanda is hosting more than 150,000 refugees “from as far as Afghanistan, from Sudan, Congolese, Burundians, and their rights were respected,” and it’s asking for a return hub system that meets “international law, European law and our national laws.”

The country wants to bring on board international organizations and put an independent monitoring mechanism in place, he said: “Everyone will be welcome to witness and monitor what’s happening.”

But civil society groups are worried return hubs would move vulnerable people far away from genuine oversight.

“Looking at what we know from previous agreements with third countries, it has proven to be very difficult to guarantee any kind of human rights standard,” Meron Ameha Knikman, senior EU advocacy adviser at the International Rescue Committee, said ahead of the announcement. “It doesn’t matter what you put on paper — as long as it’s not under your jurisdiction, it’s extremely difficult if not impossible to enforce … any kind of guarantees.”

More hubs to follow

The ministers indicated that a deal with Rwanda could be the first in a string of return hub partnerships. “We are already exploring other partner countries, and I think other European countries will participate as well,” Frederiksen said.

Return hubs aren’t just about ramping up deportations, but also about sending a signal, she argued, adding that if people don’t assume they’ll get to stay after entering the EU irregularly, many would rethink their decision to attempt it.

Frederiksen also pushed back against human rights concerns in the partnership with Rwanda.

“You have to remember that we are talking about people who don’t have a legal reason to be in Europe. It’s people who have entered illegally and that have no right to be protected in Europe or to stay,” Frederiksen said in a response to a question from POLITICO.

“What is the alternative? Is it to continue the system we have today?” she asked. “Because if you believe in human rights, I don’t like the current system. It’s broken. I have been to refugee camps outside Europe and seen with my own eyes that some of those who are most fragile … will never come to Europe because it demands a lot of money and strength to travel.”

“If the prospect of dying in the desert, being raped and tortured in Libya, or drowning at sea doesn’t deter people, it’s hard to see how the possibility of being sent to Rwanda would dissuade people,” Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO.

title: US Travel Ban 2026: Who Is Barred and What the December Review Means
description:

Federal Litigation and Separate Immigration Restrictions Federal courts have examined several immigration measures introduced or implemented alongside the 2026 entry restrictions.
United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (2026) Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. et al.
