text:
After President Donald Trump signaled in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired shortly after the midterm elections that he was willing to "work on a deal" with Democrats to allow some illegal immigrants to gain legal status, Fox News Digital spoke with several immigration experts about the potential ramifications of such an agreement.

The interview came just days after Republicans suffered crushing losses in the midterm elections, raising questions about whether Trump might be willing to compromise on immigration. But the president later ruled out amnesty, saying, "There won't be amnesty," while maintaining that his immigration policy had not changed.

While Trump has not outlined a specific proposal, his comments have raised questions about what a potential deal could look like and how granting legal status to some illegal immigrants could impact the rule of law, assimilation and fiscal policy.

TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS

Fox News Digital spoke with three immigration experts about what a potential agreement could mean for the country, including its impact on the rule of law, assimilation and taxpayers.

Rule of Law:

"I think one of the first things we have to always consider is the impact on the rule of law and does it undermine it. It's very hard to argue that the best way to restore the rule of law and deal with illegal immigration is to reward some large fraction of people who've broken the law," said Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS).

Camarota believes that amnesty begs the question of basic fairness, and impacts how people who have come to the United States legally view the immigration system.

"It seems like it mocks them," he said.

He used the example of a person who illegally overstays a visa to illustrate his point, saying that person shouldn't be rewarded with citizenship after overstaying a visa, especially when there are millions of people who have already followed the law and left the country when their visas expired.

Laura Collins, director of immigration policy at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, acknowledged those concerns but argued that the country's immigration laws are part of the problem.

AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

"I understand people's concerns about the rule of law," said Collins. "I also think you have a set of immigration laws that are not working as intended. The reason we have so many people who are here undocumented is because we have an economy that pulls in a lot of people's work, but an immigration system that restricts that labor flow."

She says the United States is at a crossroads: the country can choose a system where illegal immigrants cannot stay and fix their mistakes while also contributing to the economy, or they can stay and be offered a chance at restitution.

"Almost every single piece of legislation that has had a chance at passage on immigration that involves legalization program has had things like paying back taxes, going through a background check, paying some sort of fine or fee or restitution payment in order to make up for the fact that these people did something illegal by either overstaying a visa or crossing the border," she said.

But Camarota questioned whether a future amnesty agreement would actually require immigrants to complete those restitution payments before obtaining citizenship.

Assimilation:

Camarota also said that one of the main reasons for restricting immigration in the first place is to ensure that the United States isn't overwhelmed.

"We don't want the numbers to be so large that they overwhelm the assimilation process, where you can go to a school where everyone's from your background or you don't ever have to learn English, because there's enough people around you who you don't [and] who you speak your native tongue So that's one reason to limit immigration," he said.

"In effect, an amnesty throws that out the window and says, well, we have these limits, but we're not going to enforce them," he continued.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

Drawing from the findings of a 2022 book called "Streets of Gold: America's Untold Story of Immigrant Success," Collins argued that today's immigrants are assimilating at a pace similar to that of immigrants of prior generations. America's current foreign-born population has matched a historic peak similar to late 1800s and early 1900s levels. About 15% of the current population is foreign-born.

The book, she said, compared people's memories of how their grandparents and great-grandparents assimilated when they came to the United States.

"And what they found was actually that immigrants are integrating it pretty much the same rates," she said.

She also said that work helps people to assimilate faster, and thus, if illegal immigrants were given the opportunity to work legally, assimilation would be a smoother process.

"I do think that one of the things America really is good at is us taking newcomers and turning them into Americans, and so I worry less about that" she said. "But I understand why there is a scenario where people could be afraid of that. But the data doesn't support it."

Fiscal Policy:

Camarota estimated that households headed by illegal immigrants receive approximately $50 billion annually in government benefits, often through programs for which their U.S.-born children are eligible. He cited Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and free school lunches as examples, although illegal immigrants themselves are generally barred from receiving many federal welfare benefits.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

Illegal immigrants use welfare not because they're lazy, but because most of them do not have educations higher than 11th grade level, Camarota said.

"Legalizing folks doesn't change the fact that the illegal population is overwhelmingly less educated, and less educated people just don't pay enough in taxes to cover their consumption of public services, especially when you consider all the means-tested programs they get," he said.

Low-income people, he noted, simply don't pay much in taxes.

"Remember, half of all workers pay no federal income tax," he said. "So, yes, illegal immigrants do pay taxes, and actually we think more than half already work on the books, so there's no big boon to taxpayers anyway. But now, they themselves will become eligible for welfare programs."

Collins conceded that while many immigrants have low education levels, he said that that doesn't mean all of them are working jobs that meet their education skills. She pointed to a 2013 Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis of the Gang of Eight's immigration bill, S. 744, which estimated that the legislation would increase federal tax revenues and reduce federal deficits by approximately $158 billion over 10 years, despite increased spending on government benefits.

"You get a little bit more tax revenue," she said. "They are potentially making higher wages, they're able to negotiate for different jobs and different wages because they have that legal work authorization," Collins said.

HISPANIC VOTERS ARE NATURAL CONSERVATIVES. REAGAN KNEW. GOP NEEDS TO PROVE IT AGAIN

She argued that with legal work authorization, some illegal immigrants would be able to fulfill their full potential in higher-level jobs.

Mark Krikorian runs CIS. He said that while thinking through the pros and cons of amnesty might be a useful thought exercise, the point is probably moot.

"Well, to begin with, it's not going to happen," he said of an amnesty deal. The likelihood of anything happening, certainly until the Democrats come in, until the next Congress comes in, and even then, it is, in my opinion, close to zero."

For two reasons, Krikorian doesn't think Republicans have leverage to make a deal.

He says Democrats won't be willing to concede any restrictions on immigration, thus leaving Republicans with no incentive to make an amnesty deal for illegal immigrants.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT

He used DACA as an example. Recently, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin floated the possibility of a compromise involving DACA recipients — people who came to the United States as children and received temporary protections from deportation — that could give them permanent legal status.

"A DACA amnesty? Frankly, the DACAs already have amnesty. It's upgrading them from amnesty light to amnesty premium," he said.

He said the first Trump administration tried making a deal for tighter immigration measures using DACA recipients as a bargaining chip.

"That idea is valuable and could be productive, but there's no way that upgrading the DACA who already have Social Security numbers and work permits to regular green card status is something that the Democrats would give anything in exchange for," he said.

But Krikorian warned that giving green cards to DACA recipients could eventually allow them to sponsor additional relatives, including their parents, once they become U.S. citizens, although existing immigration restrictions could prevent some relatives from obtaining legal status.

"And that would have some effects, because once you have a green card, you can petition for certain relatives, and the five-year clock for citizenship starts," he said. "And when you become a citizen, you could then petition for your parents. There's no numerical caps for that."

Trump discussed on "60 Minutes" potentially working out a deal that would allow some illegal immigrants working in industries like hospitality and landscaping to remain in the country.

"When you go into a hotel, and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," Trump said on "60 Minutes."

MULLIN VOWS ‘ZERO CHANGE’ ON IMMIGRATION AFTER REPUBLICANS SUFFER CRUSHING MIDTERM LOSSES

He added that people whom he described as "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal immigrant is working.

The White House, meanwhile, says Trump's "strong immigration policy remains unchanged," and White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital that Democrats should work with the president to keep the border secure, remove dangerous criminal illegal immigrants from the country and stop drug trafficking.

She said the president's "commonsense immigration agenda" has resulted in the "most secure border in history."

"If Democrats choose to pursue radical left open border and mass amnesty policies, they are choosing to work against the interests of the American people," she said.

text:
A federal judge threw out a Trump administration rule limiting how long foreign students can stay in the U.S., finding it arbitrary and contrary to Congress’s intent, Politico reports.

Massachusetts District Judge Dennis Saylor, appointed by President George W. Bush, ruled Monday against the Department of Homeland Security rule issued in July. It would have ended the “duration of status” system and capped stays for F and J visa holders at four years, whatever the program’s length, forcing students, researchers and professors who needed more time to apply for extensions.

Saylor found DHS didn’t properly weigh the rule’s costs and benefits, and that its fraud and national security rationale didn’t hold up. He also found it ran counter to Congress. “DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity... that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” he wrote.

The ruling keeps the existing definition in place.

Education groups sued in August, arguing the rule was arbitrary and would deter international students. Miriam Feldblum, president of The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a plaintiff, said it would have worsened falling enrollment and burdened campuses. A report from the Institute of International Education puts the drop in new international enrollment at 15% this fall.

Administration officials say stricter student visa policies fight fraud and keep Americans from competing with international students for work. DHS earlier said the rule would fix a system in which students stay indefinitely and take advantage of U.S. generosity.

text:
Five European countries and Rwanda announced Monday that they are exploring the establishment of the first return hub outside Europe, aiming to reach an agreement and begin transferring rejected asylum seekers by 2027.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands said in a joint statement published by Denmark's Immigration Ministry that the proposed facility would accommodate migrants without legal permission to remain in the participating EU countries and who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

The initiative would allow transferred migrants to integrate into Rwandan society or voluntarily travel to their countries of origin or other countries where they can legally reside, with international support, according to the statement.

Speaking at a press conference in Vienna, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the announcement a turning point.

"For me today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system, a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens," she said.

Frederiksen said the participating countries are seeking fundamental changes to migration policy, arguing that human smuggling networks are profiting from dangerous journeys to Europe.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the partnership would provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants," while addressing economic inequalities driving irregular migration.

Danish Minister of Immigration and Integration Morten Bodskov called the announcement "a huge breakthrough," saying the proposed hub would help address difficulties in returning migrants without legal residence.

Return hubs offer "a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said, particularly when their countries of origin do not cooperate on repatriation.

Greek Minister for Migration and Asylum Athanasios Plevris said "combating illegal immigration and dismantling human trafficking networks is one of our key priorities," adding that return hubs could reduce irregular migration and increase returns.

Lastly, Dutch Minister of Asylum and Migration Bart van den Brink said the initiative aimed to "increase returns and provide a new chance for migrants to settle in Rwanda.

"This is how the Netherlands, with its partners, will contribute to a modern, effective and well-functioning asylum system," he said.

The joint statement said the proposed arrangement would comply with EU, Rwandan and international law, while the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) is providing advice on human rights standards.

Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said concrete negotiations with the East African country would begin Monday.

Karner described the initiative as a pilot project intended to curb irregular migration, disrupt smuggling networks and reduce pressure on the population.

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is no longer pursuing a lawsuit against the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), according to Collin County court records.

The state filed a notice of nonsuit without prejudice on Monday, court records show. Paxton filed the suit in February to stop CAIR and its Texas chapters from operating in the state. The lawsuit also sought to name CAIR and its Texas affiliates as foreign terrorist organizations.

CAIR's website states the group was established to challenge stereotypes about Islam and Muslims. Most of its work focuses on civil rights and anti-defamation.

Gov. Greg Abbott designated CAIR as a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization last year. Among several things in Abbott's proclamation letter, he cited accusations that CAIR was created as a "front group" for Hamas. CAIR denies those claims.

Abbott also claimed CAIR has "repeatedly employed, affiliated with, and supported individuals promoting terrorism-related activities."

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told the Washington Post that she would remove CAIR's terrorist designation when she assumes office.

"We have to use public safety measures for public safety," she said, dismissing what she called "nonsense happening with power that should be used for public safety, money that should use for public safety, that is not being used for safety."

CAIR hopes to see a push toward unity under the new administration, said Mustafaa Carroll, the CAIR-Dallas executive director.

"We're tired of fighting this fight," Carroll said. "We want to get along with folks."

KERA has reached out to Hinojosa and the attorney general's office for comment on this story and will update with any response.

But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

“Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”

On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

Bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.

The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch said.

In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

Also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s plans to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, said that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the new curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.

Teachers in the camps established the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees in 2025, which now comprises more than 125 community-led schools with up to 30,000 students, and is working to ensure quality education, including standardized exams in the Myanmar curriculum. Establishing the examination board took a year of volunteer outreach in the camps.

However, the Bangladesh government has still not accredited any curriculum for Rohingya children, and because community-led schools lack legal status, they cannot receive foreign support directly. As a result, while the UK organization’s school is able to hire and train Rohingya teachers, the project is formally being implemented through a registered Bangladeshi group. Most community-led schools have to charge students small fees to operate, limiting access, and rely on refugees to donate the use of their small living shelters as makeshift classrooms.

Eight teachers at community-led schools said that to reach more students, they need Bangladesh to grant their schools official status, allow official certification of education and a pathway to higher education, and for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and humanitarian organizations to acknowledge their work and engage with them.

A teacher at one of the schools said, “We are spending money to ensure education quality, as if we were a government, but we are not a government, we are simply refugees.” Leaders and teachers offered to collaborate with UNICEF and humanitarian organizations on examinations, quality assurance, and improved teaching.

The vast majority of Rohingya students rely on donor-funded humanitarian education programs. Humanitarian groups providing education, coordinated by UNICEF, received just US$29 million from donors towards their 2025 budget request of $72 million, resulting in “learning centers” in the refugee camps closing for months. The education sector laid off teachers, cancelled an early education program, and cut teacher trainings and other programs. In October 2026, a humanitarian education official told Human Rights Watch: “We are struggling to maintain the most basic services. Even textbooks are [insufficient].… We cannot ensure children receive materials like a pencil, a notebook.... Learning centers were damaged by mudslides and climate events, but we do not have funding to carry out repairs.”

Several Rohingya instructors at learning centers that rely on humanitarian funds confirmed the lack of resources. A grade 1 instructor said his classroom had no whiteboard, markers, desks, or benches, and students had to share textbooks, pens, and exercise books. A grade 3 instructor worried that “three students are using one set of textbooks.” Rather than teaching one class for the full school day, learning center instructors teach students in two “shifts” per day.

Even after humanitarian agencies reduced their education funding request to $53 million for 2026, donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October, leaving learning centers at risk of closing again, humanitarian officials said. The World Bank and Education Cannot Wait have provided or pledged funding, but this alone is insufficient. The United States had paid for half the Rohingya education budget before halting its funding in 2025. Globally, humanitarian education funding has fallen by 20 percent since 2023.

All states are obligated to provide children access to quality education without discrimination, regardless of their refugee status. The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies’ Minimum Standards emphasize the importance of community leadership and participation in the design and implementation of education programming.

“Rohingya children are eager to learn,” said a Rohingya teacher in the camps. “The problem is that their education has been repeatedly interrupted by circumstances beyond their control. Education needs to be treated as a right, not a temporary humanitarian project.”

text:
Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that sought to ban the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group from operating in Texas, state court records show.

The lawsuit, filed in February, had asked a Collin County judge to declare the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization. It alleged that CAIR was working with the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Muslim group, to “usurp governmental power and establish dominion through Sharia law.” At the time, CAIR said it was being punished for its opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

The petition came after Gov. Greg Abbott slapped the same designation against the two groups and urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR amid a surge in Republican candidates running anti-Islam campaigns.

Paxton’s office filed a notice of nonsuit Monday, voiding the lawsuit nearly two weeks after a blue wave sunk Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and swept Abbott out of office. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will remove the “foreign terrorist organization” label against CAIR.

The organization didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit’s end, which was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

CAIR and its Texas chapter have cheered Hinojosa’s pledge, which she announced during an interview with The Washington Post.

text:
Immigrants facing deportation would have just 10 days to appeal many immigration court decisions under a Trump administration rule that revives a major change blocked by a federal judge earlier this year.

The rule, due to be published in the Federal Register by the Department of Justice (DOJ), would cut the normal appeal period from 30 days to 10 days and restore other restrictions on appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), amid efforts to speed up a system that has become overwhelmed by a growing backlog.

The DOJ tried to do this in February, but faced legal challenges that led to a federal judge partially setting the policy aside. After a notice and comment period, the DOJ policy is back as a final rule.

Read More on U.S.

"This rule is a part of the Trump Administration's efforts to provide only a facade of due process," Jill family, a professor at Widener University Commonwealth Law School, told Newsweek. "These procedures do not provide meaningful internal review of immigration judge decisions. Addressing the backlog requires more resources and procedural innovation, but that innovation must maintain, if not improve, the process. The administration's approach is to say, 'the line is too long; let's eliminate the service.'"

Under the Trump administration, immigration court hearings have spiked, in part due to the rise in the number of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) suspected of having no legal status. The court system has also faced a growing backlog due to sweeping firings of longtime immigration judges, who have been gradually replaced.

Newsweek reached out to the Department of Justice, as well as Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which brought the original challenge, for further comment Monday afternoon.

What is Changing for Immigration Appeals?

The BIA is the Justice Department's highest administrative body for interpreting and applying immigration law, handling large numbers of appeals from removal decisions made by immigration judges.

Under the plan laid out in the Federal Register filing, the appeal window for many cases would fall from 30 to 10 days, with appellants needing to identify the issues they are raising in their Notice of Appeal. Some asylum cases would keep the 30-day window.

The new system substantially expands summary dismissal, meaning an immigration judge's decision to issue a removal order would be the final government decision unless the BIA accepts the case through a vote by the majority of BIA members.

The DOJ said the changes are needed because of a spike in the number of waiting cases, which it called a "lengthy and unprecedented" backlog.

In Fiscal Year 2017, the BIA had a pending caseload of 35,837 cases. That rose to 325,774 in Fiscal Year 2026, a near ninefold increase.

Hunter Hammill, policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) told Newsweek Monday that the changes would increase efficiency "at the great cost of dismantling due process in the court system."

"It will be nearly impossible, even for people with attorneys, to file an appeal in 10 calendar days, rather than having the 30-day window," Hammill said. "Detained individuals and people who do not have legal counsel will have a harder time because they will have barely received notice of a decision and there will be no time as a practical matter to find an attorney to help with an appeal."

Why Was the 10-Day Deadline Blocked?

On February 6, the DOJ issued its interim final rule laying out this proposal. That sparked a legal challenge to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, with plaintiffs arguing that the new deadline would severely curtail meaningful BIA reviews.

The lawsuit included claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Immigration and Nationality Act, and the Constitution.

On March 8, Judge Randolph D. Moss set aside parts of the rule, with the DOJ then telling immigration judges the 10-day deadline had been set aside and the correct appeal deadline was still 30 days.

The March ruling did not declare that immigrants were constitutionally entitled to 30 days. Instead, Moss focused on how DOJ had gone about implementing the policy, saying the department had bypassed notice-and-comment requirements for substantive changes to policy.

Does a 10-Day Deadline Violate Due Process?

The restored deadline could renew a deeper fight over how much process the Constitution requires before the government can deport someone.

The Justice Department argued that while noncitizens are entitled to due process in removal proceedings, the Constitution does not independently guarantee an administrative appeal before the BIA.

Once the government establishes an appeal process, the question becomes whether it can impose conditions that effectively prevent people from using it.

Under the 10-day time frame, an immigrant facing deportation would need to obtain the judge's decision, find counsel, understand what went wrong, and prepare a Notice of Appeal identifying the issues being challenged, potentially while in ICE custody and without English proficiency.

The organizations fighting the original rule argued it would disproportionately affect people who are detained, unrepresented, disabled, children, or speakers of less-common languages.

"The BIA Interim Final Rule makes a mockery of due process," Emilie Raber, Senior Attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said in a February press release. "In addition to taking away virtually any benefit the BIA could provide immigrants, it will wreak havoc on people with cases in immigration court or federal appellate courts."

In 1994, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals considered a 20-day immigration appeals deadline in Gonzales-Julio v. INS, which the DOJ also refers to in its 2026 rule.

The court found then that a 10-day deadline was unconstitutional in certain circumstances, with the case examining an immigrant in Hawaii who needed to file an appeal in San Diego, California, within that time.

The DOJ argues in 2026 that technology has mitigated that issue, with electronic filing allowing documents to be sent at any time over the internet.

What Happens Next

The DOJ plan is due to be published November 17, with the rule taking effect 30 days later and applying to cases filed after that date. Cases already pending would not face the shorter deadline.

The department likely expects further legal challenges, with its plan outlining concerns around due process, access to counsel, and meaningful case review.

While the BIA is the last immigration tribunal layer, immigrants who still see their cases dismissed could take their case to a federal court for further examination.

text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) led a group of 22 other Democrats in a letter to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) Joseph Cuffari urging him to investigate the nearly $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for border infrastructure projects in the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector.

Joining Congresswoman Escobar (in alphabetical order) are Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-7), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Dan Goldman (NY-10), Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), Al Green (TX-9), Jared Huffman (CA-2), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-8), Stephen Lynch (MA-8), Seth Magaziner (RI-2), Christian Menefee (TX-18), Dave Min (CA-47), Brittany Petterson (CO-7), Emily Randall (WA-6), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Gabe Vazquez (NM-2), and Nydia Velazquez (NY-7).

The full letter can be found here or below:

Inspector General Cuffari:

We write to urgently request that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) investigate the contracting process, potential political influence, and award of $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for massive border infrastructure projects in and around the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector in Texas, including Big Bend National Park.

On October 15, 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem waived virtually every provision of federal law “with respect to all contracting actions necessary for the construction of physical barriers and roads” in the Big Bend Sector of Texas. This was followed by additional waivers of environmental, historic preservation, and other laws that would ordinarily provide independent review of federal actions affecting more than 500 miles of borderlands. In addition to Big Bend National Park, one of the nation’s most treasured landscapes, these waivers also impact Big Bend Ranch State Park, Texas’ largest state park, and hundreds of miles of privately owned land.

Publicly available information raises serious questions about how these contracts were awarded, whether political relationships played any role in contractor selection, whether the circumvention of normal contracting and oversight safeguards was in the public interest, and whether the enormous expenditures are justified by an operational need.

The Big Bend Sector, and especially Big Bend National Park, encompasses some of the most remote, rugged, and waterless terrain along the southern border. Local law enforcement officials and elected leaders from across the political spectrum, as well as former National Park Service officials, have questioned the need for extensive physical barriers or other major border security infrastructure in this region.

The available data further raises questions about the justification for the waivers or these massive contracts. The Big Bend Sector includes 26% of the southern border, but CBP’s published data shows that in the 5 years that DHS used to justify these actions, it accounted for less than 1% of the apprehensions of migrants across that same border. The national park accounted for only 0.016% of apprehensions in the same period despite spanning 6% of the southern border. DHS’ own press releases cites that apprehensions in the sector have fallen sharply in recent years.

Nevertheless, DHS designated the region an "area of high illegal entry" with an "acute and immediate need" for border infrastructure. “High illegal entry” is a legal necessity established by the Congress under Section 102(a) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) to allow the Department to waive legal requirements and expedite construction.

We believe the DHS Office of the Inspector General has a responsibility to scrutinize how the Department has made the decisions, and the impact of those decisions, regarding whether the area in question is truly an area of high illegal entry, whether the subsequently awarded contracts were properly issued (even in light of the waivers), and whether the resulting expenditures are in the public interest. The scale of the expenditures is enormous. Five contracts, totaling $7.5 billion, have been awarded in the Sector.

These contracts include:

$1.0 billion to Barnard Construction (BB1 Project)

$1.2 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel (BB2 Project)

$960.4 million to Barnard Construction (BB3 Project)

$1.7 billion to Southwest Valley Constructors for work associated with Big Bend National Park. (BB4 project)

$2.6 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel for work in the Lower Canyons region downstream of the national park (BB5 project)

These expenditures warrant scrutiny because of the contracting practices and political relationships surrounding some of the companies receiving them. Public reporting has documented substantial political connections involving contractors that have received significant border construction awards.

Barnard Construction Chairman Tim Barnard and his wife donated approximately $1 million to a Trump campaign fundraising committee during the 2024 election cycle. Barnard Construction has subsequently received billions of dollars in border construction contracts, including a $1.6 billion contract for approximately 112 miles of border wall in New Mexico that was awarded without competitive bidding based on an asserted need for urgency.

Fisher Sand & Gravel has also been the subject of previous scrutiny over political influence in federal contracting. During President Trump's first term, the company received a $400 million border wall contract after President Trump personally and repeatedly urged federal officials to consider Fisher for the work. Those circumstances prompted a Department of Defense Inspector General review. Public reporting has also connected Fisher to a consulting firm formerly associated with White House Border Czar Tom Homan. Fisher reportedly paid Homan's consulting firm as much as $186,000 while seeking border wall work. The administration has stated that Mr. Homan does not participate in the actual awarding of contracts.

These facts do not by themselves establish that contracts were improperly awarded. They do, however, create a strong public interest in an independent review of whether political relationships, communications, or influence played any role in DHS contracting decisions.

The processes CBP used to award these contracts lacked any transparency, and there has been no opportunity for public oversight of the contracts, or even for the public to understand the scope of the contracts.

A lawsuit brought by a competing contractor – that was subsequently withdrawn -

- alleged that solicitations for broader Texas border work were not genuine competitive opportunities and that winningbidders were subsequently required to perform work outside the scope originally advertised. When discovery was sought in that litigation, DHS moved to seal materials including depositions and affidavits.

At the same time, DHS and CBP have repeatedly changed their public descriptions of what is being built in the Big Bend Sector.

CBP materials initially showed a border wall through the region. The wall later disappeared from public maps, then reappeared. In May, CBP publicly stated that there would be no wall in Big Bend National Park. Approximately one week later, DHS awarded a $1.7 billion contract whose contracting records described work associated with a border wall in the national park. More recently, CBP has described construction inside the park as involving roads, technology, and vehicle barriers.

Taken together, these circumstances warrant an independent investigation. We therefore request that the DHS Office of Inspector General examine:

Whether political relationships, communications, campaign contributions, or other political considerations played any role in the selection of contractors or award of contracts for border infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector;

Whether contracts awarded for work in the Big Bend Sector were awarded through full and open competition and, where they were not, whether DHS properly justified the use of noncompetitive or expedited procurement procedures;

Whether DHS adequately evaluated the operational need, cost effectiveness, and alternatives before committing billions of taxpayer dollars to border infrastructure in a region with comparatively low and declining levels of unlawful crossings;

Whether the scope of work ultimately assigned to contractors materially differed from the work described during the solicitation and bidding process, and whether any such changes disadvantaged competing bidders or increased costs to taxpayers;

Whether any current or former administration officials participated in, attempted to influence, or communicated with DHS or CBP officials concerning the selection of particular contractors;

Whether DHS's waiver of environmental and other statutory requirements, together with limitations on public access to contracting information, diminished safeguards against waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement; and

Whether the contracts and expenditures associated with these projects comply with applicable ethics, appropriations, and other federal requirements.

Big Bend National Park is an irreplaceable public resource. Taxpayers deserve confidence that decisions affecting it and the surrounding region— and billions of dollars in federal spending — are based on legitimate public needs rather than political influence or private advantage.

We expect a written response to this letter with an associated timeline for an OIG investigation no later than November 27, 2026. We further expect that the findings of such an investigation be made public.
