text:
The Trump administration is continuing its aggressive immigration enforcement crackdown despite the Republicans’ stunning loss in the midterm elections. Plans to deport more people, add more detention centers and approve fewer applications for legal status are moving forward. In the Bay Area, the recent arrests of immigrants with no criminal histories such as Dr. Ann Lawani, a well-known professor of nursing at the University of San Francisco, and UC Berkeley student Paula Albornoz Hernandez have sparked protests. We’ll talk about the latest in Trump’s immigration crackdown locally and nationally and whether the rebuke voters sent the President in the midterms could affect immigration policy.

Guests:

Jasmine Garsd, immigration correspondent, NPR

Deep Gulasekaram, professor of law and director of Byron White Center for the Study of Constitutional Law, University of Colorado Boulder Law School – where he teaches constitutional and immigration law. He is co-author of the leading immigration law textbook used in U.S. law schools.

Tyche Hendricks, senior editor covering immigration, KQED

This is a computer-generated transcript. While our team has reviewed it, there may be errors.

Alexis Madrigal: Welcome to Forum. I’m Alexis Madrigal. The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement, deporting record numbers of people through ICE. In the Bay Area, the recent arrests of immigrants with no criminal histories, including a professor of nursing and a UC Berkeley student, have sparked protests.

Here to update us first on what’s been happening with these high-profile local cases, we’re joined by Tyche Hendricks, immigration reporter here at KQED. Welcome, Tyche.

Tyche Hendricks: Thank you.

Alexis Madrigal: We’ve also got Deep Gulasekaram, who’s a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. Welcome, Deep.

Deep Gulasekaram: Thank you for having me.

Alexis Madrigal: And we’ve got Jasmine Garsd, who’s immigration correspondent with NPR. Welcome back, Jasmine.

Jasmine Garsd: Thanks for having me.

Alexis Madrigal: Okay, Tyche, let’s start with you. Can you tell us about this 23-year-old UC Berkeley student who was arrested by immigration agents at SFO?

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, we have had two pretty high-profile arrests recently of folks with university affiliations. One is a student at UC Berkeley. She’s from Colombia originally. She came here four or five years ago, applied for asylum, and is still waiting for that case to be decided. Paula Albornoz-Hernandez is her name.

She decided to take a trip to Oregon with her boyfriend for the weekend recently, and they went to SFO, where she was arrested by ICE. She spent nine days in a detention facility in California City, and then a federal judge ordered her release, basically ordered that her detention was illegal.

So she’s out now, but her asylum case has shifted from a sort of proactive asylum case to one in immigration court, where she’s now trying to defend herself against deportation.

There’s another case you mentioned of a nursing professor at the University of San Francisco, who’s been in the U.S. for 20 years or so. Dr. Anne Lewani got her PhD in the U.S. She also entered here on a lawful visa and applied for asylum. She didn’t get it, but she got something called withholding of removal, which is that the immigration judge said, “You’re more likely than not to face persecution in your home country of Nigeria, and the U.S. may not send you back there.”

But the U.S. is now sending people to third countries. And so she has been put in removal proceedings. She spent two months in detention, and she’s still in an ICE facility down in Louisiana. And now facing this risk that she could be sent to some third country, who knows where.

Alexis Madrigal: You know, Jasmine, these are the cases we’re hearing about because, you know, it’s the University of San Francisco and it’s UC Berkeley. Nationally, are similar things happening? Similar people being detained?

Jasmine Garsd: Yeah, I mean, I think these two cases that you just mentioned are super interesting in that they tell us a couple of things that are happening on a larger scale.

First of all, we’re seeing a lot of de-documentation, which means people who have been in the U.S. with paperwork of some kind, whether it’s TPS, whether it’s withholding of removal, and then that gets removed.

So, you know, this administration came to power on the promise that they were going to crack down on, you know, the worst of the worst, the criminals, the quote-unquote monsters. And also, you know, that they would go after undocumented immigrants.

What we are seeing, first of all, is that somewhere around 70% of the people who are in immigration detention have no criminal record whatsoever. I mean, that’s pretty extraordinary because we believe there are somewhere around 60,000 people in immigration detention right now.

We’re also seeing, like you mentioned, in the case of this professor and the student, people who actually did have permission to be here in the U.S. and are being taken.

And the other thing is, you know, in the case of the professor, we are seeing these long — the default for this administration is detention. And so we are seeing people being held for what feels like long and maybe indefinite periods of time.

Alexis Madrigal: Let’s come to you, Deep, on sort of the specifics of these legal situations. You know, when we think about this professor of nursing, Dr. Lewani, at USF, she’s been in the country for a super long time. She has this specific legal status that’s a little gray, but it’s not really gray. Like, for the past many decades of immigration policy, this was a kind of legal status, right?

Deep Gulasekaram: Yeah, I think that if you look at the past, people who had either pending applications for asylum or were granted things like withholding of removal, they were allowed to remain in the country. They were often given employment authorization as a matter of course.

But as Tyche pointed out in this case, that type of protection, for example, withholding of removal, does not technically prevent the removal to the country from which that person was facing or was claiming that they would face a form of persecution or torture or cruelty.

And one of the things that the Trump administration has focused on as part of its removal policy for the last two years is to remove people to what are known as third countries, right? Countries that they’re not — that’s not the country from which the individual hails, that may not be their nationality, but that country is willing to accept this individual from the United States.

And they’re doing that because —

Alexis Madrigal: It makes it seem like it fits within the letter of the law, to say nothing of the spirit, but the letter of the law.

Deep Gulasekaram: Yeah, I mean, that is technically one of the things that’s been litigated, but at this moment, it looks like the Trump administration has at least prevailed in important decisions.

The question is whether it’s okay to institute a policy by which lots of people, as a matter of course, are taken to places that are willing to accept them but are not their countries of nationality.

And so, yes, in a sense, I think you might have phrased it correctly, that it is technically, at least as currently understood, not necessarily in violation of the law. But it is a highly contested legal question and certainly a highly contested question as to whether this is a good idea, especially from the perspective of the noncitizen who may have no relationship to the place to which they are being sent.

Tyche Hendricks: Just to go back in here a second, Alexis. I mean, another thing that we’re seeing is, in the case of Dr. Lewani, there was no record of her in the ICE detainee locator, this portal that you can use to find where somebody is being held.

So she kind of disappeared into the detention system. It was a couple of days before she was able to make a call and let people know where she was.

But this is a, you know, kind of a terrifying development, I think, for a lot of families, for people and their lawyers, if they’re lucky to have lawyers, that increasingly in recent months we’ve seen folks just not being recorded, ICE not being willing to share where people are.

Alexis Madrigal: And that’s because they were doing — they were providing that portal, like, out of courtesy? It’s not, like, legally required? What’s the deal?

Tyche Hendricks: Maybe Deep can answer that.

Alexis Madrigal: Question, yeah.

Deep Gulasekaram: Well, ICE is obligated to be able to identify where an individual is. Every noncitizen put into the immigration enforcement system gets something known as an A-number. It’s the number that’s filed on the notices to appear, the documents that charge them with removability from the country.

If one has that A-number, a family member, an attorney should be able to locate this individual.

But as Tyche has explained, one of the things that ICE is doing, either inadvertently or on purpose, is to lose people in the system.

The other thing that they are certainly doing as a matter of course and on purpose is moving people far away from the jurisdictions in which they are initially apprehended.

So if these individuals were apprehended in Northern California or in the Eastern District of California, if we’re looking at specific federal judicial districts, ICE will very quickly move that person to another facility, oftentimes many states away. And the most popular destinations now are places like rural Louisiana, rural Florida, Texas, where it’s much harder to find them, A, and then B, get resources to them.

Alexis Madrigal: We are talking about the Trump administration, its continuing aggressive immigration enforcement campaign. We’ve got Deep Gulasekaram, who is professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. We’ve got Tyche Hendricks, immigration reporter here at KQED. We’ve got Jasmine Garsd, immigration correspondent with NPR.

Deep, let’s stay with you for one more second here, which is, you know, we’ve got kind of two parallel legal systems. One is our, like, real and official legal system. And one is this sort of immigration court system, which, the more shows we do on it, the more it doesn’t seem like a real legal system.

What determines what goes in what place? Like, you know, one of you mentioned earlier that a federal court — it was Tyche — mentioned the federal court was helping out this UC Berkeley student, but also their case is showing up in immigration court now, this other thing. So talk to me about those kind of two parallel tracks.

Deep Gulasekaram: It’s understandable that you’re confused, and listeners may be confused about it.

So when ICE starts a removal proceeding purely for the basis of deporting an individual, that proceeding is going to be in immigration court.

As you note, we call it immigration court, but immigration courts are held entirely within the executive branch of the United States federal government. The head of the Department of Justice, that is to say, the attorney general of the United States, is the lead actor of the agency that houses immigration courts. DHS is another executive branch.

So one of the things that happens in immigration court is that you have one part of the executive branch of the United States federal government acting as prosecutor, another agency within the executive branch of the United States government acting as the adjudicator. And of course, that creates problems or questions as to the legitimacy and neutrality of those systems.

But to get to your other question, in immigration court, when ICE files and DHS files those charges against somebody, they then have the decision whether they are going to detain or not detain the individual as they’re awaiting their removal hearing.

ICE, in our current moment, has decided to detain as many people as they can possibly detain. Whether the statute allows them to do so or not is an important legal question.

Once they are detained, awaiting their immigration hearings in immigration court, what they can do, and what many of these cases are about, is an attorney trying to file what’s known as a habeas petition on behalf of that noncitizen.

Habeas — most people have heard the word, but what it essentially means is, “I need a federal court to review the legality of this detention.”

Alexis Madrigal: Amazing. Deep Gulasekaram, professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. We’ll be back with more on immigration right after the break.

Welcome back. We’re talking about the Trump administration, its continuing aggressive immigration enforcement campaign. We want to hear from you.

What do you want the Democratic Congress to do about immigration when the new term starts? Do you expect to see any changes in immigration enforcement or policy reform after these midterms?

You can give us a call. The number is 866-733-6786. That’s 866-733-6786. The email is forum@kqed.org. And, of course, BlueSky, Instagram, Discord. We are KQED Forum.

We’re joined this morning by Deep Gulasekaram, professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. We’ve got Tyche Hendricks, our own immigration reporter here at KQED, and we’ve got NPR’s Jasmine Garsd.

Jasmine, let’s talk a little bit about these midterm results. You know, of course, any sort of massive blue tsunami like this would not have just one cause, but some people have pointed to the type of immigration enforcement that the Trump administration did as one factor in Republicans losing so many seats.

What do you see happening at the, you know, kind of Trump administration level? Do you feel like they got a message about immigration? Do you feel like they didn’t? What do you think is happening?

Jasmine Garsd: I mean, look, if anything, what I have sensed is a doubling down on the immigration agenda.

Immediately after the midterms, you had J.D. Vance, Vice President J.D. Vance, go on X, and he posts about how, you know, why did voters turn on the Republican Party? And he said a lot of it is economic issues, the war with Iran. And then he says it really wasn’t about immigration enforcement.

I think it’s very interesting that, you know, this obstinance in separating immigration enforcement from the American economy, as if it could be separated. It can’t.

But, you know, you see other indications that, you know, DHS head Markwayne Mullin tweeted, “Deportations will continue.” You know, in the days after the midterms, Homeland Security moved forward on two major projects to convert these Amazon-style warehouses into detention centers.

And perhaps the biggest indication that things will not just continue as is, but that they will double down, is that Stephen Miller got a huge promotion. Stephen Miller was promoted to White House chief of staff.

Stephen Miller is the architect of the first Trump administration’s immigration policy and the child separation policy. And he is the architect of this Trump administration’s immigration policy. This is Stephen Miller’s core issue. This is what matters to him, and he just got the promotion.

Alexis Madrigal: Is that promotion something — what does it actually do in terms of the power that he holds?

Jasmine Garsd: I mean, I think that it signals that he has President Trump’s ear and that he is really going to be setting an agenda.

But there is the question of what can Democrats really do when they get in January? What can these newly elected Democrats do?

But here’s the thing. ICE is sitting on so much money right now. They received a blank check from the current Congress with no strings attached. And the reality is that it will be difficult to rein ICE in with Stephen Miller in power and with ICE having this blank check.

Yeah.

Alexis Madrigal: I mean, Tyche, when we think about ICE having so much money, you know, the best-funded law enforcement agency in history, what do we imagine that might trickle down to locally? Like, does it just mean that we’ll just have way more ICE agents here? There’ll be more facilities? Like, what does it mean?

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, well, I mean, I think what we’re seeing right now — we’re actually seeing, you know, as we speak, over the last couple of weeks since right before the election, a big increase in immigration enforcement happening in the Bay Area.

And speaking with folks with rapid response networks in different counties, it sounds like some of that is being powered by ICE agents, not from the local field offices here, but, you know, on top of that, more agents coming in from outside.

And, you know, I mean, I think it’s fair to surmise that those are folks who, you know, have been hired up with some of this money. There’s been a lot of hiring.

So where they seem to be focused right now is outside of county jails in Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, Santa Cruz County jails.

And one thing I would say is a big difference between California and some other states, like, for example, Florida, Texas, Republican-governed states up until now, is that in California, local police are not allowed to be deputized as ICE agents and essentially make arrests.

And so that means that ICE has had to get a little creative in California about, you know, how to get the numbers of arrests up and how to arrest people themselves.

Because our sanctuary laws don’t prohibit ICE from operating in the state, but they just prohibit our state and local law enforcement, apart from the state prisons, I should say, from collaborating with ICE.

So they’re outside of jails. They’ve been questioning people. They’ve been making arrests. They’re staging a lot of times on jail or courthouse parking lots, county property, and some counties have policies in place to say, you know, that’s not allowed.

Alameda sent a cease-and-desist letter to ICE saying, like, “Get off, go away,” and ICE seems to be coming back and saying, like, “We can operate. That doesn’t apply to us.”

The Contra Costa Board of Supervisors is taking up a similar policy tomorrow.

But, yeah, this is contested territory as far as where ICE can operate. But we saw a big surge earlier in October of hundreds of arrests in the Central Valley and on the Central Coast and sort of the San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria area, agricultural areas, where I was hearing reports of people being, you know, carloads of people going to work in the agricultural fields, farmworkers getting stopped and seemingly racially profiled as Latinos and being arrested without warrants.

And so there were hundreds of arrests there, and now the movement seems to be into the Bay Area.

So, as far as where does it go from here, that’s TBD, but we’re seeing some increase already right now.

Alexis Madrigal: Let’s bring in a caller here. Let’s bring Michael in Marin County. Welcome, Michael.

Michael: Oh, hi. Yeah, I just wanted to comment that I think the American people have spoken, and they see this as mean-spirited.

And I wanted to point out that I think this is really the way ICE is operating. It’s really for show. It’s red meat for the sort of extremists, because if they really wanted to shut down immigration and actually have people self-deport, they would put together a team of inspectors and go to businesses and go to contractors.

I’m a former contractor myself, and they would find people. I mean, if the business got a $5,000 fine for every undocumented worker, they would release all their undocumented workers immediately.

And, you know, you wouldn’t have to have any of this violence. It would all be done by inspectors, and there wouldn’t be children taken away from parents, and there would be all this stuff, you know.

But I want to also point out that a lot of these people are really helping to run our economy. And we went through this right after World War II, or during World War II, when the Japanese were primarily running the Central California food production.

Interestingly, my grandfather was one of the founders of the California Landscape Contractors Association, and they hired a lot of the Japanese when they came out of the camps. But those people were, at that time, very heavily involved in agriculture, and the agricultural production plummeted.

So anyway, I don’t know. I don’t know. Yeah, the whole system, the way they’re doing this, is not to actually solve the problem.

And I want to say that to the people out there that are listening who really feel that people should have a visa and come into the country correctly, which I do — my wife is from Japan. We had to pay ten grand to do paperwork and, right, but this is being done for show.

Alexis Madrigal: That’s a great point. Thank you, Michael. Yeah, yeah. I appreciate that perspective.

I mean, this is an interesting point, right? I mean, as you said earlier, Jasmine, the idea that you could disentangle our economy from this immigration enforcement is such a good point.

I mean, I was also listening to Tyche talk about agricultural workers being arrested. Well, what about the growers who hired those people, right? Well, aren’t they also involved in skirting our immigration system?

So there’s a couple of questions that come out of this. One is, when you arrest growers’ workers in Republican areas, most of those growers are Republicans. Like, isn’t that a political liability for the president in some way?

Jasmine Garsd: Yeah, I mean, I think the listener’s point is excellent.

And, you know, to take his point about an increase in detentions in Northern California and in California, we’ve been seeing that surge nationwide. We’ve been seeing it in New Jersey. I’m based in New York. We’ve been seeing it in New York City.

And, you know, when I speak to business owners here in New York, they tell me that their business has taken such a hit, either because workers have been detained, either because customers have been taken or are too scared to come out and be consumers.

And so, absolutely, I think that’s why it’s so fascinating to me that the vice president tried to separate the current economic issues we are facing from these deportations, this mass deportation campaign.

Now, is it for show? Yes, part of it. But I would also tell our listener to follow the money. That is something I’ve been doing with my reporting.

And, you know, there are people who are making so much money off of these detentions. You know, one of the big private prison contractors that ICE works with is called CoreCivic. It has had a nearly 30% increase in revenue year over year. So compared to this time last year, their revenue increased by 30%.

That is ICE’s main — one of the main private prison contractors.

And what’s interesting is the day after the midterms, I tuned in to one of their quarterly calls with investors. And the big question investors had for the CoreCivic president was, “How will midterms affect our bottom line?”

And she had the advice, which was, “We would urge you to hurry up.”

And so I think when we’re talking about ICE, when we’re talking about this enforcement, we have to acknowledge that there are entire industries that are making a lot of money off of this.

Alexis Madrigal: One of our listeners, Matthew, has a question I think I want you to take, Deep. Matthew writes:

“The administration is normalizing unconstitutional and unchecked secret police actions, outrunning the courts and the legislature in a clear power grab. The Constitution provides one clear remedy for an executive like this: impeachment, removal from office, not just for the president, but for a wide range of members of the executive branch. Democrats should follow the process, do what America voted for, stop this un-American abuse of power.”

So that would be sort of like one poll of what Democrats could attempt to do. What do you see, Deep, as the legal remedies that an empowered Democratic Congress could pursue? There’s legislative ones, but they could get blocked. So what else can they do?

Deep Gulasekaram: Yeah, this is a great question.

Because legislation is likely to be vetoed, first of all, it would be possible for Congress to explicitly create liability and other forms of constraint on federal officer action. So they could do so and dare the president to veto that type of legislation, which is likely to happen. The president has said he’s going to use his veto power.

The other option is sort of a much softer check, but to engage in significant congressional oversight. Congress has the power to subpoena various agency heads, pull them in front of them, to question them in front of the American people about how they’ve chosen to use their authority to allow, on the streets of American cities like Minneapolis, Charlotte, Los Angeles, Chicago, now the Bay Area, this type of occupying force, as Tyche Hendricks has stated, the movement of thousands of agents into those areas.

I think the other significant check is probably not going to come from federal authorities and the federal Congress, but is really going to have to be thought about at the state and local level.

So these types of enforcement activities, where hundreds of officers are moved from the border — so lots of CBP officers, Customs and Border Patrol officers, being moved into places to do these types of surges — they are violating basic constraints on law enforcement, including racialized enforcement, not complying with Fourth Amendment guarantees, et cetera.

The emerging legal debates are what states and localities can do about them. So can localities use their power over zoning and property control to make sure that ICE cannot use local property, county property, to stage their activities?

Can states create forms of liability that are applicable to state officers, but also federal officers, when they go about unconstitutional enforcement?

They’re by no means legally guaranteed, but these are where some of the hard lines of legal fight are going to happen.

Tyche Hendricks: Oh, go ahead. Oh, just to say, I mean, California did just recently pass a bunch of laws, and the governor signed them, to try to do just that.

Alexis Madrigal: And are there any in particular you want to mention, or just like it’s sort of a —

Tyche Hendricks: Well, I mean, it’s not top of mind right now, but there are, I mean, like a sort of a bill of rights for how people are treated in immigration detention. And, you know, some accountability on how — there’s this No Kings Act that would allow an individual in California to sue in state court if their rights were, you know, if they felt their rights were being violated by a federal officer, like an ICE agent.

So these are some of the new policies that are going to start taking effect in the new year. And I think California’s been quite deliberate about trying to do what Deep was describing, at the state level, trying to put some checks on immigration enforcement.

Alexis Madrigal: Which is fascinating, you know, vis-à-vis the midterm elections, because, you know, we’ve talked a lot — everyone in the entire world has talked a lot — about the House and the Senate, but Democrats, as part of this blue wave, also flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, Texas, and other places. They got a bunch of state legislatures in the Democratic column, too.

So what I’m hearing from you, Deep, is that that may actually be more significant for checking immigration enforcement than necessarily the stuff at the federal level.

Deep Gulasekaram: I think it’s certainly much more likely that you can get action there, which will then be tested in courts for its legality.

One example is California in 2025 did pass an anti-masking act, which courts struck down, but you can imagine other types of interventions that might be upheld.

I also want to note that the Supreme Court of the United States has a role to play here. They are the ones who have written opinions, mainly by Justices Thomas and Alito, that have taken away the ability to sue ICE agents and CBP agents when they violate fundamental aspects of our law, including constitutional restrictions on the way in which they operate.

Alexis Madrigal: We’re talking about the current moment in immigration enforcement with Deep Gulasekaram from the University of Colorado Boulder Law School, NPR’s Jasmine Garsd, and KQED’s Tyche Hendricks.

We’ll be back with more right after the break.

Welcome back to Forum. We’re talking about how the Trump administration is continuing its aggressive immigration enforcement campaign, even after the midterm shellacking.

We’re joined by Jasmine Garsd, immigration correspondent with NPR; Deep Gulasekaram, who’s a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School, where he teaches constitutional and immigration law; and we also have Tyche Hendricks, immigration reporter with KQED, of course.

We’re taking your questions about the current state of immigration enforcement and policy. Maybe you think the Trump administration should alter its immigration enforcement policies. Maybe you think they’ve worked in some sense.

866-733-6786. That’s 866-733-6786. You can email forum@kqed.org. You can find us on social media, BlueSky, Instagram, and Discord.

Tyche, you know, you mentioned in the last segment that ICE enforcement appears to be increasing in the Bay Area. One of the things I find so tricky about covering this on the show is how hard it is to know, like, are they actually increasing enforcement? Part of some of the work that they’re doing is trying to get people to think there’s more enforcement, you know?

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah. So, I mean, there is data on arrests, detentions, deportations. There’s an outfit at UC Berkeley, the Deportation Data Project, that has a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against ICE, and they are getting tranches of data every so often.

The last numbers that we saw, though, were from July. And, you know, there was a sharp increase in arrests then.

At this point, absent that kind of hard numbers, the numbers are coming from, you know, how many calls are rapid response hotlines getting?

Alameda’s told me that the number of calls is up three or four times what it has been on average over the past year.

And so the folks who are on the ground responding — these rapid response teams are typically driven by immigrant legal aid organizations, sometimes with some state and county money to help their budgets, and a lot of volunteer power to provide legal observers on the ground.

If somebody calls in and says, “I think I see some unmarked black vehicles in my neighborhood, and they’re boxing in a car. What’s going on?” they send somebody who’s trained out to the scene to ascertain what it is.

Or similarly, if a person is arrested by ICE, like, “Where is my person? What do I do?” Well, we’re going to get a lawyer connected and find your person and help them fight their deportation.

So those are the folks who kind of have their finger on the pulse. And those are folks that I’ve been talking to the most about that.

Alexis Madrigal: Yeah. Yeah.

You know, we have a listener on BlueSky, obviously opposed to immigration. MJ writes on BlueSky:

“Do the guests really believe that the millions who strolled across the border over four years are somehow all now integral parts of our economy? At one point, New York City was paying a billion dollars a year to house and feed migrants. What happened?”

I just want to note for the record that, you know, during the Biden administration, the Biden administration actually turned back, via Title 42 expulsions and normal deportations, way more people, actually, than the Trump administration has, just for the record.

But let’s take the point, Jasmine, here. There were large numbers of migrants who came into the country. It did put stress on some cities, both at the border and in other places.

So what do you make of that? Like, did people, in fact, get integrated into the economy? Did they go home? Like, what happened with the migrant surges that we saw happen?

Jasmine Garsd: Well, first of all, I would address that comment and say people didn’t just stroll over the border.

I spent much of the Biden years working on the border at open-air detention camps. They had points of entry, and nobody was strolling over the border. I mean, the people who were coming in, they were, you know, either coming in through the CBP One app or, you know, so people weren’t strolling over.

You know, part of the thing that people, when they talk about, like, well, you know, this wave of migration overwhelmed New York, it overwhelmed Chicago — well, it was weaponized.

I mean, you know, I was in New York when people were being bused by either Texas Governor Greg Abbott or by Ron DeSantis, Governor Ron DeSantis in Florida. They were being bused to blue cities and states with the intention to overwhelm these blue cities and states prior to the presidential election.

So I do think it is really important. I had the experience of going to certain Midwestern towns or places in Appalachia where I would have political officials and business owners tell me, “I wish we had more laborers. Why are they being sent to these other cities?”

And the response was political.

There is a really interesting — I was watching this the other day — there’s a really interesting exchange on C-SPAN from, I think it’s from 2024, between then-head of the Fed, Jerome Powell, and several members of Congress, in which they talk about the economy. And Jerome Powell himself says that one of the reasons that the U.S. economy at that moment was starting to return to pre-COVID levels was in part because we got an injection of workers, of young workers, who brought inflation rates down.

And, you know, that was one of the reasons.

And so I think that, no, you cannot extricate the current immigration crackdown, the removing of millions of workers and millions of consumers, from the American economy. They are interlinked.

People who are living here, whether they have papers or not, they are working and they are spending their money. And that’s not just me talking. That is an abundance of economic reports that have been studying this for decades.

Tyche Hendricks: And I think it’s also worth mentioning that apart from the folks who arrived during those Biden years — and there were, you know, large numbers then who were being granted parole and so forth — there have been, you know, otherwise undocumented people in this country who have been here for decades in many cases.

And this is very much true of our agricultural labor force in California, but with no way to legalize their status.

And that sort of then goes to the question of our immigration laws in a bigger-picture way. Are there avenues for people to come legally? Or could there be more avenues for people at different points in the skill and economic level to come in legally and work? Or ways for people who have been here for a long time to adjust their status, to get on a path to legal status?

Comprehensive immigration reform?

Jasmine Garsd: Right. And to that effect, we’re talking about de-documentation. If the concern is undocumented immigration, then why do the goalposts keep moving? Why does the government keep expanding the population of people who are undocumented?

When you take away TPS for millions of people, some of whom have been here for practically lifetimes, then you are creating a bigger undocumented population.

So I think, you know, there’s some duplicitousness in that.

Alexis Madrigal: Let’s bring in Bob in Santa Rosa. Welcome, Bob.

Bob: Thank you. Thank you very much. And it’s a great show.

I’m part of a band here in Santa Rosa and Sonoma County that plays at the protests and deportation demonstrations. And we are aligned with a group here called the Sanctuary Coalition, as well as La Raza.

And the Hispanic community here has decided recently, last week, in getting an anti-collaboration ordinance passed, a very strong one, in the city that is comprehensive. And we hope, because we have a progressive Board of Supervisors now after the election, to get it countywide.

I wondered if your guests could comment on the effectiveness.

This ordinance details down the line that no city or county employee will collaborate with any federal law enforcement official without a judicially signed order. And it goes on to say they won’t use property, won’t use buildings, will not be allowed entrance to buildings without a warrant.

Caller: Mm-hmm.

Bob: Now, you know, that doesn’t mean we’ve effectively, you know, put that in process yet, but I just wanted to say this is the result of two years of considerable focused work. But I just wonder —

Alexis Madrigal: Bob, no, I really appreciate it. Let’s take it to the panel here. Tyche, let us get your perspective first, and then, Deep, I’m going to ask you about this kind of thing nationally.

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, this is something that we’re seeing, in addition to our statewide laws, which over, you know, really beginning in the first Trump administration, were saying, look, law enforcement — you know, the job of state and local law enforcement is to protect public safety. It’s not to conduct immigration operations.

But on top of those statewide laws, a lot of localities are increasingly being pushed by grassroots efforts, like the caller was describing, to specify and spell out, like, unless they have a judicial warrant signed by a judge, not just a warrant for somebody that was signed by an ICE supervisor, then we’re not going to, you know, let them onto the property or so forth.

And our attorney general has spelled out some best practices for public institutions, going all the way to public hospitals, public schools, and universities, for how to interact with ICE and keep nonpublic spaces off-limits and so forth. And records, also, documents.

But the enforcement is the question, or the implementation. It seems we’re seeing ICE basically saying, “Yeah, that doesn’t apply to us.”

So then I think it’s most likely to get kicked to the courts.

But one other thing I wanted — we started out talking about the nursing professor at USF and the student at UC Berkeley. And another area where we have seen kind of a response has been from the universities that those women are affiliated with.

And a real — I mean, their advocates say that the universities just sprang into action to connect these people with legal support, to provide letters from the chancellor, and to rally support from members of Congress, to open channels through the congressional offices with ICE to try to locate them and so forth.

And a kind of a protocol, and in particular, UC Berkeley’s protocol.

Advocates have said, and lawyers who are doing this work — in fact, this young woman, Paola’s lawyer, was saying, “I spoke with my other stakeholders in the county and said, like, this protocol that UC Berkeley’s developed is a great model for other institutions.”

And so there’s other kinds of pushback where universities, in some cases, early in the Trump administration, were a little bit wary of standing up to this administration, but here they really seem to be coming to these women’s support.

So there’s a lot of different parts of society that seem to be stepping into this arena.

Alexis Madrigal: Deep, what else? Yeah, I mean, this is interesting. Maybe there’s a proliferation of different models by local actors who are kind of opposing this one larger national or federal force. What else do you see?

Deep Gulasekaram: Yeah, so I think, to the listener’s question, certainly these local ordinances, state ordinances, county ordinances that highly restrict the communication, what local officers can do, what types of questions they can ask, who they can communicate with, can be highly effective and are completely within the control of state and local county boards and supervisory legislative bodies.

And so I think that is an important right to assert.

Tyche was saying public institutions like universities — they have rights with regard to the types of privacy they can create for their students, the nature under which they need to allow enforcement officers on their campuses. They have rights they can assert.

It gets trickier, though, as to the question that was asked, when we deal with public property. Certainly counties and localities own property and therefore can assert some rights over it.

But the tricky legal question is that you cannot, as a state and local county or jurisdiction, simply have a blanket prohibition on federal authorities coming upon your public property.

Federal authorities, like everyone else, have rights to access, especially when it’s a public area. And this is where it gets tricky, right?

So if there’s a public area where people are generally allowed to go on that public land, so should ICE agents and federal agents.

On the other hand, if the presence of those ICE agents is starting to compromise the types of services provided, so especially thinking about state courts and scaring away witnesses and litigants, county health institutions, and the presence of ICE officials is scaring away people who need care, it becomes a much harder question.

And these are the questions that are currently being litigated in federal court.

Alexis Madrigal: So interesting. Let’s bring in one last caller here. Let’s bring in Amy in Concord.

Amy: Thank you so much for taking my call. Thank you very much, Alexis. I feel like I know you even though we’ve never met. I’ve been with you every day, and I feel a good day to you.

Alexis Madrigal: Thank you, Amy. Thank you.

Amy: Well, I’ve been thinking about this. The main thing is they’ve got to shut down the money because they can’t have an unlimited amount of money to go out and violate human rights.

These immigrants are being put in jail without any due process, and they aren’t really even criminals. You know, Trump sold it to us that we were going to be taking criminals away, but no, we’re just taking immigrants away. They may have been under a protected status just a few short months ago. That’s part of the biggest problem.

The other part is that these jails are not ever — there’s no oversight. There are young women who are pregnant, who are becoming pregnant in these jails. How is that happening? And there’s not oversight.

You know, I’m just wondering, when is the time going to come where we decide that we have to collect all the people who have red hair and freckles and put them in jail? Because that’s really all that we’re doing. We’re just selecting a group of people, and we’re putting them in jail.

And it’s not even a jail. It really is. You can call it a detention center if you have to, but —

Alexis Madrigal: Amy, I appreciate it. Thanks, friend, for this perspective.

You know, maybe I’ll give you the last kind of sense. I do think there’s many people who are expressing Amy’s sense of frustration about this and maybe are expecting Congress to be able to go after the money. Is there any sense that might happen?

Tyche Hendricks: Well, I mean, yeah, I guess a question, and maybe our folks who are looking at the federal picture: Can the Democratic Congress claw back some of those tens of billions of dollars that were appropriated by this current Congress? Can they put restrictions on how ICE conducts itself? Can they, you know, dare the president to veto legislation?

I mean, these are going to be the questions that face the next Congress. And there’s a lot of questions that are going to face the next Congress.

So how much of a priority immigration rises to is partly going to come from constituents and from the grassroots, as far as, you know, making that a priority with their lawmakers.

Alexis Madrigal: Thank you so much, Tyche Hendricks, immigration reporter at KQED. Thanks so much for joining us.

Tyche Hendricks: My pleasure.

Alexis Madrigal: We’ve also had Deep Gulasekaram, who is professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. Thank you so much, Deep.

Deep Gulasekaram: Thank you for having me.

Alexis Madrigal: And we’ve had Jasmine Garsd, immigration correspondent at NPR. Thank you so much for coming back, Jasmine.

Jasmine Garsd: Always a pleasure.

Alexis Madrigal: Thanks so much to all of our callers, our listeners, and commenters. Thanks so much.

I’m Alexis Madrigal. Stay tuned for another hour of Forum ahead with Mina Kim.

text:
WASHINGTON — Some Texas Democrats argue Congress should immediately tackle immigration reform following their party’s decisive victories across the country this month, including in Hispanic-majority districts in South Texas that have experienced the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

In his first public appearance after winning the U.S. Senate race in Texas, Democrat James Talarico visited the memorial of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Houston man fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer. Talarico, like many others, placed his “I Voted” sticker at the site.

“People were moved by this situation, and I do think it was the turning point in the election and in our country as a whole,” Carlos Eduardo Espina, a Spanish-language content creator from Houston, told Spectrum News.

Espina said President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration approach was a motivating factor for many Texans to vote. Espina has more than 25 million followers across different social media platforms, where he discusses immigration and politics.

“There's a difference between going after someone who has a criminal record who's done things they shouldn't do, and going after someone who's been here for 10, 15, 20 years, working hard, paying taxes, contributing to society,” Espina said.

Espina joined Texas Democrats, immigration advocates and business leaders at a press conference in Washington last week, calling for protections for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the U.S. for years.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, a Democrat who flipped a Hispanic-majority district in South Texas, said mixed-status families have been living in fear.

“I do want to fight for a pathway to citizenship for those that have been here, and I say this because that's going to be their protection. We don't know. What if we in the future get somebody even more anti-immigrant than Donald Trump? The only thing that would protect them is citizenship, because we don't know what the future holds,” Pulido said.

Before leaving the White House Monday for the Philippines and China, President Trump was asked about the possibility of immigration reform.

“A lot of people would like me to look at it, and I'll always look at it, and it'd be wonderful, but we'll see. I mean, it has to be tough, and no amnesty, et cetera, et cetera,” the president told reporters.

The president said his immigration policies “helped and hurt” him at the polls and that they may have been “too tough.” But the president’s promotion of Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his hardline immigration policies, to White House chief of staff is being seen by many as a sign that a dramatic change of course is unlikely.

“To me, immigration and the economy go hand in hand,” Espina said. “When someone gets detained by ICE, let's say the head of household, that creates economic issues for that family. Immigration becomes an economic issue when you own a business and half your clients don't want to show up anymore because they're afraid of ICE enforcement."

Espina said Republicans need to strike a deal on immigration reform if they want to be successful in the 2028 elections.

“People on both sides of the aisle can agree that the current system just doesn't work. It's completely broken. It's completely outdated, and there needs to be some change, and I think we can make it happen,” Espina said.

Some Texas Democrats argue there is no need to wait for the new Congress to begin in January to tackle immigration. Meanwhile, the Trump administration recently touted its 483,000 deportations and nearly half a million immigration arrests made this year.

description:
The coalition challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.
The court set aside the rule in its entirety under the Administrative Procedure Act and denied the government’s motion for summary judgment.
If implemented, this rule would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses.
This outcome underscores the importance of defending international education through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy.
International students and scholars deserve to have a level of predictability in pursuit of their dreams and it is in our nation’s best interest to provide it.
text:
Media Contacts: media@nafsa.org, press@presidentsalliance.org, press@aft.org, highered@uaw.net, press@newsguild.org

Washington, D.C. — Today, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts ruled in favor of NAFSA: Association of International Educators; the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM); the American Federation of Teachers (AFT); Graduate Labor Organization, AFT Local 6516 (GLO); International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW); United Auto Workers Local 2322; and The NewsGuild-CWA. The coalition challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.

The court set aside the rule in its entirety under the Administrative Procedure Act and denied the government’s motion for summary judgment. The ruling preserves the longstanding D/S framework and prevents the rule’s new fixed admission periods, extension-of-stay requirements, and restrictions on academic mobility from taking effect.

The court held that the rule was arbitrary and capricious because DHS failed to appropriately weigh its costs and benefits, justify the changes based on its stated fraud and national security concerns, consider less burdensome alternatives, or adequately respond to significant public comments. The court further emphasized that DHS failed to meaningfully consider improvements to the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) as an alternative to imposing a costly new system.

The court also held that the rule’s restrictions on academic studies exceeded DHS’s statutory authority because they were not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 student visa program. As the court explained, “The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program.”

The rule would have replaced the longstanding D/S policy with fixed admission periods of no more than four years and required international students and exchange visitors to apply for extensions of stay. It also would have restricted students’ ability to change educational objectives, transfer institutions, or pursue additional programs of study. The coalition challenged the rule in court because of the uncertainty and administrative burdens it would create, their interference with academic decision-making, and the disruption it would cause to educational and professional plans.

The coalition is represented by Paul Hughes, Partner, at McDermott Will & Schulte.

Jon Schleuss, President of The NewsGuild-CWA, stated:

“International journalists working in the United States have been on pins and needles waiting for a decision in this case and we are thrilled that Judge Saylor struck down the Trump administration’s rule. We are grateful that Judge Saylor understands that a free press is an essential ingredient to protect democracy. We will continue to defend journalists everywhere.”

Miriam Feldblum, President and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, stated:

“Today’s ruling is a clear and important victory for international students and scholars and the colleges and universities that welcome them. Preserving Duration of Status gives students greater certainty as they pursue their education and allows institutions to support their academic progress without arbitrary hurdles and unnecessary barriers. The harmful consequences of the current administration’s policy actions and efforts are already evident in the significant declines in international student enrollment and interest we are witnessing. If implemented, this rule would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses. We are proud to stand with our coalition partners in defending international education, and the contributions that international students and researchers bring to our campuses, communities, and country.”

Fanta Aw, PhD, Executive Director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, stated:

“With this ruling, the judge has sent an unequivocal and resounding message: the longstanding Duration of Status policy is retained. This outcome underscores the importance of defending international education through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy. At a time when uncertainty continues to affect our field, this decision is a powerful reminder that our collective voice matters and that standing firm in defense of educational opportunity can make a meaningful difference for institutions, students and this nation. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to our legal counsel, our fellow plaintiffs, and the many members and institutions whose experiences and expertise helped inform this effort. International students and scholars deserve to have a level of predictability in pursuit of their dreams and it is in our nation’s best interest to provide it. Their contributions, combined with domestic talent, make our country stronger.”

Robert J. McCarron, President and CEO of the Association of Independent Colleges & Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), stated:

“We are pleased that the court vacated the entire Duration of Status rule as arbitrary and capricious and reiterated in its ruling that the “nature and purpose” of the F-1 visa is to permit, and indeed encourage, international students to pursue educational opportunities here. International students add to the vibrancy of our campuses, drive innovative research, and support the Commonwealth’s economic vitality.”

Randi Weingarten, President of AFT, stated:

“Today’s final order will have resounding impacts for generations of scientists and scholars from every corner of the globe that make America the worldwide leader in cutting-edge research. The Trump administration’s proposed limits on how long international scholars have to complete their studies were arbitrary and hostile. We stand united with our 420,000 higher education members, international and American alike, so they can continue to pursue difficult questions, challenge conventional wisdom, publish findings without political interference and make US colleges and universities the envy of the world.

text:
WASHINGTON — Today, the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that CBP’s October encounters reached the lowest level ever recorded to start a fiscal year. Additionally, October marked the 18th consecutive month of zero releases at the border.

“President Trump unleashed the full strength of DHS to secure the border and enforce the law,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “The results speak for themselves. In Fiscal Year 2026, our officers and agents drove illegal crossings to historic lows. DHS carried that momentum into October, when CBP saw its fewest nationwide encounters ever to open a fiscal year. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will continue to deliver the most secure border in American history and save American lives.”

The sustained decline in illegal border crossings and apprehensions—at levels not seen in over three decades—shows the profound impact of robust enforcement policies. With daily Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border down 95% over the past year compared with the previous administration, the border remains more secure than at any point in history.

“Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, CBP has been empowered to enforce the law, giving us an unprecedented level of control over our borders,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “We know more about who and what is entering our homeland than at any time in our nation’s history. America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities, and putting the security of the American people first.”

Below is a snapshot of October’s key figures. Full monthly reporting can be viewed on CBP’s Stats and Summaries webpage.

Border Enforcement at Historic Levels

Illegal crossings remain historically low:

CBP’s nationwide encounters in October were the lowest ever to start a fiscal year

Additionally, CBP’s nationwide encounters in October (27,890) were 7% lower than September, and the lowest for a month since February.

U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions decreased in October

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 7% lower than September.

Southwest border apprehensions in October were 95% lower than under Biden

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 95% lower than the monthly average of the Biden administration; 97% below the peak of the Biden administration (December 2023); and less than the number of apprehensions recorded in 5 days in October 2024.

Drug Interdictions That Save Lives

CBP remains on the frontline against drug smuggling, seizing dangerous narcotics before they reach American communities.

Nationwide in October, seizures of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, and marijuana (combined, by weight) increased 44% from September 2026. Total drug seizures in October 2026 (combined, by weight) increased 13% from October 2024 during the Biden administration.

Individual drugs compared to September 2026:

Marijuana seizures increased 29% in October (14,748 pounds seized in October 2026)

Methamphetamine seizures increased 59% in October (14,745 pounds seized in October 2026)

Cocaine seizures increased 60% in October (9,032 pounds seized in October 2026)

Heroin seizures increased 95% in October (246 pounds seized in October 2026)

Trade and Tariff Enforcement

CBP plays a central role in enforcing U.S. trade law and supporting economic security.

$391 billion in imports processed in October 2026.

$26 billion in duties identified for collection in October 2026.

Agriculture Stats/Seizures – Securing American Agriculture

In October, CBP agriculture specialists helped protect America’s agriculture, natural resources, and economic prosperity.

CBP issued 6,020 emergency action notifications for restricted and prohibited plant and animal products.

title: FP Predictions: SCOTUS Will Hand Major Win to Agricultural Employers by Blocking DOL ...
description:
Quick Background Sun Valley Orchards, a family-run farm in New Jersey, was investigated by the DOL over its H-2A practices during the 2015 growing season.
While a federal district court in New Jersey sided with the DOL, the 3rd Circuit reversed in favor of Sun Valley Orchards.
The Supreme Court heard arguments in DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards on November 10.
On behalf of Sun Valley Orchards, Robert Johnson argued that this is fundamentally an employment and contract dispute, not an immigration proceeding.
This could potentially significantly reduce H-2A employers’ exposure to such financial liability.
text:
The Supreme Court will likely rule in favor of a family farm in a critical separations-of-power case, ending the Department of Labor’s ability to adjudicate proceedings to collect financial penalties from agricultural employers for alleged violations of the H-2A temporary visa program. That’s according to the predictions of our firm’s thought leaders monitoring DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards, a pending case that centers on whether the agency’s use of administrative law judges (ALJs) to impose H-2A penalties is constitutional (if authorized by federal law at all) or whether ag employers have a right to a trial before an independent federal judge. Read on for an analysis of the issues, our specific predictions on how SCOTUS will decide the case, and how a final decision in 2027 could impact ag employers for years to come.

Quick Background

Sun Valley Orchards, a family-run farm in New Jersey, was investigated by the DOL over its H-2A practices during the 2015 growing season. The agency determined that the farm had committed several violations and owed back wages and civil penalties. After Sun Valley requested a hearing, an ALJ issued a decision that mostly aligned with the DOL’s determination, requiring the farm to pay over $500K to the agency. The DOL’s Administrative Review Board affirmed the ALJ’s decision on appeal.

The farm then sued the DOL in federal court, claiming, among other things, that the agency’s administrative system for imposing financial liability was unconstitutional, and that cases involving orders to pay money to the government must be tried before an Article III court. While a federal district court in New Jersey sided with the DOL, the 3rd Circuit reversed in favor of Sun Valley Orchards. Earlier this year, the DOL officially asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case, and SCOTUS granted that petition on April 27.

Overview of the Issues Before SCOTUS

The Supreme Court will ultimately decide whether the DOL’s adjudication system for collecting monetary remedies from employers that have allegedly violated the terms and conditions of employment of H-2A workers (and domestic workers in corresponding employment) is:

prohibited by Article III of the Constitution; and, if not,

authorized by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. §1188(g)(2)).

The DOL argues that that agency’s administrative penalty procedure for H-2A violations is permissible because:

this procedure involves immigration-related “public” rights;

Congress may empower the executive branch to impose monetary penalties in cases involving public rights; and

Congress has done so through Section 1188(g)(2) of the INA, which authorizes the Secretary of Labor to “take such actions, including imposing appropriate penalties…as may be necessary to assure employer compliance with terms and conditions of employment under this section.”

On the other hand, Sun Valley Orchards argues that:

this case is fundamentally a labor dispute involving private contractual rights and therefore falls outside of the narrow “public rights” exception (especially in light of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in SEC v. Jarkesy); and

Section 1188(g)(2) of the INA allows the DOL to pursue penalties in court, but not to create this type of in-house agency court system where they write the rules, prosecute cases, provide witnesses, and then issue judgments.

What’s the Latest?

The Supreme Court heard arguments in DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards on November 10. Below are some of the highlights.

Chief Justice Roberts repeatedly challenged the government’s attempt to characterize this dispute as an exercise of immigration authority, drawing a line between admission to the country via the H-2A program versus subsequent employment conditions.

Sarah Harris, a principal deputy solicitor general for the Department of Justice, argued on behalf of the DOL that the H-2A program’s conditions are governmental obligations rather than private employment contracts, and that immigration authority over those continuing obligations does not stop at the physical border.

On behalf of Sun Valley Orchards, Robert Johnson argued that this is fundamentally an employment and contract dispute, not an immigration proceeding. He said the nature of the allegations in this case are employment-related (“for instance, almost half the liability, a large chunk of the liability, involves the three-quarters guarantee issue”), whereas “immigration adjudication involves the question of whether to admit, exclude, or deport.”

Justice Kagan pushed back and said that the H-2A program has nothing to do with contract rights: “Essentially, this is a kind of visa fraud or immigration fraud. The employer says I’m certifying a set of things in order to get a set of foreign workers, and in exchange for that, I’m going to treat them a certain way, treat them the way that will not undercut domestic workers. And then, allegedly, the employer does the exact opposite, treats them in ways that do undercut domestic workers.”

Justices Alito, Kavanaugh, and Barrett, who seemed the most undecided, raised concerns about the broadest possible arguments on both sides and where lines should be drawn.

FP SCOTUS Predictions: Court Will Strike Down DOL’s ALJ Use for H-2A Penalties

Rebecca Hause-Schultz and Joshua Viau, leaders of FP’s Agriculture Industry Team, predict that the Court will rule 6-3 for Sun Valley Orchards, with Chief Justice Roberts writing the majority opinion. We anticipate that the decision will continue this Court’s recent trend limiting administrative agency authority and deference. The majority is likely to emphasize the substance of the underlying claims rather than the immigration-policy-based purpose and preserve the distinction between the government’s authority to regulate participation in a federal program and its authority to adjudicate monetary liability.

What’s at Stake for Agricultural Employers?

If the Supreme Court rules in favor of Sun Valley Orchards, agricultural employers will gain a new tool to fight back against back wages and monetary penalties by the DOL for H-2A program violations. The DOL would have to bring these types of claims in federal court, which is a slower, more burdensome, and less favorable process for the government. This could potentially significantly reduce H-2A employers’ exposure to such financial liability.

Further, a win for agricultural employers could benefit employers across all industries as it could potentially influence other courts to curb ALJ authority in similar challenges. Stay tuned for an upcoming FP Insight that will dive deeper into the broader implications at stake for all employers.

Conclusion

title: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee's Collarbone
description:
“I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator.
They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.
The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.
Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets.
Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.
text:
Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.

Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.

According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”

Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”

The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.

On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.

“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”

Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.

According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.

Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.

In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”

Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”

“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”

Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.

It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.

Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.

The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.

“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”

The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse. The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.

Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.

In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.

“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”

The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”

Roca Estrada tells a very different story.

He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.

Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.

“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”

According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.

The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”

Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.

The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.

According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”

Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.

For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.

“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”
