title: Centreville Immigration Forum et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al. - ACLU of Virginia
description:
Despite this clear law – and repeated rulings against these practices by federal courts across the country – ICE is arresting Virginians without a warrant and without probable cause.
In fact, ICE’s own data reflect 8,835 non-custodial arrests in Virginia between January 20, 2025, and August 5, 2026.
The people represented by today’s filing were stopped on ordinary trips to work or to run errands.
Centreville Immigration Forum et al.
v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al.
text:
For more than 70 years, immigration law has strictly limited federal agents’ authority to make arrests by requiring them to have a warrant when arresting someone for an immigration violation, or to have probable cause that a person is both in the United States in violation of the law and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

Despite this clear law – and repeated rulings against these practices by federal courts across the country – ICE is arresting Virginians without a warrant and without probable cause. In fact, ICE’s own data reflect 8,835 non-custodial arrests in Virginia between January 20, 2025, and August 5, 2026. That represents a 1,724 percent increase in the average weekly rate of such arrests, from approximately six per week in 2024 to 109 per week after January 20, 2025.

The people represented by today’s filing were stopped on ordinary trips to work or to run errands. But they never made it: armed ICE agents driving unmarked vehicles boxed in their cars, confronted them, forcibly removed them from their vehicles, and then handcuffed and transported them to immigration facilities that routinely lacked adequate medical care and other basic necessities.

Centreville Immigration Forum et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al. was filed in the Alexandria division of the Eastern District of Virginia and asks the court to prevent DHS and ICE from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests without a warrant or probable cause, as required by law.

title: Stephen Miller Is Already Planning For After Trump | The New Republic
description:
Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller have reportedly become much closer in the second Trump administration, reports The Wall Street Journal.
The Trump administration is blaming everyone but itself for the nationwide flight stoppage that the Federal Aviation Administration instituted on Friday.
And President Trump and I are gonna fix it.
But when other leaders of state and other people come here—the White House was in terrible condition.
The Trump administration blamed the rare nationwide ground stop on faulty copper wiring and a bum router located in Arkansas.
text:
Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller have reportedly become much closer in the second Trump administration, reports The Wall Street Journal. Together, the duo is one of the most powerful influences on policy in Washington.

Now that Miller has been made White House chief of staff, he and Rubio will have even more sway over the president. Miller’s xenophobic views and extreme approach to immigration enforcement certainly didn’t help Republicans in the midterms, but despite that, President Donald Trump seems to be doubling down on Miller’s brutal, racist tactics.

Rubio, meanwhile, has a lot of influence in his dual role as secretary of state and national security adviser, and knows how to sell potentially controversial policies. Together, the two men have cooked up some of the most brazen foreign policy moves of the last two years: the plan to seize Greenland, the likely illegal deadly boat strikes, and the abduction of Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, according to the Journal.

For anyone who knows Rubio and Miller’s history, their close relationship may come as a surprise: The two initially butted heads when Rubio was working on immigration reform and Miller was an adviser to Republican Senator Jeff Sessions. Miller reportedly worked fiercely to undermine Rubio, and called him an “extremist who wants unlimited immigration.”

However, during the second Trump administration, Rubio has reportedly done all he can to enforce Miller’s hardline immigration crackdown, and personally flew to El Salvador to negotiate a deal to send U.S. deportees to the country’s megaprison, where many have suffered abuse.

The Trump administration is blaming everyone but itself for the nationwide flight stoppage that the Federal Aviation Administration instituted on Friday.

“The FAA administrator apologized to the American people during the news conference you held yesterday,” NBC’s Kristen Welker asked Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Monday morning. “Do you feel you also owe an apology to the American people? This happened on your watch.”

“It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or the [Department of Transportation] in decades. And I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy replied. “But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us. And I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them! It goes back 25, 30 years of a lack of investment … waving the flag to say, ‘Hey, this is a problem, let’s fix it.’ Why they didn’t do that, I don’t know.”

“They gave me a system that needs to be fixed. And President Trump and I are gonna fix it. I’m well on my way, but I need more money to do it,” he continued.

Thousands of flights were cancelled over the weekend due to the Trump administration’s nationwide grounding, leaving countless Americans stranded and deeply inconvenienced. The administration has attributed the stoppage to faulty copper wiring and a router malfunction in Arkansas, denying reports that it had anything to do with the massive artificial intelligence systems overhaul the FAA performed just a day before. Regardless, for Duffy to refuse to apologize to them—dumping the issue on previous administrations—is weak and uncompelling, especially given that this was the first nationwide ground stop in years.

President Trump wasn’t keen on apologizing either.

“How much responsibility do you take for the ground stop on Friday given that you’re the president?” a reporter asked Trump on the White House lawn Monday.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” he replied. “Everybody was safe, nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing. The only responsibility should be for 40 years they should’ve done this.”

He blamed the Biden administration more explicitly over the weekend.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” he wrote Sunday on Truth Social. “We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.” On Monday, he called a Black female reporter a “loser” for even asking about it.

But despite the will of the American people, Evans is not ready to lose his grip on power. The MAGA politico announced Monday that he’s going to run for Congress again in 2028, albeit in a different district.

“I know what it means to live rurally and depend on water, energy, and agriculture, because that’s how three generations of my family have lived in Douglas, Elbert, and Weld counties,” Evans said in a statement on Facebook. “Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls’ sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable.”

The Fort Lupton resident also suggested that the people of Colorado’s 4th district—which constitutes the Centennial State’s most conservative region—were at risk of losing their values to Democratic Socialists.

“The people of the 4th District grow our food, produce our energy, work in defense, aerospace, healthcare, and so many other sectors. They raise their families on values that Democrat Socialists and their allies keep trying to regulate out of existence. They deserve a representative with deep roots in the community who shows up for them, not one who answers to the coastal donors who just bought this seat,” Evans wrote, apparently referring to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, who bested Representative Lauren Boebert earlier this month.

(Interestingly enough, Boebert herself switched districts in 2023 after a close race in order to ensure herself an easier return to Congress. Although she won in 2024, she lost this time around in yet another stunning Democratic flip.)

The unusually early announcement will give Evans a remarkable head start in the 2028 race, entering the new year with $300,000 in campaign funds and regional name recognition that will make it difficult for new candidates to compete, according to the Colorado Sun.

But the region’s incoming lawmaker is ignoring the noise.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted five times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher wrote in a statement obtained by Colorado Public Radio’s Caitlyn Kim. “While Gabe Evans focuses on finding his way back to Washington, Eileen is focused on making Washington deliver for the people of Colorado’s 4th District.”

Just two days after the midterm elections, Crosbie announced her candidacy in a letter to the RNC’s 168 members. She questioned whether Republicans had done enough to address voter concerns to avoid the sweeping party losses. “Tuesday’s results were a serious setback,” she wrote. “We owe ourselves an honest account of why.”

The White House did not take kindly to the first major challenge to Trump’s authority within the Republican Party ranks. “The White House was blindsided by KC’s bid for RNC Chair and people are infuriated that she did not give anybody a courtesy call,” an administration official told Axios.

During a meeting in the White House on November 6, Trump warned that if Crosbie was crowned, he’d cut the financial cord. Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other administration and Cabinet officials would no longer be permitted to appear at fundraising events. Trump would also bar the RNC from using his likeness and signature as part of fundraising efforts.

The president was sent over the edge Monday by a simple question about the FAA’s ground stop, resulting in a lengthy tirade and a series of demeaning remarks against an inquiring Black woman reporter.

“Mr. President, what do you say to critics who say you were too focused on D.C. construction projects while our airline systems were crumbling, given the fact that Republicans have been in control?” NBC News White House Correspondent Yamiche Alcindor asked Donald Trump as he departed the White House for a trip to Asia.

But Trump was apparently uninterested in acknowledging the multibillion-dollar national airline crisis spurred by his administration on Friday, which required practically every plane in U.S. airspace to cut short its route and land at the nearest airport.

Instead, the president took the opportunity to exalt his White House renovations for the umpteenth time, all while disparaging Alcindor as “pathetic” and a “loser” for daring to question his vanity projects. When Alcindor attempted to ask a follow-up question, Trump shot her down.

“You’re so pathetic,” he fumed. “This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts. I pay for it. This doesn’t cost money. This is called talent. You don’t have talent. You don’t know what a broken column is. When you see a broken column you don’t notice. But when other leaders of state and other people come here—the White House was in terrible condition. Now it’s in beautiful condition.”

“Cost me very little money to do it. I spent very little time to do it, and losers like you say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country, and the White House should look like that,” Trump said, extending his arm to gesture to the executive mansion behind him.

The Trump administration blamed the rare nationwide ground stop on faulty copper wiring and a bum router located in Arkansas. Senior officials denied that the rapid expansion of the agency’s artificial intelligence tools—which were rolled out the day prior—had anything to do with the critical failure.

text:
Congresswoman Veronica Escobar is leading a group of 22 House Democrats who are urging the Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General to investigate the nearly $7.5 billion in contracts awarded for border barrier infrastructure in the Big Bend region of West Texas.

In a Monday letter to Inspector General Joseph Cuffari, the group — which includes 10 representatives from Texas — wrote that the contracts need to be investigated due to known political ties between President Donald Trump and selected border wall contractors. They also cited how contracting and procurement laws were among those waived by the DHS Secretary to expedite the project.

“Publicly available information raises serious questions about how these contracts were awarded, whether political relationships played any role in contractor selection, whether the circumvention of normal contracting and oversight safeguards was in the public interest, and whether the enormous expenditures are justified by an operational need,” the letter states.

DHS did not immediately respond to Marfa Public Radio’s request for comment on a potential investigation.

The move comes as Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, are promising a slew of investigations into the Trump administration driven by corruption concerns.

The letter states that the Big Bend region, which includes Bend Bend National Park, “encompasses some of the most remote, rugged and waterless terrain,” along the border and cites statistics about its low levels of migrant crossings.

In 2025, the region accounted for just 1.3% of total Border Patrol apprehensions along the U.S.-Mexico border. Within the national park itself, officials recorded 133 apprehensions in 2025, according to National Park Service data.

House Democrats wrote that Inspector General Ciffari “has a responsibility to scrutinize” whether the Big Bend Sector is truly an area of “high illegal entry” — a designation that unlocked the use of the waivers — and whether the resulting contracts and expenditures are in the public interest.

The Trump administration’s known political ties to both Barnard Construction Company and Fisher Sand and Gravel, two companies awarded multiple Big Bend border wall contracts, was another key reason cited by House Democrats as to why an independent investigation is needed.

The lawmakers also took aim at how the project’s plans have continuously changed over the past year. U.S. Customs and Border Protection has still not revealed updated plans for Big Bend National Park, which CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott teased after the Supreme Court ruled last week that construction can continue in the area following a lower court’s pause.

“The processes CBP used to award these contracts lacked any transparency, and there has been no opportunity for public oversight of the contracts, or even for the public to understand the scope of the contracts,” the letter argues.

Escobar, whose congressional district includes El Paso, and the other House Democrats requested a response to their letter and a timeline for an Office of the Inspector General investigation by November 20.

title: ICE under Trump is unlawfully arresting Virginians without a warrant
description:
“ICE agents are arresting people first and assuming they’ll figure out a reason to justify it later, flagrantly ignoring federal law that’s been in place for decades,” said ACLU-VA Senior Supervising Attorney Sophia Gregg.
“The law is clear: ICE must have a warrant or probable cause before it can arrest someone.
Despite this clear law – and repeated rulings against these practices by federal courts across the country – ICE is arresting Virginians without a warrant and without probable cause.
“ICE agents cannot arrest someone without a warrant or probable cause,” said Rebecca Guterman, counsel at Washington Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs.
The filing asks the court to prevent DHS and ICE from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests without probable cause, as required by law.
text:
11/16/26 – Legal Aid Justice Center, The ACLU of Virginia, Bailey & Glasser, LLP, Covington & Burling LLP, and the Washington Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs filed a class action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on behalf of Centreville Immigration Forum (CIF), a Virginia organization, and six Virginia residents to end the Trump administration’s unlawful policy and practice of executing immigration arrests in Virginia without a warrant or probable cause.

“ICE agents are arresting people first and assuming they’ll figure out a reason to justify it later, flagrantly ignoring federal law that’s been in place for decades,” said ACLU-VA Senior Supervising Attorney Sophia Gregg. “The law is clear: ICE must have a warrant or probable cause before it can arrest someone. Federal agents can’t endanger Virginia communities to advance the Trump administration’s inhumane, anti-immigrant agenda.”

For more than 70 years, immigration law has strictly limited federal agents’ authority to make arrests by requiring them to have a warrant when arresting someone for an immigration violation, or to have probable cause that a person is both in the United States in violation of the law and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

Despite this clear law – and repeated rulings against these practices by federal courts across the country – ICE is arresting Virginians without a warrant and without probable cause. In fact, ICE’s own data reflect 8,835 non-custodial arrests in Virginia between January 20, 2025, and August 5, 2026. That represents a 1,724 percent increase in the average weekly rate of such arrests, from approximately six per week in 2024 to 109 per week after January 20, 2025.

“Federal agents are terrorizing Virginia communities by indiscriminately stopping and arresting people who are simply trying to go about their lives,” said Legal Aid Justice Center Senior Supervising Attorney Emily Lopynski. “This kind of lawlessness does nothing to keep the Commonwealth safe — in fact, it is a threat to the safety of every Virginian, and it cannot be allowed to continue.”

The people represented by today’s filing were stopped on ordinary trips to work or to run errands. But they never made it: armed ICE agents driving unmarked vehicles boxed in their cars, confronted them, forcibly removed them from their vehicles, and then handcuffed and transported them to immigration facilities that routinely lacked adequate medical care and other basic necessities.

“The Trump administration is encouraging federal agents to escalate their tactics, causing chaos and confusion and putting everyone’s safety at risk in Virginia,” said Bailey & Glasser partner Michael L. Murphy. “ICE cannot violate people’s civil rights and civil liberties in the name of a violent, anti-immigrant agenda.”

The Trump administration has imposed on ICE a national quota of 3,000 immigration arrests every day, ripping Virginia families and communities apart. As ICE roams the Commonwealth looking for people to arrest to fill their quotas, Brown and Black Virginians in particular live in fear of being arbitrarily arrested, and because ICE agents often do not wear any insignia or otherwise identify themselves, these violent confrontations are functionally indistinguishable from armed kidnappings.

“ICE agents cannot arrest someone without a warrant or probable cause,” said Rebecca Guterman, counsel at Washington Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs. “Congress specifically enacted laws that protect the public from arbitrary arrests and federal agents who remove Virginians from their families and communities must be held accountable for their illegal actions.”

Today’s class action complaint was filed in the Alexandria division of the Eastern District of Virginia. The filing asks the court to prevent DHS and ICE from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests without probable cause, as required by law.

description:
Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.
Costs remain unclear The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda.
“The agreement is a shame” Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.
Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.
The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.
text:
Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.

Although the details of the agreement are still being negotiated, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece say they are confident of reaching a deal and beginning deportations of irregular migrants in 2027.

The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

“I think this [agreement] is a game changer. We will take back control and remove the incentive for illegal migration,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, during the announcement in Vienna, along with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and the interior ministers of other countries involved, including Rwanda’s Vincent Biruta.

The initial hub will be a small-scale pilot project, with plans to expand the scheme once it is operational and the risk of deportations being blocked by legal challenges has diminished.

Who will be sent to the return hubs?

The five countries will deport only rejected asylum seekers who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

Minors will be excluded, while each country will apply its own criteria for selecting those to be deported.

The Netherlands will focus on adult men from countries in Rwanda’s region, while Germany will target migrants who refuse to cooperate with efforts to establish their identity and come from countries reluctant to readmit their own nationals, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.

The EU border agency Frontex will not have a role in deportations in the initial stages, despite a reform of its mandate recently proposed by the European Commission, which would allow it to do so.

Costs remain unclear

The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda. However, no estimate for the initial facility was provided at the press conference, as negotiations are still ongoing.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, services in Rwanda will be considerably cheaper than equivalent services in Europe.

What Rwanda will get in return is also unclear at this stage. Kigali is, however, set to sign a partnership agreement with Denmark next week, related to cooperation on migration.

“The agreement is a shame”

Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.

Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

“The agreement is a shame,” said French lawmaker Mélissa Camara, of the Greens/EFA group, considering the countries involved are “crossing another disgraceful moral line by reaching an agreement with an authoritarian regime.”

The group of five countries said that all procedures will be carried out in line with international human rights standards.

However, legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may be subjected to violations of fundamental rights.

The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.

A similar agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, under which Britain planned to send asylum seekers to the African country, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk that those transferred could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution.

According to the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

text:
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands are advancing a controversial plan to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, establishing what would be an unprecedented arrangement under European Union migration policy. The five countries intend to create a "return hub" in the East African nation for migrants whose asylum applications have been rejected and who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

Although the initial program is expected to involve only a small number of people, its supporters hope the prospect of deportation to a third country will discourage migrants from making dangerous journeys to Europe. Human rights organizations, however, warn that transferring people to a country with which they have no connection could violate their fundamental rights.

The initiative comes amid mounting political pressure on European governments to adopt tougher immigration policies, driven partly by the growing influence of far-right parties across the continent. In June, the European Parliament approved regulatory changes that opened the door to establishing return centers outside EU territory. According to reports, the five countries began preliminary discussions with Rwanda in August.

MAKE ynetGlobal MY TRUSTED SOURCE

Austria formally announced Monday that negotiations with Rwanda were underway, saying the parties hoped to reach an agreement quickly enough for the first deportations to begin in 2027. The arrangement would apply to asylum seekers who have exhausted their legal options but cannot be deported to their countries of origin.

Rwanda's growing role in Western deportation plans

Rwanda, led by President Paul Kagame, has increasingly positioned itself as a destination for migrants removed from Western countries. Last year, the government reached a limited agreement with the United States under which it agreed to receive up to 250 migrants who had been living in the U.S. without authorization.

Britain previously pursued a similar arrangement under the Conservative government that lost power in the 2024 general election. The plan faced repeated legal challenges and never resulted in deportation flights. The Labour government abandoned it after taking office.

The British proposal differed from the new European initiative in one important respect: It would have allowed asylum seekers to be transferred to Rwanda before all their legal appeals had been exhausted. The five EU countries, by contrast, say their arrangement would apply only to people whose asylum claims have already been rejected following the completion of legal proceedings.

Rwanda had already prepared reception facilities for the British program before it was canceled. During a visit to the capital, Kigali, in September, two European lawmakers were shown accommodation sites, including a hotel, that could now be used to house migrants transferred from EU countries.

Diplomatic sources told AFP that the initiative would begin as a small pilot program involving approximately 100 people, with each participating country sending around 20 rejected asylum seekers. Officials from the five governments insist that the arrangement will comply with EU regulations and international law.

Supporters say the goal is not mass deportation but deterrence. They argue that migrants may reconsider paying smugglers thousands of euros for perilous journeys to Europe if they know that even reaching EU territory will not necessarily allow them to remain there. Under the proposed system, people who lose their asylum cases could ultimately be transferred to Rwanda rather than returned to their countries of origin.

Human rights groups warn of serious consequences

The plan has drawn sharp criticism from organizations working with refugees and migrants, which question both its legality and the practical safeguards available to people transferred thousands of kilometers from Europe.

"What remedies are available to people if their rights are violated, and who will be held accountable?" asked Celine Mias of the Danish Refugee Council. "If responsibility lies with the EU member state, how would that work in practice?"

The Council of Europe, a separate pan-European organization responsible for promoting human rights, democracy and the rule of law, raised similar concerns in July. It warned that the establishment of return centers outside the EU carried a "significant risk of human rights violations."

Critics also dispute the central argument behind the initiative: that tougher enforcement will persuade people not to migrate. They say evidence that restrictive policies reduce migration over the long term remains limited, particularly when people are fleeing conflict, persecution or severe economic hardship.

"Enforcement measures change how people travel, not their decision to travel in the first place," said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a research organization that studies migration routes and patterns. He explained that migrants may delay their journeys or choose different routes, while smuggling networks adapt to new restrictions and raise their prices.

Why Rwanda is particularly controversial

Much of the opposition focuses on Rwanda itself. Kagame has received international recognition for his role in ending the country's 1994 genocide and overseeing its subsequent reconstruction. But after 26 years in power, he has also faced persistent allegations of authoritarian rule, political repression and efforts to silence opponents.

Clémentine de Montjoye, a senior Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch, said Rwanda has a well-documented record of repressing political opponents, arbitrary detention and mistreatment of detainees. She also pointed to allegations that Rwanda supports armed rebels in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo who have been accused of killings and sexual violence.

"Paying Kigali for a deportation scheme will not only cause suffering and harm to deportees, but will also finance a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad, while giving it political leverage," she warned.

For opponents of the plan, these concerns raise a fundamental question about whether European governments can guarantee the rights and safety of deportees once they are transferred to a country outside their jurisdiction. Supporters maintain that appropriate legal safeguards can be established, but critics argue that oversight and accountability may prove difficult in practice.

Illegal border crossings decline across Europe

The proposed deportation center comes as irregular migration into the European Union has fallen substantially compared with last year, although some routes have recently experienced renewed pressure.

According to Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, nearly 110,000 irregular border crossings were recorded during the first 10 months of 2026, a decline of 29% compared with the corresponding period in 2025.

In October, approximately 18,100 irregular crossings were detected, down 6% from October last year but 22% higher than in September. The monthly increase was largely attributed to a sharp rise in migrants arriving via the West African route to Spain's Canary Islands.

text:
Victory for Annunciation HouseAnnunciation House and FIEL Houston after the soon-to-be-former Texas attorney general gives up his fight to shutter their doors

It turns out some of the winners from this month’s historic midterm elections weren’t even on the ballot. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is leaving his position come January and was resoundingly trounced in the U.S. Senate race, announced that his office is dropping its baseless, politically-motivated lawsuits that targeted two non-profit organizations for their vital immigrant advocacy work.

The two organizations, EL Paso-based Annunciation House and FIEL Houston, are breathing a much-needed sigh of relief following the news, which came exactly a week after State Rep. James Talarico defeated Paxton to become Texas’ first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.

“It’s very gratifying that this has now ended. It’s over,” said Ruben Garcia, Executive Director of Annunciation House, which has historically worked to provide nutrition, water, temporary shelter, and other vital services to migrants who have already been processed and released by the federal government. “What I would want next is for the state Legislature to say, ‘We have to find a way to prevent this from happening,’” Garcia continued.

WITH LEGAL DISTRACTION OVER, TIME TO GET BACK TO WORK

Cesar Espinosa, Executive Director of immigrant-led civil rights organization FIEL Houston, expressed a desire to get back to focusing on the community’s needs without distractions. “This lawsuit has been very burdensome for us as an institution,” he said. “Now that this is over, we can return to committing 100% of our time and energy to protecting, educating, and empowering our community.”

That’s precisely why Paxton abused his power to target them. Despite the fact that Annunciation House has years of partnering with the federal government under its belt, Paxton sued the faith-based organization in 2024, baselessly accusing staffers and volunteers of facilitating human smuggling. Paxton’s claims and despicable effort to revoke its registration drew condemnation from Catholic bishops and more than 150 organizations.

“The Annunciation House has accompanied migrants for nearly 50 years, partnering with local and federal law enforcement and the U.S. Border Patrol,” the California Catholic Conference of Bishops Executive Committee said at the time. “For the AG to claim the nonprofit is responsible for ‘worsening illegal immigration’ shows a lack of fundamental understanding of the gravity of immigration as a humanitarian concern and unjustly attacks a long-standing partner in relief efforts.”

Later that year, a sound-minded judge blocked Paxton’s political stunt, finding that his office violated the organization’s religious freedoms and used a records request as an excuse to go after humanitarian workers and vulnerable migrants.

IT WAS ALWAYS A POLITICAL STUNT

“The record before this Court makes clear that the Texas Attorney General’s use of the request to examine documents from Annunciation House was a pretext to justify its harassment of Annunciation House employees and the persons seeking refuge,” 205th District Judge Francisco Dominguez wrote in his decision. “In fact, the record before the Court now establishes that the Attorney General was seeking evidence of alleged criminal activity all along. This is outrageous and intolerable.”

Paxton’s attacks on FIEL Houston were similarly outrageous and intolerable. That same year, Paxton accused the group of violating federal regulations by speaking out about immigration policies that affect families in the state. But like in the case of Annunciation House, Paxton’s lawsuit was not about rule of law, but instead about shutting them down. The lawsuit was “the first to target a group far from the border and the first to target what is essentially political speech,” The Texas Tribune reported at the time.

FIEL Houston had an initial victory in court that summer, when a judge rejected Paxton’s demand to close the organization. “Harris County Attorney Christian Menefee Aug. 20 filed a written argument in support of the organization, asserting Paxton misused his power,” Houston Public Media reported. “It’s clear that the Attorney General is overstepping his role by singling out organizations like FIEL that advocate for immigrants and their families,” Menefee said. “Lawsuits like this not only undermine the hard work of organizations that provide critical resources to immigrants but also perpetuate a climate of fear and division.”

However, later that year, an appeals court cleared the way for Paxton’s office to continue hounding FIEL Houston over its work. Paxton gloated over the ruling, attacking the community-led organization as “Anti-American” and continuing to accuse it of “flagrantly violating our laws.”

Those are some big claims coming from someone who faced securities fraud charges, was impeached by the Republican-led Texas House over allegations of misconduct that included bribery and abuse of office, once stole a fancy pen like some office supply closet thief, and has been slammed as the “most corrupt politician in Texas.”

NON-PROFITS EVERYWHERE OVERCOME ABUSE OF POWER

Had Paxton’s lawsuit against FIEL Houston succeeded, the legal precedent could have sent “a chill through every nonprofit in the state,” the American Immigration Council noted in 2024.

“History will remember who was on the right side and on the wrong side of it,” Espinosa said about FIEL Houston’s victory over Paxton. “Today proves once again that we continue to be on the right side of history.” Thomas Saenz, MALDEF President and General Counsel, said that the dismissal notice “brings an early end to one of Paxton’s many shady litigation tactics; this case epitomized Paxton’s overt politicization of his office. Targeting immigrant-serving organizations was biased, improper, and cruel, demonstrating an overarching interest in serving Paxton’s political masters rather than the Texas public.”

Paxton abused his office and power by throwing the full weight of the state against vulnerable groups. Now he goes out with a whimper.

This week’s Judicial Notice is sponsored by

Welcome to all—especially my many new subscribers. You’re reading the latest edition of Judicial Notice (JN), my weekly legal news roundup.

If you’re a free subscriber, you’ll receive much of JN (just as you’ll receive most of what I write here at Original Jurisdiction). If you’re a paid subscriber, you’ll receive the complete version of JN—which this week includes an update on Cahill Gordon & Reindel, under Law Firm of the Week. If you’re reading this post as an email and it gets cut off at some point (which happens most commonly in Gmail), simply click “view entire message” to read the whole thing.

Zach and I spent last weekend in Washington, D.C., where we attended the Federalist Society’s 2026 National Lawyers Convention. It was, as always, an excellent opportunity for me to catch up with my readers and sources on the right side of the aisle—and for Zach to connect with some of the columnists he edits for SCOTUSblog, an ideologically diverse group—and to take the pulse of conservative and libertarian lawyers after Republican losses in the recent midterm elections. For two insightful write-ups on the overall mood or vibe at the conference, see the pieces by Joan Biskupic in CNN and Jacqueline Thomsen in Bloomberg Law—which capture both the disappointment felt by some attendees over the election results and the possibility that those results could present an opportunity to move on from Donald Trump.

In addition to a brief personal update, I try to offer a practical pointer in each installment of JN. This week, I’ll repeat some advice I’ve previously offered in the fourth quarter: As the year draws to a close, it’s time for financial housekeeping. Have you maxed out your 401(k)? Have you contributed to your child’s 529? Are there capital gains or losses you want to realize before the year’s end? And if you end up with extra cash and need to park it somewhere that’s FDIC-insured, sign up for Wealthfront using my referral code, which will give us both a 4.30% interest rate for the next three months (an offer several of you have taken me up on in the past).

Now, on to the news.

Lawyers of the Week: Joon Kim, Melinda Haag, Walter Brown, and other attorneys involved in the Jensen Huang affair(s).

There was no shortage of crazy news last week. On Thursday, we experienced the Microsoft Outlook outage—which hit Biglaw hard. On Friday, air travelers suffered through a nationwide ground stop. These events could eventually lead to litigation; the Outlook outage reminded me of the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which gave rise to (still ongoing) litigation filed by Delta Air Lines against CrowdStrike.

For now, though, the general news story from last week with the most implications for lawyers and the legal industry is the abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of NVIDIA, the AI chipmaking giant and one of the world’s most valuable companies. Huang, 63, resigned from the top job at NVIDIA, which he co-founded in 1993, amid allegations of two extramarital affairs: one with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based data company (and a possible Chinese spy or intelligence asset), and another with Kimberly Powell, a senior executive at NVIDIA.

The situation remains fluid—and Huang might even end up returning as CEO, as reported by The Financial Times. How things ultimately shake out could depend in part on the actions taken by the many lawyers involved in L’Affaire Huang:

On Sunday, November 8, the NVIDIA board announced that it was commissioning an independent investigation, “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The investigation will be overseen by a committee of independent directors advised by Joon Kim and his law firm, Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz, as first reported by The New York Times. A former acting U.S. attorney (S.D.N.Y.) turned Chambers Band 1 white-collar defense attorney, Kim is relatively new to Wachtell, having joined the firm from Cleary Gottlieb earlier this fall.

And who’s representing Jensen Huang? As one of the 20 wealthiest people in the world, worth somewhere between $136 billion (Bloomberg) and $142 billion (Forbes), he can afford some of Biglaw’s best: former U.S. attorney Melinda Haag (N.D. Cal.) and former assistant U.S. attorney Walter Brown (C.D. Cal.), both with the San Francisco office of Paul Weiss. They’re both Chambers-ranked for white-collar defense in California, with Melinda Haag as a Star Individual and Walt Brown in Band 1.

On Monday, November 9, the first trading day after NVIDIA’s board announced its investigation, the company’s stock dropped 4%; by the end of the week, it was down more than 12%. So not surprisingly, given these sizable dips in share price, “The race is on to sue NVIDIA,” as a headline in TechCrunch put it. Here are some early entrants, based on coverage by Law360:

On November 9, Laurence Rosen of The Rosen Law Firm PA filed Kistenmacher v. Nvidia Corp. (N.D. Cal.), a proposed class action against the company and Jensen Huang, alleging that they misled investors regarding national-security concerns and risks to NVIDIA’s reputation arising out of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

On November 11, three lawyers—Olimpio Lee Squitieri of Squitieri & Fearon LLP, Fletcher Moore of Moore Law PLLC, and Kristopher Diulio of The Diulio Firm PC—filed Vanegas v. Huang (N.D. Cal.). A derivative lawsuit against NVIDIA’s board of directors and executive leadership, Vanegas alleges that the defendants earned $2 billion in insider trades while ignoring warning signs about Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

And additional plaintiffs’ firms, including Schall Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, could get involved, per TechCrunch. So stay tuned.

[UPDATE (11:42 a.m.): For additional discussion of NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, and the role of lawyers, see Vivia Chen’s latest Substack post, Did the Lawyers in the Jensen Huang Scandal Screw Up?]

Other lawyers in the news:

In case you missed the update appended to last week’s Judicial Notice, District Attorney Scott Colom (D-Miss.) won the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi. And in case you’re wondering, it’s pronounced kuh-LOAM, basically rhyming with “cologne.” (Yes, Senator-elect Colom will be in my lawyer and judge pronunciation guide—feel free to nominate someone for inclusion.)

In my latest podcast episode—a (delightful) conversation with Alyssa DaCunha, co-chair of the congressional investigations practice at WilmerHale—we discussed the aggressive oversight the Trump administration should expect from the new Democratic majorities in Congress next year. Firing a shot across the Democrats’ bow, White House Counsel Will Scharf sent a three-page letter to Representative Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), chair of the House Oversight Committee, in which Scharf declared that “process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.” But as Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the Cato Institute, told CBS News, “I think it’s incredibly unlikely that any court would find merit in any criminal charge against a member of Congress for their vote on issuing a subpoena.” (While criminal prosecutions of members of Congress are far-fetched, lower courts and ultimately SCOTUS could stymie investigations by ruling in the Trump administration’s favor on issues such as executive privilege, as discussed by Adam Liptak in The Docket.)

Meanwhile, over at the U.S. Department of Justice, things aren’t going so great for Attorney General Todd Blanche and his shrinking coterie of top advisers.

Last Thursday, the Trump administration sent to the Senate a bipartisan slate of nominees to serve as members of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or commissioners of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC):

For the SEC: Kristin Johnson (Democrat), a GW Law professor who served as a ​CFTC commissioner during the Biden administration, and Steven Levine ​(Republican), former general counsel to the Council of Economic Advisers.

For the CFTC: Matthew Rowland (Democrat), a senior assistant general counsel, and Nathan Anonick (Republican), counsel for the U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry.

Poor Alina Habba: Concord Partners—the family company controlled by a Venezuelan billionaire who received a presidential pardon from Trump, a few weeks after Concord gave Habba a $50 million employment contract—canceled the contract, in the wake of controversy (and criticism from Trump himself). But Habba gets to keep $6.5 million that was already paid to her, as well as an $8 million signing bonus (because we live in a just universe).

Back in January, Richard Rollo of Richards Layton & Finger, one of Delaware’s top corporate-law firms, filed a brief containing AI hallucinations in Delaware Chancery Court. Last Friday, the court sanctioned Rollo, to the tune of $2,500.

In memoriam:

Michael Ward Stout, a leading art lawyer who represented clients such as Robert Mapplethorpe and Salvador Dalí, passed away at 83.

Gail Bopp Agrawal—who clerked for the late Justice O’Connor before entering academia, where she served as the dean of both the University of Kansas Law School and the University of Iowa College of Law—passed away at 75 after being diagnosed with bulbar ALS.

David Corwin James, a longtime assistant U.S. attorney (E.D.N.Y.) who focused his practice on appeals, passed away at 71 after battling Parkinson’s disease.

Christopher W. Schwarz, a 2024 graduate of Catholic Law and associate at Hartel DeSantis & Murray, passed away at 31 after a long illness.

May they rest in peace.

Judge of the Week: Judge Richard Posner.

On a handful of occasions over the history of Original Jurisdiction (which turns six next month), I have posthumously recognized a Lawyer or Judge of the Week. And if anyone deserves this honor, it is Judge Richard Posner (7th Cir.), who passed away on November 10. A brilliant and prolific jurist and scholar, Posner was “a towering figure in the law,” to quote Adam Liptak’s obituary that ran on the front page of The New York Times. (A friend and I tried to think of another lower-court judge who was the subject of an obituary that ran on page A1 of The Times, but we came up empty; if you can think of one, please drop the link in the comments.) [UPDATE (10:50 a.m.): As pointed out by Liptak in the comments, Judge Learned Hand (2d Cir.) has a front-page Times obituary—back in 1961.]

As I mentioned on LinkedIn and Twitter, I was honored to call Judge Posner—or Dick Posner, as he asked to be called—a friend. So I will actually be writing a separate post about him—because I can’t do justice to him here, and I put special care and thought into my obituaries (which I like to think represent some of my better writing).

So keep an eye out for that. In the meantime, you can read some of the many obituaries and tributes to Judge Posner, which Howard Bashman has been collecting at How Appealing. Or you can listen to an event that Posner and I did together back in February 2008: “Judges as Public Figures,” a conversation hosted by the U. Chicago FedSoc and moderated by Professor Lior Strahilevitz. As you can tell from all the laughter on the recording, Posner was not only brilliant but hilarious. Dick Posner, RIP.

In other news about judges and the judiciary:

Much ado about a golf course: DC Preservation League v. Department of Interior, the drama pitting the Trump DOJ against Judge Ana Reyes (D.D.C.), is far from over. Last Friday, in a hearing that lasted almost six hours, Judge Reyes made clear that she intends to get to the bottom of whether government lawyers made misrepresentations to the court about the Trump administration’s plans for the East Potomac Golf Links. Then on Saturday, Judge Reyes temporarily blocked the administration from closing the property so that it can be transformed into the championship-level golf course touted by Trump himself on social media.

Last Tuesday, in an 87-page decision, the California Commission on Judicial Performance ordered the removal of Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper, 84. As reported by The New York Post—and you know it’s going to be bad when an L.A. judge is getting covered by a Manhattan tabloid—the allegations against Judge Draper “included making sexually explicit comments to female attorneys, directing racially charged remarks at others, and improperly sharing confidential records containing nude images of minors—as well as a nude photograph of himself” (thankfully taken from behind, so no full frontal).

In nominations news:

The Senate confirmed Alabama Supreme Court Justice Gregory Cook to serve on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama.

Donald Trump publicly announced three judicial nominees whose paperwork had been previously sent over to the Senate Judiciary Committee: T. Elliot Gaiser (N.D. Tex.), assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel; Justice James Sullivan (W.D. Tex.), who lost his reelection bid to remain on the Texas Supreme Court; and William Grayson Lambert (D.S.C.), chief legal counsel to Governor Henry McMaster (R-S.C.).

Working with the White House, Republican senators are hoping to confirm around 25 judicial nominees, including four circuit-court picks, during the current lame-duck session, before Senate control switches in January. But the process hasn’t been going very smoothly, thanks to… Republican senators.

Last Tuesday, the Trump administration withdrew the Eighth Circuit nomination of Judge Lee Rudofsky (E.D. Ark.), then nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland in his place. What explains this strange sequence of events? For the backstory, involving disagreement between the White House and the two (Republican) Arkansas senators—Senators John Boozman and Tom Cotton, but mainly Senator Boozman—see Professor Josh Blackman at The Volokh Conspiracy and Patrick McNeil at Nomination Notes.

Finally, Senator Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.) appears to be causing problems for the nomination of Zach West (E.D. Okla.), a lawyer in the Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office. For the details on that, see Michael Fragoso in National Review.

text:
A federal lawsuit filed by a Chelsea mother has raised concerns about the operations of federal immigration enforcement and the constitutional protections afforded to immigrant communities throughout Massachusetts.

The lawsuit was filed Oct. 28 by Hilda Ramirez Sanan, a permanent lawful resident. She describes how Immigration and Customs Enforcement violently removed her from her vehicle, shattering its windows, then pushed her against a chain-link fence before kicking her and twisting her arms in Sept. 2025. She then claims being forced to the ground face-first when she briefly lost consciousness, all in front of her two children, including her then 13-year-old autistic son.

Ramirez Sanan alleges approximately eight armed and masked federal agents surrounded her vehicle while the family accompanied a relative to a court hearing. She also claimed her son was pulled from the vehicle and questioned about his immigration status. The family filed that the incident resulted in physical injuries and emotional distress.

The encounter with federal law enforcement only concluded in a release after Chelsea police intervened and called for ICE to verify Ramirez Sanan’s identification. She has since then declared her rights under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments, corresponding to unlawful search and seizure and due process respectively, were violated. These declarations have not yet been formally adjudicated in court.

Associate Professor of Political Science, Luis Jiménez of UMass Boston, states that although the Fourth Amendment offers protection for everyone against unreasonable searches, those protections are not being consistently respected and applied under the Trump administration.

“In reality, ICE has been racially profiling and then making up their probable cause for suspicion,” Jiménez said.

He explained the decent number of significant obstacles immigrants face when they attempt to challenge their detention under the Fifth Amendment.

“ICE has been deliberately making this more difficult because they hide information from lawyers and communities. Sometimes they will deport people even before their loved ones know where they are,” he said.

ICE has argued against the family’s account of the events and declared that officers used appropriate force. An ICE spokesperson told GBH reporters that agents were conducting a vehicle stop, aiming to arrest a family member with an alleged criminal charge. The family’s attorneys, Zimmer, Citron & Clarke LLP and Lawyers for Civil Rights, have challenged the agency’s recall of the incident.

According to WBUR, ICE removed 1,833 people apprehended in Massachusetts from Sept. 2025 through early Aug. 2026. This included about 200 minors and concluding to nearly six removals a day. 301 people out of the 1,833 deported had previous criminal convictions.

For those connected or belonging to immigrant communities in Greater Boston, questions surrounding legal protections extend beyond Chelsea’s District Courthouse and to the city itself. Federal immigration law provides more protections against removal for permanent lawful residents like Ramirez Sanan, but certain convictions offer legal grounds for deportation.

“The government cannot just deport people on a whim,” declared Jiménez. “But again, in practice, it’s difficult to give protection if lawyers do not know where their client is.”

Questions regarding courthouse protections have increased significantly in light of similar cases to Ramirez Sanan’s. The PROTECT Act, signed into effect Aug. 5, 2026, establishes judicial authorization requirements for immigration arrests inside a courthouse. Civil arrests are forbidden inside courtrooms as well as on certain surrounding courthouse grounds. Jiménez, however, clarifies that being near a courthouse does not provide people with automatic protections from ICE arrests.

“Near is none. A public sidewalk is just like anywhere else, but Massachusetts is a sanctuary state,” said Jiménez, “That means that the police are not supposed to cooperate with ICE.”

Massachusetts laws restrict police from both assisting federal immigration enforcement and their ability to prevent ICE from carrying out its federal operations. Jiménez continued, questioning the effectiveness of federal accountability and identifying federal courts as an important pathway for challenging alleged misconduct.

The allegations against ICE remain subject to review in court as the lawsuit proceeds.

text:
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon due to a communications issue affecting air traffic control centers across the country, disrupting thousands of flights. MPR News host Catharine Richert was on a plane at Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport when the pilot told her flight the ground stop was enacted and “I really don’t know what to do here. Never seen this before.” The U.S. Homeland Security secretary said on Friday afternoon there were no signs this was “a nefarious attack against us. It is just a telecommunication outage.” Check mprnews.org for updates. Video captured by Catharine Richert and edited by Anne Guttridge.

A mural titled “The Procession of St. Paul” stretches over 500 feet across Mounds Boulevard in east St. Paul. It features vibrant imagery of animals marching south towards Wakaŋ Tipi, a 27-acre sacred site formerly known as Bruce Vento Nature Sanctuary. Artist Bobby Wilson designed the mural, and local artists helped paint it. He is a citizen of the Sisseton Wahpeton Dakota in North Dakota, and is known for his role as a writer and producer for TV shows including “Reservation Dogs,” “Rutherford Falls” and “Echo.” Wilson was raised in east St. Paul and lived in the Twin Cities metro area for much of his life. He now lives in Arizona. “The idea behind the procession is the people of this land, the first people and the next and the next, all walking on the same path towards my ancestral burial mounds up on Mounds Park,” he said. Wilson represented the cultural diversity of the area through animals such as an elephant, a bison and a beaver. He says each animal has different cultural connections depending on the community. Story, video and thumbnail by Chandra Colvin

On Election Day, Twin Cities voters made another stop after the polls: The memorials for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, so they could leave their “I Voted” stickers. Some voters told MPR News they were voting on Pretti and Good’s behalf. “I just want this nightmare to end for our city and for our country,” Minneapolis resident Peg Ihinger said. “And damn it, they shouldn’t have died. None of them should have died.” In the days since, those voters have been joined by dozens from outside of Minnesota mailing in their stickers to be placed on the Pretti memorial on Nicollet Avenue. Teresa Fox, who owns Glam Doll Donuts across the street from the memorial, told MPR News she’s been working with caretakers to field submissions. Memorial caretaker Julia Lopez-Kaley told MPR News, “To see people come and lay down a piece of what they’ve been able to do, an action they’ve been able to take in honor of and in remembrance of Alex, has been life-sustaining.” Story and video capture by Winter Keefer. Video edited by Payton Whaley.

Spring Lake Park’s mayoral election came down to a film canister pulled from a bag Monday night. That’s because the small north metro city’s mayoral race ended in a draw between incumbent Robert Nelson and challenger Halyn Roth — each candidate received exactly 1,401 votes. Under Minnesota law, a city’s canvassing board must break an election tie by drawing lots. Story and video capture by Ahmed Hassan Video edited by Anne Guttridge Thumbnail photo by Jackson Forderer for MPR News

Neighborhood groups in south Minneapolis threw an outdoor party Nov. 8 to celebrate the long-awaited reopening of Nicollet Avenue near Lake Street. Around 100 people strolled back and forth across the bridge over the Midtown Greenway bike and pedestrian path to the site of the former derelict Kmart that divided Nicollet. Barring last-minute construction or weather delays, Minneapolis plans to officially reopen the street to traffic on Nov. 24 for the first time since the city plopped the Kmart and parking lot on the site nearly 50 years ago. Story by Alanna Elder Video by Feven Gerezgiher and Anne Guttridge

A petition to allow Minnesotans to choose their voter sticker designs launched this week. The petition, created by local content creator Olivia Iverson, gained almost 1,000 signatures from its launch on Wednesday to Friday evening. Petition signers agree, saying voting deserves to look cool and express Minnesotan creativity. Story by Ava Grace Video by Anne Guttridge

Hortman advocated for the buildout and helped secure financing for the highway that connects Interstate 94, County Road 81 and County Road 130 to U.S. Route 10. The unveiling follows a vote by lawmakers to designate the highway in the north metro in memory of the Hortmans. The couple was assassinated at their Brooklyn Park home in 2025. Gov. Tim Walz and Hortman family members, including the couple’s daughter Sophie and son Colin, unveiled the placement signs in Brooklyn Park. Also in attendance was state Sen. John Hoffman, who survived an assassination attempt the same June 2025 night. Story by Dana Ferguson Video captured by Dana Ferguson and edited by Anne Guttridge

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border.

One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims.

A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision.

The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months.

This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.

The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border.

The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court late last week agreed to take on a case central to the Trump administration's immigration agenda concerning the conditions under which migrants can request asylum.

While the announcement ended up being buried in a Friday afternoon news cycle that saw the unforeseen ground stop of U.S. air travel, it means that the top court will now hear at least three major immigration-related cases in its session that runs through June 2027.

The Trump administration's "retinterpretation of certain detention and deportation policies" has led to a "particularly high number of immigration disputes" compared to previous sessions," according to SCOTUSblog, which tracks the work of the top court. The blog, in an October post, also highlighted a handful of other cases that, while narrower in scope in terms of their ramifications, could also be described as immigration-related.

The top court in the 2025-2026 session rejected a Trump administration bid to end birthright citizenship going forward, but it made an impactful ruling that has paved the way for the federal government to deport large numbers of Haitian Americans and other residents who have been in the U.S. for years after fleeing natural disasters or turmoil in their home countries.

Overall, these new cases could lead to Supreme Court rulings that further reshape the American immigration and asylum system, or at least provide clarity in response to actions, some very controversial, that have been undertaken by President Donald Trump's second administration.

Here is a look at the three major cases, so far, of the 2026-2027 docket:

Executive authority to limit asylum

Generally speaking, U.S. laws have recognized through the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and other legislation the rights of migrants to make an asylum claim when arriving at a border entry point, or even if they are caught trying to cross into the country between entry points. In most years, denials have been greater than asylum claims being granted, though the percentage has fluctuated.

In his final year in office, former president Joe Biden sought to stem the tide of surging arrivals at the southern border and encourage appointment-based claims with what was described as an executive order meant to be temporary, which limited asylum eligibility based on the daily number of encounters at the border.

On the very first day of his second presidential term in 2025, Trump signed an executive order deemed necessary due to an "invasion" at the southern border.

Trump's order has essentially amounted to a blanket asylum ban for migrants caught crossing between border points. The prohibition has also applied to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.

It was blocked first by a federal judge and then in April by the U.S. Court of Appeals in D.C. The panel ruled 2-1 that the INA doesn't "allow the president to remove [migrants] under summary removal procedures of his own making."

In a partial dissent, Judge Justin Walker wrote that the administration can broadly deny asylum applications, but that the INA and other laws forbid sending people back to countries where they would be persecuted.

Whether that has been practised in the asylum claims the government does consider is arguable. Denial rates in some cases have climbed to over 90 per cent, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. Denial rates that high have not been seen for decades, if ever.

Democratic House Rep. Rob Menendez of New Jersey, posting Friday after it was learned the Supreme Court would take on the case, said "fixing our broken immigration system means upholding our values as a nation of immigrants" while "protecting the right to seek asylum."

Third-country deportations

The Supreme Court justices will gather to hear oral arguments on Dec. 9 regarding a controversial plank of the Trump administration's deportation policies, also related to executive orders the president signed on his first day back in the Oval Office in 2025.

The U.S. traditionally has followed a principle of non-refoulement. That is, not returning persons to countries where it could be reasonably expected they'd face persecution or torture due to race, religion, sexuality, political views or other factors.

Flowing through the Trump executive orders, however, the administration has sought workarounds through third-country deportations. According to a website run by two human rights organizations, the Trump administration has spent more than $95 million US to deport over 28,000 people to 31 different countries and has struck agreements to potentially send people to four additional countries.

In many cases, people are being sent to countries to which they have no connection. In addition, some of the countries that have struck agreements with the U.S. have had questionable track records in terms of upholding human rights and freedoms.

"These migrants are being transferred to countries or territories with which they have no ties, which can be a traumatizing and isolating experience that compounds harms already suffered which triggered their fleeing to the U.S. in the first place," the UN's Human Rights Council said in a statement earlier this year condemning the practice.

The administration has said that it has struck deals with foreign governments where the safety of the deportees has been assured. But the New York Times reported last week after an extensive investigation that it had it identified 110 persons who were deported to a third country but then put on a plane back to their home country of origin, even after U.S. courts had established they had reasonable fears in leaving those countries to seek asylum.

LISTEN | Amy Fischer, director for Refugee and Migrant Rights at Amnesty International USA:

Access to bond hearings

Under past administrations, most non-citizens without a criminal record who were arrested away from border points had an opportunity to request a bond hearing. In many cases, that allowed them to work and remain free while their cases, which would ultimately determine if they would be deported, wound their through immigration court.

The Trump administration has ended that practice, citing an interpretation of existing 1996 legislation. After conflicting rulings in federal courts across the U.S., the Supreme Court will take up the issue after the American Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit on behalf of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha.

The Brazilian man entered the U.S. without authorization two decades ago and, according to his lawyers, has never been charged or convicted of a crime. Nevertheless, after federal immigration agents detained him on his way to work in September 2025, an immigration judge subsequently denied him a bond hearing.

According to the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, the number of detention beds for people arrested within the U.S. has more than quadrupled in the past two years, meaning the stakes for this case are considerable.

As with the asylum case just announced Friday, no date has been set yet for oral arguments.

text:
Today, a federal district court vacated the Department of Homeland Security regulation that sought to subject F, J, and I nonimmigrants to fixed periods of admission. Judge Dennis Saylor of the federal district court for the district of Massachusetts granted the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment and struck down the regulation, finding that the regulation exceeded DHS’s authority and was inconsistent with Congress’s intent in creating the affected visa programs. The case is Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al., 1:26-cv-13799 (D. Mass., filed Aug. 18, 2026).

In August, a coalition of educational organizations and unions – including NAFSA, the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the American Federation of Teachers, and the UAW – filed a lawsuit in the federal district court of Massachusetts, alleging that the regulation that sought to replace duration-of-status admissions with fixed admission periods for F-1 foreign students, J-1 exchange visitors, I representatives of foreign information media, and their dependents violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). In September, the court temporarily postponed the effective date of the rule while the litigation proceeded.

The Trump Administration is expected to appeal the ruling.

authors: Amina Ismail and Francois Murphy, Amina Ismail, Francois Murphy
description:
BRUSSELS/VIENNA ― Five European countries are set to announce plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, two sources familiar with the plans said.
With elections approaching in several EU countries and anti-immigration sentiment widespread, governments are under pressure to show they can control migration.
Deportation hubs offer a highly visible demonstration of that resolve, analysts say.
The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.
During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain's abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.
text:
BRUSSELS/VIENNA ― Five European countries are set to announce plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, two sources familiar with the plans said.

Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said in September they were working towards a deal with a non-EU country to host so-called return hubs, part of a broader European push to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.

The deal, expected to be announced in Vienna, follows the approval of the EU's new Returns Regulation, which seeks to speed up deportations and allows member states to establish return hubs outside the block.

With elections approaching in several EU countries and anti-immigration sentiment widespread, governments are under pressure to show they can control migration. Deportation hubs offer a highly visible demonstration of that resolve, analysts say.

The scheme differs from Britain's abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.

Accountability questions

Leaders from the five countries have repeatedly said their plans would comply with EU and international law, but rights advocates have questioned whether migrants' rights could be violated if they are transferred to a country they have no connection to.

"What recourse do people have if their rights are violated and who is accountable?" said Céline Mias, EU director at the Danish Refugee Council. "If responsibility rests with the European member state, how would that work in practice?"

The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."

European officials backing the hubs say the policy's main purpose is deterrence rather than large-scale removals.

They argue that the prospect of paying smugglers thousands of euros for a dangerous journey to Europe, only to be sent to a third country, could dissuade some migrants from making the trip.

Critics, however, say there is little evidence that tougher enforcement measures and deportation schemes reduce migration over the long term.

“Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or change route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices,” said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a research institute that collects data along migration routes.

A willing host

Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants that Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its human rights record.

President Paul Kagame has won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda's 1994 genocide and rebuilding the country into a destination for investment and aid.

Critics, however, accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo, which rights groups say has committed killings, rapes and other abuses.

Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.

Freedom House rates it "Not Free" and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.

The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.

Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country's Supreme Court 2023. Kigali sought a 50 million pound ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.

During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain's abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.

description:
The Netherlands and four other European Union countries are preparing to establish a deportation center in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers.

The plan follows changes to European migration rules introduced in June, which expanded the legal options for transferring rejected asylum seekers to countries outside the European Union.
