text:
The Netherlands and four other European Union countries are preparing to establish a deportation center in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers. The proposed facility would house migrants who cannot be returned to their home countries. The plan is expected to be formally announced at a meeting in Vienna on November 16.

The proposed facility would allow European governments to transfer rejected asylum seekers to a third country while arrangements are made for their eventual return home. Migrants would not need to have any previous connection to Rwanda.

The agreement is expected to be formally announced at a migration conference in Vienna on November 16, according to sources cited by RTL. Germany, Austria, Denmark and Greece are joining the Netherlands in the initiative after months of discussions about establishing deportation facilities beyond European borders.

Rwanda is the first country selected for the proposed arrangement. One possible location is the Hope Hostel in Rwanda’s capital, Kigali. The facility was originally developed under a British agreement to accommodate migrants deported from the United Kingdom. The agreement collapsed following legal challenges, and Britain’s new government abandoned the plan in 2024.

The plan follows changes to European migration rules introduced in June, which expanded the legal options for transferring rejected asylum seekers to countries outside the European Union. However, the legality of the arrangements has yet to be tested in court.

The previously mentioned Hope Hostel now stands empty and has space for about 100 people. Its facilities include shared bedrooms, communal washing areas, a dining hall, gardens and sports fields. A nearby residential development, also financed by Britain, could provide accommodation for hundreds more.

Rwanda already accommodates refugees from neighboring Congo and other countries. It also works with the United Nations and the African Union to receive migrants evacuated from detention centers in Libya. Dutch Asylum Minister Bart van den Brink has also backed the concept but has been more cautious about setting a timetable or specifying how many people could be transferred.

The proposal is included in the Dutch governing coalition agreement, which commits the government to pursuing reception facilities for rejected asylum seekers outside the European Union. In February, the Tweede Kamer adopted a motion introduced by the JA21 party calling for a concrete plan within six months.

The financial terms of the Rwanda agreement have not been settled. Rwanda is expected to seek economic compensation for hosting the migrants, but the participating countries have not disclosed how much the arrangement could cost.

The financial implications are a particular concern because only a relatively small number of asylum seekers are expected to be transferred initially. Britain previously paid Rwanda hundreds of millions of pounds under its abandoned deportation agreement. The two countries have since disputed the payments, with Rwanda refusing to return the money.

The proposal has exposed some differences within the Dutch governing coalition. The conservative VVD and Christian Democratic CDA support the plan, while the centrist D66 party has raised serious objections. D66 considers Rwanda, as well as Uganda, an unsuitable destination for transferred migrants.

Human rights organizations and refugee advocacy groups have opposed the use of third countries to accommodate rejected asylum seekers. They argue that transferring migrants to countries outside Europe could expose them to inadequate protections and make independent monitoring more difficult.

The Dutch Council for Refugees has criticized the proposal, citing concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record. “One of the primary reasons for our opposition is our serious concern regarding the human rights situation in Rwanda,” said Sjoerd Warmerdam, the organization’s director.

“Independent human rights monitoring is virtually impossible in Rwanda. Furthermore, the Dutch Immigration and Naturalization Service (IND) has itself concluded that Rwanda cannot be classified as a safe third country. The United Kingdom previously attempted to negotiate an agreement with Rwanda, but that arrangement was rightfully rejected because of concerns surrounding the country’s human rights record.”

The European coalition is also considering similar arrangements with Kenya, Uzbekistan, Ghana and Uganda. The Netherlands previously held discussions with Uganda about establishing a return hub but suspended its participation in those talks.

text:
The Briefing

On November 13, 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Mullin v. RAICES, a challenge to President Trump's January 2025 proclamation that eliminated asylum access at the entire southern border — including at official ports of entry.

Both a D.C. federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit have already ruled the proclamation unlawful, but the ban has remained in effect while the case works its way to the justices.

A final ruling is expected before the Court closes its term in June 2027; the decision will settle whether an executive proclamation can override a congressional statute specifically designed to protect people fleeing persecution.

A presidential order that has shut people out of the asylum system at the southern border for nearly two years is now on its way to the highest court in the country. On November 13, 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to review the Trump administration's asylum restrictions in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services — widely known as Mullin v. RAICES. The justices will decide whether a sitting president can use an executive proclamation to override a statute that Congress wrote specifically to give people fleeing persecution the right to request protection on American soil.

A Proclamation That Left No Door Open

On the first day of his second term, President Trump signed Proclamation 10888, declaring an "invasion" along the southern border and suspending asylum access for everyone crossing there — including those who approached official ports of entry. That last detail set the order apart from previous Trump-era restrictions: unlike earlier policies, this one left no legal pathway to asylum whatsoever, closing even the door that had traditionally remained open at official checkpoints.

The legal scaffolding for the proclamation rested primarily on Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which authorizes a president to suspend the entry of noncitizens when deemed in the national interest. The administration added the "invasion" framing to invoke what it argued were additional emergency powers under both the Constitution and the statute.

The legal problem, as courts below identified it: Congress separately enacted INA § 208, which explicitly grants any person physically present in the United States — regardless of how they arrived — the right to apply for asylum. No executive proclamation, however sweeping, can override a congressional statute that was written to function as an unconditional floor of protection.

Two Courts Said No — Yet the Ban Kept Running

The federal district court in Washington, D.C. ruled the proclamation unlawful, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld that ruling in April 2026. Even so, the appellate panel paused its own decision to allow the Supreme Court to weigh in — meaning the ban has remained operational throughout, permitting the rapid removal of people who crossed the border without authorization.

The plaintiffs in the case include 13 individuals who fled countries including Afghanistan, as well as three nonprofits that provide legal services to migrants at the border: RAICES, the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, and Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center. Some of the individual plaintiffs were deported to third countries and then pushed back to the very nations they had originally fled; others endured extended detention without meaningful access to legal proceedings.

The Two Questions the Justices Will Answer

The Supreme Court narrowed its grant of review to two specific legal questions. The first asks whether the proclamation and related Department of Homeland Security guidance lawfully bar both asylum claims and withholding-of-removal claims. The second involves a procedural question about scope: whether a provision of federal immigration law, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), prohibited the lower court from extending its relief to an entire class of migrants rather than adjudicating each case individually.

The stakes of the first question could not be higher. A ruling in the administration's favor would validate the use of a presidential proclamation to override a federal statute — a legal tool that future administrations of either party could then deploy against any congressionally protected right. A ruling for the plaintiffs would reaffirm that Congress, not the White House, sets the floor for who may seek safety in the United States.

"Our system of checks and balances exists for moments precisely like this — to ensure no single branch can consolidate power at will," said Faisal Al-Juburi, co-chief executive officer of RAICES.

A Supreme Court Term Defined by Immigration

Mullin v. RAICES does not stand alone on the Court's docket. This term has shaped up as one of the most consequential for immigration law in decades, with the justices having accepted review in a cluster of related cases since late spring.

One companion case involves the administration's practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders — a third-country removal policy the Court has repeatedly allowed to continue while litigation plays out. That case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., was scheduled for oral argument in December and centers on whether migrants have the right to contest a deportation destination before being removed to a country where they have no ties.

The other, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, concerns the government's policy of holding immigrants in mandatory detention without access to bond hearings, regardless of how long a person has lived in the United States or how deep their community ties run. In July 2025, the Department of Homeland Security issued guidance declaring that immigrants who entered the country without inspection are subject to mandatory detention for the entire duration of their removal proceedings — a sharp break from nearly three decades of established practice.

Together, these three cases form an interlocking framework: Can the president eliminate asylum at the border? Can those already living in the country be held indefinitely without a hearing? Can they be deported to countries they never identified as home? The answers — arriving from a Court with a 6-3 conservative majority — will define the rights of millions of immigrants, disproportionately from Latin America, for a generation.

What Happens Between Now and the Ruling

Until the Supreme Court issues its decision, the asylum ban remains in force. Oral arguments in Mullin v. RAICES are expected in spring 2027, with a final ruling anticipated before the Court wraps up its term that June. No specific argument date has been set.

text:
Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.

The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. “I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”

Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe.

He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”.

When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency.

Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there.

In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.

The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.

A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”.

Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda.

text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.

Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she is part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area.

A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows.

Footage filmed by Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera, captured a tumultuous scene as several people protested the agents making the arrest. The circumstances of the man’s arrest were not immediately clear, and he has not been identified. Agents wore law enforcement vests and ICE badges, and at least two of them had masks covering their faces.

It was unclear what exactly happened right before Vargas Andrade’s arrest, with the sound on the footage repeatedly cutting out. One woman was heard screaming at the agents to get away from her and another cursed at the agents, telling them, “You should be embarrassed … you guys are so fucked up.”

Vargas Andrade had her phone in one hand as she and an agent then appeared to bump into each other, footage showed. That agent then grabbed her and started to handcuff her. Another agent then pulled out what appeared to be a pepper-spray canister and pointed it at the direction of Vargas Andrade and her husband who was filming.

The footage partially captured the agent deploying the pepper spray, though it was difficult to discern how long he sprayed it and where the chemicals landed. Soon after, the footage captured Talavera shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents moved to detain his wife. Seconds later, two agents took Vargas Andrade to the ground where she was handcuffed on her stomach with her hands behind her back, before one of the agents moved her onto her side.

Vargas Andrade was taken into custody and transported to an ICE field office in Stockton, according to her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski. Vargas Andrade’s sister had called for an ambulance, which then arrived at the ICE facility and transported her to a hospital, her family and a local advocate said at the press conference.

Vargas Andrade said officers had told her she was accused of assaulting an ICE agent, an accusation she denied. She was released later that day, and she has not been charged with any crimes, according to Kolasinski.

Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Monday. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice (DoJ) declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Stanislaus sheriff’s office, which runs the jail, said sheriff deputies were not involved in Vargas Andrade’s arrest.

“They threw me to the ground, they maced me, then they handcuffed me,” Vargas Andrade recalled to reporters on Sunday night. “I told the ICE agent … ‘I’m pregnant, so don’t put your hands on me.’ … They right away threw me on the floor … I was burning. I couldn’t breathe. The mace went up my nose.”

Another ICE agent then gave her water to wash her face, she recalled.

“I got scared,” Talavera said. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”

Vargas Andrade said she was particularly worried because she had suffered two previous pregnancy losses, but she said doctors did an ultrasound after the incident and did not identify any concerns.

The encounter happened amid reports of increased ICE activity in California’s central valley region, which is home to the state’s agricultural industry. DHS and the justice department have repeatedly accused anti-ICE protesters of assaulting agents, though many of those prosecutions in California have fallen apart in federal court.

“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

text:
By Georg von Harrach

Five European countries have announced that they will send failed asylum seekers to Rwanda after reaching an agreement in principle with the central African country.

In a deal with Austria, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, migrants, who have had their right to asylum rejected, could be sent to Rwanda to seek a new life.

The model differs from the now defunct British scheme to send migrants to Rwanda while their asylum applications were processed.

Announcing the outline of a deal in Vienna this afternoon, Denmark’s Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen, pictured at the top, said “we need to take back control of our borders”.

Ministers would not be drawn on the number of migrants involved or the cost, which they insisted were still under negotiation.

Pilot phase

Some reports suggest a pilot phase could involve up to 100 migrants, but Frederiksen said it would put off a much bigger number - in the “thousands” - from making the attempt to try to get to Europe in the first place.

Standing alongside European ministers at the press conference, Rwanda’s Foreign Minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, said migrants would be given the option to settle in Rwanda or volunteer to return to their home country.

Unlike the British scheme, which saw dedicated facilities built in Kigali, Nduhungirehe said migrants from the five EU member states would not be “kept in a camp or a dedicated area, they will be integrated in our society”.

But the details still need to be finalised.

Denmark’s Immigration Minister, Morten Bødskov, said he hoped the full agreement could be completed “within the next few months”, with the aim of sending the first set of migrants to Rwanda before the end of 2027.

‘Safe third country’

Under EU rules, it was previously only possible for member states to send failed asylum seekers to a country where they have some kind of family connection and one with which the EU, or a member state, had a bilateral agreement, if they refused to return home voluntarily.

But under the terms of a new European law, which only recently came into force, migrants can be sent to a designated “safe third country”, even if it is a country with which the migrant has no previous connection.

Share Channel 4 News

According to data from the European Commission, 28% of all non-EU migrants “ordered to leave” actually did so last year.

An estimated 350,000 failed asylum seekers neither voluntarily left nor could be forced to do so.

The EU has been signing more so-called readmission agreements, including one with Nigeria last week. But many countries refuse to take migrants back or - like war-torn Syria - are not in a position to do so.

Tougher stance

Immigration has become a political hot potato across Europe with governments under pressure - particularly from right wing parties - to take a tougher stance.

In the first 10 months of this year, there were around 110,000 attempts to illegally enter the EU, according to the EU’s border agency, Frontex. That’s down 29% on last year, but the numbers are still seen as too high.

Before the announcement, Human Rights Watch said the Rwanda scheme was a “deceitful misnomer” to send migrants to a country where they have never set foot.

“Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad,” said Clementine de Montjoye.

Share

The EU’s Return Regulation requires that deals “may only be concluded with a third country where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law, including the principle of non-refoulement, are respected”.

But the regulation is untested and many expect the scheme to end up in court. In the past that has put paid to other similar schemes.

Huge political pressure

The British government previously reached a deal worth £715 million to send migrants to Rwanda while their asylum claims were being assessed in the UK.

The UK paid for asylum facilities to be built in Rwanda that could house up to 200 people per year at Hope Hostel in Kigali.

After facing hurdles from the European Court of Human Rights and huge political pressure, the scheme was dropped when Labour came to power.

Meanwhile, Italy has struggled with its deal to send migrants to Albania, with court cases forcing the Italian government, under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, pictured below, to move the goalposts.

But only a handful of migrants have ended up there.

Other countries to follow suit?

Meloni has called it an “innovative solution” that set the precedent for the change in European law.

The Italian scheme is set to cost taxpayers €653 million over five years.

The European Commission said that it “welcomed” the initiative taken by five member states to work towards a deal with Rwanda which it said had been taken following “careful preparatory work, including with regard to ensuring respect for human rights and the close cooperation with UN agencies”.

The Rwandan government said it believed other countries would likely follow suit and accept migrants from Europe once the concept was proven to be a success.

The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border.

One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims.

A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision.

The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months.

This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.

The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border.

The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

text:
Media contacts:

media@sikhcoalition.org

media@asianlawcaucus.org

Federal Court Strikes Down Determination, Reaffirms NY Immigrant Truck Drivers’ Ability to Work

SAN FRANCISCO — Last week, a federal appeals court struck down the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s (FMCSA) determination that the State of New York and its Department of Motor Vehicles’ (DMV) are out of compliance with the federal commercial drivers license (CDL) program, FMCSA issued its Final Determination in April which risked the removal of $73.5 million in highway funds and threatened the decertification of the state’s entire CDL program.

“The decision is a much-needed win for immigrant commercial drivers,” said Josh Rosenthal, workers’ rights program director at Asian Law Caucus. ‘They have done everything right only for the Trump administration to take away their livelihoods and thrust thousands of families into economic instability. Commercial drivers are essential workers that our communities depend on, and the entire country suffers when the government targets immigrant workers with these hurtful policies.”

“Following the devastating attack on California truckers’ livelihoods as a result of FMCSA’s threats, this development in New York is a significant victory,” continued Sahel Kaur, Managing Attorney at the Sikh Coalition. “We continue to believe that it is callous to deprive law-abiding drivers of the ability to provide for their families—and that it is reckless to threaten entire states’ transportation funding packages in service of doing so.”

Asian Law Caucus and Sikh Coalition submitted an amicus brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in July urging the court to set aside FMCSA’s determination as it would mean the loss of 25,000 CDL holders’ livelihoods and it attempted to rewrite long-standing policy. The brief was submitted on the behalf of Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund, Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, Chinese for Affirmative Action, National Immigration Law Center, Sikh American Legal Defense and Education Fund, South Asian Legal Defense Fund, Stop AAPI Hate, Truckers Movement for Justice, and United Sikhs.

California received a similar determination from FMCSA, which led it to cancel thousands of CDLs this spring. Asian Law Caucus, Sikh Coalition, and Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP brought a class-action lawsuit on the behalf of the class of commercial drivers and the Jakara Movement challenging these cancellations. California later challenged the FMCSA determination in a separate lawsuit.

The affected California drivers—as well as many immigrant drivers with lawful status in New York and across the country— remain unable to renew expiring CDLs, due to a Trump administration rule. That rule is also subject to a lawsuit in the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

###

About the Organizations

For nearly 25 years, the Sikh Coalition has fought to defend and expand Sikh civil rights in the United States. For more information about this lawsuit, the Sikh community’s impact on the U.S. trucking industry, or the Sikh Coalition’s additional work to fight for truckers’ rights, email media@sikhcoalition.org.

text:
The American Nurses Association (ANA) and the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) condemn the continued detention of Ann Lawani, PhD, MSN, RN, a nurse educator at the University of San Francisco. Detained in Lodi, California, on September 16, she remains in federal immigration detention thousands of miles from her family and community. We call for her immediate release and return to California while her legal proceedings continue.

Dr. Lawani’s detention raises broader concerns about the consequences of separating nurses from the people who depend on them. Nurses provide essential patient care, educate the next generation of healthcare professionals, strengthen public health, and care for their own families. Their absence can disrupt care and education, with consequences that extend throughout their communities.

ANA and AACN are deeply concerned about the detention of nurses who hold valid federal work authorization, as Dr. Lawani reportedly does. Federal authorities must account for the human and community consequences of enforcement decisions, including disruptions to healthcare and nursing education.

Guided by the Code of Ethics for Nurses and our shared commitment to the nursing profession, ANA and AACN advocate for the dignity, human rights, and fair treatment of every person, regardless of immigration status. These principles apply to the patients nurses serve and to nurses themselves.

We urge federal authorities to uphold due process and humane treatment and ensure that enforcement practices take account of the effects on nurses, their families, and the patients, students, and communities who rely on them.

###

About the American Nurses Association

As the preeminent organization representing more than 5 million nurses, the American Nurses Association harnesses The Power of Nurses® to champion the profession and drive transformation in healthcare. Through legislative and political advocacy, comprehensive educational services, and the profession’s leading Code of Ethics and Scope and Standards, the association empowers nurses across every specialty and practice setting. The association is committed to ensuring healthy work environments, shaping pioneering policies, and cultivating partnerships that enhance both the nursing profession and the broader healthcare experience.
